Lesson focus: Comparing Two or More Distributions
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will compare two sections by hand with a written paragraph, build an Excel side-by-side table and report it as text, read three box plots on one axis, choose a summary pair for two towns' rents, and find errors in two students' claims. Practice set: scored on completeness and visible reasoning. All data are constructed.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
How do you compare two groups fairly, and what can a comparison honestly say?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
By hand (application). A teacher records minutes of homework done on one night (constructed). Section A (11 students): 22, 25, 28, 30, 31, 33, 35, 36, 38, 40, 44. Section B (12 students): 18, 26, 29, 32, 34, 36, 38, 39, 41, 43, 45, 95. For each section find the five-number summary (median of each half, leaving out the median when n is odd), the IQR, the 1.5 × IQR fences, and the mean (to two decimals). Then write a comparison paragraph of at least four sentences covering center, spread, shape and unusual features, each with a number and a direction, and say where B's median sits relative to A's box.
2
Excel side-by-side table (answered as text). Two players' points in eight games (constructed). Player A: 14, 17, 18, 21, 22, 25, 27, 30. Player B: 19, 21, 24, 25, 27, 28, 31, 33. Type each list into a column of a blank Excel workbook. Build a table with a row for Count, Mean, Median, SD (sample), Q1, Q3, IQR, Min, Max and Range, a column for each player, and a B minus A column, using QUARTILE.INC for the quartiles. Report the formulas you typed for Player A's column, and give the full table of values (rounded to two decimals) in your submission. Then write two sentences comparing the players. (You do not upload a workbook.)
3
Three groups. A workshop times how many minutes it takes to assemble a kit at three stations (constructed, 10 kits each). Five-number summaries (min, Q1, median, Q3, max): Station 1: 12, 16, 19.5, 23, 28. Station 2: 17, 21, 24.5, 28, 31. Station 3: 18, 21, 23.5, 25, 44. (a) Find each IQR. (b) Station 3's largest value is 44 and its next-largest is 27. Use the fence rule to decide whether 44 is an outlier. (c) Sketch the three box plots on one axis (end the Station 3 whisker at 27 and show 44 as a separate dot). (d) Which two stations' boxes overlap the most, and which station has the lowest median? (e) Station 3's mean is 24.9 and Station 2's is 24.5. Does the mean or the median give the fairer comparison of these two, and why? (f) In one sentence, say what these samples do not tell us about the stations.
4
Which summary, and why. Monthly rent in dollars for ten apartments in each of two towns (constructed). Town 1: 1150, 1200, 1250, 1300, 1350, 1400, 1450, 1500, 1600, 3400. Town 2: 1100, 1250, 1300, 1400, 1500, 1550, 1600, 1650, 1700, 1800. (a) Find the median and IQR of each town (by hand), the upper fence for Town 1, and the mean of each town. (b) Decide which summary pair to use to compare the towns and justify it using the data. (c) Write one comparison sentence using your chosen pair, with numbers and directions. (d) Say what the means alone would have suggested, and why that would be misleading.
5
Find the mistakes. Maya says: “Team A's mean score is 74 points and Team B's is 72, so Team A is the better team.” (Team A's SD is 14; Team B's SD is 3.) Jonas says: “Class P has 40 students and 9 of them earned an A; Class Q has 20 students and 6 earned an A. Nine is more than six, so Class P's students are better prepared, and the teacher must be better.” Find at least three errors in total. For each, say what is wrong and write a corrected statement with numbers.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All five parts complete, with the by-hand five-number summaries and fences shown.
☐
The comparison paragraph covers center, spread, shape and unusual features, each with a number and a direction.
☐
The Excel part gives the formulas typed and the table of values.
☐
No claim of “proof” or cause is made from a sample difference.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Completeness
6 pts		 All five parts attempted in full. One part missing or clearly rushed. Two or more parts missing. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Part 1: A: 22, 28, 33, 38, 44, IQR 10, fences 13 to 53, mean 32.91, no outliers. B: 18, 30.5, 37, 42, 95, IQR 11.5, fences 13.25 to 59.25, mean 39.67, 95 is an outlier. Paragraph: B's median is 4 minutes higher (37 against 33); B's IQR is 11.5 against 10 (1.5 wider); B has one outlier (95) and A has none; B's mean is 6.76 higher, much larger than the median difference, because of the 95; B's median (37) lies inside A's box (28 to 38) and the boxes overlap from 30.5 to 38, so the sections are not clearly different. Part 2 (QUARTILE.INC): Count 8, 8, 0; Mean 21.75, 26, 4.25; Median 21.5, 26, 4.5; SD 5.39, 4.75, −0.64; Q1 17.75, 23.25, 5.5; Q3 25.5, 28.75, 3.25; IQR 7.75, 5.5, −2.25; Min 14, 19, 5; Max 30, 33, 3; Range 16, 14, −2; formulas such as =COUNT(A2:A9), =AVERAGE(A2:A9), =MEDIAN(A2:A9), =STDEV.S(A2:A9), =QUARTILE.INC(A2:A9,1). Sentences: B's median is 4.5 higher and B's IQR is 2.25 narrower, in these eight games. Part 3: IQRs 7, 7, 4; fence for 44 is 25 + 1.5 × 4 = 31, so 44 is an outlier; boxes of Stations 2 and 3 overlap most (Station 3's box 21 to 25 sits inside Station 2's 21 to 28), Stations 1 and 2 overlap from 21 to 23; Station 1 has the lowest median (19.5); the median is fairer because Station 3's mean (24.9) is lifted by the 44, and its median (23.5) is 1 below Station 2's (24.5); the samples do not show whether the stations differ in general or why. Part 4: Town 1 median 1375, IQR 250 (Q1 1250, Q3 1500), upper fence 1500 + 375 = 1875, mean 1560; Town 2 median 1525, IQR 350, mean 1485; use median and IQR because Town 1 has an outlier (3400 > 1875); Town 2's median is 150 higher; the means suggest Town 1 is 75 higher, which is misleading because of the 3400. Part 5: Maya ignores spread (A's SD 14 against B's 3; a 2-point difference in means is small against that spread, so the scores overlap heavily) and calls a mean difference “better”; Jonas compares counts when sizes differ (9 of 40 = 22.5% against 6 of 20 = 30%, so Q has the larger share); and Jonas claims causation (better prepared, better teacher) from a comparison of counts. Mostly correct but with one wrong value, a missing fence, a comparison sentence with no number or no direction, or a claim stated as proof. Bare answers with little visible reasoning. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts

Outliers and Their Effects on Center and Spread

Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 24.2
Assignment 24.2 — Outliers in Action
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
One value, many summaries
Practice set · graded on complete, honest work
Covers: which statistics move when the maximum moves; how n sets the mean's sensitivity; shifts and rescales (including a unit change); deciding what to do with an outlier; with-and-without reporting.
Lesson focus: Outliers and Their Effects on Center and Spread
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will build an effect table on made-up data, predict the effect of a unit conversion without recomputing, compare a small and a large group, decide what to do with a flagged value in two stories, and find the error in one student's claim. Practice set: scored on completeness and visible reasoning.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What does one unusual value do to the numbers we report, and what do we owe the reader about it?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Effect table. A made-up set of seven puzzle times (minutes) is 8, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 19. Build a table with three columns: the original set; the set with the largest value doubled (19 → 38); and the set with the largest value removed. For each, give n, the mean, the median, the range, the IQR (median of each half), and the sample SD (use Excel's STDEV.S or show the Desmos arithmetic), and say whether the largest value is flagged by the 1.5 × IQR fences in the doubled version (show the fences). Then write two sentences: which summaries held still when the max doubled, and which moved?
2
Transformation. A made-up list of seven afternoon temperatures in degrees Fahrenheit is 41, 50, 50, 59, 68, 77, 86. Find the mean, median, IQR, range, and sample SD in °F. The conversion to Celsius is \(C = (F - 32) \times \tfrac{5}{9}\): subtract 32 (a shift), then multiply by \(\tfrac{5}{9}\) (a rescale). Without converting the whole list, predict the mean, median, IQR, range, and SD in °C and explain which of the five are changed by the shift and which only by the rescale. Then convert the seven values and recompute to check.
3
Does n matter? (made up) Class A has 10 students and a mean score of 70; Class B has 40 students and a mean of 70. In each class, one student's score is re-graded from 70 to 100 and no other score changes. (a) By how much does each class mean move? (b) What would the move be in a class of 5? (c) What is the smallest class size for which a re-grade of that size (+30) moves the mean by no more than 0.5? Explain in a sentence why the median of each class could stay the same.
4
Decide what to do. A made-up volunteer group recorded the minutes of travel to a service day for 11 volunteers: 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 24, 25, 28, 30, 35, 450. (a) Compute the mean, median, IQR (by hand), and sample SD with all 11 values. (b) Compute the upper fence and say which value is flagged. (c) Recompute the mean, median, IQR, and SD without it. (d) Write what you would do first, and what you would report, in two different stories: the 450 was meant to be 45.0 (a misplaced decimal on the sign-in sheet), or the 450 is a verified trip from a volunteer who came a long way. Write one sentence on why quietly deleting it would be wrong either way.
5
Find the error. A teacher curves a made-up quiz by adding 5 points to every score. The eight scores before the curve are 5, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19. A student writes: “After the curve the mean, the median, and the standard deviation all go up by 5, since every score is bigger. Also, the 5 is flagged as an outlier, so I will delete it so the class average looks better.” Compute the mean, median, IQR, and sample SD before and after the curve, say exactly what the student got wrong, and say what the student should do about the flagged 5 instead.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All five parts are complete, with arithmetic shown.
☐
The effect table separates the resistant summaries (median, IQR) from those that follow the max (mean, range, SD).
☐
The transformation is predicted from the shift-and-scale rules before it is checked.
☐
The decide-what-to-do part reports with and without, names the reason for any removal, and does not delete to improve the story.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Completeness
6 pts		 All five parts attempted in full. One part missing or clearly rushed. Two or more parts missing. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Part 1: original n 7, mean 12.57 (88÷7), median 12, range 11, \(Q_1 = 9\), \(Q_3 = 15\), IQR 6, SD 3.78; doubled (19 → 38): mean 15.29 (107÷7), median 12, range 30, IQR 6, SD 10.32, fences 0 and 24 so 38 is flagged; removed: n 6, mean 11.5, median 11.5, range 7, \(Q_1 = 9\), \(Q_3 = 14\), IQR 5, SD 2.74; median and IQR held still when the max doubled, mean (up 19÷7, about 2.71), range, and SD moved. Part 2: °F mean 61.57, median 59, \(Q_1 = 50\), \(Q_3 = 77\), IQR 27, range 45, SD about 16.20; °C predictions: mean \((61.57 - 32) \times 5/9 = 16.43\), median \((59-32) \times 5/9 = 15\), IQR \(27 \times 5/9 = 15\), range \(45 \times 5/9 = 25\), SD \(16.20 \times 5/9 = 9.00\); the shift (subtract 32) changes mean and median but not IQR, range, or SD; the rescale (× 5/9) changes all five; converted list 5, 10, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30 confirms mean 16.43, median 15, IQR 15 (\(Q_1 = 10\), \(Q_3 = 25\)), range 25, SD 9.00. Part 3: (a) Class A moves by 3 (to 73), Class B by 0.75 (to 70.75); (b) a class of 5 moves by 6; (c) 60 students, since 30÷60 = 0.5 (and 30÷59 is above 0.5); one value changing need not cross the middle, so the median can stay the same. Part 4: with all 11: mean 61.73, median 24, \(Q_1 = 18\), \(Q_3 = 30\), IQR 12, SD 128.95; upper fence \(30 + 1.5 \times 12 = 48\), so 450 is flagged (lower fence 0); without it: n 10, mean 22.9, median 23, \(Q_1 = 18\), \(Q_3 = 28\), IQR 10, SD 7.02. Story 1 (typo): check the sign-in sheet, correct it to 45.0 (the corrected list has mean 274÷11, about 24.9) and say so; Story 2 (verified): keep it, report both sets of summaries and lead with the median and IQR; deletion without a stated reason would hide information and make the story prettier, not truer. Part 5: before the curve: mean 13.875 (13.88), median 14.5, IQR 4 (\(Q_1 = 12.5\), \(Q_3 = 16.5\)), SD 4.22; after: mean 18.875 (18.88), median 19.5, IQR 4, SD 4.22; mean and median go up by 5 but the SD (and IQR) do not change, since a shift leaves the spread alone; the 5 (now 10) is flagged by the lower fence \(12.5 - 6 = 6.5\) (before the curve), but it should be investigated (a data entry slip? a student who did not take the quiz? a genuine low score?) and, if it is real, kept and reported, not deleted to improve the average. Mostly correct but with one slip in arithmetic or a thin explanation. Bare answers with little visible reasoning. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts

Assignment 24.3 — Capstone Data Story
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Two lists of numbers, one honest story
Module capstone · graded on correct work and an honest, traceable data story
Covers: Five-number summaries and IQR by hand; fences and outliers; mean and sample standard deviation; a display on a shared axis; with-and-without for an outlier; a 150 to 250 word data story; the honesty checklist.
Lesson focus: Case Study: Telling a Dataset's Story Honestly
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will analyze two constructed lists of lunch-line waits: five-number summaries, standard deviations, a display on a shared axis, and an outlier decision. Then you will write a 150 to 250 word data story and check it against the seven-point honesty checklist. Because the story and the checklist are the reasoning, they carry the Work shown & reasoning points.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Can you tell a true story about two sets of numbers, so that a reader would not be surprised by what you left out?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Summaries by hand. A made-up school measured the minutes a student waited in each of two lunch lines on 20 school days. (Constructed data, in day order.) Line 1: 8, 9, 7, 10, 8, 9, 8, 7, 9, 8, 17, 9, 8, 10, 7, 9, 8, 9, 10, 8. Line 2: 5, 11, 8, 13, 6, 10, 7, 12, 8, 9, 4, 14, 8, 9, 7, 10, 6, 12, 5, 8. Order each list from smallest to largest and show the two halves. Find, by the median-of-each-half method, the five-number summary, the IQR, and the 1.5 × IQR fences for each line, and say which values (if any) are flagged.
2
Mean and standard deviation. Find the mean and the sample standard deviation of each line (use Excel's AVERAGE and STDEV.S, or compute by hand; show the sum of squared deviations if you work by hand). Compute the mean and sample SD of Line 1 again without the flagged value.
3
Display. Draw one dot plot (or histogram) for each line on the same labeled number line, and a box plot for each beneath it. Mark flagged values. Give each graph a title with units. The axis must show the whole range of the data and be labeled.
4
Write the data story. In 150 to 250 words, write one data story that answers: “Which line is better if you want a short wait?” Use the summaries that fit the shape, use the same pair for both lines, and report with-and-without for the flagged value. Every number in the story must come from your work. Label the data as constructed.
5
Checklist. Under your story, copy the seven checklist questions (n and units; what the summary hides; no cause claimed; honest axis; both views; spread as well as center; what the data cannot tell). Next to each, write the words or number in your story that show you did it. You may type the story and checklist; the hand work and graphs may be a photo or scan.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Both five-number summaries, IQRs, fences, and flags are correct, with the halves shown.
☐
Means and SDs are correct, including Line 1 without the flagged value.
☐
The display uses one labeled axis for both lines and marks the flagged value.
☐
The 150 to 250 word story uses the fitting summaries, reports both views, and passes all seven checklist items, with every number traceable to your work.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Completeness
6 pts		 Five-number summaries by hand: Line 1 (ordered 7, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8, 8 | 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 9, 10, 10, 10, 17): min 7, Q1 8, median 8.5, Q3 9, max 17, IQR 1, fences 6.5 and 10.5, flagged 17. Line 2 (4, 5, 5, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 8, 8 | 8, 9, 9, 10, 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14): min 4, Q1 6.5, median 8, Q3 10.5, max 14, IQR 4, fences 0.5 and 16.5, nothing flagged. Means 8.90 and 8.60; sample SDs 2.13 and 2.80; Line 1 without the 17 (n = 19): mean 8.47, SD 0.96, median 8, Q1 8, Q3 9. Display: both dot plots or histograms on one labeled axis (about 3 to 18 minutes), box plots beneath, the 17 marked. Story of 150 to 250 words, labeled constructed. Most of the work is present, but a summary, the with-and-without comparison, the display, or the word count is missing or has a slip (a wrong quartile or a mislabeled axis). Two or more parts missing, or the values are mostly wrong. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 The story uses median and IQR (8.5 and 1 versus 8 and 4) for both lines, notes the flagged 17 and reports both views (the Line 1 mean is 8.90 with it and 8.47 without, so the mean difference flips from 0.30 above Line 2's 8.60 to 0.13 below it, while the medians stay 8.5 and 8), says Line 1 is steadier (IQR 1 versus 4; SD 2.13 with the 17 and 0.96 without versus 2.80) but has the one long wait, states n = 20 days each and minutes, claims no cause, and says what the data cannot tell. The checklist maps each of the seven items to words or numbers in the story, and the story does not use a number that is not in the work. A story is present but it relies on the mean alone, leaves out the spread or the flagged value, or the checklist does not point to specific words in the story. A list of numbers with no story, or a story with claims the data cannot support (a cause, or a recommendation with no evidence). 4 pts
Total: 10 pts

assignments.title: VR Lab — Walking the Distribution
assignments.html:
Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company
PROBABILITY & STATISTICS HONORS
Quarter / Module
Q3 · Module 8
Descriptive Statistics
Type
VR Module Lab
Optima · Week 24 · the module's capstone in headset
Time in headset
20–30 minutes
One session, one submission
Points
Rubric-scored
15 pts
Module 8 · VR Lab
Walking the Distribution
VR Lab · 15 pts · rubric-graded
🥼 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
This module's virtue is courtesy, and Lessons 23.1 and 23.2 showed you what it means for a summary: a number you hand to a reader should fit the data it stands for, and you owe the reader an honest word about what it leaves out. Today you will not read the summary numbers off a page; you will walk them. In the Location a set of 15 data values stands as markers on a numbered floor strip. You will stand on the mean, pace out one standard deviation each way, count how many markers fall inside that band, place the median and quartiles, and walk from median to mean to measure the gap in paces. Then you will tell the story of the distribution aloud in a short spatial recording: which way it leans, what pulled the mean, which pair of summaries you would hand a reader, and one thing every summary hides. A skew you have walked is a skew you will recognize on sight. All of the data in this lab are constructed (made up).
📋 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset with Optima installed (desktop Optima works if a headset is unavailable, but walking out a spread and feeling a gap in paces is the heart of this lab).
▶
Your Lesson 22.2, 23.1, and 23.2 notes (notebook page): quartiles by hand (the median of each half), the sample standard deviation, and how skew moves the mean relative to the median. Review them before you put the headset on; re-reading inside a headset is hard.
▶
The data, to work on at your desk before the session (constructed; the minutes 15 made-up students spent on one homework set): 7, 8, 8, 10, 11, 11, 12, 12, 13, 15, 17, 18, 20, 24, 24. Using the free Desmos Scientific Calculator (desmos.com/scientific), find the sample standard deviation (divide the sum of squared deviations by \(n - 1\); this is the course default, as in Lesson 23.1) and write it on paper to two decimal places. The same 15 values will be posted on the Whiteboard IFX inside; you will not need to re-read this list in the headset.
▶
About 30 uninterrupted minutes. The “twist” at the end is optional and takes about five more; if you are past 30 minutes when you get to it, skip it.
🚀 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (preferred) or desktop Optima
Session type: Persistent Session (your work saves between visits)
Session ID: [SESSION ID — teacher enters before publishing]
Location: [LOCATION NAME — an open, flat-floored Location with a long numbered floor strip; teacher enters before publishing]
On arrival: Find the Whiteboard IFX near the spawn point labeled “Walking the Distribution — start here.” It lists the 15 values. Ahead of you a long strip on the floor is numbered 0 to 26, with one numbered spot for each whole number and a small tick halfway between neighboring spots; the distance between neighboring spots is one pace. Fifteen identical tokens stand on it in stacks, one token for every value on the whiteboard (two students who spent 24 minutes appear as a stack of two on spot 24). Beside the whiteboard wait loose marker IFX in two colors: three in one color (for the mean and for the two ends of the standard-deviation band) and three in the other (for the median, \(Q_1\), and \(Q_3\)).
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Read the floor. Walk the strip once from spot 0 to spot 26. Count the tokens aloud and check that you get 15, the same as the list on the Whiteboard IFX. Say the shape you see before you compute anything: where do the tokens pile up, and where do they trail off?
2
Stand on the mean. On the whiteboard, add the 15 values and write the sum, then divide by 15 and write the mean. It should match what you found at your desk. Walk to that spot and place one of the first-color markers there, with a sticky note: “Mean = __ minutes.” Look down: is a token standing here? Say aloud what that tells you about the mean as a summary.
3
Pace out one standard deviation each way. Write your sample standard deviation (divided by \(n - 1\)) on the whiteboard and round it to the nearest half pace. Stand on the mean and walk that many paces toward the left end; place a first-color marker there. Walk back to the mean, then that many paces toward the right end, and place the last first-color marker. Add sticky notes: “Mean − 1 SD = __” and “Mean + 1 SD = __.”
4
Count the band. Walk between your two SD markers and count every token that stands inside, counting stacks token by token. Place a sticky note in the middle of the band: “Inside ±1 SD: __ of 15 tokens.”
5
Place the median and the quartiles. The median is the 8th token from the left. \(Q_1\) is the median of the 7 tokens to its left (use the by-hand method; the median itself is left out of both halves), and \(Q_3\) is the median of the 7 tokens to its right. Place a second-color marker on each, with sticky notes “Median = __,” “Q1 = __,” and “Q3 = __.” Then pace the IQR from \(Q_1\) to \(Q_3\) and write it on the whiteboard.
6
Measure the gap. Stand on the Median marker, face the Mean marker, and walk to it, counting spots. Write “Mean − median = __ paces” on a sticky note between them. Say aloud which marker is on the left.
7
Capture the layout. Stand back far enough that one snapshot catches the whole strip: the tokens, the Mean marker, both SD markers, the Median, \(Q_1\), and \(Q_3\) markers, and their sticky notes. Take it and check it before moving on; every note must be readable. If not, retake it from closer.
8
Narrate, then try the twist. Stand where the whole strip is in view and start a spatial recording. Speak for 60 to 90 seconds, in your own words, answering all four: (a) which way is this distribution skewed, and how can you tell from where you are standing; (b) how far apart are the mean and the median in paces, and which tokens pulled the mean; (c) which pair of summaries would you hand to a reader, the mean with the SD or the median with the IQR, and why; (d) one thing that every one of these summaries hides. Use your own numbers. Do not read your sticky notes aloud; look at the floor and tell what you see. Twist (optional, if you are under 30 minutes): without stopping the recording, move the three tokens farthest to the right to the mirror-image spots, the same number of paces to the left of the median (a token 8 paces right of the median goes 8 paces left of it). Add up the new sum on the whiteboard, find the new mean, count to the new median (it may have moved), and say in a sentence what happened to the gap between mean and median. Stop the recording.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Canvas Assignment Name: VR Lab — Walking the Distribution
Upload two things: (1) your snapshot from step 7 (image file) showing the placed markers and their sticky notes; and (2) your spatial recording from step 8 (60–90 seconds of narration, plus the twist if you did it), shared as a link or file exactly as your teacher shows on the Canvas page for this assignment.
Below them, in the text entry box, write one line giving your numbers: the mean, the median, the sample SD, \(Q_1\), \(Q_3\), the count inside \(\pm 1\) SD, and the gap in paces, so your teacher can check them without replaying your recording.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment. · Estimated time: 20–30 minutes in headset.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Completeness
5 pts		 Mean, both SD markers, median, \(Q_1\), and \(Q_3\) markers are all placed with sticky notes; the snapshot shows the whole layout readably; the spatial recording runs about 60–90 seconds and answers all four questions (skew, gap and what pulled the mean, which pair of summaries, what the summaries hide); the numbers line is typed. One element missing or clearly rushed: a marker or sticky-note set missing, an unreadable snapshot, a recording that skips one of the four questions or runs under about 45 seconds, or the numbers line missing. Two or more required elements missing. 5 pts
Accuracy
5 pts		 Mean 14 (sum 210, divided by 15); sample SD about 5.52, rounded to 5.5 paces, so the band runs from 8.5 to 19.5 with 9 of 15 tokens inside; median 12, \(Q_1\) = 10, \(Q_3\) = 18 (IQR 8); the gap from median to mean is 2 paces with the mean on the right; the distribution is named right-skewed. One value wrong (for example, the population SD of about 5.33 used instead of the sample SD, a quartile off by Excel's method, or the gap miscounted) while the rest is correct and the skew is named correctly. Multiple errors in the mean, SD, band count, quartiles, or gap, or the skew named backward. 5 pts
Evidence of engagement
5 pts		 The narration is in the student's own words and uses their own numbers: it says the mean sits to the right of the median because of the long tail of high tokens (the 20 and the two 24s), chooses a pair of summaries and defends it with the shape, and names a specific thing the summaries hide (for example, nobody at all stands on the mean, the two 24s sit in a pair far from the pile, or the full spread of the tail). The twist, if attempted, is described honestly, including what moved. A correct narration that is generic or read from notes (“skewed right, mean is bigger”), or a pair of summaries chosen without a reason from the shape, or something the summaries hide that is vague. Narration missing the questions, or no evident engagement with the layout. 5 pts
Total: 15 pts
👋 FACILITATOR NOTE
Stage the Location before publishing. Floor strip: an IFX with a collider, about 13 m long, with 27 numbered spots (0 to 26) spaced 0.5 m apart and a small tick at every half spot (0.25 m), so that one pace is one numbered spot and a half pace is one tick. Large digits. Data: exactly 15 identical tokens stacked on the spots, one token per data value, in these stack sizes: spot 7: 1; spot 8: 2; spot 10: 1; spot 11: 2; spot 12: 2; spot 13: 1; spot 15: 1; spot 17: 1; spot 18: 1; spot 20: 1; spot 24: 2 (values 7, 8, 8, 10, 11, 11, 12, 12, 13, 15, 17, 18, 20, 24, 24; minutes spent on one homework set; made up). Lock all tokens except the three that stand on spots 20 and 24 (students move them in the twist). Markers: six loose marker IFX near the spawn point, unlocked: three in one color (mean and the two SD markers) and three in a second color (median, \(Q_1\), \(Q_3\)). A Whiteboard IFX at the spawn point labeled “Walking the Distribution — start here” that lists the 15 values in order and gives the legend (“1 token = 1 student”; “1 pace = 1 numbered spot”). Confirm the IFX names and sizes, and the place to start and stop a spatial recording, against the current IFX library and ENGAGE app before publishing; any identical stackable shape works. Answer key. The sum is 210, so the mean is \(210 \div 15 = 14\) (spot 14 holds no token). The median is the 8th value, 12. By-hand \(Q_1\) is the median of 7, 8, 8, 10, 11, 11, 12, which is 10; \(Q_3\) is the median of 13, 15, 17, 18, 20, 24, 24, which is 18; IQR = 8. (QUARTILE.INC gives 10.5 and 17.5; accept these if the student says they used Excel's method.) No value is flagged by the 1.5 × IQR rule: the fences are \(10 - 12 = -2\) and \(18 + 12 = 30\), so the walk stays about shape and not about outliers. The sum of squared deviations is 426, so the sample SD is \(\sqrt{426 \div 14} \approx 5.52\) (the population SD, 5.33, is the wrong choice here because these 15 students are a sample; it rounds to the same 5.5 paces, so check the SD the student wrote on the whiteboard, 5.52, not just the markers); rounded to the nearest half pace it is 5.5 paces, so the band runs from 8.5 to 19.5 and contains the 9 tokens on 10, 11, 11, 12, 12, 13, 15, 17, 18 (60% of the 15). No token stands within half a pace of either band edge, so the count is unambiguous (the tokens on 8 and 20 are just outside). Mean − median = 2 paces, the mean to the right of the median: skewed right. The tokens that pull the mean are the 20 and the two 24s (all more than 7 paces above the median). Which pair? For this right-skewed shape the better answer is the median with the IQR (12 and 8), because the tail drags the mean (and the SD) away from where the typical student sits; accept mean and SD if the reason is tied to the shape. What is hidden (accept any true specific): nobody stands on the mean; the two 24s are a pair far from the pile; no summary shows the clump at 10 through 13. Twist key. The tokens on 20, 24, and 24 mirror about the median (12) to spots 4, 0, and 0. The new data are 0, 0, 4, 7, 8, 8, 10, 11, 11, 12, 12, 13, 15, 17, 18. The new sum is 146 (a drop of 64), so the new mean is about 9.73. The median also moved, from 12 to 11, because three values crossed it. The gap is now about 1.25 paces, with the mean to the left of the median: the tail moved to the other side, and the mean followed it. Common sticking points: using \(n\) instead of \(n - 1\); mixing up the mean's spot with a token's spot; counting a stack as one token; finding the median of the whole strip when computing \(Q_1\) and \(Q_3\) (the halves leave the median out); and going over 90 seconds or reading sticky notes aloud. What to demo: placing a marker on a half-pace tick with the Gizmo; starting and stopping a spatial recording; creating and placing sticky notes. If a student finishes early, ask what would happen to the mean and the SD if one more token stood on spot 26.

Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 25.1
Assignment 25.1 — z-Scores: Computing, Comparing, and Checking
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
z-scores: how far from the mean, in standard deviations
Practice set · graded on complete, honest work
Covers: computing and interpreting z-scores; working backward from z to a value; comparing values from different distributions; the standard normal; STANDARDIZE in Excel; checking an AI's answer.
Lesson focus: The Normal Model and z-Scores
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will compute z-scores and interpret them, work backward from a z-score to a value, compare two scores from different tests, use Excel's STANDARDIZE (answered as text), judge an unusual value in an applied setting, and check an AI's answer against Excel. All data are constructed. Practice set: scored on completeness and visible reasoning.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
How can one number tell you where a value stands, whatever the units?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
z-scores by hand. Show the subtraction in parentheses and the division. (a) A constructed test has mean 76 and SD 6; find the z-score of 88. (b) A constructed test has mean 70 and SD 4; find the z-score of 61. (c) Cereal boxes have mean 500 g and SD 4 g; find the z-score of a 500 g box. For each, say in a sentence how many standard deviations above or below the mean the value is.
2
Working backward. Constructed heights follow N(170, 8) cm. (a) Find the height with z = 1.5. (b) Find the height with z = −2. (c) Find the z-score of a height of 175 cm, rounded to two decimals. Check (a) and (b) by running them forward.
3
Compare across tests. Priya scores 71 on a constructed Test P (mean 62, SD 5). Sam scores 166 on a constructed Test Q (mean 140, SD 20). Find both z-scores and say who did better relative to their own test, and why raw scores cannot be compared directly. Then, in one sentence, describe the standard normal distribution (give its mean and SD) and say what z = (x − μ) ÷ σ does to a normal curve.
4
Excel (answered as text). A constructed process has mean 25 and SD 5. Open a blank workbook, put the mean in B1 and the SD in B2, and type the four values 31, 18, 25, 40 in A5 through A8. In B5 type =STANDARDIZE(A5,$B$1,$B$2) and fill down to B8. Report the formula you typed in B5, the four z-scores, and one other formula that gives the same z-score without using STANDARDIZE. (You do not upload a workbook for this item; type the formulas and values into your submission.)
5
Application. A constructed filling machine puts cereal in boxes with mean 500 g and SD 4 g. One box weighs 489 g. (a) Find its z-score. (b) Is it unusual? State a clear rule of thumb for how large |z| must be, and say what it means. (c) Name one possible reason for such a box other than “the machine is broken,” and say what you would check before deciding.
6
AI check. Ask an AI tool: “For a standard normal distribution, what is P(z > 1.5)? Show your steps.” Before you read the answer, write your own estimate of the size (closer to 0.5, 0.1, or 0.01?). Then use Excel to compute =1-NORM.S.DIST(1.5,TRUE) and report the value rounded to four decimals. Report what the AI said, whether it was right, and anything it got wrong or left vague.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All six parts are complete, with the subtraction in parentheses and the division shown for every z-score.
☐
Every z-score is interpreted as a number of standard deviations above or below the mean, and backward answers are checked by going forward.
☐
The Excel part gives the exact formula typed, the four values, and an equivalent formula without STANDARDIZE.
☐
The AI check records your prediction, the AI's claim, the Excel value, and an honest verdict.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Completeness
6 pts		 All six parts attempted in full. One part missing or clearly rushed. Two or more parts missing. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Part 1: (a) z = (88 − 76) ÷ 6 = 2.0; (b) z = (61 − 70) ÷ 4 = −2.25; (c) z = (500 − 500) ÷ 4 = 0 (each with an interpretation: SDs above or below the mean, or exactly at it). Part 2: (a) 170 + 1.5(8) = 182 cm; (b) 170 + (−2)(8) = 154 cm; (c) z = (175 − 170) ÷ 8 = 0.625, about 0.63. Part 3: Priya z = (71 − 62) ÷ 5 = 1.8; Sam z = (166 − 140) ÷ 20 = 1.3; Priya did better relative to her own test; raw scores are on different scales. The standard normal has mean 0 and SD 1; z = (x − μ) ÷ σ slides any normal curve to center 0 and rescales it to SD 1. Part 4: mean 25, SD 5: =STANDARDIZE(A5,$B$1,$B$2) gives 1.2 for 31, −1.4 for 18, 0 for 25, 3 for 40; the equivalent =(A5-$B$1)/$B$2 gives the same values (accept consistent references). Part 5: z = (489 − 500) ÷ 4 = −2.75, 2.75 SDs below the mean; unusual by a stated rule of thumb (|z| beyond about 2); accept reasoning that it is a question about why (random fluctuation, drift, a mis-weighed box), not a verdict. Part 6: P(Z > 1.5) = 1 − NORM.S.DIST(1.5, TRUE) = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668 (about 6.7%). Credit a prediction, the AI's claim reported honestly, the Excel entry and value, and a clear verdict; the grade rewards the checking, not the AI being right. Mostly correct but with one wrong value, a missing interpretation, a missing Excel formula, or an AI check that skips the prediction or the verification. Bare answers with little visible reasoning. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 25.1 — z-Scores: Computing, Comparing, and Checking
Submit a clear photo or scan of your notebook pages (JPG, PNG, or PDF), or type your work directly into the text entry box. Make sure every step, entry, and answer is legible.
For the Excel parts, type the formulas and the values Excel gave you into your answer. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Lesson 25.2
Assignment 25.2 — The Empirical Rule in Practice
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
The 68–95–99.7 rule: intervals, percents, counts, and its limits
Practice set · graded on complete, honest work
Covers: intervals from a mean and SD; percents above, below, and between whole-SD cutoffs by symmetry; working backward to a mean and SD; counts from a population; an Excel interval table; when the rule does not apply; checking an AI answer.
Lesson focus: The Empirical Rule (68–95–99.7)
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will write intervals for a normal distribution, estimate percents by symmetry, work backward from an interval, turn percents into counts, build a small Excel table (answered as text), find the mistakes in two claims, and check an AI’s answer against your own. All data are constructed. Practice set: scored on completeness and visible reasoning.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Why can one set of three percents describe so many different bell curves, and when must we refuse to use them?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Intervals. A constructed test has scores that are approximately normal with mean 100 and SD 15. Write the interval that holds about (a) 68%, (b) 95%, and (c) 99.7% of the scores. Show the arithmetic (for example, 100 − 2×15), and check one endpoint in Desmos by typing it as plain arithmetic.
2
Percents. Same test (mean 100, SD 15). Sketch a curve for each part and estimate the percent of scores (a) above 115, (b) below 70, (c) between 85 and 130, (d) above 145. Use the word “about” and say which slices you added or subtracted.
3
Work backward. Constructed lengths of bean pods are approximately normal. The middle 95% of lengths run from 9.2 cm to 14.8 cm. (a) Find the mean. (b) Find the SD. (c) About what percent of pods are longer than 13.4 cm? Explain each step.
4
Counts. A constructed city has 5,000 commuters whose commute times are approximately normal with mean 30 minutes and SD 6 minutes. About how many commuters take (a) between 24 and 36 minutes, (b) more than 42 minutes, (c) between 18 and 36 minutes?
5
Excel (answered as text). Build a three-row table for a normal distribution with mean 30 and SD 6, as in the lesson: k = 1, 2, 3 in column A; lower endpoint in B (mean − k×SD); upper endpoint in C (mean + k×SD); exact share inside in D using =NORM.DIST(upper, mean, sd, TRUE)-NORM.DIST(lower, mean, sd, TRUE) with your own cell references. In your answer type (i) the three formulas you typed in row 5, (ii) the values of B, C, and D for all three rows (D as a percent to two decimals), and (iii) one sentence comparing column D to 68, 95, and 99.7. (You do not upload a workbook for this item.)
6
Find the mistake, and when not to use the rule. (a) Sam says, “A value 1 SD above the mean has about 34% of the data above it.” Find the error and give the correct percent. (b) Twelve constructed repair times, in hours, are 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 9, 14, 40 (mean about 7.92, sample SD about 10.67). Give two reasons the Empirical Rule should not be applied to this list. Include the lower end of the “mean − 1 SD” interval, and say how many of the 12 values lie within 1 SD of the mean.
7
Check an AI. Ask an AI tool: “A made-up exam has scores that are normally distributed with mean 60 and SD 8. Using the Empirical Rule, what percent of scores are below 44?” Before you read its answer, write your own prediction and the arithmetic behind it. Then report: the prompt you typed, the AI’s answer, whether it matches yours, and one thing it got right, vague, or wrong (or, if it was fully correct, one thing it did not say that a careful reader would want, such as the word “about”). If no AI tool is available to you, say so and describe what a typical wrong answer would look like and why.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All seven parts complete, with a sketch or stated slices for each percent problem.
☐
Every interval, percent, and count shows its arithmetic and says “about” where the rule gives an estimate.
☐
The Excel part gives the exact formulas typed and the values for all three rows.
☐
The error analysis names why the rule fails for the skewed list; the AI part shows your prediction made before the AI’s answer.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
CriteriaFull creditPartial creditMinimal creditPts
Completeness
6 pts		 All seven parts attempted in full. One or two parts missing or clearly rushed. Three or more parts missing. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Part 1: (a) 85 to 115; (b) 70 to 130; (c) 55 to 145. Part 2: (a) above 115 is +1 SD, about 16%; (b) below 70 is −2 SD, about 2.5%; (c) 85 to 130 is −1 SD to +2 SD, 34 + 47.5 = about 81.5%; (d) 145 is +3 SD, about 0.15%. Part 3: (a) mean = (9.2 + 14.8) ÷ 2 = 12 cm; (b) 14.8 − 12 = 2.8 = 2 SD, so SD = 1.4 cm; (c) 13.4 = 12 + 1.4 is +1 SD, about 16%. Part 4: (a) ±1 SD, 68% of 5,000 = 3,400; (b) 42 is +2 SD, 2.5% = 125; (c) −2 SD to +1 SD, 81.5% = 4,075 (exact normal counts about 3,413, 114, 4,093; accept the rule values). Part 5: B5 =$B$1-A5*$B$2 (or equivalent), C5 =$B$1+A5*$B$2, D5 =NORM.DIST(C5,$B$1,$B$2,TRUE)-NORM.DIST(B5,$B$1,$B$2,TRUE). Rows: k=1: 24, 36, 68.27%; k=2: 18, 42, 95.45%; k=3: 12, 48, 99.73%. Column D is slightly larger than 68, 95, 99.7 because the rule rounds. Part 6: (a) the 34% is the slice between the mean and +1 SD; the share above +1 SD is about 16%. (b) The list is strongly right-skewed (median 4, far below the mean of about 7.92, with 14 and 40 pulling the right tail); mean − 1 SD is about −2.76 hours, impossible for a repair time; 11 of the 12 values (about 92%) lie within 1 SD (about −2.76 to 18.59), not about 68%. Accept any two valid reasons. Part 7: 44 is 2 SD below the mean (60 − 2×8), so about 2.5% (exact 2.28%). Common AI slips: 5%, 95%, 97.5%. Award full credit for a prediction written before the AI answer plus an honest comparison; do not require a particular AI response. Mostly correct but with one or two wrong values, a missing sketch or slice explanation, or an AI part with no earlier prediction. Bare answers with little visible reasoning. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts

Estimating Population Percentages from a Normal Fit
Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 25.3
Assignment 25.3 — Normal Areas Workbook
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Areas, cutoffs, and the honest word “estimate”
Spreadsheet lab · graded on a correct, complete workbook and clear reasoning
Covers: NORM.DIST (cumulative), NORM.S.DIST and NORM.INV; percent below, above, and between; working backward from a percent to a cutoff; turning a percent into a count; stating a result as an estimate that depends on the normal model fitting; checking an AI answer.
Lesson focus: Estimating Population Percentages from a Normal Fit
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
This is the week’s Excel lab. You will upload one workbook with three sheets (Areas, Cutoffs, Notes) built from typed formulas. You will also type four numeric answers, one applied answer, and one AI check into the Canvas text box. All scenarios are constructed; none are real data.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
If a normal curve can answer any question about a population in one step, what must be true before you believe the answer?
📁 M365 REMINDER
Name your Excel file Wk25_Normal_YourName.xlsx, save it to your OneDrive Optima → Math folder, and upload the .xlsx file to Canvas. Excel work happens outside Canvas; you will submit the finished workbook. Do not submit screenshots in place of the workbook.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Build the Areas sheet. Follow the Excel section of Lesson 25.3. Name the first sheet Areas. Use the headings from the lesson (Scenario, Mean, SD, a, b, z for a, Below a, Above a, Between a and b, Check: NORM.S.DIST). Enter these three constructed scenarios in rows 4 to 6: Quiz scores mean 75, SD 10, a = 68, b = 82; Cereal fill (g) mean 500, SD 4, a = 498, b = 507; Heights (cm) mean 170, SD 8, a = 158, b = 176. Use typed formulas with cell references (NORM.DIST for below and between, 1 minus the below cell for above, NORM.S.DIST for the check column), fill them down, and format the areas as percents with one decimal.
2
Build the Cutoffs sheet. Add a sheet named Cutoffs with headings Scenario, Mean, SD, Percent below, Cutoff, Round-trip check. Use NORM.INV to find: the top 5% of quiz scores (mean 75, SD 10); the bottom 25% of cereal fills (mean 500, SD 4); the top 20% of heights (mean 170, SD 8); and the lower and upper cutoffs of the middle 90% of cereal fills (the 5th and 95th percentiles; use two rows). Put the percent below in column D (a top 5% means 0.95 below), and fill the round-trip check with NORM.DIST. Format the cutoffs to 2 decimals.
3
Write the Notes sheet. Add a sheet named Notes with three items. (a) One sentence reporting the Heights row between a and b result in words, as an estimate for the population of students, with the unit. (b) One or two sentences naming the assumption behind every number in your workbook and saying what you would need to check. (c) One sentence explaining why the Cutoffs sheet needs the percent below and how you handled the “top” percents.
4
Part B — numeric answers (type into the Canvas text box). Use your workbook. Give areas as decimals to 4 places and cutoffs to 2 decimals. B1: the area below 68 for quiz scores (mean 75, SD 10). B2: the area between 498 g and 507 g for cereal fill (mean 500, SD 4). B3: the cutoff for the top 20% of heights (mean 170, SD 8). B4: in a school of 1200 students whose heights are modeled by mean 170 and SD 8, the estimated number of students between 158 cm and 176 cm (round to a whole number).
5
Part C — applied item. A constructed cereal line fills boxes with mean 500 g and SD 4 g. A box is acceptable if it holds between 494 g and 506 g. (i) Estimate the percent of boxes that are acceptable, showing both z-scores. (ii) In a run of 5000 boxes, estimate how many are outside tolerance. (iii) In one sentence, say what could make this estimate unreliable for a real production line.
6
Part D — AI check. Ask an AI tool: “Student heights are normally distributed with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 8 cm. What percent are between 160 cm and 180 cm? Show your steps.” Before reading its answer, write your own prediction. Then report: the AI’s final percent, the value you verified with Excel or the widget, whether the AI was right, and one thing to flag (rounding, standard deviation versus variance, a missing “estimate,” or a wrong step). If the AI got everything right, say what you checked to be sure. Save the workbook as Wk25_Normal_YourName.xlsx and upload it.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The workbook has Areas, Cutoffs, and Notes sheets, and the values come from typed formulas with cell references.
☐
Every area and cutoff matches the expected values (to rounding), and the check columns agree.
☐
The numeric answers, the applied item, and the AI check are in the Canvas text box and use the word “estimate.”
☐
The notes name the model assumption and say honestly what the AI got right or wrong.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Workbook & numeric answers
6 pts		 Areas (below / above / between): Quiz scores a=68, b=82: z = −0.7 and +0.7; 0.2420 / 0.7580 / 0.5161. Cereal a=498, b=507: z = −0.5 and +1.75; 0.3085 / 0.6915 / 0.6514. Heights a=158, b=176: z = −1.5 and +0.75; 0.0668 / 0.9332 / 0.7066. Check column equals Below a. Cutoffs: scores top 5% (0.95) = 91.45; cereal bottom 25% (0.25) = 497.30; heights top 20% (0.80) = 176.73; cereal middle 90%: 493.42 and 506.58 (0.05 and 0.95). Round-trip cells return the percent in column D. Part B: B1 0.2420 (±0.001); B2 0.6514; B3 176.73 (±0.05); B4 848 (0.7066 × 1200 = 847.9; accept 847 to 849). Formulas typed, not values. This row is worth 6 pts: Areas 2, Cutoffs 2, Part B 2 (0.5 each). One sheet or one formula block missing, a few values wrong because of a slip (wrong tail, 1 minus forgotten, percent below not used for a top percent), or one or two numeric answers wrong. Two or more parts missing, or values typed in instead of formulas. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Part C: z = ±1.5; area between = 0.9332 − 0.0668 = 0.8664, about 86.6% acceptable; outside = 0.1336 × 5000 = about 668 boxes (accept 665 to 670 from rounding); a sound reason such as fill weights not being roughly normal, a drifting machine, or needing actual sampling alongside the model. Part D: the verified value is 0.7887, about 78.9% (z = ±1.25); a prediction was written before reading the AI; the report names the AI’s answer, says whether it was right, and names one specific flag (for example rounding to 80% or 68%, 8 treated as variance giving about 99.96%, or no ‘estimate’ or assumption stated). The Notes sheet names the assumption (population roughly normal) and reads results as estimates. assignments.html:
Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company
PROBABILITY & STATISTICS HONORS
Quarter / Module
Q3 · Module 9
The Normal Distribution
Type
VR Solo Activity
Optima · Week 25 · pairs with Lessons 25.1 and 25.2
Time in headset
20–30 minutes
One session, one submission
Points
Completion-scored
5 pts
Module 9 · VR Solo Activity
The z-Score Lineup
VR Activity · 5 pts · completion
🥼 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
Lesson 25.1 gave you one ruler for every normal measurement: the z-score, \(z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\), the number of standard deviations a value stands from its mean. On paper that is a subtraction and a division. Today it is a place on the floor. Five made-up bean plants stand in a lineup, each with its height posted, and a strip on the floor is numbered by z. You will work out each plant's z-score, walk the plant to the spot where it belongs, and then watch what happens to every position when the group's spread changes and the heights do not. Measurements in centimeters, in minutes, or in points all land on the same ruler. That is the wonder of it: very different things measured in very different units can stand in one line. All of the data in this activity are constructed (made up).
📋 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset with Optima installed (desktop Optima works if a headset is unavailable, but walking a value to its place on the ruler is the heart of this activity).
▶
Your Lesson 25.1 notes (notebook page): the z-score formula, what a negative z means, and the reverse step \(x = \mu + z\sigma\). Review them before you put the headset on; re-reading inside a headset is hard.
▶
A pencil and notebook beside you for after the session. You will not need a calculator inside the headset: every number is small enough to work out on the Whiteboard IFX.
▶
About 30 uninterrupted minutes.
🚀 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (preferred) or desktop Optima
Session type: Persistent Session (your work saves between visits)
Session ID: [SESSION ID — teacher enters before publishing]
Location: [LOCATION NAME — an open, flat-floored Location with a long numbered floor strip; teacher enters before publishing]
On arrival: Find the Whiteboard IFX near the spawn point labeled “The z-Score Lineup — start here.” Ahead of you a row of five identical figures stands on a low platform, labeled A, B, C, D, E. Each has a sign giving the height in centimeters of one made-up bean plant. A second sign on the platform says: “Group 1: mean 50 cm, standard deviation 6 cm.” In front of the platform a long strip on the floor is numbered −3 to +3, with one numbered spot for each whole number and a small tick halfway between neighboring spots; the distance between neighboring spots is one pace. Beside the whiteboard wait five sticky notes and a second whiteboard marked “Group 2.”
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Read the lineup. Walk along the platform and say each plant's letter and height aloud. Before computing anything, say which plant you think is the most unusual and which is the most ordinary, judging only by how far each height is from 50.
2
Compute five z-scores. On the Whiteboard IFX, make a table with a row for each plant and write \(z = \frac{x - 50}{6}\) worked out in full for each one. Put the answer on a sticky note and attach it to the figure.
3
Walk each figure to its place. Pick up each figure in turn and set it on the floor strip at its z-score. A plant with \(z = -1.5\) goes on the tick halfway between −2 and −1. Then stand on the spot where z = +1 and say aloud which plant stands next to you and how many centimeters above the mean it is.
4
Change the spread. Go to the Group 2 whiteboard. It says: “Group 2: the same five heights, but the mean is 50 cm and the standard deviation is 3 cm.” Work the five new z-scores on the whiteboard, and move each figure to its new place. If a figure's z-score falls off the end of the strip, set it at the end of the strip and attach a sticky note: “Off the strip: z = __.” Say aloud which figures moved, which stayed put, and why the heights did not change.
5
Capture the lineup. Stand where one snapshot catches the strip with the five figures in their Group 2 places, their sticky notes, and the Whiteboard IFX with both sets of z-score work. Take the snapshot and check it before you go on: every number must be readable. If not, retake it from closer.
6
Put it back. Return the five figures to the platform in order A to E, so the next student finds the lineup as it was written. Leaving a place as you found it is the plainest courtesy there is.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Canvas Assignment Name: VR Activity — The z-Score Lineup
Upload your snapshot (image file) from step 5, showing the five figures in their Group 2 places, their sticky notes, and the Whiteboard IFX with your z-score work in frame.
Below it, in the text entry box, write a reflection of 2–3 sentences: (1) which plant was the most unusual in Group 1 and how its z-score shows it; and (2) why the same five heights got different z-scores in Group 2, and what that says about what a z-score measures.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment. · Estimated time: 20–30 minutes in headset.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA (COMPLETION)
☐
The snapshot shows the five figures at Group 2 positions with their z-score sticky notes, and the Whiteboard IFX with the z-score work for both groups readable in frame.
☐
All ten z-scores are correct, shown as a worked fraction (not just the answer).
☐
Any figure that falls off the strip carries an “Off the strip” sticky note with its z-score.
☐
The text entry contains the 2–3 sentence reflection.
👋 FACILITATOR NOTE
Stage the Location before publishing. Floor strip: an IFX with a collider, about 6 m long, with 7 numbered spots (−3 to +3) spaced 1 m apart and a small tick at every half spot (0.5 m), so that one pace is one numbered spot. Large digits, readable from a standing height. Lineup: five identical simple figures (one IFX, one color), unlocked, labeled A to E on a low platform with signs: A 56 cm, B 41 cm, C 50 cm, D 62 cm, E 47 cm (made-up bean plants). Platform sign: Group 1, mean 50 cm, SD 6 cm. A second whiteboard marked “Group 2” with the sentence in step 4. A Whiteboard IFX at the spawn point labeled “The z-Score Lineup — start here” with the first instruction and the legend (“1 pace = 1 z-score unit”; “a tick is half a unit”). Confirm the IFX names and sizes against the current IFX library before publishing; any identical simple shape works. Answer key. Group 1 (SD 6): A \(\frac{56-50}{6} = +1\); B \(\frac{41-50}{6} = -1.5\); C \(0\); D \(\frac{62-50}{6} = +2\); E \(\frac{47-50}{6} = -0.5\). The plant next to you at z = +1 is A (6 cm above the mean). Most unusual in Group 1: D (z = +2, the farthest from 0); most ordinary: C. Group 2 (SD 3): A +2; B −3; C 0; D +4 (off the strip; the end is +3); E −1. Only C stays put. The heights did not change; the ruler's unit did: with a smaller SD, each centimeter is worth more standard deviations. Reflection. Accept any true, specific statement: a z-score measures distance from the mean in units of the group's own spread, so the same raw height can be ordinary in one group and unusual in another. Common sticking points: dividing before subtracting; losing the sign (B is below the mean); placing −1.5 on the wrong side of −1; treating z = 4 as impossible (it is only rare, which is why it runs off the strip); and forgetting that the Group 2 plants kept the same heights. What to demo: picking up and placing an IFX on a numbered spot (with the Gizmo for fine placement), creating a sticky note and attaching it to an object, and taking and reviewing a snapshot. If a student finishes early, ask what height a plant would have at z = +1 in Group 2 and in Group 1 (53 cm and 56 cm).

Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 26.1
Assignment 26.1 — Does the Bell Fit?
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Checking whether the normal model fits, and saying so honestly
Practice set · graded on complete, honest work
Covers: shape, mean versus median, the 68–95–99.7 comparison, impossible values, outliers and heavy tails; why matching the mean and SD does not make data normal; the Excel checks; checking an AI’s diagnosis.
Lesson focus: When the Normal Model Is the Wrong Model
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will diagnose fit from described histograms and summary numbers, run the rule check on a constructed list, use Excel on a second list (answered as text), explain why two datasets with the same mean and SD can differ, judge an applied report, and check an AI’s diagnosis. All data are constructed. Practice set: scored on completeness and visible reasoning.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
How do you know when a beautiful model is the wrong one for your data?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Diagnose from descriptions. For each constructed dataset, say whether a normal model fits (fits, does not fit, or fits only in the middle) and give a reason that uses at least one of the checks. (a) A quantity that cannot be negative: mean 12, median 7, SD 14. (b) A single symmetric hump: mean 70, median 71, SD 8; 69% within 1 SD, 95% within 2 SD, 100% within 3 SD. (c) A histogram with two humps near 30 and 70: mean 50, median 50, SD 20.
2
Run the rule check. A constructed list of 16 values: 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 14, 17, 22, 30, 52. A spreadsheet reports mean = 13.81 and sample SD = 12.27. (a) Find the median. (b) Write the intervals mean ± 1, 2, and 3 SD, count the values inside each, and give the percents. (c) About how many of the 16 values would a normal model put inside each band (use 68, 95, 99.7)? (d) Compute mean − 2 × SD and say what it means if these values cannot be negative. (e) Give a verdict with two reasons, and say which check was most convincing and which was least.
3
Excel (answered as text). A constructed list of 15 values: 48, 52, 55, 57, 58, 60, 61, 62, 63, 64, 66, 67, 69, 72, 76. Open a blank workbook, type the values in A2 through A16 (heading Value in A1), and compute in Excel the mean, median, and sample SD, then the number and percent of values within 1 SD of the mean and within 2 SD. Report the exact formulas you typed (including the one that counts values within 1 SD), the values Excel gave, and your verdict on whether a normal model fits. (You do not upload a workbook for this item; type the formulas and values into your submission.)
4
Same mean, same SD, different shape. Dataset P is a single symmetric hump. Dataset Q has two humps, one near 30 and one near 70, with almost no values near 50. Both have mean 50 and SD 20. A classmate says, “They have the same mean and SD, so the same normal model describes both.” In three to five sentences, respond. Say what the classmate has right, what is wrong, and which check would tell the two datasets apart.
5
Application. A constructed report on made-up delivery wait times, in minutes, gives: mean 24, median 15, SD 26. (a) Compute mean − 2 × SD and say what it shows about a normal model. (b) State which center you would report and why. (c) The report says “95% of waits are within 2 SD of the mean.” Explain why that sentence is not safe to repeat. (d) Name what you would look at before deciding what to do.
6
AI check. Ask an AI tool: “Here are 15 values: 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 13, 20, 35, 80. Does a normal model fit this data? Explain how you decided.” Before you read its answer, write your own diagnosis in two or three sentences using at least two checks. Then report what the AI said and grade its diagnostic: did it look at shape, compare the mean with the median, run the rule check with actual counts, or watch for impossible values, or did it simply say yes? Recompute any number it quotes. State whether the AI was right, and anything it got wrong or left vague.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All six parts are complete, with each verdict supported by named checks (shape, mean versus median, rule check, impossible values, outliers).
☐
Counts, percents, and interval endpoints are shown, and every verdict is worded as a judgment with reasons, not as a proof.
☐
The Excel part gives the exact formulas typed, the values Excel gave, and a verdict.
☐
The AI check records your own diagnosis first, then grades the AI’s diagnostic honestly.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Completeness
6 pts		 All six parts attempted in full. One part missing or clearly rushed. Two or more parts missing. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Part 1: (a) Does not fit: mean 12 is well above median 7 (right skew) and 12 − 2(14) = −16 is impossible for a quantity that cannot be negative. (b) Fits: one symmetric hump, mean 70 and median 71 close, 69/95/100 close to 68/95/99.7, and 70 − 2(8) = 54 is far from zero (credit “fits reasonably” with reasons; the answer is a judgment, not a proof). (c) Does not fit: the shape check (two humps) fails even though the mean and median agree. Part 2: the sorted list has 16 values, so the median is the average of the 8th and 9th: (9 + 10) ÷ 2 = 9.5, well below the mean 13.81. Intervals: 1 SD is 1.54 to 26.08 (14 of 16, 87.5%); 2 SD is −10.73 to 38.35 (15 of 16, 93.75%, about 93.8%); 3 SD is −23.0 to 50.62 (15 of 16, 93.8%; 52 is outside). A normal model would put about 0.68(16) = 10.9, 0.95(16) = 15.2, 0.997(16) = 15.95 inside, so about 11, 15, 16. Mean − 2 SD = 13.81 − 24.54 = −10.73: impossible if values cannot be negative. Verdict: does not fit. Reasons: mean above median, right skew, impossible lower end, the value 52 is (52 − 13.81) ÷ 12.27 = 3.1 SD above the mean, and 87.5% inside 1 SD versus 68%. The 2 SD and 3 SD counts are near the prediction, so the rule check is the least convincing here (accept a reasoned ranking). Part 3: mean 62, median 62, SD about 7.47. Formulas such as =AVERAGE(A2:A16), =MEDIAN(A2:A16), =STDEV.S(A2:A16), and =COUNTIFS(A2:A16,">="&(mean cell − SD cell),A2:A16,"<="&(mean cell + SD cell)). Within 1 SD (54.53 to 69.47): 11 of 15, 73.3%. Within 2 SD (47.05 to 76.95): 15 of 15, 100%. Verdict: fits reasonably (one hump, mean equals median, nothing impossible, nothing far out); 73% versus 68% is under one value’s difference at n = 15 (each value is 6.7%). Accept consistent formulas that give these values. Part 4: the classmate is right that the mean and SD match, and a normal curve with that mean and SD can be drawn over either dataset; wrong that the same model fits both, because mean and SD do not determine shape. Dataset Q puts few values where the normal model puts the most (near 50). The histogram (shape check) separates them; the rule check or mean versus median would not necessarily. Part 5: (a) 24 − 2(26) = −28 minutes, an impossible wait, so a normal model is poor. (b) The median 15, because the mean 24 is pulled up by a few long waits (mean well above median). (c) A normal interval for 95% would start at −28, which is impossible, and the data are probably right-skewed, so the 95% claim does not apply. (d) The histogram and the actual percents within 1, 2, and 3 SD. Part 6: the list has median 6 and mean 13.67 (205 ÷ 15), SD about 20.26, 13, 14, 14 of 15 values within 1, 2, 3 SD (86.7%, 93.3%, 93.3%), mean − 2 SD = −26.8, and the largest value 80 is (80 − 13.67) ÷ 20.26 = 3.27 SD above the mean. Diagnosis: does not fit (right-skewed). Credit a prediction, an honest report of the AI’s claim, a verdict on its diagnostic (shape, mean versus median, rule check, impossible values), and evidence that its numbers were recomputed; the grade rewards the checking, not the AI being right. Mostly correct but with one wrong value, a verdict with no named check, a missing Excel formula, or an AI check that skips the prediction or the grading of the AI’s diagnostic. Bare verdicts with little visible reasoning. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 26.1 — Does the Bell Fit?
Submit a clear photo or scan of your notebook pages (JPG, PNG, or PDF), or type your work directly into the text entry box. Make sure every step, entry, and answer is legible.
For the Excel part, type the formulas and the values Excel gave you into your answer. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Lesson 26.2
Assignment 26.2 — The Binomial and the Normal
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Binomial counts, normal curves, and when one can stand in for the other
Practice set · graded on complete, honest work
Covers: the mean np and SD √(np(1−p)); normal estimates with the continuity correction; checking when the approximation is appropriate; BINOM.DIST versus NORM.DIST in Excel; what a Galton board shows; checking an AI's answer.
Lesson focus: The Binomial and the Normal: Galton’s Board
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will compute the mean and SD of binomial counts, estimate binomial probabilities with a normal curve and the continuity correction, decide when that estimate is appropriate, compare BINOM.DIST with NORM.DIST (answered as text), reason about a Galton board, and check an AI's answer. All settings are constructed. Practice set: scored on completeness and visible reasoning.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Why does a crowd of unpredictable choices make a predictable bell, and when can you trust the bell as a shortcut?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Mean and SD. For each constructed binomial setting, find the mean np and the standard deviation √(np(1−p)), the SD rounded to two decimals, and say whether both np and n(1−p) are at least 10. (a) n = 60, p = 0.25. (b) n = 200, p = 0.4. (c) n = 500, p = 0.02. Show the number under the root before you take the root.
2
Normal estimates with the continuity correction. Let X ~ Binomial(100, 0.5), a constructed 100-trial setting. Using a normal curve with the continuity correction, estimate (a) P(X ≤ 55), (b) P(X ≥ 60), and (c) P(X = 50). For each, state the cutoff(s) you used, the z-score(s), and the area, rounded to four decimals (use Excel's NORM.DIST or NORM.S.DIST).
3
When is it okay? For each constructed setting, check both np and n(1−p) against the rule of thumb of 10 and say whether the normal approximation is appropriate: (a) n = 20, p = 0.5. (b) n = 60, p = 0.05. (c) n = 500, p = 0.97. Then, for the setting that fails, explain in one or two sentences what goes wrong with a normal curve there (think about the shape of the pile and about negative counts).
4
Excel: BINOM.DIST versus NORM.DIST (answered as text). Let X ~ Binomial(50, 0.3). Open a blank workbook and type the formulas for P(X ≤ 18) in three ways: the exact answer with BINOM.DIST; the normal approximation with the continuity correction, using NORM.DIST; and the normal approximation without it. Report the formula you typed for each, the three values to four decimals, and one sentence saying which approximation is closer to the exact value and why. Then report what you get when you add up BINOM.DIST(k,50,0.3,FALSE) for k = 0 through 18 (for instance with SUM over a column of those 19 values). (You do not upload a workbook for this item; type the formulas and values into your submission.)
5
The Galton board. A constructed Galton board has 12 rows of pegs. (a) With a 50% chance of going right, what are the mean and SD of the slot a ball lands in, and does the board pass the check of 10? (b) The chance is changed to 10% with the same 12 rows. Find the mean and SD, run the check again, and describe how the pile will look and why. (c) In one sentence, explain what a Galton board shows about a single ball versus a crowd of many balls.
6
AI check. Ask an AI tool: “What does a Galton board show, and why do the balls form a bell shape? For a board with 12 rows and a 50% chance of going right, what are the mean and standard deviation of the slot a ball lands in?” Before you read its answer, write your own prediction of the mean and SD. Check the AI's numbers with Desmos or Excel and compare with the Galton board widget (12 rows, 50%, 1000 or more balls). Report what the AI said, whether it was right, and anything it got wrong or left vague (for example, saying the balls “prefer” the middle, saying more balls change the spread, or leaving the square root out of the SD).
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All six parts are complete, with the number under the root shown before the root is taken and every z-score written with its subtraction in parentheses.
☐
Every normal estimate of a binomial probability states the cutoff used and applies the continuity correction.
☐
The when-is-it-okay judgments check both np and n(1−p) against the rule of thumb and give a reason.
☐
The Excel part gives the exact formulas typed, the three values, and a one-sentence comparison, without uploading a workbook.
☐
The AI check records your prediction, the AI's claim, your verification, and an honest verdict.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Completeness
6 pts		 All six parts attempted in full. One part missing or clearly rushed. Two or more parts missing. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Part 1: (a) mean 60 × 0.25 = 15; under the root 60 × 0.25 × 0.75 = 11.25; SD = √11.25 ≈ 3.35; np = 15 and n(1−p) = 45, both at least 10. (b) mean 80; under the root 200 × 0.4 × 0.6 = 48; SD = √48 ≈ 6.93; 80 and 120, both at least 10. (c) mean 10; under the root 500 × 0.02 × 0.98 = 9.8; SD = √9.8 ≈ 3.13; 10 and 490, both at least 10 (just meets it). Part 2: mean 50, SD 5. (a) cutoff 55.5, z = 1.1, area 0.8643 (the exact binomial value is about 0.8644). (b) cutoff 59.5, z = 1.9, area above = 1 − 0.9713 = 0.0287 (exact about 0.0284). (c) between 49.5 and 50.5, z = −0.1 and 0.1, area 0.0797 (exact about 0.0796). Accept answers within 0.0002 of these if a different rounding path was used; an answer that uses 55, 60, or 49.5 to 50.5 incorrectly (no correction) should lose credit for that part. Part 3: (a) np = 10 and n(1−p) = 10: the check is met (barely), so the approximation is appropriate. (b) np = 3 is below 10: not appropriate; use the exact binomial. (c) np = 485 and n(1−p) = 15: both at least 10, so appropriate. For (b): with a small np the exact distribution is lopsided and bunched near 0 (the mean is only 3, and the SD is about 1.69), but the normal curve is symmetric and extends below zero (mean minus 2 SDs is negative), so it assigns area to counts that are impossible and misstates the probabilities near 0. Part 4: for X ~ Binomial(50, 0.3), mean 15, SD √10.5 ≈ 3.24. =BINOM.DIST(18,50,0.3,TRUE) gives about 0.8594; =NORM.DIST(18.5,15,SQRT(50*0.3*0.7),TRUE) gives about 0.8600; =NORM.DIST(18,15,SQRT(50*0.3*0.7),TRUE) gives about 0.8227. The corrected version is far closer (off by about 0.0006 against 0.037) because the bar for 18 reaches up to 18.5. The sum of =BINOM.DIST(k,50,0.3,FALSE) for k = 0 through 18 is the same as the cumulative value, about 0.8594. Accept equivalent formulas with the same values. Part 5: (a) mean 12 × 0.5 = 6, SD √3 ≈ 1.73; np = 6 and n(1−p) = 6, both below 10, so the board does not quite meet the check of 10 (accept a remark that the rule is a screening check and that some sources use 5; the pile is still roughly bell-shaped at 50%). (b) mean 12 × 0.1 = 1.2, SD √1.08 ≈ 1.04; np = 1.2 fails clearly (n(1−p) = 10.8 is fine). The pile leans hard against the left side (most balls go right only 0, 1, or 2 times) and trails off to the right, so it is not a symmetric bell; the heap cannot go below slot 0. (c) One ball is unpredictable, but the crowd of many balls builds a predictable, bell-shaped pile. Part 6: for 12 rows at 50%, mean 6 and SD √3 ≈ 1.73 (Desmos: 12*0.5 and sqrt(12*0.5*0.5)); the widget's observed values should be close to these. Credit a prediction, the AI's claim reported honestly, the check against Desmos or the widget, and a clear verdict; the grade rewards the checking, not the AI being right. Mostly correct but with one wrong value, a missing continuity correction, a check of only one of the two conditions, a missing Excel formula, or an AI check that skips the prediction or the verification. Bare answers with little visible reasoning. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts
