📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
This is the week’s Excel lab. You will upload one workbook with four sheets (Tolerance, Scores, Survey, Notes) built from typed formulas, using the layout you built in Lesson 26.3 with the new numbers below. You will also type your Part B numeric answers, one applied item, and one AI check into the Canvas text box. All scenarios are constructed; none is real data.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Before you trust a normal-model answer, what do you check, and what do you say when the check fails?
📁 M365 REMINDER
Name your Excel file Wk26_NormalLab_YourName.xlsx, save it to your OneDrive Optima → Math folder, and upload the .xlsx file to Canvas. Excel work happens outside Canvas; you will submit the finished workbook. Do not submit screenshots in place of the workbook.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Build the Tolerance sheet. Use the Tolerance layout from Lesson 26.3 (inputs in B3:B8, results in B10:B17, a what-if table in A20:C24 with absolute references). Use these constructed numbers for pipe segment lengths: mean 120.0 mm, SD 0.5 mm, lower limit 119.0, upper limit 121.0, batch size N = 4000, target share too long 0.01. In the what-if table use upper limits 120.5, 121.0, 121.5, and 122.0. Use typed formulas with cell references, and format shares as percents.
2
Build the Scores sheet. Use the Scores layout from the lesson with Test C (mean 70, SD 12) in row 4 and Test D (mean 50, SD 6) in row 5. Look up the score 85 on Test C (percentile), and find the cutoff for the top 10% (B9 = 0.10). In the comparison table enter Ana, Test C, score 85, and Ben, Test D, score 62, with D, E, F, and G as formulas.
3
Build the Survey sheet. Use the Survey layout from the lesson with two claims. Claim 1 (column B): n = 120, p = 0.25, k = 24 (at most 24). Claim 2 (column C): n = 25, p = 0.04, k = 1. Include np, n(1-p), the PASS/FAIL audit, SD, exact BINOM.DIST, normal with no correction, normal with the continuity correction, the error, and the normal area below 0. Fill column B to column C.
4
Write the Notes sheet. In three sentences (A3, A4, A5), answer “What would make this estimate wrong?” for Tolerance, Scores, and Survey. Each sentence must name a specific condition (the shape of the data, independence, random sampling, or the audit) and say how it would affect the estimate. Do not copy the sentences from the lesson.
5
Part B — numeric answers (type into the Canvas text box). Use your workbook. Give areas as decimals to 4 places, limits and cutoffs to 2 decimals, and counts as whole numbers. B1: the share of pipe segments in specification (Tolerance). B2: the expected number of pipe segments out of specification in the batch of 4000. B3: the upper limit that would reject only 1% of segments for being too long. B4: the score needed for the top 10% on Test C. B5: Ana’s z-score and Ben’s z-score, and who did better relative to their own test. B6: for Claim 1, np, n(1-p), whether the audit passes, the exact probability, and the normal estimate with the continuity correction. B7: for Claim 2, np, whether the audit passes, and the one probability you would report.
6
Part C — applied item. A made-up student team claims that 15% of the students at a school would prefer a later start time. They plan a random sample of n = 80 students. (i) Show the audit for np and n(1 − p) and say whether the normal approximation is allowed. (ii) Estimate the probability that at most 8 students in the sample prefer a later start, using the continuity correction (show the z-score), and compare with the exact BINOM.DIST value. (iii) The team then considers a smaller sample of n = 40. Run the audit again and say what they should use instead, and why. (iv) In one sentence, say what could make these probabilities misleading for a real school.
7
Part D — AI check. Ask an AI tool: “A made-up claim says 30% of the students at a school play an instrument. In a random sample of 150 students, use a normal approximation to find the probability that at most 40 play an instrument. First check that the approximation is appropriate, and show every step including any continuity correction.” Before reading its answer, write your own prediction. Then report: the AI’s final probability, your verified value, whether the AI computed np and n(1-p) and compared them with 10, whether it used the correct continuity correction (40.5), and one specific thing to flag (a skipped check, no correction, SD versus variance, or no mention of random sampling and independence). If the AI got everything right, say what you checked to be sure. Save the workbook as Wk26_NormalLab_YourName.xlsx and upload it.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The workbook has Tolerance, Scores, Survey, and Notes sheets, and the values come from typed formulas with cell references (with absolute references where a value must not move).
☐
Every value matches the expected numbers (to rounding), the audit row reads PASS or FAIL from a formula, and the Survey sheet reports the exact value whenever the audit fails.
☐
The numeric answers, the applied item, and the AI check are in the Canvas text box and use the word “estimate.”
☐
The notes and the applied item name specific conditions (fit, independence, random sampling) and say honestly what the AI got right or wrong.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Workbook & numeric answers
6 pts		 Tolerance (mean 120, SD 0.5, limits 119 and 121, N = 4000, target 0.01): z = −2 and +2; below 0.0228, above 0.0228, in spec 0.9545, out of spec 0.0455, expected rejects 182.0 (accept 181 to 183), upper limit for 1% too long 121.16. What-if table (above 120.5, 121.0, 121.5, 122.0): 15.9%, 2.3%, 0.1%, 0.0%, with expected counts about 635, 91, 5, 0. $B$ references used in the table. Scores (Test C 70 and 12, Test D 50 and 6): Test C percentile of 85 = 0.8944; top 10% cutoff = 85.38; Ana z = 1.25 (0.8944), Ben z = 2.00 (0.9772). Survey: Claim 1 np = 30, n(1-p) = 90, PASS, SD 4.7434, exact 0.1217, no correction 0.1030, correction 0.1231, error +0.0015, area below 0 about 0.0000. Claim 2 np = 1, n(1-p) = 24, FAIL, SD 0.9798, exact 0.7358, no correction 0.5000, correction 0.6951, error −0.0407, area below 0 = 0.1537. Part B: B1 0.9545; B2 182; B3 121.16 (±0.01); B4 85.38 (±0.05); B5 1.25 and 2.00, Ben did better; B6 30, 90, PASS, 0.1217, 0.1231; B7 np = 1, FAIL, report the exact 0.7358. Formulas typed, not values. This row is worth 6 pts: Tolerance 1, Scores 1, Survey 2, Part B 2. One sheet or one block missing, a few values wrong because of a slip (wrong tail, 1 minus forgotten, top percent entered as 0.10 instead of 0.90 below, continuity correction left out, absolute references missing so the table fails), or one or two numeric answers wrong. Two or more parts missing, or values typed in instead of formulas. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Part C: (i) np = 80 × 0.15 = 12 and n(1-p) = 68, both at least 10, allowed (SD = 3.194); (ii) z = (8.5 − 12) ÷ 3.194 = −1.10, estimate 0.1366 (accept 0.136 to 0.137), exact 0.1342, close; (iii) n = 40 gives np = 6, less than 10, so the audit fails and they should use the exact BINOM.DIST (for example P(X ≤ 4) = 0.2633); (iv) a sound reason such as a non-random or self-selected sample, students influencing each other, or a claim of 15% that is itself unverified. Part D: the verified values are np = 45, n(1-p) = 105, SD 5.612, z = −0.80, estimate 0.2113, exact 0.2126; a prediction was written before reading the AI; the report names the AI’s probability, says whether it checked np and n(1-p) and used 40.5, and names one specific flag (for example no audit shown, 40 used instead of 40.5 giving about 0.1865, variance 31.5 used as the SD giving about 0.44, or no mention of random sampling and independence). The Notes sentences name specific conditions and say how each would change the estimate. This row is worth 4 pts: Part C 2, Part D 2 (Notes sentences count toward the reasoning in either part). Correct numbers but the audit reasoning, the word “estimate,” or the conditions are missing, or the AI check reports only the AI’s answer without a verified value or a specific flag. Bare numbers with no reasoning, or no AI check. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts

Upload your Excel workbook (.xlsx) as a file, and type your Part B, Part C and Part D answers in the text box. Label each answer (B1, B2, and so on).

assignments.html:
Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company
PROBABILITY & STATISTICS HONORS
Quarter / Module
Q3 · Module 9
The Normal Distribution
Type
VR Module Lab
Optima · Week 26 · the module's capstone in headset
Time in headset
20–30 minutes
One session, one submission
Points
Rubric-scored
15 pts
Module 9 · VR Lab
Inside the Bell
VR Lab · 15 pts · rubric-graded
🥼 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
This module's virtue is wonder, and the Galton board in Week 26 showed why: a thousand small left-or-right choices pile up into a bell, and the bell is nearly the same bell wherever it appears. Today you will stand inside one. In the Location a bell has been built to room scale: twelve towers, each standing over a half-unit slice of the z-ruler, with the number of made-up bean plants in each tower posted on it. You will walk the ruler from \(z = -2\) to \(z = +2\), place three banners that mark the Empirical Rule's bands, add up what is inside each, and compare your percents with 68, 95, and 99.7. Then two made-up visitors arrive with a measurement each, and you will find where each one stands and how many plants stand beyond. Finally you will tell the story in a short spatial recording, including one thing that this bell, as lovely as it is, cannot tell you. All of the data in this lab are constructed (made up).
📋 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset with Optima installed (desktop Optima works if a headset is unavailable, but standing at \(z = 2\) and looking back at the whole bell is the heart of this lab).
▶
Your Lesson 25.1, 25.2, 26.1, and 26.2 notes (notebook page): the z-score formula, the 68–95–99.7 rule, how to tell when a normal model does not fit, and why the binomial makes a bell. Review them before you put the headset on; re-reading inside a headset is hard.
▶
To do at your desk before the session: the made-up bean plants in this lab have a mean of 50 cm and a standard deviation of 8 cm. Write on paper the height of a plant at each of \(z = -2, -1, 0, +1, +2\), using \(x = \mu + z\sigma\). You will check these on the floor.
▶
About 30 uninterrupted minutes.
🚀 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (preferred) or desktop Optima
Session type: Persistent Session (your work saves between visits)
Session ID: [SESSION ID — teacher enters before publishing]
Location: [LOCATION NAME — an open, flat-floored Location with a long numbered floor strip and the staged bell; teacher enters before publishing]
On arrival: Find the Whiteboard IFX near the spawn point labeled “Inside the Bell — start here.” Ahead of you a long strip on the floor is numbered −3 to +3, with one numbered spot for each whole number and a tick halfway between neighboring spots; the distance between neighboring spots is one pace. Over the strip stand twelve towers, each covering half a unit of z (from −3 to −2.5, then −2.5 to −2, and so on to +3). Each tower carries a sticky note giving how many of the 1,000 made-up bean plants fall in that slice, and a taller tower means more plants. Two further sticky notes at the ends say how many plants lie beyond −3 and beyond +3. Beside the whiteboard wait three banner-shaped IFX in three colors, a marker labeled “You are here,” and a second marker in another color.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Read the bell. Walk the strip once from −3 to +3 under the towers. Read each tower's count aloud and write the twelve numbers and the two end counts in a row on the Whiteboard IFX. Add them. You should get 1,000. Say the shape you see before you compute anything else.
2
Stand at the landmarks. Walk to \(z = 0\), then to \(-1\), \(+1\), \(-2\), and \(+2\). At each place a sticky note on the floor with the height in centimeters of a plant that stands there (your desk numbers). Say aloud at each place how many paces you are from the center, and what a z-score of 2 means in the group's own units.
3
Place the banners. Stretch the first banner across the strip from \(z = -1\) to \(+1\), the second from \(-2\) to \(+2\), and the third from \(-3\) to \(+3\). For each, add up the posted counts of the towers it covers (include the end counts only for the third banner) and write on the whiteboard: “Inside \(\pm k\): __ of 1,000 = __%.” Next to each, write the Empirical Rule's percent and say aloud why your percent is close but not exactly equal to it.
4
Find where ‘you’ fall. Two made-up visitors are posted on the whiteboard. Visitor 1: a bean plant 66 cm tall. Visitor 2: a bean plant 42 cm tall. Work each z-score on the whiteboard, walk to that place on the strip, and set the “You are here” marker for Visitor 1 and the second marker for Visitor 2. For each visitor count how many plants stand beyond them (to the right of Visitor 1, to the left of Visitor 2), using the tower and end counts, and write the share as a percent of 1,000.
5
Capture the bell. Stand back far enough that one snapshot catches the strip, the towers with their counts, the three banners, both markers, and the Whiteboard IFX with your sums. Take it and check it before moving on; every number must be readable. If not, retake it from closer.
6
Narrate. Stand where the whole bell is in view and start a spatial recording. Speak for 60 to 90 seconds, in your own words, answering all three: (a) what your three banner percents were, how they compare with 68, 95, and 99.7, and why the bell in the room can only approximate the rule; (b) where each visitor stands, their z-scores, and what share of plants lie beyond; (c) one thing this bell cannot tell you, for example whether real bean plants, or real test scores, really make a bell (what you learned to check in Lesson 26.1). Use your own numbers. Do not read your sticky notes aloud; look at the floor and tell what you see. Stop the recording. Then put the markers and banners back where you found them, so the next student finds the bell as it was built.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Canvas Assignment Name: VR Lab — Inside the Bell
Upload two things: (1) your snapshot from step 5 (image file) showing the towers, the three banners, both markers, and your sums; and (2) your spatial recording from step 6 (60–90 seconds of narration), shared as a link or file exactly as your teacher shows on the Canvas page for this assignment.
Below them, in the text entry box, write one line giving your numbers: the three banner counts and percents, the z-scores of the two visitors, and the share of plants beyond each, so your teacher can check them without replaying your recording. Then add the spreadsheet check: type =1-NORM.S.DIST(2,TRUE) in Excel, write the value it gives, and say in one sentence how it compares with your count for Visitor 1.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment. · Estimated time: 20–30 minutes in headset.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
CriteriaFull creditPartial creditMinimal creditPts
Completeness
5 pts		 The three banners, both markers, and the landmark sticky notes are placed; the snapshot shows the whole bell readably with the sums on the whiteboard; the spatial recording runs about 60–90 seconds and answers all three questions; the numbers line and the spreadsheet check are typed. One element missing or clearly rushed: a banner or marker missing, an unreadable snapshot, a recording that skips one of the three questions or runs under about 45 seconds, or the numbers line or spreadsheet check missing. Two or more required elements missing. 5 pts
Accuracy
5 pts		 Inside \(\pm 1\): 682 of 1,000 (68.2%); inside \(\pm 2\): 954 (95.4%); inside \(\pm 3\): 998 (99.8%); Visitor 1: \(z = +2\), 23 plants beyond (2.3%); Visitor 2: \(z = -1\), 159 plants beyond (15.9%); Excel gives about 0.0228, close to 2.3%. One value wrong (for example, a tower omitted from a sum, the end counts added to the wrong banner, or a visitor's z-score computed with the wrong sign) while the rest is correct. Multiple errors in the sums, percents, z-scores, or counts beyond. 5 pts
Evidence of engagement
5 pts		 The narration is in the student's own words and uses their own numbers: it explains that the posted counts are rounded and the bell is a finite staged model, so percents are close to but not equal to the rule; it says where each visitor stands in z-units and in the group's own units; and it names a specific thing the bell cannot tell you (for example, that a normal model only fits if the real data have that shape and must be checked, or that it says nothing about any one plant). Honest remarks about what the model assumes are welcome. A correct narration that is generic or read from notes (“the percents are close to the rule”), or a limit that is vague. Narration missing the questions, or no evident engagement with the layout. 5 pts
Total: 15 pts
👋 FACILITATOR NOTE
Stage the Location before publishing. Floor strip: an IFX with a collider, about 6 m long, with 7 numbered spots (−3 to +3) spaced 1 m apart and a tick at every half spot, so that one pace is one numbered spot. Large digits. Towers: twelve identical box-shaped IFX, each 0.5 m wide, standing over the half-unit slices from −3 to +3, scaled to heights proportional to the counts (for example 1 cm per plant, so the tallest, 191, stands 1.91 m; any consistent scale that fits the Location works). Posted counts, left to right: 5, 17, 44, 92, 150, 191, 191, 150, 92, 44, 17, 5 (sum 998), with end sticky notes 1 beyond −3 and 1 beyond +3, for exactly 1,000 made-up bean plants. Lock all towers. Markers: three banner-shaped IFX in three colors; a marker labeled “You are here” and a second marker in another color, all unlocked. A Whiteboard IFX at the spawn point labeled “Inside the Bell — start here” with the legend (“1 pace = 1 z-score unit”; “1,000 made-up bean plants, mean 50 cm, SD 8 cm”) and the two visitors. Confirm the IFX names and sizes, and the place to start and stop a spatial recording, against the current IFX library and ENGAGE app before publishing. How the counts were made. Each is 1,000 times the normal area in its half-unit slice, rounded to whole plants. They come from a model, not from real measurements, which is why the page says made up. Answer key. Heights at \(z = -2, -1, 0, +1, +2\): 34, 42, 50, 58, 66 cm. Inside \(\pm 1\) (the four central towers): \(150 + 191 + 191 + 150 = 682\), 68.2%. Inside \(\pm 2\) (the eight central towers): \(44 + 92 + 150 + 191 + 191 + 150 + 92 + 44 = 954\), 95.4%. Inside \(\pm 3\) (all twelve towers): 998, 99.8%; the two plants beyond \(\pm 3\) make up the last 0.2%. Visitor 1: \(z = \frac{66 - 50}{8} = +2\); plants beyond +2: \(17 + 5 + 1 = 23\), 2.3%. Visitor 2: \(z = \frac{42 - 50}{8} = -1\); plants beyond −1 on the left: \(92 + 44 + 17 + 5 + 1 = 159\), 15.9%. Excel: \(1 - \) NORM.S.DIST(2, TRUE) \(\approx 0.0228\) (2.28%), close to the room's 2.3%; the exact value for Visitor 2 is about 15.87%. The percents match the rule's 68, 95, and 99.7 to within about half a percent because the towers are rounded and the staging is finite. Limits the student might name (accept any true, specific one): fit must be checked in real data; a normal model says nothing about one plant; the made-up bell is built to be normal, so of course it fits. Common sticking points: adding the end sticky notes to the wrong banner; mixing up “beyond” with “inside”; losing the sign for Visitor 2; reading z as centimeters; and going over 90 seconds or reading sticky notes aloud. What to demo: stretching a banner IFX with the Gizmo; placing a marker; starting and stopping a spatial recording; creating and placing sticky notes. If a student finishes early, ask what would change about the posted heights in centimeters if the standard deviation were 4 cm instead of 8 cm (the z-positions and counts would not change).

An Education Experience Company
PROBABILITY & STATISTICS HONORS
Quarter / Module
Q4 · Module 10
Bivariate Data & Regression
Lesson
Lesson 27.1
Paired Lesson
Scatter Plots and Association
Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 27.1
Assignment 27.1 — Reading the Scatter
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Describing association and reading r, with careful claims
Practice set · graded on complete, honest work
Covers: direction, form, strength, and unusual features; the meaning of r; curved patterns with r near 0; a labeled Excel scatter chart; wording that does not claim cause; checking an AI’s estimate of r.
Lesson focus: Scatter Plots and Association
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will describe scatter plots in four parts, match values of r to patterns, explain a curved pattern whose r is near 0, build an Excel scatter chart (answered as text), judge a causal claim, and check an AI’s estimate of r. All data are constructed. Practice set: scored on completeness and visible reasoning.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What can a scatter plot and a correlation honestly tell us, and what must we leave unsaid?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Describe it in four parts. (a) A constructed dataset of 8 plants: x is days of sunlight per week, y is height in cm. The pairs (x, y): (2, 10); (3, 16); (4, 12); (5, 17); (6, 15); (7, 22); (8, 18); (9, 24).
Plant height and sunlight (made up)
Constructed (made-up) data.
Give direction, form, strength, and unusual features in a sentence or two, and estimate r to the nearest tenth. (b) A different plot has most points falling from left to right along a tight band, but one point at the far right sits high above the band. Which of the four parts does that point belong to, and would it make r closer to 0 or farther from 0?
2
Match r to the pattern. Match each value of r to one description: r = −0.95, −0.4, 0.0, +0.5, +0.9. (i) Points rise tightly along a straight line. (ii) Points fall steeply and very tightly along a straight line. (iii) Points form a round cloud with no tilt. (iv) Points rise loosely, with a lot of scatter. (v) Points fall loosely, with a lot of scatter. Then explain in one sentence why the number r = 0.0 alone cannot tell you whether the points have a pattern.
3
A curved pattern. A constructed dataset: x is the temperature setting of an oven (in tens of degrees above a baseline) and y is a made-up “doneness score.” Nine points: (1, 3); (2, 9); (3, 14); (4, 17); (5, 18); (6, 16); (7, 13); (8, 8); (9, 2). (a) Sketch the scatter plot. (b) Describe it in four parts. (c) A spreadsheet reports r = −0.08. A classmate says “r is almost 0, so the setting and the score are unrelated.” Respond in two or three sentences.
4
Excel (answered as text). A constructed dataset of 10 students: x is minutes of daily reading, y is a vocabulary quiz score. x: 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35, 40, 45, 50, 55. y: 12, 10, 15, 14, 19, 17, 22, 21, 24, 27. Open a blank workbook, type the headings and values (x in column A, y in column B), and build a scatter chart with axis titles and a chart title. In your answer, list (a) the exact menu clicks you used, in order, (b) the three titles you typed, (c) the four-part description of your chart, and (d) your estimate of r to the nearest tenth. (You do not upload a workbook for this item; type your answers into your submission.)
5
Application: careful wording. A constructed news line: “A made-up study of 40 adults found that people who own more houseplants report better moods (r = +0.5). Experts say plants boost your mood.” (a) Describe the association the study reports, using “is associated with.” (b) Explain why the data alone do not show that plants boost mood, and give two other explanations. (c) Write a revised, responsible version of the headline.
6
AI check. Ask an AI tool: “Nine measurements: (x, y) = (0, 10); (1, 22); (2, 31); (3, 36); (4, 38); (5, 35); (6, 30); (7, 21); (8, 11). Describe the scatter plot and estimate the correlation coefficient r.” Before you read its answer, sketch the points and write your own description and estimate of r. Then report what the AI said, and grade it: did it name the shape, give a sensible r, avoid false precision, and avoid claiming cause? Name anything it got wrong or left vague.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All six parts are complete, and each description names direction, form, strength, and unusual features.
☐
Estimates of r are given to about one decimal place and match the direction and strength described.
☐
The Excel part gives the clicks, the titles, the description, and an estimate of r.
☐
Claims about relationships use “is associated with,” not “causes,” and the AI check records your own prediction first.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Completeness
6 pts		 All six parts attempted in full. One part missing or clearly rushed. Two or more parts missing. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Part 1: (a) The points rise: positive; roughly linear; moderately strong to strong (the computed r is +0.85, so accept an estimate of +0.8 or +0.9 and accept “moderate to strong”); no outliers or clusters. (b) The far point is an unusual feature (an outlier). Because it sits off the line, it would pull r toward 0 (weaker than the tight band alone gives); it should be investigated, not simply deleted. Part 2: (i) +0.9; (ii) −0.95; (iii) 0.0; (iv) +0.5; (v) −0.4. Reason for r = 0: r only measures straight-line association, so a curved pattern can also give r near 0; the plot must be looked at. Part 3: (a) the sketch is an arch; (b) direction: rises then falls; form: curved (arch); strength: tight along the curve; no unusual points. The computed r is −0.08, near 0. (c) r near 0 only says there is no straight-line trend; the pattern is a strong curve, so the setting and score are clearly related (the highest scores come at a middle setting). Part 4: sample answer: select A1:B11, Insert tab, Scatter (X, Y), dots-only option, then Chart Elements (+) for Axis Titles and Chart Title; titles such as “Minutes of daily reading,” “Vocabulary quiz score,” “Reading time and vocabulary score (made-up data)”; description: positive, linear, strong, no outliers; computed r is +0.96, so accept estimates of +0.9 or +1.0. Part 5: (a) among the 40 adults, owning more houseplants is associated with better reported mood, a moderate positive association (r = +0.5); (b) a study like this cannot show cause: people in a good mood may be more likely to keep plants, or a third factor such as free time, income, or a sunny home may raise both; chance and how the 40 were chosen also matter; (c) e.g. “In one study of 40 adults, those with more houseplants reported better moods; the study cannot say whether the plants play a part.” Part 6: the points rise then fall (an arch); the computed Pearson r is −0.009, essentially 0. A good AI answer notes the arch and says r is near 0 while the relationship is strong but not linear; a weak answer says “no relationship,” gives r to many decimals, or ignores the shape. Credit a prediction, an honest report of the AI’s answer, and a reasoned grade; the grade rewards the checking, not the AI being right. Mostly correct but with a missing part of a four-part description, an r estimate with the wrong sign, a causal verb in Part 5, or an AI check that skips the prediction or the grading. Bare answers with little visible reasoning. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 27.1 — Reading the Scatter
Submit a clear photo or scan of your notebook pages (JPG, PNG, or PDF), or type your work directly into the text entry box. Make sure every step, entry, and answer is legible.
For the Excel part, type the clicks, titles, and your description into your answer. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Lesson 27.2
Assignment 27.2 — Fitting a Line
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Reading a line exactly, and claiming no more than it says
Practice set · graded on complete, careful work
Covers: slope and intercept in context with units; when an intercept has no sensible meaning; a line from two points; comparing lines by the sum of squared misses; an Excel trendline with its equation; association versus cause; checking an AI's interpretation.
Lesson focus: Fitting a Line: Slope and Intercept in Context
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
You will interpret constructed models, build lines from two points, compare lines using squared misses you compute yourself, use Excel to add a trendline (answered as text), rewrite overreaching sentences, and check an AI's interpretation. All data and equations are constructed. Practice set: scored on completeness and visible reasoning.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What does a fitted line say, and what does it not say?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Read the model. All three models are constructed. For each, write the slope sentence with units (use the word predicts), say whether x = 0 lies inside the data, and say whether the intercept has a sensible meaning. (a) ŷ = 50 + 6.5x, where x is hours studied (data from 0.5 to 6 hours) and ŷ is quiz score in points. (b) ŷ = 28 − 2x, where x is the age of a used car in years (data from 1 to 10 years) and ŷ is asking price in $1000s. (c) ŷ = −80 + 0.85x, where x is height in cm (data from 150 to 190 cm) and ŷ is weight in kg.
2
A line from two points. (a) A constructed line passes through (3, 40) and (7, 64). Find the slope, the intercept, and the equation, check it against the second point, and predict ŷ at x = 5. (b) A second line passes through (10, 90) and (30, 50). Find its equation and write its slope in words, using predicts. Show the rise and the run.
3
Which line is better? Five constructed points: (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 7), (5, 8). Student A draws ŷ = 1 + 1.5x. Student B draws ŷ = 2 + x. (a) For each line, make a table with columns x, y, predicted ŷ, miss (y − ŷ), and miss squared, and add up the squared misses (the SSE). (b) Which line is better by the least-squares rule, and why? (c) The least-squares line for these points is ŷ = 1.8 + 1.2x. Show that it passes through (x̄, ȳ) and compute its SSE. How does it compare with A and B?
4
Excel trendline (answered as text). A constructed table of 7 students: hours of practice per week (x) are 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and skills-test scores in points (y) are 14, 17, 15, 21, 24, 23, 28. Open a blank workbook, type the data (headings Hours and Score in A1 and B1), make a Scatter chart with axis titles that include units, add a linear trendline, and display the equation and R-squared on the chart. Report in your answer: the equation exactly as Excel shows it, the R-squared value Excel shows (you do not interpret it yet), the equation rewritten in the form ŷ = a + bx with the variable names, the slope sentence with units, and a check that the line passes through (x̄, ȳ). (You do not upload a workbook for this item; type your answers into your submission.)
5
Say it carefully. Each sentence below claims more than a fitted line can support. Rewrite each so it says only what the model says. (a) “Because the slope is 6.5, every extra hour of studying raises a student's score by 6.5 points.” (b) “The slope of −2 proves that each year of age makes a car lose $2 thousand of value.” (c) “The intercept of −80 says a person who is 0 cm tall weighs −80 kg, so the model must be broken.” (Hint for (c): where is the model meant to be used?)
6
AI check. Ask an AI tool: “A made-up household study fitted a line: predicted monthly water bill in dollars = 18 + 14 × (number of people in the household). The households in the data had 1 to 6 people. Interpret the slope and the intercept in context, with units, and predict the bill for 4 people.” Before you read its answer, write your own interpretation and prediction. Then report what the AI said and grade it: did it give the units, say predicts rather than causes, and handle the intercept honestly, or did it treat 0 people as meaningful? Recompute any number it quotes. State whether the AI was right and anything it got wrong or left vague.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All six parts are complete, with units on every slope sentence and the word predicts used instead of causal words.
☐
Slopes are found as rise over run and intercepts with a = y − bx, with the equation checked against a point.
☐
The SSE table is shown line by line, and the Excel part gives the equation, the R-squared Excel shows, and the slope sentence.
☐
The AI check records your own interpretation first, then grades the AI's units, wording, and intercept honestly.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Completeness
6 pts		 All six parts attempted in full. One part missing or clearly rushed. Two or more parts missing. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Part 1: (a) For each additional hour studied, the model predicts a quiz score about 6.5 points higher. x = 0 is just outside the data (smallest 0.5), so the intercept of 50 points is a rough anchor and should be hedged; accept meaningful with caution or not meaningful if the student notes that 0 is outside the data and justifies it. (b) For each additional year of age, the model predicts an asking price about $2 thousand ($2000) lower. x = 0 (a new car) is just outside the data (smallest 1 year); the intercept of $28 thousand is a rough anchor, same grading as (a). (c) For each additional centimeter of height, the model predicts a weight about 0.85 kg higher. x = 0 is far outside 150 to 190 cm, and −80 kg is impossible, so the intercept has no sensible meaning; it only positions the line. Part 2: (a) b = (64 − 40) ÷ (7 − 3) = 24 ÷ 4 = 6; a = 40 − 6(3) = 22; ŷ = 22 + 6x; check at x = 7: 22 + 42 = 64; at x = 5: 22 + 30 = 52. (b) rise = 50 − 90 = −40, run = 30 − 10 = 20, b = −2; a = 90 − (−2)(10) = 110; ŷ = 110 − 2x; check at x = 30: 110 − 60 = 50. Slope in words: for each additional unit of x, the model predicts y about 2 units lower. Part 3: Line A predictions 2.5, 4, 5.5, 7, 8.5; misses 0.5, 1, −1.5, 0, −0.5; squares 0.25, 1, 2.25, 0, 0.25; SSE = 3.75. Line B predictions 3, 4, 5, 6, 7; misses 0, 1, −1, 1, 1; squares 0, 1, 1, 1, 1; SSE = 4. Line A is better by the least-squares rule (3.75 is less than 4): smaller sum of squared vertical misses. (c) x̄ = 15 ÷ 5 = 3 and ȳ = 27 ÷ 5 = 5.4; 1.8 + 1.2(3) = 5.4, so it passes through (3, 5.4). Predictions 3, 4.2, 5.4, 6.6, 7.8; misses 0, 0.8, −1.4, 0.4, 0.2; squares 0, 0.64, 1.96, 0.16, 0.04; SSE = 2.8, smaller than both A and B (as the least-squares line must be). Part 4: Excel shows about y = 2.25x + 9.0357 and R² = 0.8891 (digits may be rounded differently, for example 9.0357 or 9.04, 0.8891 or 0.889). Rewritten: ŷ = 9.0357 + 2.25x (hours of practice per week to skills-test points). Slope sentence: for each additional hour of practice per week, the model predicts a skills-test score about 2.25 points higher. Check: x̄ = 35 ÷ 7 = 5 and ȳ = 142 ÷ 7 = 20.29; 9.0357 + 2.25(5) = 20.29. The chart must show axis titles with units, a trendline, the equation, and R²; the student should not interpret R². (Independent least-squares on these 7 points gives slope 2.25, intercept 9.035714, R² = 0.88911.) Part 5: (a) For each additional hour studied, the model predicts a score about 6.5 points higher (students who studied more tended to score higher in these data); raises claims a cause. (b) For each additional year of age, the model predicts an asking price about $2 thousand lower; the line describes an association and does not prove that age alone causes the drop (condition, mileage, and so on travel with age); proves and makes are too strong. (c) The model is meant for heights from 150 to 190 cm; 0 cm is far outside, so the intercept has no meaning and the model is not broken; it only positions the line. Credit any rewrite that says predicts, keeps the units, and drops the unsupported claim. Part 6: slope: for each additional person in the household, the model predicts a monthly water bill about $14 higher. Intercept: $18 when there are 0 people, but a household has at least 1 person (the data start at 1), so it has no sensible meaning. Prediction at 4 people: 18 + 14(4) = 18 + 56 = $74, inside the data (1 to 6). Credit a prediction written first, an honest report of the AI's claims, a verdict on its units, its use of predicts, and its handling of the intercept, and evidence that its numbers were recomputed; the grade rewards the checking, not the AI being right. Mostly correct but with one wrong value, a slope sentence missing units or using causal wording, a missing SSE row, a missing Excel element, or an AI check that skips the prediction or the grading of the AI's wording. Bare answers with little visible reasoning. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 27.2 — Fitting a Line
Submit a clear photo or scan of your notebook pages (JPG, PNG, or PDF), or type your work directly into the text entry box. Make sure every step, entry, and answer is legible.
For the Excel part, type the trendline equation, the R-squared value Excel showed, and your answers into your submission. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Lesson 27.3
Assignment 27.3 — Prediction Workbook
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Predict it, flag it, and say how far you trust it
Spreadsheet lab · graded on a correct, complete workbook and clear reasoning
Covers: a scatter chart with a trendline equation; a prediction table built with typed formulas; an automatic inside-the-range or beyond-the-data flag with MIN and MAX; spotting impossible predictions; reporting a prediction as an estimate with its limits and no cause claim; checking an AI answer that extrapolates.
Lesson focus: Prediction: Interpolation vs. Extrapolation
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
This is the week's Excel lab. You will upload one workbook with three sheets (Data, Predictions, Notes) using the layout you built in Lesson 27.3 with the new data below. The formulas must be typed. You will also type your Part B numeric answers, one applied item, and one AI check into the Canvas text box. All data and scenarios are constructed; none is real.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
When a line gives you a prediction, how do you decide how far to trust it, and what do you say about it?
📁 M365 REMINDER
Name your Excel file Wk27_Prediction_YourName.xlsx, save it to your OneDrive Optima → Math folder, and upload the .xlsx file to Canvas. Excel work happens outside Canvas; you will submit the finished workbook. Do not submit screenshots in place of the workbook.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Build the Data sheet. Name the first sheet Data. Constructed data: a made-up phone is charged fully and the battery percent is read each hour. Type headings in A1 and B1 (Hours and Battery %) and these values in A2:B9: hours 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 and battery 91, 83, 78, 66, 60, 51, 44, 35. Make a Scatter chart (markers only) of the data, add a Linear trendline with Display Equation on chart ticked, and give the chart a title and both axis titles (with units).
2
Build the Predictions sheet. Use the Predictions layout from Lesson 27.3. In B1 type a and in B2 type b by hand from your chart's trendline equation. B3 is =MIN(Data!A2:A9) and B4 is =MAX(Data!A2:A9). Headings in row 6 (x, Predicted y, Range check, Sense check). Put the x values 0.5, 4.5, 9, 15 in A7:A10. Type a prediction formula in B7 with absolute references (=$B$1+$B$2*A7), a range-check formula in C7 using IF, AND, and the cells B3 and B4 (it must print “inside the data range” or “beyond the data”), and a sense-check formula in D7 that prints “possible” when the predicted battery percent is between 0 and 100 and “impossible” otherwise. Fill B7:D7 down to row 10. In A12 type x where prediction reaches 0 and in B12 a formula that finds it from a and b. In E6 add Report (whole number) with a ROUND formula in E7:E10. Format the predictions to two decimals.
3
Write the Notes sheet. Name the third sheet Notes. In A3, write one sentence stating the range of hours your line can reasonably be used for and why. In A4, write one sentence about the prediction at 15 hours: what is wrong with it and what you would do instead. In A5, write one sentence that explains in your own words why this line does not show that time causes the battery to drain, or what else could be going on. Use your own words; do not copy sentences from the lesson.
4
Part B — numeric answers (type into the Canvas text box). Use your workbook. Give a and b to 3 decimals and predictions to 2 decimals. B1: the trendline a and b, and the equation written as ŷ = a + bx. B2: the smallest and largest hours in the data. B3: for each of x = 0.5, 4.5, 9, 15, the predicted battery percent, whether it is an interpolation or an extrapolation, and whether it makes sense. B4: the number of hours at which the line reaches 0%, and whether that value is inside the data range. B5: which of the four predictions you would report, how you would word each (use “about”), and which you would refuse to report.
5
Part C — applied item. A made-up coach fits a line to data from players who trained 2 to 6 sessions per week: fitness score (out of 100) = ŷ = 30 + 5x. (i) Predict the score for a player who trains 4.5 sessions and for one who trains 20 sessions, and tag each as interpolation or extrapolation. (ii) For the 20-session prediction, say whether the value makes sense and why. (iii) Find the number of sessions at which the line reaches 100, and say whether it is inside the data range. (iv) The coach says, “This line proves training more makes players fitter, so train 20 sessions.” In two or three sentences, rewrite the coach's claim honestly, using a range, the word “about,” and no cause claim.
6
Part D — AI check. Ask an AI tool: “A made-up line for used guitars says price in dollars = 600 − 45 × age in years, fitted to guitars aged 1 to 9 years. What price does it predict for a guitar that is 20 years old?” Before you read its answer, write your own prediction. Then report: the AI's final number, your verified value, whether the AI warned that 20 is outside the data, whether it noticed (or gave without comment) an impossible value, whether it used causal words, and one specific thing to flag. If the AI got everything right, say what you checked to be sure. Save the workbook as Wk27_Prediction_YourName.xlsx and upload it.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The workbook has Data, Predictions, and Notes sheets, with a scatter chart, a linear trendline, and its equation on the Data sheet, and the Predictions values come from typed formulas that use cell references (absolute references for a and b).
☐
Every value matches the expected numbers (to rounding), and the range check and the sense check are formulas that read the right label for each x.
☐
The numeric answers, the applied item, and the AI check are in the Canvas text box, use the word “estimate” or “about,” and name the range the data support.
☐
Nothing claims cause from a fitted line, and no impossible prediction is reported as fact.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Workbook & numeric answers
6 pts		 Data sheet (hours 1 to 8; battery 91, 83, 78, 66, 60, 51, 44, 35): scatter chart with titles and axis labels, linear trendline, displayed equation y = −8.0238x + 99.607 (accept a = 99.607 to 99.61 and b = −8.024 to −8.023). Predictions sheet: B3 = 1, B4 = 8; x = 0.5: 95.60, beyond the data, possible; x = 4.5: 63.50, inside the data range, possible; x = 9: 27.39, beyond the data, possible; x = 15: −20.75, beyond the data, impossible. B12 = 12.41 (formula =-B1/B2). Rounded column E agrees with the predictions (about 96, 63, 27, −21; the value 63.4999 shows as 63.50 but rounds to 63, so accept 63 or 64). Formulas typed with $B$1 and $B$2 locked, range-check IF(AND(...)) using B3 and B4, sense check testing 0 to 100. Part B: B1 a = 99.607, b = −8.024; B2 1 and 8; B3 as above; B4 12.41 hours, beyond the data range; B5 report 4.5 as “about 63.5%” (or “about 63% or 64%”), report 0.5 and 9 only with a beyond-the-data caution (“about 96%” and “about 27%”), refuse 15. This row is worth 6 pts: Data sheet and chart 1, Predictions formulas and flags 3, Part B numbers 2. One sheet or block missing, a few values wrong because of a slip (a and b swapped, a sign error, an absolute reference missing so the fill-down breaks, MIN or MAX range wrong, 0.5 labeled inside the data range), or one or two numeric answers wrong. Two or more parts missing, no chart or no trendline equation, or values typed in instead of formulas. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Part C: (i) 30 + 5(4.5) = 52.5, interpolation (4.5 is between 2 and 6); 30 + 5(20) = 130, extrapolation; (ii) 130 is not possible for a score out of 100, and 20 sessions is far beyond the observed 2 to 6; (iii) 30 + 5x = 100 at x = 14, beyond the data range; (iv) an honest rewrite such as “In players who trained 2 to 6 sessions, more sessions went with higher scores, about 5 points per session; the line should not be used for 20 sessions, and it does not show that training is the only reason scores differ,” with a range, “about,” and no cause claim. Part D: verified value 600 − 45(20) = −300 dollars, an extrapolation (20 is far beyond 1 to 9) and an impossible negative price; the line reaches 0 at 600 ÷ 45 = 13.33 years, still beyond the data; a prediction was written before reading the AI; the report says whether the AI warned about extrapolation, whether it gave −300 as a price without comment or declined to trust it, and whether it used causal words (such as “age makes the price drop”) or gave an unqualified single number, and names one specific flag. Notes: A3 names 1 to 8 hours as the supported range; A4 says 15 hours is far beyond the data and gives −20.75%, an impossible battery level, so the line should not be used there; A5 gives a reason the line does not show cause (a pattern in data, other things such as phone use or temperature, a made-up data set). This row is worth 4 pts: Part C 2, Part D 1, Notes 1. Correct numbers but the interpolation/extrapolation labels, the impossible-value reasoning, or the hedged wording are missing; or the AI check reports only the AI's answer without a verified value or a specific flag. Bare numbers with no reasoning, a cause claim left standing, or no AI check. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 27.3 — Prediction Workbook
Upload your Excel workbook (.xlsx) as a file, and type your Part B, Part C and Part D answers in the text box. Label each answer (B1, B2, and so on).

Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 28.1
Assignment 28.1 — Residuals
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
What did the line miss, and where?
Mostly auto-scored items · one Excel item and one short written item
Covers: computing a residual and reading its sign; the residual sum and the sum of squared residuals; reading residual plots; outliers versus points that pull the line; a residual column in Excel; an applied residual; checking an AI's residuals.
Lesson focus: Residuals: Assessing a Linear Fit
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
There are 10 items worth 1 point each. Items 1 to 8 have one correct answer (a number or a choice) and are scored automatically. Item 9 is an Excel task answered as text; Item 10 is a short written AI check. All data are constructed. Show a line of work in your notebook for the numeric items in case a teacher needs to review them.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
How do we know a straight line is a fair description of the data?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Compute a residual. (1 pt) A constructed model is ŷ = 18 + 2.5x. An observation has x = 6 and y = 29. What is the residual, y − ŷ? Enter a number (include the sign).
2
Read the sign. (1 pt) In Item 1, what does the sign of the residual mean? Choose one. (a) The observed value is above the line; the model underpredicted. (b) The observed value is below the line; the model overpredicted. (c) The observed value is exactly on the line. (d) The model is wrong, so the point should be removed.
3
A missing residual. (1 pt) A least-squares line is fitted to five constructed points. Four of the residuals are +1.2, −0.7, +0.4, −1.5. What is the fifth residual? Enter a number (include the sign).
4
Sum of squared residuals. (1 pt) Another fit leaves residuals +2, −1, 0, −3, +1. What is the sum of the squared residuals (the SSE)? Enter a number.
5
Read the plot. (1 pt) A constructed least-squares fit to 8 points (x = 1 to 8) leaves residuals −3, −1, +1, +3, +3, +1, −1, −3, in order of x. The residuals add to 0. What should you conclude? Choose one. (a) Random scatter, so a straight line is adequate. (b) The residuals form a curved pattern (an arch), so a straight line is not adequate. (c) A fan shape, so the line is only reliable at large x. (d) The sum is 0, so the line is a perfect fit.
6
Outlier or influential? (1 pt) Eight constructed points have x values from 2 to 12 and follow a clear upward trend. A ninth point is at x = 30, far to the right of the others and well below the trend. Adding it changes the slope from positive to nearly flat. Which description is best? Choose one. (a) An influential point: it is far from the others in the x direction and pulls the line toward itself. (b) Not a problem, because the slope of a line never depends on a single point. (c) An outlier only because it has a large y. (d) A point that makes the residuals stop adding to 0.
7
Applied: a delivery. (1 pt) A made-up delivery service fits the line predicted trip time (minutes) = 8 + 3.2 × (miles). A trip of 5 miles took 27 minutes. What is the residual, in minutes? Enter a number (include the sign).
8
Applied: say what it means. (1 pt) In Item 7, what does the residual mean in context? Choose one. (a) The trip took about 3 minutes longer than the model predicted for 5 miles. (b) The trip took about 3 minutes less than the model predicted. (c) The driver was 3 miles off the route. (d) The model predicts every 5-mile trip will take 27 minutes.
9
Excel: a residual column. (1 pt, text) Make a blank workbook. In A1:B6 enter the headings x and y and the constructed data x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 5, 9, 8, 13, 15. The least-squares line is ŷ = 2.8 + 2.4x. In C2 type a predicted-value formula and in D2 a residual formula, then fill both down to row 6. Add a sum cell, and make a scatter chart of the residuals against x with axis titles. Answer as text, in this order: (i) the formula you typed in D2, (ii) the residual at x = 3, (iii) what the sum of the residuals showed in Excel (give the value you saw), (iv) whether the residual plot looks random or patterned, in a few words. (You do not upload the workbook.)
10
AI check (short written). (1 pt, text) Ask an AI tool: “A made-up study fitted predicted y = 2.3 + 1.9x to the points (1, 4), (2, 6), (3, 9), (4, 9), (5, 12). List each residual (observed minus predicted) and say whether each point is above or below the line.” Before you read its answer, work out the five residuals yourself. Then, in 2 to 4 sentences, report whether the AI's residuals and above/below statements match yours, and name any error (an order-of-subtraction slip, a wrong sign, or an arithmetic mistake). Recompute any number it gives.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Every residual is computed as observed minus predicted, with its sign, and the sign is read correctly in context.
☐
Residual plots are read for a pattern (curve or fan) and not only for the sum.
☐
The Excel answer gives the residual formula, a correct residual, the sum Excel showed, and a reading of the plot.
☐
The AI check records your own residuals first, then grades the AI's signs and arithmetic honestly.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC AND ANSWER KEY
Item Type Correct answer / full credit Pts
Item 1 Numeric −4 (predicted 18 + 2.5(6) = 33; 29 − 33 = −4). Accept −4 or −4.0. 1
Item 2 Multiple choice (b): observed below the line; the model overpredicted. 1
Item 3 Numeric +0.6 (the five residuals must add to 0: 1.2 − 0.7 + 0.4 − 1.5 = −0.6, so the fifth is +0.6). Accept 0.6 or +0.6. 1
Item 4 Numeric 15 (4 + 1 + 0 + 9 + 1). 1
Item 5 Multiple choice (b): signs − − + + + + − − form an arch (a streak pattern), so a straight line is not adequate; the zero sum says nothing about shape. 1
Item 6 Multiple choice (a): far out in x means high leverage, and here it changes the slope a lot (influential). 1
Item 7 Numeric +3 (predicted 8 + 3.2(5) = 24; 27 − 24 = +3). Accept 3 or +3. 1
Item 8 Multiple choice (a): the trip took about 3 minutes longer than predicted. 1
Item 9 Text (Excel) (i) =B2-C2 (with C2 holding =2.8+2.4*A2); (ii) −2 (observed 8, predicted 10); (iii) 0 or a tiny number such as 1E-15 or −1.8E-15, i.e. essentially 0; (iv) the residuals are −0.2, 1.4, −2, 0.6, 0.2, so the plot looks random with no clear curve or fan (only five points, so a pattern is hard to judge). Full credit for a correct formula, the residual −2 and a sum of about 0; the plot comment is not required to be exact. 1
Item 10 Text (written) Correct residuals: −0.2, −0.1, +1.0, −0.9, +0.2 (predictions 4.2, 6.1, 8.0, 9.9, 11.8). Below the line: points 1, 2 and 4; above: points 3 and 5. They add to 0. Credit a prediction written first, an honest report of where the AI matched or differed, a named error type if any, and evidence that numbers were recomputed; the grade rewards the checking, not the AI being right. 1
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 28.1 — Residuals
Enter your answers to Items 1 to 8 in the matching Canvas questions (they are scored automatically). For Items 9 and 10, type your answers into the text boxes. You do not upload a workbook for Item 9. Keep your notebook work in case a teacher asks to see it.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Lesson 28.2
Assignment 28.2 — Correlation Workbook
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Compute it, check it, and say only what it shows
Spreadsheet lab · graded on a correct, complete workbook and clear reasoning
Covers: CORREL, SLOPE, INTERCEPT, and RSQ on a made-up dataset; checking that the formulas agree with a chart trendline and with the rule b = r · (sy / sx); what happens to r and the slope when the roles of x and y are swapped; the effect of one extra point; interpreting r and r-squared in context without a cause claim; checking an AI answer.
Lesson focus: Correlation: Strength, Direction, and r
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
This is the week’s Excel lab. You will upload one workbook with three sheets (Data, Analysis, Notes) built from the data below. The formulas must be typed, not pasted as values. You will also type your Part B numeric answers, one applied item, and one AI check into the Canvas text box. All data and scenarios are constructed (made up); none is real.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
When a computer hands you an r, how do you read it, check it, and report it so that you claim no more than the data show?
📁 M365 REMINDER
Name your Excel file Wk28_Correlation_YourName.xlsx, save it to your OneDrive Optima → Math folder, and upload the .xlsx file to Canvas. Excel work happens outside Canvas; you will submit the finished workbook. Do not submit screenshots in place of the workbook.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Build the Data sheet. Open Excel, start a Blank workbook, and rename the first sheet Data (right-click the sheet tab at the bottom, choose Rename, type the name, press Enter). Constructed data: twelve made-up students recorded their weekly typing practice and the typing errors per page on a test. Type headings in A1 and B1 (Practice (hours per week) and Typing errors per page), then type these values in A2:B13, x in column A and y in column B. Hours: 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9. Errors: 14, 10, 13, 11, 12, 9, 10, 8, 9, 5, 7, 6. Then, in row 14, type one extra made-up student: 10 in A14 and 14 in B14, and type extra point in C14. Select A1:B13 only (not row 14), click Insert > Scatter (X, Y) (dots only), and add a chart title and both axis titles with units. Click the + (Chart Elements) button, tick Trendline, then right-click the trendline, choose Format Trendline, and tick Display Equation on chart and Display R-squared value on chart.
2
Build the Analysis sheet. Click the + beside the sheet tabs to add a sheet and rename it Analysis. In A1 type Measure and in B1 type Value. Type these labels in A2:A16, one per row, and type the formula beside each in column B (the formulas refer to the Data sheet, so click the cells or type Data! before each range): A2 n with =COUNT(Data!A2:A13); A3 r (CORREL) with =CORREL(Data!A2:A13,Data!B2:B13); A4 Slope b (SLOPE) with =SLOPE(Data!B2:B13,Data!A2:A13); A5 Intercept a (INTERCEPT) with =INTERCEPT(Data!B2:B13,Data!A2:A13); A6 r-squared (RSQ) with =RSQ(Data!B2:B13,Data!A2:A13); A7 sx with =STDEV.S(Data!A2:A13); A8 sy with =STDEV.S(Data!B2:B13); A9 r * sy / sx with =B3*B8/B7; A10 r squared by hand with =B3^2; A11 CORREL, roles swapped with =CORREL(Data!B2:B13,Data!A2:A13); A12 SLOPE, roles swapped with =SLOPE(Data!A2:A13,Data!B2:B13); A13 Share not accounted for with =1-B6; A14 r with the extra point with =CORREL(Data!A2:A14,Data!B2:B14); A15 Slope with the extra point with =SLOPE(Data!B2:B14,Data!A2:A14); A16 Change in r with =B14-B3. Widen column A (double-click the line between the A and B column headers) so the labels show. Remember: in SLOPE and INTERCEPT the y range comes first.
3
Write the Notes sheet. Add a third sheet and rename it Notes. In A3, write a 2 to 3 sentence interpretation, in the context of practice hours and typing errors, of the direction and strength of the relationship and of what r-squared means (about what share of what, accounted for by what). In A4, write one sentence about what the extra point did to r and why. In A5, write one sentence saying what r cannot show here (for example, whether practice causes fewer errors). Use your own words; do not copy sentences from the lesson. To keep a long sentence readable, click the cell and choose Home > Wrap Text.
4
Part B — numeric answers (type into the Canvas text box). Use your workbook. Give r, a, b, sx, and sy to 4 decimal places (or as Excel shows them). Label each answer. B1: r and a one-line description of the direction and strength. B2: the slope b and intercept a, and the fitted equation written as ŷ = a + bx; confirm in one sentence that they match your chart’s trendline equation. B3: r-squared, written as a percent, and what it means in a careful sentence. B4: sx, sy, and the value of r · sy / sx; say what it equals. B5: with the roles swapped, the new r and the new slope, and one sentence on what stayed the same and what changed. B6: r and the slope with the extra point, and the change in r.
5
In a made-up study of 40 adults, the correlation between steps walked per day and a mood rating is r = +0.35. Part C — applied item. (i) Describe the direction and strength, and compute r-squared and say what it means. (ii) A headline says: “35% of people who walk more are happier, so walking makes you happier.” Name the two mistakes in it and rewrite the sentence honestly in one or two sentences. (iii) Back to the typing data: if the practice time had been recorded in minutes per week instead of hours (every x multiplied by 60), what would happen to r and what would the slope be? Give the number for the slope and explain in one sentence.
6
Part D — AI check. Ask an AI tool: “Here are twelve made-up pairs (hours, errors): (1, 14), (2, 10), (2, 13), (3, 11), (4, 12), (4, 9), (5, 10), (6, 8), (6, 9), (7, 5), (8, 7), (9, 6). Compute the correlation coefficient r and the least-squares slope of errors on hours, and interpret them.” Before you read its answer, use your Analysis sheet as the check. Then report: the AI’s r and slope, your verified values, whether the AI’s numbers match, whether it described direction and strength correctly, whether it used causal words, and one specific thing to flag. If the AI got everything right, say what you checked to be sure. Save the workbook as Wk28_Correlation_YourName.xlsx and upload it.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The workbook has Data, Analysis, and Notes sheets, a scatter chart with titles and a trendline equation and R² on the Data sheet, and every Analysis value comes from a typed formula that refers to the Data sheet.
☐
The values match the expected numbers (to rounding), the check cells agree (r · sy / sx equals the slope; r squared by hand equals RSQ), and SLOPE and INTERCEPT have the y range first.
☐
The numeric answers, the applied item, and the AI check are in the Canvas text box, labeled, and the interpretations use direction, strength, context, and careful wording such as “tends to,” “accounted for by,” and “about.”
☐
Nothing claims that practice (or walking) causes the result, and r is never reported as a percent.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Workbook & numeric answers
6 pts		 Data sheet: x = 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9; y = 14, 10, 13, 11, 12, 9, 10, 8, 9, 5, 7, 6; extra point (10, 14) in row 14; scatter chart of A1:B13 with title, both axis titles, linear trendline, equation y = −0.9609x + 14.064 and R² = 0.7814 displayed (accept small rounding differences in the digits). Analysis sheet (typed formulas referring to Data): B2 n = 12; B3 r = −0.8840; B4 slope = −0.9609; B5 intercept = 14.0641; B6 R² = 0.7814; B7 sx = 2.5271; B8 sy = 2.7469; B9 = −0.9609 (equals B4); B10 = 0.7814 (equals B6); B11 = −0.8840 (same as B3); B12 = −0.8133 (not the same as B4); B13 = 0.2186; B14 = −0.4632; B15 = −0.4775; B16 = +0.4208. SLOPE and INTERCEPT with the y range first. Part B: B1 r = −0.8840, negative, strong; B2 ŷ = 14.064 − 0.961x, matching the trendline; B3 78.14% (about 78%) of the variation in errors per page is accounted for by the straight-line relationship with practice hours; B4 2.5271, 2.7469, −0.9609 (equals the slope); B5 r = −0.8840 (same), slope −0.8133 (different); B6 r = −0.4632, slope −0.4775, change +0.4208 (r moves toward 0). Worth 6 pts: Data sheet and chart 1, Analysis formulas and values 3, Part B numbers 2. One sheet or block missing, a few values wrong because of a slip (SLOPE or INTERCEPT with the ranges in the wrong order, a range that stops at row 12 or runs to row 14 by mistake, the extra point left out or put into the chart), or one or two numeric answers wrong. Two or more parts missing, no chart or trendline, or values typed in instead of formulas. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Notes: A3 states in context that more weekly practice hours tend to go with fewer typing errors (negative, strong, roughly linear) and that about 78% of the variation in errors is accounted for by the line using hours (not “caused by”); A4 says the extra point (10 hours, 14 errors) sits far from the pattern and pulled r from about −0.88 to about −0.46 (one point can change r a lot); A5 says r cannot show cause (other factors, such as typing skill or motivation, or a made-up dataset). Part C: (i) positive, weak (0.35 is in the 0.2 to 0.5 weak range of the rough guide), more steps tend to go with higher mood; r² = 0.35² = 0.1225, so about 12% of the variation in mood ratings is accounted for by the line using steps; (ii) the two mistakes are reading r as a percentage of people (35%) and claiming cause from a correlation; an honest rewrite such as “In this study, people who walked more steps tended to report somewhat higher mood, a weak positive straight-line association; this does not show that walking is the reason”; (iii) r does not change (still −0.8840) because it has no units; the slope becomes −0.9609 ÷ 60 = −0.0160 errors per page per minute of weekly practice (the same relationship in new units). Part D: verified r = −0.8840 and slope = −0.9609 from the workbook; the report compares the AI’s numbers with them, says whether direction (negative) and strength (strong) were right, whether any causal words appeared, and names one specific flag (for example, an arithmetic slip, a percent misreading of r, or “practice causes fewer errors”). If the AI was fully right, the report names what was checked. Worth 4 pts: Notes 1, Part C 2, Part D 1. Correct numbers but the interpretation lacks context, treats r or r-squared loosely (for example “78% correlated”), or misses one of the two mistakes in Part C; or the AI check reports only the AI’s answer without a verified value or a specific flag. Bare numbers with no reasoning, a cause claim left standing, or no AI check. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 28.2 — Correlation Workbook
Upload your Excel workbook (.xlsx) as a file, and type your Part B, Part C and Part D answers in the text box. Label each answer (B1, B2, and so on).
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Lesson 28.3
Assignment 28.3 — Careful Claims
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Association, confounders, and what a study can support
Seven auto-graded items · one short written item
Covers: careful reading of a correlation; reverse direction; testing a confounder by recomputing r within groups; random assignment versus observation; rewriting an overclaiming headline.
Lesson focus: Correlation Is Not Causation
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (7 pts, auto-graded): four multiple-choice questions and three numeric answers. Part B (3 pts, teacher-scored): one short written response. All data and scenarios are constructed (made up). Use Excel for the numeric answers in Part A.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
When two things go together, what may I honestly say, and what must I leave unsaid?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
Careful reading. In a made-up comparison of 25 cities, the number of public libraries and the number of coffee shops have a correlation of r = +0.91. Which statement is the most careful?
(a) Libraries cause people to open coffee shops.
(b) Coffee shops cause cities to build libraries.
(c) Cities with more libraries tended to have more coffee shops; the data alone cannot say why, and city population is a plausible third variable.
(d) Because r is high, population must be the only reason, and neither one has any effect on the other.
2
Reverse direction. In made-up records, people who take more pain medicine report more pain. Which explanation does the idea of reverse direction most directly suggest?
(a) More pain leads people to take more medicine.
(b) Hot weather drives both pain and medicine use.
(c) The result is entirely due to chance.
(d) Pain medicine is the only possible cause of pain.
3
Study design. A researcher wants to know whether a new study guide raises quiz scores for 100 student volunteers. Which plan can best support a cause-and-effect claim?
(a) Let each student choose whether to use the guide, then compare quiz scores.
(b) Survey students about whether they used the guide and how they did, then compute r.
(c) Randomly assign 50 students to receive the guide and 50 not to, then compare quiz scores.
(d) Compare this year’s volunteers with last year’s class.
4
Testing a confounder. You suspect temperature drives both sunscreen sales and sunburn cases. Which check is most useful?
(a) Recompute the correlation after rounding the data to whole numbers.
(b) Compute r separately within groups of days that have about the same temperature, and see whether the association shrinks.
(c) Add more days to the data and see whether r gets bigger.
(d) Delete the days with the most sunscreen sales.
5
Numeric: use Excel. Eight made-up weeks, grouped by weather. x is dozens of cups of hot cocoa sold and y is pairs of gloves sold at a market stall.
WeekWeatherCocoa sold x (dozens)Gloves sold y (pairs)
1Mild28
2Mild310
3Mild412
4Mild56
5Cold1430
6Cold1638
7Cold1942
8Cold2234
Use =CORREL on all eight weeks. Enter r for all eight weeks, rounded to two decimals.
6
Numeric. Using the same table, enter r for the four Cold weeks only (weeks 5 to 8), rounded to two decimals.
7
Numeric. Using the same table, enter r for the four Mild weeks only (weeks 1 to 4), rounded to two decimals.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (3 PTS)
8
Application: the careless headline. A constructed news line: “Video Games Are Ruining Teens’ Grades. A made-up study of 60 teens found that those who play more video games have lower grades (r = −0.45).” In three to five sentences, write: (a) the claim the data actually support, using “is associated with” or similar words; (b) one plausible confounder (or a reverse-direction story) and how you would check it; (c) a careful rewrite of the headline.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I computed each correlation in Excel from the table and rounded to two decimals.
☐
My written answer states what the data support without a cause verb.
☐
My confounder could plausibly affect both variables, and my check holds it about the same.
☐
My rewritten headline names the sample and says what the data cannot show.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Part A: auto-graded
7 pts		 1 pt per item. Answer key: (1) c; (2) a; (3) c; (4) b; (5) 0.94; (6) 0.33; (7) -0.20 (accept ±0.01 on the numeric items). Not applicable: each item is right or wrong. Not applicable. 7 pts
Part B: the claim
1 pt		 States that, in this sample, more video game play is associated with lower grades (a moderate negative association) using “is associated with,” “tends to,” or similar, with no cause verb. Describes the pattern but with one causal verb (“leads to,” “hurts”) or omits the sample (60 teens). Only repeats the headline, or says “video games cause lower grades.” 1 pt
Part B: confounder and check
1 pt		 Names a plausible third variable that could affect both (for example, free time, sleep, home situation, or stress) or a reverse-direction story (teens who are struggling may play more to escape), and gives a check: compare grades and play within groups alike on that variable, or note that random assignment would be needed. Names a plausible confounder or reverse story but gives no check, or the check is vague. Names something that could not affect both variables, or only says “other factors.” 1 pt
Part B: careful rewrite
1 pt		 A rewritten headline that names the sample, uses associated or tends-to language, and says the study cannot show why or does not show cause. Example: “In a made-up study of 60 teens, those who played more video games tended to have lower grades; the study cannot say why.” Softer wording, but still implies cause or leaves out the sample or the limit. Unchanged, or still uses a cause verb. 1 pt
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 28.3 — Careful Claims
Enter the four multiple-choice letters and the three numeric answers for Part A, and type your Part B response in the text box. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

25–30 minutes
One session, one submission
Points
Completion-scored
5 pts
Module 10 · VR Solo Activity
Guess the Correlation Gallery
VR Activity · 5 pts · completion
🥼 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
The correlation coefficient \(r\) is one number that tries to say how closely a cloud of points hugs a straight line, and in which direction. Lessons 28.2 and 28.3 showed you how to compute it and what it cannot tell you. Today you test your eye. Six scatter plots hang on the walls of a gallery, each built from ten small dots. At each wall you will write your guess for \(r\) first, and only then lift the covered panel that shows the true value. Honesty here is simple and a little humbling: the guess you post is the guess you actually made, written down before you look. After six walls you will know something about yourself that no one else can tell you: whether your eye runs high or low, and which kinds of picture fool it. All of the data in this activity are constructed (made up).
📋 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset with Optima installed (desktop Optima works if a headset is unavailable, but walking from wall to wall and standing in front of each picture is part of the activity).
▶
Your Lesson 28.2 and 28.3 notes (notebook page): what the sign of \(r\) means, what values near 0 and near ±1 mean, and the warning that \(r\) measures straight-line association only. Review them before you put the headset on; re-reading inside a headset is hard.
▶
A pencil and notebook beside you for after the session. You will not need a calculator inside the headset: the only arithmetic is one subtraction per wall and one average at the end.
▶
About 30 uninterrupted minutes.
🚀 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (preferred) or desktop Optima
Session type: Persistent Session (your work saves between visits)
Session ID: [SESSION ID — teacher enters before publishing]
Location: [LOCATION NAME — an open, flat-floored Location with room for six wall-mounted displays; teacher enters before publishing]
On arrival: Find the Whiteboard IFX near the spawn point labeled “Guess the Correlation Gallery — start here.” Ahead of you, six walls stand in a row, numbered 1 to 6. Each wall carries a scatter plot made of ten identical small dots on a grid from 0 to 10 across and 0 to 10 up. Beside each plot a cover panel hides a sticky note. At the far end waits a second whiteboard, the Calibration Board, with six empty rows and a blank pad of sticky notes.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Read the legend. At the starting whiteboard, read the rules: \(r\) runs from −1 to +1; a value near +1 means the points rise along a tight straight line; near −1, they fall along one; near 0, no straight-line pattern. Every plot is made-up data.
2
Look, then guess. Stand in front of Wall 1 and look for at least ten seconds. Ask: Do the points rise, fall, or neither? How tightly do they hug a line? Does any point sit far from the rest? Then create a sticky note, write your guess for \(r\) to two decimal places (for example −0.60), and attach it to the wall before you touch the cover panel.
3
Lift the reveal. Pick up the cover panel and read the true \(r\) on the sticky note beneath it. On a second sticky note, write your signed error: your guess minus the true value, keeping the sign. A guess of 0.60 against a true 0.80 is −0.20. Set the panel back in place when you have copied the numbers.
4
Repeat for Walls 2 to 6. Same order every time: look, guess, attach the guess, lift, compare, write the error. Do not go back and change a guess after you have seen the reveal.
5
Fill the Calibration Board. At the Calibration Board, write one row per wall: wall number, your guess, the true \(r\), and your signed error. Under the table, find the average of your six signed errors. A positive average means you tend to guess high; a negative average means you tend to guess low.
6
Write the reflection. On the board, write one line answering: do I run high or low, did the curve wall or the far-off-point wall fool me, and what clue did I use (direction, tightness, outliers)? Then write one sentence of your own: a high \(r\) shows association, not that x causes y, in your own words.
7
Capture the board. Stand where one snapshot catches the whole Calibration Board: all six rows, the average, and your reflection. Take the snapshot and check it before you go on: every number must be readable. If not, retake it from closer. If you like, also take a snapshot of one wall with your guess and the reveal beside it.
8
Put it back. Make sure every cover panel is back over its reveal, so the next student can make an honest guess. Leaving a place as you found it is the plainest courtesy there is.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Canvas Assignment Name: VR Activity — Guess the Correlation Gallery
Upload your snapshot (image file) from step 7, showing the Calibration Board with your six guesses, the six true values, the six signed errors, and your average error readable in frame.
Below it, in the text entry box, write 2–3 sentences: (1) whether you ran high or low overall, and which wall fooled you most and why; and (2) one sentence in your own words saying that a high \(r\) shows association, not that x causes y.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment. · Estimated time: 25–30 minutes in headset.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA (COMPLETION)
☐
The snapshot shows the Calibration Board with six rows: guess, true \(r\), and signed error for each wall, all readable.
☐
Each signed error equals your guess minus the true \(r\), with the sign kept, and the average of the six errors is shown.
☐
The board shows your one-line pattern reflection (high or low, which wall fooled you, what clue you used).
☐
The text entry contains the 2–3 sentences, including the sentence that a high \(r\) shows association, not that x causes y.
👋 FACILITATOR NOTE
Stage the Location before publishing. Walls: six wall-mounted displays in a row, numbered 1 to 6, each with a plot area of about 1.5 m by 1.5 m whose bottom edge is about 0.6 m above the floor. Draw a grid from 0 to 10 on each axis (0.15 m per unit) with large axis digits, labeled only “x” and “y” and a small sign “Made-up data, 10 points.” Dots: ten copies of one small identical simple shape per wall (a sphere or disc about 0.12 m across, one color), locked in place so students cannot knock a point off its coordinate. Place each dot at (0.15 m × x) from the left edge and (0.15 m × y) above the bottom edge of the plot area. Dots on the same wall must not overlap; all coordinates below are distinct. Coordinates (x, y), made up:
