Lesson 31.1
Assignment 31.1 — Sampling Variation Workbook
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Run the experiment yourself: twenty samples, then twenty bigger ones, and see the spread shrink
Spreadsheet simulation lab · graded on a correct, consistent workbook and honest reasoning
Covers: simulating a 40% population with IF and RANDBETWEEN; the sample proportion with AVERAGE; freezing with Paste Special > Values; the mean and typical swing of 20 estimates with AVERAGE and STDEV.S; COUNTIFS tallies and column charts; comparing n = 25 with n = 100; sampling variation versus bias; a check against the theory in Desmos; checking an AI answer.
Lesson focus: Sampling Variation: Many Samples, Many Estimates
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
This is the week’s Excel lab. You will upload one workbook with five sheets (Draws25, Draws100, Results, Tallies, Notes). Because every draw is random, your numbers will not match your classmates’ numbers, and that is expected: it is the lesson itself. You are graded on building the simulation correctly, on freezing and summarizing your estimates consistently, and on what you can honestly say about the pattern (the center near 0.40, and the n = 100 pile about half as spread out as the n = 25 pile). You will also type your Part B numbers, the Part C reasoning, and one AI check into the Canvas text box. All data and scenarios are simulated or constructed (made up); none is real.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
When every sample is drawn fairly, why do the estimates still scatter, and what happens to the scatter when the sample size is four times as big?
📁 M365 REMINDER
Name your Excel file Wk31_SamplingVariation_YourName.xlsx, save it to your OneDrive Optima → Math folder, and upload the .xlsx file to Canvas. Excel work happens outside Canvas; you will submit the finished workbook. Do not submit screenshots in place of the workbook. Freeze your estimates as values before you compute anything from them, or your numbers will change every time you edit.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Draws25: simulate 20 samples of 25. Open Excel, start a Blank workbook, and rename the first sheet Draws25 (right-click the sheet tab at the bottom, choose Rename, type the name, press Enter). In A1 type Sample, in B1 type 25 answers (1 = yes, 0 = no), and in AA1 type Proportion. In A2 type 1 and in A3 type 2, select A2:A3, and drag the small square at the bottom right corner of the selection down to A21 (sample numbers 1 to 20). Click B2, type =IF(RANDBETWEEN(1,100)<=40,1,0), and press Enter. (This simulates one person from a population where 40% say “yes”: a random whole number from 1 to 100 that is 40 or less gives a 1.) With B2 selected press Ctrl + C, click the Name Box (left of the formula bar), type B2:Z21, press Enter, and press Ctrl + V. That fills 20 rows of 25 answers. Click AA2, type =AVERAGE(B2:Z2), and press Enter; click AA2, press Ctrl + C, select AA3:AA21 in the Name Box, and press Ctrl + V. Check: every number in column AA should be a multiple of 0.04 (such as 0.36, 0.40, 0.44); press F9 (on some laptops Fn + F9) and watch them all change.
2
Draws100: simulate 20 samples of 100. Click the + beside the sheet tabs to add a sheet and rename it Draws100. In A1 type Sample, in B1 type 100 answers (1 = yes, 0 = no), and in CX1 type Proportion. Number the samples 1 to 20 in A2:A21 as before. In B2 type the same formula =IF(RANDBETWEEN(1,100)<=40,1,0), press Enter, copy it, then select B2:CW21 in the Name Box and press Ctrl + V (that is 100 columns, B through CW, by 20 rows). In CX2 type =AVERAGE(B2:CW2), copy it, select CX3:CX21 in the Name Box, and paste. Check: every number in column CX should be a multiple of 0.01, and they should be bunched closer together than the column in Draws25.
3
Results: freeze your estimates. Add a new sheet and rename it Results. In A1 type Sample, in B1 type n = 25, and in C1 type n = 100. Number A2:A21 1 to 20. Go to Draws25, select AA2:AA21, and press Ctrl + C. Go to Results, right-click B2 and, under Paste Options, choose Values (the clipboard icon marked 123); or use Home > Paste > Paste Special > Values. Do the same for Draws100!CX2:CX21, pasting as values into Results!C2. Check: click a cell in B and in C and look at the formula bar: each should show a plain number, not a formula. Press F9; nothing on Results should change. (From now on, Draws25 and Draws100 will keep changing when you press F9. That is fine; only Results matters.)
4
Results: the mean and the typical swing. On the Results sheet type these labels in column E and these formulas in F (for n = 25) and G (for n = 100). E1 Statistic, F1 n = 25, G1 n = 100. E2 Mean of the 20 estimates: F2 =AVERAGE(B2:B21), G2 =AVERAGE(C2:C21). E3 Typical swing (STDEV.S): F3 =STDEV.S(B2:B21), G3 =STDEV.S(C2:C21). E4 Smallest: F4 =MIN(B2:B21), G4 =MIN(C2:C21). E5 Largest: F5 =MAX(B2:B21), G5 =MAX(C2:C21). E6 Within 5 points of 0.40 (out of 20): F6 =COUNTIFS(B2:B21,">=0.35",B2:B21,"<=0.45"), G6 =COUNTIFS(C2:C21,">=0.35",C2:C21,"<=0.45"). E7 Theory: SQRT(0.4*0.6/n): F7 =SQRT(0.4*0.6/25), G7 =SQRT(0.4*0.6/100). E8 Swing at n = 25 divided by swing at n = 100: F8 =F3/G3. Select F2:G5, F7:G7, and F8 and choose Home > Number group > Increase Decimal until they show 3 decimals.
5
Tallies: group the estimates. Add a sheet named Tallies. For n = 25: in A1 type From, in B1 Up to (not including), in C1 Count. Type the lower edges 0.04, 0.12, 0.20, 0.28, 0.36, 0.44, 0.52, 0.60, 0.68, 0.76 down A2:A11 and the upper edges 0.12, 0.20, 0.28, 0.36, 0.44, 0.52, 0.60, 0.68, 0.76, 0.84 down B2:B11. Click C2 and type =COUNTIFS(Results!$B$2:$B$21,">="&A2,Results!$B$2:$B$21,"<"&B2), press Enter, and drag the fill square down to C11. In C12 type =SUM(C2:C11): it must show 20. For n = 100: in E1 type From, in F1 Up to (not including), in G1 Count. Type the lower edges 0.16, 0.20, 0.24, 0.28, 0.32, 0.36, 0.40, 0.44, 0.48, 0.52, 0.56, 0.60 down E2:E13 and the upper edges 0.20, 0.24, 0.28, 0.32, 0.36, 0.40, 0.44, 0.48, 0.52, 0.56, 0.60, 0.64 down F2:F13. In G2 type =COUNTIFS(Results!$C$2:$C$21,">="&E2,Results!$C$2:$C$21,"<"&F2), fill down to G13, and in G14 type =SUM(G2:G13): it must also show 20. If either total is not 20, an estimate fell outside the bins or an edge was mistyped: fix it before going on.
6
Tallies: two column charts. For n = 25, select C1:C11. On the Insert tab, in the Charts group, choose Insert Column or Bar Chart > Clustered Column. Right-click the chart, choose Select Data, under Horizontal (Category) Axis Labels click Edit, drag across A2:A11, and click OK twice. Add a chart title 20 sample proportions, n = 25 and axis titles (select the chart, then Chart Design > Add Chart Element > Axis Titles, or use the + button beside the chart): horizontal Sample proportion (bin starts at), vertical Number of samples. Drag the chart below the table (around A14). Repeat for n = 100: select G1:G13, insert a Clustered Column chart, set the category labels to E2:E13, title it 20 sample proportions, n = 100, add the same axis titles, and drag it below its table (around E14). Look at the two charts: the n = 100 columns should be bunched nearer the middle.
7
Notes sheet. Add a sheet and rename it Notes. In A1 type your name. In A3 write 2 to 3 sentences comparing your two piles of 20 estimates, using your own numbers from the Results sheet: where is each centered compared with 0.40, and which has the smaller typical swing, and by about how much? In A4 write one sentence saying why the mean of your 20 estimates is near 0.40 but probably not exactly 0.40. In A5 write one sentence on how this is sampling variation and not bias. Use your own words; do not copy sentences from the lesson. To keep a long sentence readable, click the cell and choose Home > Wrap Text.
8
Part B — numeric answers (type into the Canvas text box). Use your workbook and label each answer. B1: for n = 25, your mean of the 20 estimates, typical swing (STDEV.S), smallest, and largest, each to 3 decimals. B2: the same four numbers for n = 100. B3: your ratio F8 (swing at n = 25 divided by swing at n = 100) to 2 decimals. In Desmos Scientific type sqrt(0.4*0.6/25) and sqrt(0.4*0.6/100) and report both answers to 3 decimals, then divide the first by the second and report the theory ratio. B4: your counts F6 and G6 of estimates within 5 points of 0.40 (out of 20), and each as a percent. The lesson’s big simulation found about 46% (n = 25) and about 74% (n = 100); say in one sentence whether your percents are in the same neighborhood.
9
Part C — reasoning and applied items. C1. In three or four sentences, describe the pile of estimates at n = 25 and at n = 100 in terms of center, shape, and spread, and say what happened to the spread when the sample size was four times as big. C2. Applied (made up). A school board member says: “Our random survey of 100 students found 47% like the new schedule, so 47% of all students like it.” Using the typical swing for n = 100 that you found (it is about 0.05 when the true percent is near 50%), rewrite her sentence so that it is honest about sampling variation, in two sentences. C3. Variation or bias? A different made-up survey asks only the 100 students who stay after school for the club fair. It finds 70% like clubs, while the whole-school figure is believed to be about 50%. A teacher says: “Ask 400 students at the club fair instead and the gap will mostly disappear.” Explain, in two or three sentences, whether the teacher is right, using the words sampling variation and bias.
10
Part D — AI check. Ask an AI tool: “If the true proportion is 0.4, how much do sample proportions vary from sample to sample at n = 25 and at n = 100, and how does that differ from bias?” Before you read its answer, decide what a careful answer must say. Then report: the AI’s numbers for the typical swing and whether they match your Results sheet (to within about 0.02) and the Desmos values; whether it said the swing roughly halves when n is four times as big; whether it mixed up sampling variation with bias (and how you can tell); and one sentence you would change to make it true. If the AI got everything right, say what you checked. Save the work in your OneDrive folder.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The workbook has Draws25, Draws100, Results, Tallies, and Notes sheets. Draws25 and Draws100 contain live IF(RANDBETWEEN...) formulas (20 rows of 25 and of 100 answers) and a sample-proportion column; Results holds 20 plain-number (frozen) estimates for each n.
☐
The Results statistics (mean, STDEV.S, smallest, largest, within-5 count, theory, ratio) are computed from your own frozen estimates, and the Tallies sheet totals 20 in both tables and has two labeled column charts.
☐
Part B numbers match the workbook, include the Desmos theory values (0.098 and 0.049) and the ratio, and use careful wording such as “about” and “in my 20 samples.”
☐
The reasoning says the center is near 0.40, the shape is roughly bell-shaped (lumpy with only 20 samples), the n = 100 spread is about half the n = 25 spread, and that a miss is sampling variation, not bias; it does not claim a bigger sample fixes a biased method.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Workbook & numeric answers
6 pts		 Grading note: every student’s numbers differ because the draws are random. Grade structure, internal consistency, and shape claims, not fixed values. Structure: Draws25 has a live formula =IF(RANDBETWEEN(1,100)<=40,1,0) in B2:Z21 and =AVERAGE(B2:Z2) (filled to AA21); every AA value is a multiple of 0.04. Draws100 has the same formula in B2:CW21 and =AVERAGE(B2:CW2) in CX2:CX21; every CX value is a multiple of 0.01. Results B2:C21 are 20 plain numbers each (not formulas) that match the Draws sheets at the moment they were pasted (the Draws sheets may have changed since, so do not require a match). Consistency: F2 = AVERAGE of their B, G2 = AVERAGE of their C; F3, G3 = STDEV.S of their columns (sample SD, divide by 19); F4:G5 = MIN and MAX; F6, G6 = counts from 0.35 to 0.45 inclusive; F7 = 0.098 and G7 = 0.049 (0.0980 and 0.0490); F8 = F3 ÷ G3. Tallies: both totals equal 20 (C12, G14); counts match their Results values (spot-check two bins); two column charts with titles and axis titles. Part B must match their own cells (3 decimals); Desmos: 0.098 and 0.049; theory ratio = 2 (exactly, because √4 = 2). Tolerances (from a Python simulation of 20,000 complete workbooks of this exact design, true proportion 0.40): 95% of workbooks fall in these ranges: mean of 20 estimates at n = 25: 0.36 to 0.44 (simulated 0.358 to 0.444); at n = 100: 0.38 to 0.42 (0.379 to 0.422); typical swing (STDEV.S of the 20) at n = 25: 0.067 to 0.128; at n = 100: 0.034 to 0.064; ratio of swings (n = 25 over n = 100): 1.27 to 3.16 (median about 2.0); within-5-points count at n = 25: 5 to 14 of 20; at n = 100: 11 to 18 of 20. Accept without comment anything inside the 99% ranges: means 0.34 to 0.46 (n = 25) and 0.37 to 0.43 (n = 100); swings 0.059 to 0.138 (n = 25) and 0.030 to 0.069 (n = 100); ratio 1.1 to 3.7; within-5 count 4 to 15 (n = 25) and 9 to 19 (n = 100). In 99.8% of simulated workbooks the n = 100 swing is smaller than the n = 25 swing, so a workbook where it is not should be checked for a formula or freezing error (but is possible by chance, about 1 in 650). A value outside the 99% range, or a claim that contradicts the student’s own cells, points to a formula slip (for example VAR instead of STDEV.S, an estimate column of counts instead of proportions, or mixed-up columns). Part B: B1 to B4 match the workbook; B3 theory 0.098, 0.049, ratio 2.00; B4 counts are whole numbers from 0 to 20 and percents are count ÷ 20 (n = 25 about 46% and n = 100 about 74% in the large simulation; small piles of 20 vary a lot, so any value in the ranges above earns credit as long as the student comments honestly). One sheet or block missing, or a few values wrong because of a slip (estimates left as live formulas, an off-by-one range, tallies that do not total 20, counts used instead of proportions, VAR instead of STDEV.S), or one or two Part B numbers wrong or missing the Desmos theory values. Two or more parts missing, estimates typed in by hand instead of simulated with RANDBETWEEN, or numbers that do not come from the student’s own workbook. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Notes A3: compares the two piles using the student’s own numbers (both centers near 0.40; the n = 100 swing about half the n = 25 swing). A4: only 20 samples, each random, so the mean is near but not exactly 0.40 (sampling variation of the mean itself). A5: the scatter comes from chance in who is sampled, the method is fair and the pile is centered on the truth, so it is not bias. C1: center near 0.40 for both; shape roughly bell-shaped or lumpy and mound-like (20 samples is a small pile); spread at n = 100 is about half that at n = 25 (cite their ratio); four times as big gives about half the swing because of the square root. C2: honest rewrite such as “Our random sample of 100 students gave 47% in favor. Because different random samples would give somewhat different numbers, typically within about 5 points, the true figure for all students could reasonably be a few points higher or lower.” Must say it is an estimate and use a swing of about 0.05 (5 points). Do not require the words margin of error. C3: the teacher is not right. The gap (70% versus about 50%) is mostly bias (convenience or self-selection: students at the club fair are more likely to like clubs). A sample of 400 from the same place would reduce the sampling variation (the swing would roughly halve) but would stay centered near the biased value, so the gap would remain. Part D: reports the AI’s numbers (typical swing should be about 0.098 and 0.049 if correct), compares them with the workbook and Desmos, says whether it noted the halving and whether it mixed up variation and bias, and gives a specific rewrite of one sentence; if the AI was fully correct, the student says what was checked. Do not require that the AI be wrong. Correct numbers, but the reasoning is thin: omits the halving or the ratio, treats the scatter as bias, answers C3 without distinguishing variation from bias, or the AI check reports only the AI’s answer without a specific flag. Bare numbers with no reasoning, a claim that a bigger sample cures bias, a claim that a good sample would equal the truth, or no AI check. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

Upload your Excel workbook (.xlsx) as a file, and type your Part B, Part C and Part D answers in the text box. Label each answer (B1, B2, and so on).
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

assignments.html:
Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company
PROBABILITY & STATISTICS HONORS
Quarter / Module
Q4 · Module 11
Sampling & Study Design
Lesson
Lesson 31.2
Paired Lesson
Bias: How Samples and Questions Go Wrong
Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 31.2
Assignment 31.2 — Spot the Bias, Fix the Question
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Naming a survey’s bias, computing what a self-selected poll reports, and fixing a loaded question
Seven auto-graded items · one short written item
Covers: undercoverage, voluntary response, nonresponse, double-barreled and leading wording; why a larger sample cannot repair bias; the reply percent from a group table; the direction and size of a poll’s error; proposing a fix.
Lesson focus: Bias: How Samples and Questions Go Wrong
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (7 pts, auto-graded): five multiple-choice questions and two numeric answers. Part B (3 pts, teacher-scored): one short written response. All scenarios are constructed (made up). A calculator or Excel is fine for the arithmetic. You do not need to upload a workbook.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
If a survey leans, which way does it lean, why, and what would a responsible surveyor do about it?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
Name the bias. A made-up town clerk wants to know how many homes have high-speed internet. She draws 150 households at random from the landline phone directory and calls them. Many homes in town have only mobile phones and are not in the directory. What is the main problem?
(a) Voluntary response
(b) Nonresponse
(c) Undercoverage: some households have no chance to be picked
(d) A double-barreled question
2
Name the bias. A made-up radio show asks listeners to text in their opinion of a new road, and 400 people do. What is the main problem?
(a) Voluntary response: people chose themselves, and those with strong feelings are the most likely to text
(b) Undercoverage: the list of listeners was incomplete
(c) Measurement bias: the phones recorded the votes wrongly
(d) Chance variation: 400 is too few for a random sample
3
Name the bias. A made-up school mails a questionnaire to 300 randomly chosen families. Only 60 families return it. What is the main concern?
(a) The sample was a convenience sample
(b) A random sample cannot be biased
(c) The families were not chosen by chance
(d) Nonresponse: the 60 who replied may differ from the 240 who did not
4
Spot the flaw. A made-up survey asks, “Do you support extending the school day and requiring uniforms?” What is wrong with this question?
(a) It uses a loaded word
(b) It is double-barreled: it asks about two different things in one question
(c) It has too many answer choices
(d) It asks about a topic students know nothing about
5
Bigger sample? A made-up call-in poll gets 150 replies and reports a result that is too high. The station runs the same call-in poll again and gets 1,500 replies. Which statement is correct?
(a) The result will be about right, because 1,500 is a large sample
(b) The result will be exactly right, because 1,500 replies is ten times as many
(c) The result will still lean too high, because more replies from the same self-selected group do not remove the lean
(d) The result will now lean too low, because the bias cancels with more replies
6
Compute the reply percent. A made-up school has 400 students and posts an online link asking, “Should the school add a club period?” The table shows who would say yes (if everyone were asked) and who actually replied.
GroupStudentsWould say yesReply rateRepliesYes replies
Club members1008050%5040
Everyone else30012010%3012
Whole school4002008052
What percent of the replies say yes? Enter a number from 0 to 100 (no % sign).
7
Size of the miss. Using the same table, the true share of all 400 students who would say yes is 200 / 400 = 50%. By how many percentage points does the poll’s result (your answer to item 6) overstate the truth? Enter a whole number.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (3 PTS)
8
Application: bias hunt. The made-up Lincoln Park Gazette, a school newspaper, posts a link on its web page: “Wouldn’t you agree that the cafeteria’s new menu is a huge improvement?” Forty students click and answer, and 34 say yes, so the paper reports that “85% of students love the new menu.”

In three to five sentences, write: (a) the name of at least one bias in this survey; (b) which way the bias pushes the reported 85% (too high or too low) and why; and (c) a specific fix, either a rewritten neutral question or a better way to choose whom to ask, and one sentence on why it helps.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I asked two questions about each survey: who answered, and how was it asked?
☐
My answers to items 6 and 7 came from a calculation I wrote out and checked.
☐
My written answer says which direction the error goes, with a reason, not only that the survey is “biased.”
☐
My fix addresses the problem I named: a neutral question for a loaded one, a chosen (not self-selected) group for a voluntary poll.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Part A: auto-graded
7 pts		 1 pt per item. Answer key: (1) c; (2) a; (3) d; (4) b; (5) c; (6) 65; (7) 15. Items 6 and 7 are numeric (accept 65, 65.0, 65%; and 15, 15.0). Not applicable: each item is right or wrong. Not applicable. 7 pts
Part B: name the bias
1 pt		 Names a valid bias: voluntary response (self-selected link) and/or leading or loaded wording (“Wouldn’t you agree”, “huge improvement”). Also accept undercoverage (students who do not visit the page cannot answer) or a clear plain-language description of any of these. Says the poll is “unfair” or “biased” without naming a source, or names a bias that does not apply here (for example nonresponse from a random sample). Names no bias, or blames only the sample size (“40 is too small”). 1 pt
Part B: direction of the error
1 pt		 States the 85% is likely too high and gives a reason tied to the survey: the question pushes toward yes, and/or students who like the menu (or follow the paper) are more likely to click. A student who notes that we cannot know the true share but the error leans upward also earns full credit. Says the result is “off” or “not accurate” without a direction, or gives the correct direction with no reason. Gives the wrong direction with a reason that does not fit, or gives no direction. 1 pt
Part B: propose a fix
1 pt		 Gives a specific fix that matches the named bias and says why it helps. Examples: rewrite to “How do you feel about the cafeteria’s new menu? (Like it a lot, … Dislike it a lot)”; draw a random set of students from the full roster and ask each one (and follow up with those who do not reply); or both. Accept any neutral wording with balanced choices. Gives a fix that is only partly specific, such as “ask a random sample” with no steps, or rewrites the question but leaves it leading or double-barreled. Suggests only more responses to the same link, or repeats the original plan. 1 pt
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 31.2 — Spot the Bias, Fix the Question
Enter the five multiple-choice letters and the two numeric answers for Part A, and type your Part B response in the text box. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

An Education Experience Company

Lesson
Lesson 31.3
Paired Lesson
Is the Model Consistent with the Data?
Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 31.3
Assignment 31.3 — Does the Claim Fit the Data?
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Models that make data, simulated spread, and careful conclusions about consistency
Seven auto-graded items · one short written item
Covers: describing a claim as a model, expected counts, exact chances of results at least as far from expected, borderline results, what “consistent” does and does not allow, and the multiple-looks caution.
Lesson focus: Is the Model Consistent with the Data?
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (7 pts, auto-graded): three multiple-choice questions and four numeric answers. Part B (3 pts, teacher-scored): one short written response. All scenarios are constructed (made up). Excel’s BINOM.DIST, the model checker from the lesson, and a calculator are all fine to use. You do not need to upload a workbook.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
If this claim were true, how surprising would my result be, and what am I honestly entitled to say about it?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
The model. A made-up shop claims that its die is fair. Which statement is the best description of the claimed model (the data-generating process)?
(a) The die will show a six exactly once in every six rolls.
(b) Each roll shows a six with chance 1/6, and one roll does not affect the next.
(c) The next roll will not be a six if the last roll was a six.
(d) The die has been rolled enough times that it must be fair.
2
Expected count. Under the fair-die model in item 1, how many sixes do you expect in 60 rolls? Enter a whole number.
3
Exact chance. A made-up game claims its coin is fair. In 50 flips it lands heads 36 times, which is 11 above the expected 25. Using Excel’s BINOM.DIST (the lesson shows how), find the exact chance of a result at least this far from expected on either side: 36 or more heads, or 14 or fewer. Round to 4 decimal places.
4
Borderline result. A made-up fair-coin claim is checked against 60 heads in 100 flips. Using the either-side idea (60 or more, or 40 or fewer), what is the exact chance? Round to 3 decimal places.
5
Simulation wobble. A spinner is claimed to land on section A with chance 25%. In 50 spins, section A comes up 19 times. The exact chance of a result at least this far from expected, on either side, is 0.0481. Two students each use the model checker with the rule of thumb “unusual if fewer than 5 in 100 runs.” One simulation shows 47 of 1000 runs at least as far as 19, and the other shows 55 of 1000. Which statement is best?
(a) At least one student must have made a mistake, because two simulations of the same model should give the same count.
(b) The result is clearly unusual, because 47 and 55 are both much smaller than 1000.
(c) Both counts are reasonable readings of a chance near 0.048, and they fall on opposite sides of the cutoff, so the result is borderline and should be reported that way.
(d) The second student is right and the first is wrong, because 55 is the larger count.
6
A careful conclusion. A made-up seed packet claims that 30% of its seeds sprout. A student plants 50 seeds and 21 sprout. The expected count is 15, and the exact chance of a result at least this far from 15, on either side, is 0.0880 (a 1000-run simulation will read near 88, give or take about 9). Which conclusion is the most careful?
(a) The result is not unusual under the claim, so the data are consistent with 30%, but they do not prove it.
(b) The result proves that 30% of the seeds sprout.
(c) The result proves that the packet is wrong, because 21 is not 15.
(d) The result is unusual under the claim, because 21 is more than 15.
7
Multiple looks. A made-up lab checks 20 different fair models, each against its own independent result. For each check, the chance that a true model lands in the unusual zone (the 5-in-100 tail) is 0.05. What is the chance that at least one of the 20 checks lands in its unusual zone, even though every model is true? Round to 3 decimal places.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (3 PTS)
8
Application: does the claim fit? The made-up Hollow Creek Garden Club buys a seed packet that says 80% of these seeds sprout. A member plants 40 seeds, and 28 of them sprout. (This is made-up data.)

Open the model checker, choose Custom claim, enter a Claimed chance of success (%) of 80, Number of trials n = 40, and Observed count of successes = 28. Run Simulate 1000 runs again a couple of times. In four to six sentences, write: (a) the claimed model, including the expected number of sprouts; (b) how your observed result compares with what the simulation shows (the count out of 1000 and what it says about the result under your rule of thumb); and (c) a careful conclusion about the 80% claim, including one thing you cannot conclude.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
For items 2, 3, 4, and 7, my answer came from a calculation I wrote out and checked.
☐
My written answer states the claimed model and the expected count before it looks at the result.
☐
I compared the observed result with what the simulation showed, using numbers from the model checker.
☐
My conclusion matches the strength of the evidence and does not say that anything is “proved.”
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Part A: auto-graded
7 pts		 1 pt per item. Answer key: (1) b; (2) 10; (3) 0.0026 (accept 0.0025 to 0.0027); (4) 0.057 (accept 0.0565 to 0.0575); (5) c; (6) a; (7) 0.642 (accept 0.641 to 0.643; also accept 0.64). Exact values: item 3 is 2 × 0.001301 = 0.002602; item 4 is 0.0569; item 7 is 1 − 0.9520 = 0.6415. Item 5 uses simulated counts only as a tolerance statement: any 1000-run reading from about 35 to 62 is consistent with the exact 0.0481, so the result is borderline. Not applicable: each item is right or wrong. Not applicable. 7 pts
Part B: state the claimed model
1 pt		 States that each seed sprouts with chance 80% (a claimed chance of success of 0.8), with 40 seeds planted, so the expected count is 40 × 0.8 = 32 sprouts. Both the chance and the expected count are present. Gives the 80% claim but not the expected count of 32 (or the reverse), or gives 32 with no statement of the chance. Does not state a model, or restates only the observed 28 of 40 (70%). 1 pt
Part B: compare to the simulation
1 pt		 Says the observed 28 is 4 below the expected 32, and reports the model checker’s count: about 163 of 1000 runs were at least as far (28 or fewer, or 36 or more); accept any reading from about 125 to 200 because each simulation wobbles around the exact 0.1634. Concludes that this is well above the rule-of-thumb cutoff of fewer than 50 in 1000, so the result is not unusual under the claimed model. Reports a count or a verdict but not both, or compares 28 to 32 without using the simulated count, or reads a count that is clearly off with no explanation. Compares the result with nothing (for example, only says “28 is less than 32”) or reaches the opposite verdict (unusual) with no justification. 1 pt
Part B: careful conclusion
1 pt		 Concludes the 80% claim is consistent with the data and there is no good reason to drop it (stick with the model), and names one thing that cannot be concluded: for example, that the data do not prove the 80% claim (other rates such as 75% would also fit), or that one run of 40 seeds cannot settle the packet’s true rate. Does not use “proved” or “proves” in a positive sense. Reaches the right verdict (consistent / stick with the model) but names no limit, or names a limit but states the verdict loosely (for example, “the packet is basically right”). Says the data prove or confirm the 80% claim, or says the data prove the packet is false, or gives no conclusion. 1 pt
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 31.3 — Does the Claim Fit the Data?
Enter the multiple-choice letters (items 1, 5, and 6) and the numeric answers (items 2, 3, 4, and 7) for Part A, and type your Part B response in the text box. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Sampling and Study Design
Type
VR Solo Activity
Optima · Week 31 · pairs with Lessons 31.1 and 31.2
Time in headset
25–30 minutes
One session, one submission
Points
Completion-scored
5 pts
Module 11 · VR Solo Activity
The Bias Museum
VR Activity · 5 pts · completion
🥼 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
A poll is a claim about people nobody asked. To make that claim responsibly, you must be able to say how the people who answered came to be in the sample, and who was left out. Lessons 31.1 and 31.2 gave you the names for the ways a sample goes wrong. Today you walk through a small museum of sampling failures. There are six exhibits. Five are constructed (made up) for this activity and are labeled that way; the sixth is a short, hedged retelling of a famous 1936 poll, and you are asked to check that account yourself. At each exhibit you will read the placard, study the data wall (what the poll says against what is true), then post a sticky note naming the bias type and a one-sentence fix. Responsibility here means two things: you name the flaw honestly, and you leave the exhibits exactly as you found them for the next visitor. Counts on the walls are exact for the made-up groups, to keep the arithmetic clean; a real poll would wobble a little.
📋 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset with Optima installed (desktop Optima works if a headset is unavailable, but walking from exhibit to exhibit and standing in front of each placard is part of the activity).
▶
Your Lesson 31.1 and 31.2 notes (notebook page): the six bias types (undercoverage, voluntary response, nonresponse, convenience, response bias, loaded wording), what random sampling from a complete list does, and why a larger sample shrinks random variation but not bias. Review them before you put the headset on; re-reading inside a headset is hard.
▶
A pencil and notebook beside you for after the session. You will not need a calculator inside the headset: every number you need is posted on a data wall.
▶
About 30 uninterrupted minutes.
🚀 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (preferred) or desktop Optima
Session type: Persistent Session (your work saves between visits)
Session ID: [SESSION ID — teacher enters before publishing]
Location: [LOCATION NAME — an open, flat-floored Location with room for six exhibit stands, a wall of option panels, and a summary board; teacher enters before publishing]
On arrival: Find the Whiteboard IFX near the spawn point labeled “The Bias Museum — start here.” Ahead of you, six exhibits stand in a gentle curve, numbered 1 to 6. Each has a placard (a short story), a data wall (what the poll says against what is true), and a note rail beneath it where your sticky note goes. Beside the entrance hangs the Sticky-Note Wall with six bias-type options, and by the exit stands the Summary Board.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Read the legend. At the starting whiteboard, read the museum rules: Exhibits 1 to 5 are constructed (made up) and say so; Exhibit 6 is a hedged retelling with no figures, so check it yourself outside the headset. On each data wall, “the poll says” is what the survey reported, and “the truth” is what asking the whole made-up group would have shown.
2
Walk to Exhibit 1 and read before you judge. Read the placard, then the data wall: the poll’s number, the true number, and the table showing who is in each group and how likely each group was to be asked or to answer. Allow about three minutes per exhibit. Ask: Why is the poll’s number off? Which group is too loud, or missing?
3
Pick the bias type. Go to the Sticky-Note Wall and choose the option that best explains the gap: undercoverage / frame problem, voluntary response, nonresponse, convenience, response bias, or loaded wording. If two seem to fit, choose the main one and name the second in your note. Do not pull options off the wall; copy the name onto your own sticky note.
4
Write the note and the fix. Create a sticky note and attach it to that exhibit’s note rail. Write it in this form: Exhibit N — Bias: ______. Fix: ______. The fix is one sentence and must name a better method: for example, random sampling from a complete list of the population, a neutral rewrite of the question, or a plan for reaching people who did not answer. “Ask more people” is not a fix, as you will see.
5
Repeat for Exhibits 2 to 6. Same order every time: placard, data wall, option, note, fix. At Exhibit 6 there are no numbers on the wall; use the story and the mailing-list and response clues.
6
Write the summary sentence. At the Summary Board write: A bigger sample does not fix a biased method. Under it, name the exhibit that shows this best and give the two sample sizes and the percent the poll reported at each, in your own words.
7
Capture your annotated exhibits. Stand where a snapshot catches Exhibits 1 to 3 with your sticky notes on their rails, then take it and check it; every note must be readable. Take a second snapshot of Exhibits 4 to 6 the same way. If a note is too small to read, retake it from closer. Optionally, add a snapshot of the Summary Board.
8
Leave the museum as you found it. Do not move, turn or resize any placard, data wall or option panel, and do not remove anyone else’s notes. Keep your notes on your own note rails. Leaving a shared place as you found it is the plainest courtesy there is.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Canvas Assignment Name: VR Activity — The Bias Museum
Upload your snapshots (image files) from step 7, showing the six exhibits with your sticky notes (bias type and one-sentence fix for each) readable in frame. You may upload one snapshot if a single view catches all six readably.
Below them, in the text entry box, write 2–3 sentences: (1) the summary sentence a bigger sample does not fix a biased method, in your own words, and which exhibit shows it best and why; and (2) one question you will ask about the sample before you trust the next poll you read.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment. · Estimated time: 25–30 minutes in headset.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA (COMPLETION)
☐
The snapshot(s) show all six exhibits, each with your sticky note naming a bias type, all readable.
☐
Each note includes a one-sentence fix that names a better method (random sampling from a complete list, a neutral question, or a way to reach nonresponders), not just “ask more people.”
☐
The text entry contains the summary sentence that a bigger sample does not fix a biased method, names the exhibit that shows it best, and gives one question you will ask about a poll’s sample.
☐
You left the museum as you found it (no exhibit moved, nobody else’s notes removed).
👋 FACILITATOR NOTE
Stage the Location before publishing. Layout: six exhibit stands in a gentle curve, numbered 1 to 6, each with three parts: a placard (about 1.2 m wide, bottom edge about 1.0 m above the floor) at the left; a data wall (about 2.0 m wide by 1.4 m tall, bottom edge about 0.6 m) to its right; and a note rail (a shelf or labeled strip about 0.8 m wide, about 0.5 m above the floor) beneath the data wall where students attach their sticky notes. Lock placards, data walls and option panels so students cannot move or resize them. Put a sign on every constructed exhibit: “CONSTRUCTED (made up) for this activity. Not real data.” Exhibit spacing about 2.5 m so a snapshot of three exhibits fits in one view; the six data walls use large text (at least 0.08 m digits) so numbers stay readable in a snapshot.
Other items: a Whiteboard IFX at the spawn point labeled “The Bias Museum — start here” with the legend from step 1; the Sticky-Note Wall near the entrance (six labeled panels, locked, text below); the Summary Board (Whiteboard IFX) near the exit headed “A bigger sample does not fix a biased method,” with a blank line for the best exhibit and the two sample sizes; a pad of sticky notes. Sticky-Note Wall options (post exactly these six, each with one line): (1) Undercoverage / frame problem: the list you draw from leaves some people out, so they have no chance to be picked. (2) Voluntary response: people choose themselves, and strong feelings answer. (3) Nonresponse: chosen people do not answer, and those who do may differ. (4) Convenience: whoever is easiest to reach. (5) Response bias: people answer untruthfully or are pushed by the setting. (6) Loaded wording: the question itself pushes toward one answer. These names match Lesson 31.2.
Exhibit 1 — The Gym Call-In (CONSTRUCTED). Placard: “Fairmont Gym (made up) has 1,000 members. The manager wants to know whether members favor raising the gym’s budget, so she posts a hotline number and invites members to call and leave a yes or no. Constructed for this activity.” Data wall: The poll says: 62 of 95 callers said yes = 65.3%. The truth (ask all 1,000 members): 520 said yes = 52.0%. Mechanism table:
GroupMembersTruly yesChance a member callsCallsYes calls
Heavy users30080% (240)20%6048
Light users70040% (280)5%3514
Total1,00052.0% (520)—9562
Heavy users are 30% of members but 63.2% of callers (60 of 95).
Exhibit 2 — Outside the Greenleaf Market (CONSTRUCTED). Placard: “Lindenvale (made up) has 2,000 residents. A reporter stands outside the Greenleaf Market, the only place she asks, and puts one question to shoppers: ‘Do you buy organic produce every week?’ Constructed for this activity.” Data wall: The poll says (40 shoppers asked): 28 yes = 70.0%. Ask 200 shoppers instead: 140 yes = 70.0%. The truth (ask all 2,000 residents): 550 yes = 27.5%. Mechanism table:
GroupResidentsWeekly organicChance of being asked
Shop at Greenleaf30070% (210)100% (all the people asked come from here)
Everyone else1,70020% (340)0% (never asked)
Total2,00027.5% (550)—
Five times as many people asked (40 to 200) and the poll still says 70.0%. This is the cleanest “bigger sample, same bias” exhibit.
Exhibit 3 — Two Wordings (CONSTRUCTED). Placard (a pair of cards, A and B, side by side): “A town (made up) has 5,000 residents. Two random samples of 200 residents, each drawn from the complete resident list, were asked about a skate park. Card A read: ‘Should the town add a skate park? Yes or no.’ Card B read: ‘Do you favor spending town money on a skate park that few people will use? Yes or no.’ Constructed for this activity.” Data wall: Card A poll: 110 of 200 yes = 55.0%. Card B poll: 84 of 200 yes = 42.0%. The truth on the fair wording (all 5,000 asked Card A): 2,750 yes = 55.0%. Mechanism table (the 200-person samples split 80 / 60 / 60 across the three groups):
GroupResidentsYes on Card AYes on Card B
Firm supporters2,000100% (2,000)90% (1,800)
Firm opponents1,5000% (0)0% (0)
Persuadable1,50050% (750)20% (300)
Total5,00055.0% (2,750)42.0% (2,100)
Both samples are random from a complete list, so the sampling method is sound; the gap comes only from the words. The 13-point drop is entirely from the persuadable group and the wording’s effect on firm supporters.
Exhibit 4 — The Phone Book Poll (CONSTRUCTED). Placard: “Harbor County (made up) has 8,000 adults. A pollster draws names at random from the Harbor County Phone Book (a made-up list that includes 3,200 of those adults) and asks: ‘Do you support a new bus route?’ Everyone she picks answers. Constructed for this activity.” Data wall: The poll says (400 names drawn): 140 yes = 35.0%. Draw 2,000 names instead: 700 yes = 35.0%. The truth (all 8,000 adults): 4,240 yes = 53.0%. Mechanism table:
GroupAdultsSupportChance of being picked
Listed in the phone book3,200 (40%)35% (1,120)400 of 3,200 = 12.5% (or 2,000 of 3,200 = 62.5%)
Not listed4,800 (60%)65% (3,120)0% (not on the list)
Total8,00053.0% (4,240)—
Sixty percent of adults had no chance of being picked, however many names are drawn. The second sample is five times as large and gives the same 35.0%.
Exhibit 5 — Say It to My Face (CONSTRUCTED). Placard: “Oakdale High (made up) has 600 students. A random sample of 150, drawn from the complete roster, is interviewed aloud by their own teachers: ‘Did you finish all your homework this week?’ A private, anonymous log (also made up) shows what really happened. Constructed for this activity.” Data wall: The poll says: 120 of 150 said yes = 80.0%. The truth (anonymous log, all 600 students): 360 finished = 60.0%. Mechanism table:
GroupStudentsIn the sample of 150Say yes aloud

Did not finish2406050% (30)
Total60015080.0% (120)
The sample is random and everyone answered; the problem is that half of those who did not finish said they had when asked face to face.
Exhibit 6 — The 1936 Magazine Poll (a story, not a data set). This is the only exhibit not made up, and it is deliberately told in outline with no figures, no quotations and no dates beyond 1936, the same hedged account used in Week 30 Lesson 2. Placard (post exactly): “In 1936 a magazine ran a poll before a presidential election. As the story is usually told: it got back millions of ballots, and it predicted that the challenger, Landon, would beat Roosevelt. Check this account yourself.” Data wall (two columns, no numbers): “As the story is usually told”: (a) the mailing lists were drawn from sources such as telephone directories and automobile registrations; (b) only some of the people who received a ballot sent it back (nonresponse); (c) smaller, more carefully drawn polls came closer to the result. “What this wall does not show”: exact counts, percentages, quotations. “Your job”: look it up in more than one reliable source before you repeat any of it. Do not add figures, quotes or dates to this exhibit.
Answer key (bias type per exhibit; accept defensible alternatives with a reason).
ExhibitBest answerAlso defensibleA good fix names
1 Gym call-inVoluntary responseNonresponse (most members did not call)random sample from the membership list, with follow-up for those who do not answer
2 One-store shoppersConvenienceUndercoverage (non-Greenleaf residents have no chance)random sample from a complete list of residents
3 Two wordings (Card B)Loaded wordingNone; Card A is the neutral baselineneutral rewrite, such as Card A: “Should the town add a skate park? Yes or no.”
4 Phone bookUndercoverage / frame problemConvenience (using the list at hand)a frame that covers all adults, then a random sample from it
5 Say it to my faceResponse biasNone strongly; mention social desirability as the reasonanonymous written or electronic form, so students need not look good to a teacher
6 1936 pollNonresponse (and the list problem)Undercoverage (lists limited to certain groups); voluntary responsea careful random sample from a complete list, with follow-up on nonresponse
Check every fix for a method: random sampling from a complete list, a neutral question, an anonymous format, or a plan to reach nonresponders. Reject “ask more people” or “sample more” as the fix; that is the misconception the Summary Board corrects. Summary sentence. Accept any wording that keeps the idea that a larger sample does not repair a flawed method. The best exhibits are 2 (40 and 200 askers both give 70.0%, truth 27.5%) and 4 (400 and 2,000 names both give 35.0%, truth 53.0%); accept Exhibit 6 if the student says millions of ballots could not repair the method, and note that it relies on the hedged story. Why it holds: more data shrinks random variation (Lesson 31.1) but the same method keeps pulling from the same slanted group, so the poll aims at the wrong number more precisely.
Expected common errors: labeling Exhibit 3 “undercoverage” or “convenience” because the town is small (the sample is random; the words are the flaw); calling Exhibit 1 “convenience” (callers choose themselves, which is voluntary response); calling Exhibit 4 “nonresponse” (everyone picked answered; the trouble is who was on the list); writing “ask more people” as the fix; mixing up response bias (untruthful answers) with nonresponse (no answer); treating Exhibit 6 as established fact rather than something to check. Common sticking points: not knowing where to attach a note, writing the note before reading the data wall, taking a snapshot too far away to read, and moving a placard while attaching a note. What to demo: creating a sticky note and attaching it to a note rail, copying (not removing) an option from the Sticky-Note Wall, writing on a Whiteboard IFX, and taking and reviewing a snapshot. If a student finishes early, ask them to rewrite the Card B question so it is both neutral and short, or to design a better frame for Exhibit 4 and say who would still be missed.
Items to confirm in the IFX library and in ENGAGE before publishing (none of this has been tested in ENGAGE): the names and sizes of the placard, data-wall and rail IFX you use; whether tables can be shown on a Whiteboard IFX or must be built from sticky notes or text; how a sticky note attaches to a rail and whether students can create and attach notes in their own Session; whether a persistent Session keeps each student’s notes (if not, use a fresh Session per student and say so in the Session ID line); how to lock placards, data walls and the option panels so they cannot be moved; whether students can copy an option name without removing it; whether one snapshot can catch three exhibits legibly at your spacing (if not, change the number of snapshots in the submission text and the success criteria together); and whether 25–30 minutes holds for six exhibits. The page asks for two snapshots (Exhibits 1–3 and 4–6) as a reasonable plan; adjust if your Location needs a different split. All numbers on Exhibits 1 to 5 are constructed and were recomputed; none come from real polls. Exhibit 6 is a hedged outline of a historical account and should be checked against reliable sources before you rely on it.

Surveys, Experiments, and Observational Studies
Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 32.1
Assignment 32.1 — Match the Design to the Claim
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Classifying a study, separating random sampling from random assignment, and writing the conclusion a design can carry
Eight auto-graded items · one Excel formula answer · one short AI-check item
Covers: survey, observational study, and experiment; explanatory and response variables; confounding; random sampling versus random assignment; the conclusion each design supports; a difference of group means; the AVERAGEIF formula.
Lesson focus: Surveys, Experiments, and Observational Studies
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (8 pts, auto-graded): seven multiple-choice questions and one numeric answer. Part B (2 pts, quick teacher check): one typed Excel formula and one short AI-check response. All scenarios are constructed (made up). A calculator or Excel is fine for the arithmetic. You do not need to upload a workbook.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What did the researchers do, who got picked, who got which treatment, and so what can they honestly say?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
Classify the study. A made-up bakery draws 120 of its customers at random and asks each which bread they prefer. Nothing is changed for anyone. What kind of study is this?
(a) An experiment
(b) An observational study with a treatment group
(c) A sample survey
(d) A randomized comparative trial
2
Classify the study. A made-up gardener numbers 30 bean plants, draws 15 numbers from a hat to decide which plants sit by a sunny window, and puts the other 15 in a shaded corner. After three weeks she measures each plant’s height. What kind of study is this?
(a) A sample survey
(b) An observational study, because she measures heights
(c) An experiment, because she imposed the light condition
(d) A census
3
Classify the study. A made-up researcher reads school records for 400 students and compares the grades of those who joined the school band with those who did not. What kind of study is this?
(a) A sample survey
(b) An experiment, because the researcher compared two groups
(c) A randomized experiment
(d) An observational study
4
Identify the variables. In a made-up experiment, 12 runners are assigned by a draw from a hat to Shoe A or Shoe B and each runs 5 km. Researchers compare the times. What is the response variable?
(a) The shoe type (A or B)
(b) The 5 km time
(c) The group of 12 runners
(d) The draw from the hat
5
Sampling or assignment? A made-up school asks for volunteers for a study. Forty students volunteer, and names drawn from a hat put 20 on a morning tutoring session and 20 on an afternoon one. Which statement correctly describes the use of chance?
(a) There is random sampling and random assignment
(b) There is random sampling but no random assignment
(c) There is random assignment but no random sampling
(d) There is neither random sampling nor random assignment
6
What conclusion is justified? A made-up researcher draws 400 students at random from a large school district and records each student’s weekly screen time and hours of sleep. Students with more screen time tend to sleep less. Which conclusion is best supported?
(a) More screen time causes less sleep for students in the district
(b) In this district, screen time and sleep appear to be associated; the design cannot show that one causes the other
(c) The result applies to every teenager in the country
(d) Nothing can be concluded because the students were not assigned to groups
7
What conclusion is justified? In a made-up study, 60 volunteers from one running club are assigned to Shoe A or Shoe B by random draw. Shoe A runners are faster. Which conclusion is best supported?
(a) Shoe A makes every runner faster
(b) Shoe A probably made these volunteers faster; the study cannot show it would hold for runners in general
(c) Shoe A and speed are associated, but cause cannot be considered at all
(d) Nothing can be said because the volunteers were not a random sample
8
Compute the difference. A made-up bakery has 12 identical dough balls, and names drawn from a hat decide which 6 rise in a hot proofing box and which 6 in a cool one. The heights after one hour, in millimeters, are:
Hot box: 12, 14, 11, 15, 13, 13
Cool box: 10, 9, 12, 11, 8, 10
Find the mean height for each group. By how many millimeters does the hot-box mean exceed the cool-box mean? Enter a number.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (1 PT EACH)
9
Excel formula. In a worksheet, group labels (A or B) are in A2:A13 and 5 km times are in B2:B13. Type the exact Excel formula that gives the mean time for the runners in group A. (Typed as you would type it in a cell, beginning with =.)
10
Check an AI. A made-up AI tool was given the bean-plant study from item 2 (plants randomly assigned to sun or shade) but was told the 30 plants were the ones the gardener happened to have in her yard. It replied: “Because the plants were randomly assigned, these results apply to all bean plants everywhere.” In two or three sentences, say whether the AI is right, and explain, using the words random assignment and random sampling, what the design does and does not allow.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I decided the design by asking what the researchers did: asked, measured, or imposed a treatment.
☐
I kept random sampling (who is in) apart from random assignment (who gets which treatment).
☐
My answer to item 8 came from two means I wrote out and checked.
☐
My conclusions in items 6, 7, and 10 are no bigger than the design allows.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Part A: auto-graded
8 pts		 1 pt per item. Answer key: (1) c; (2) c; (3) d; (4) b; (5) c; (6) b; (7) b; (8) 3. Item 8 is numeric (hot-box mean 13, cool-box mean 10; accept 3, 3.0, 3 mm). Not applicable: each item is right or wrong. Not applicable. 8 pts
Part B: Excel formula (item 9)
1 pt		 Types =AVERAGEIF(A2:A13,"A",B2:B13). Accept absolute references ($A$2:$A$13) and straight or curly quotes around A. Accept a label in a cell (for example =AVERAGEIF(A2:A13,D2,B2:B13)) if the student says D2 holds A. Right idea with a small slip: omits the leading equals sign, or the range arguments are in a valid but wrong order for the intended result, or uses AVERAGE with a filter that would work (for example AVERAGE(B2:B7)) and says rows 2 to 7 are group A. Uses COUNTIF, SUM, or plain AVERAGE(B2:B13) of both groups, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Part B: AI check (item 10)
1 pt		 Says the AI is wrong or overreaching, and explains that random assignment supports a claim of cause among the 30 plants, but because the plants were not randomly sampled from all bean plants, the result cannot be generalized to bean plants everywhere. Both ideas present, correctly attached. Says the AI is wrong but names only one of the two ideas, or swaps the terms but reaches a correct overall point. Agrees with the AI, or says only that the sample is “too small.” 1 pt
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 32.1 — Match the Design to the Claim
Answer items 1 to 8 in Canvas (seven multiple-choice letters and one number), then type your Excel formula for item 9 and your short response for item 10 in the text boxes. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Points

Lesson 32.2
Assignment 32.2 — Randomization Workbook
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Let chance make the groups, check the balance, then estimate the effect honestly
Spreadsheet lab · graded on a correct, complete workbook and honest reasoning
Covers: a made-up study of 24 subjects; RAND and sort to form two groups of 12; freezing with Paste Special > Values; AVERAGEIF group means; a baseline balance check; an estimated effect compared with the known truth; careful causal wording; control group, placebo, double-blind, and what randomization cannot fix.
Lesson focus: Randomized Assignment: The Key to Causal Claims
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
This is the week’s Excel lab. You will upload one workbook with two sheets (Experiment and Notes). Because the groups are made by chance, your groups will not match your classmates’ groups, and that is expected. You are graded on doing the method correctly and on computing your own numbers correctly, not on getting any particular split. A few numbers (the all-subjects mean and the true average effect) are the same for everyone, and you can use them to check your work. You will also type your Part B numbers and your Part C short answers into the Canvas text box. All data and scenarios are constructed (made up); none is real.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
When chance makes the groups, what can the difference in outcomes honestly tell us, and what can it not?
📁 M365 REMINDER
Name your Excel file Wk32_Randomization_YourName.xlsx, save it to your OneDrive Optima → Math folder, and upload the .xlsx file to Canvas. Excel work happens outside Canvas; you will submit the finished workbook. Do not submit screenshots in place of the workbook. Freeze your random numbers as values before you sort or compute anything, or your groups will change every time the sheet recalculates.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Open the workbook and enter the subjects. Open Excel, start a Blank workbook, and rename the first sheet Experiment (right-click the sheet tab at the bottom, choose Rename, type the name, press Enter). This is a made-up memory-training study of 24 subjects. In A1:D1 type the headings ID, Baseline, ScoreIfRoutine, ScoreIfUsual (Tab between cells). Baseline is each subject’s score on a 60-point memory quiz before the study. ScoreIfRoutine and ScoreIfUsual are the score the subject would get after the study if assigned to the new study routine, or to the usual way of studying. (In real life you see only one of the two for each person. Because this data set is made up, we can show both, which lets you check your work against the truth afterward.) Enter the data below in A2:D25: type it, or drag across the table with the mouse, press Ctrl + C, click A2, and press Ctrl + V (delete the pasted header row if it lands on row 2). Check your typing: in spare cells, =SUM(B2:B25) should give 650, =SUM(C2:C25) should give 848, and =SUM(D2:D25) should give 694.

2
Add random numbers. In E1 type RAND. Click E2, type =RAND(), press Enter, then drag the small square at the bottom right corner of E2 down to E25. Every cell in E now holds a random decimal between 0 and 1.
3
Freeze the random numbers (before sorting). Select E2:E25 and press Ctrl + C. Right-click the same selection and, under Paste Options, choose Values (the clipboard icon marked 123); or use Home > Paste > Paste Special > Values. Press Esc. Click a cell in E and check the formula bar: it must show a plain number, not a formula. Press F9 once; nothing in E should change.
4
Sort by the random numbers. Select A1:E25. On the Data tab choose Sort. In the box, check My data has headers, set Sort by to RAND, Sort On to Cell Values, and Order to Smallest to Largest, then click OK. Your IDs are now in a scrambled order, with each subject’s numbers moving together.
5
Make the two groups. In F1 type Group. In F2 type Routine and copy it down through F13 (the first twelve rows). In F14 type Usual and copy it down through F25. Check: =COUNTIF(F2:F25,"Routine") and =COUNTIF(F2:F25,"Usual") must both give 12.
6
Compare the groups before the study (baseline balance). In H1 type Baseline check. Then type these labels in column H and formulas in column I: H2 Routine group baseline mean with I2 =AVERAGEIF(F2:F25,"Routine",B2:B25); H3 Usual group baseline mean with I3 =AVERAGEIF(F2:F25,"Usual",B2:B25); H4 Difference (Routine minus Usual) with I4 =I2-I3; H5 All 24 subjects baseline mean with I5 =AVERAGE(B2:B25). If assignment worked, the two group means should be close to each other and to the all-subjects mean. Note that the two group means average to the all-subjects mean, because the groups are equal in size: =(I2+I3)/2 must equal I5.
7
Pick each subject’s observed score. In G1 type Observed. Click G2 and type =IF(F2="Routine",C2,D2), press Enter, and fill down to G25 (drag the small square). This picks the “ScoreIfRoutine” for subjects in the Routine group and “ScoreIfUsual” for subjects in the Usual group: the one score a real researcher would actually get to see.
8
Estimate the effect. In H7 type After the study. Then: H8 Routine group mean with I8 =AVERAGEIF(F2:F25,"Routine",G2:G25); H9 Usual group mean with I9 =AVERAGEIF(F2:F25,"Usual",G2:G25); H10 Estimated effect (Routine minus Usual) with I10 =I8-I9. Because the data are made up, you can also find the truth: H11 True average effect, all 24 with I11 =AVERAGE(C2:C25)-AVERAGE(D2:D25), and H12 Estimate minus truth with I12 =I10-I11. Save the file.
9
Write the Notes sheet. Click the + beside the sheet tabs and rename the new sheet Notes. In A1 type your name. In A3, write a careful 2 to 3 sentence conclusion about the routine, using your own numbers (the size of the estimated effect, the direction, how it compares with the true value, and the fact that random assignment supports but does not prove a causal claim). In A4, write one sentence about what your baseline check showed. In A5, write one sentence naming a limit of this study that random assignment cannot fix. Use your own words. To keep a long sentence readable, click the cell and choose Home > Wrap Text.
10
Part B — numeric answers (type into the Canvas text box). Label each answer. B1: the all-subjects baseline mean (I5) to 2 decimals. B2: your two group baseline means and their difference (I2, I3, I4), to 2 decimals, and one sentence saying whether the groups looked balanced to you. B3: your two group means after the study and your estimated effect (I8, I9, I10), to 2 decimals. B4: the true average effect (I11) and your estimate minus truth (I12), to 2 decimals. B5: in Desmos Scientific, the chance that 24 fair coin flips give exactly 12 heads (the chance that a coin-flip assignment would make two equal groups): type 2704156/2^24 and give the answer to 3 decimals and as a percent, and say in one sentence why RAND with sort is a better way to make equal groups than a coin flip for each subject.
11
Part C — short answers (type into the Canvas text box, in your own words). C1: define control group, placebo, and double-blind, and say in one phrase why each is used. C2: for each constructed study, say whether it supports a causal claim about the treatment and why. (i) A coach lets players choose whether to try a new warm-up; the players who chose it ran faster. (ii) A coin flip decides which 20 of 40 volunteer runners do the new warm-up; the new-warm-up group ran faster on average. (iii) Researchers compare the race times of people who report stretching with those who do not. C3: name two problems that random assignment cannot fix, and give a one-sentence example of each.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The workbook has an Experiment sheet and a Notes sheet; the data match the table (sums 650, 848, 694); the random numbers in E are plain values (not formulas); the rows are sorted by E; F has 12 “Routine” and 12 “Usual”; G uses the IF formula; the baseline and outcome means use typed AVERAGEIF formulas.
☐
The baseline check, the estimated effect, and the true effect are computed from your own groups; the answers in the Canvas box match your workbook cells.
☐
The Notes conclusion and the short answers use careful wording such as “supports,” “about,” “in this experiment,” and “estimate.”
☐
Nothing claims that random assignment proves a cause, eliminates every confounder, or guarantees identical groups.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
CriteriaFull creditPartial creditMinimal creditPts
Workbook & numeric answers
6 pts		 Grading note: every student’s random split differs; grade structure and consistency, not a fixed value. Experiment sheet: A2:D25 match the table (sums 650, 848, 694); E2:E25 are plain numbers (not formulas) and the rows are sorted by E; F has 12 “Routine” and 12 “Usual”; G2:G25 is the IF formula; I2, I3, I8, I9 are AVERAGEIF; I4 = I2 − I3; I10 = I8 − I9. Fixed values to check exactly: I5 (all-subjects baseline mean) = 650 ÷ 24 = 27.0833 (27.08); I11 (true average effect) = (848 − 694) ÷ 24 = 154 ÷ 24 = 6.4167 (6.42); (I2 + I3) ÷ 2 must equal 27.0833, so I2 + I3 = 54.1667 for every student. Values that depend on the student’s split (check against their own groups): in 20,000 simulated random splits of these 24 subjects, the baseline difference I4 fell between -3.0 and +3.0 in 95% of splits, and the estimated effect I10 fell between about 2.9 and 9.9 in 95% of splits (average about 6.4, close to the true 6.42). A value outside these ranges happens for about 1 student in 20 from an honest random split, so do not penalize it by itself: confirm 12/12 groups and that the means recompute from their own F column. A baseline difference near 0 does not mean the student did anything special, and one far from 0 does not mean the method failed. Part B: B1 27.08; B2 consistent with I2, I3, I4 (signed difference) and a sentence that is honest about balance; B3 consistent with I8, I9, I10; B4 true effect 6.42 and I12 = I10 − 6.42 (signed); B5: 2,704,156 ÷ 16,777,216 = 0.161, about 16.1%, with a sentence that a coin flip per subject often produces unequal groups (about 84% of the time), whereas RAND with sort always gives exactly 12 and 12. One block missing or a few values off because of a slip (random numbers still formulas, sorted before freezing so groups changed, groups not 12/12, AVERAGEIF range off by a row, mean computed on the wrong column, a sign error in a difference), or one or two Part B answers wrong. Two or more parts missing, groups chosen by hand rather than by RAND, or numbers that do not come from the student’s own groups. 6 pts
Work shown & reasoning
4 pts		 Notes: A3 reports the student’s own estimated effect (I10), says it is positive (the routine group scored higher) and about how large, compares it with the true value 6.42 (the estimate misses by chance, and the recorded spread over many random splits is about 3 to 10), and says random assignment supports a causal claim as evidence, not proof; A4 compares the baseline group means honestly (small differences are expected from chance; random assignment balances on average); A5 names a valid limit (for example: only these volunteers took part, so it may not apply to everyone; a measurement problem; dropout; a small study; the quiz measures only one kind of memory). Part C: C1 control group = the comparison group that does not get the treatment (so the effect has something to be compared with); placebo = a look-alike with no active part (so belief and attention are equal in both groups); double-blind = neither subjects nor the staff measuring outcomes know the group (so expectations and hopes do not change the results). C2 (i) no: players chose, so keenness or fitness may differ (confounding), observational comparison; (ii) yes, it supports a causal claim for runners like these volunteers (random assignment balances other variables on average), worded as evidence; (iii) no: observational, stretchers may differ in training, age, and so on. C3 any two of: bad measurement (a faulty stopwatch gives bad data in both groups), dropout (people leaving unevenly unbalances the groups), an unrepresentative sample (volunteers only, so limited generalization), very small groups (chance imbalance), expectation effects (needs placebo and blinding). Credit two correct problems with an example each. Correct numbers, but the Notes conclusion lacks the size or direction of the effect, says “proves” or “eliminates,” or one of C1 to C3 is missing or partly wrong. Bare numbers with no reasoning, or a claim that random assignment guarantees equal groups or proves a cause left standing. 4 pts
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 32.2 — Randomization Workbook
Upload your Excel workbook (.xlsx) as a file, and type your Part B and Part C answers in the text box. Label each answer (B1, B2, and so on).
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Optima Academy Online
