PROBABILITY & STATISTICS HONORS
Quarter / Module
Q4 · Module 11
Sampling & Study Design
Lesson
Lesson 32.3
Paired Lesson
Design-a-Study Workshop: From a Vague Question to a Plan
Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 32.3
Assignment 32.3 — Design a Study
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Turning a question into a design, and claiming only what the design earned
Three auto-graded warm-ups · one written one-page design
Covers: choosing between a sample survey, an observational study, and an experiment; explanatory and response variables; sampling plans; random assignment; bias, confounding, and nonresponse; and writing an honest statement of what the study can and cannot show.
Lesson focus: Design-a-Study Workshop: From a Vague Question to a Plan
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (3 pts, auto-graded): three multiple-choice warm-ups. Part B (7 pts, teacher-scored with the rubric below): a one-page study design, typed in the Canvas text box, for one of four prompts. All scenarios are constructed (made up). Use Desmos or Excel for any arithmetic. You do not need to upload a workbook.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Is this design fair to the people in it, fair to the question, and honest about what it cannot show?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
Classify the study. A made-up researcher takes 60 volunteers and uses a random number generator to place 30 of them in a group that practices a new breathing routine for a month and 30 in a group that does not. She then compares the two groups’ stress scores. What kind of study is this?
(a) A sample survey
(b) An observational study
(c) An experiment
(d) A census
2
Why observational? Which is the best reason to choose an observational study instead of an experiment?
(a) Observational studies prove cause more strongly than experiments do.
(b) Assigning people to the condition would be unethical or impossible, so we study groups as they already are.
(c) Observational studies do not need a population.
(d) Observational studies have no confounding variables.
3
Name the variables. A made-up study asks whether students who drink more water during the school day have fewer headaches. Which pairing is correct?
(a) Explanatory: headaches per week. Response: liters of water per day.
(b) Explanatory: the school. Response: headaches per week.
(c) Explanatory: the number of students. Response: liters of water per day.
(d) Explanatory: liters of water per day. Response: headaches per week.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (7 PTS)
4
Design a study. Choose one of the four prompts below and write a one-page study design (about 300 to 450 words) in the text box. Say which prompt you chose. Use the eight checklist questions from the lesson as your headings, in order, and end with a short paragraph on what the study can and cannot conclude.
Prompt A — Compost and beans. The made-up Cedar Lane Middle School garden club has 36 bean seedlings of the same variety and wants to know whether adding compost to the soil makes bean plants grow taller in 6 weeks. The greenhouse has two shelves: a bright shelf by the window and a shaded shelf by the door. Each shelf holds 18 pots.

Prompt B — Walking and attendance. The made-up Ridgeview High (900 students) wonders whether students who walk or bike to school have fewer absences than students who ride in a car or bus. The school keeps attendance records for every student, and a survey could ask how each student usually gets to school. Decide how to study this, and be careful about what you claim.

Prompt C — The vacant lot. The made-up town of Willow Run has 8,000 households in four neighborhoods of 3,000, 2,500, 1,500, and 1,000 households. The town council has a vacant lot and wants to know whether households would prefer a new playground or a new skate area. A complete address list exists for each neighborhood.

Prompt D — Flashcards. The made-up Delmar High has an app that makes vocabulary flashcards. 120 sophomores (40 from each of three English classes) have volunteered to try it for two weeks. The teachers want to know whether students who study with the app score higher on a vocabulary quiz than students who study the usual way.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA · YOUR CHECKLIST BEFORE YOU SUBMIT
☐
Question and aim: I stated the question in one sentence and said whether I want to describe, find a link, or find a cause.
☐
Population and sampling: I named exactly who or what I am speaking about, and I gave a specific plan for choosing them (with the numbers adding up).
☐
Variables and design: I listed the explanatory and response variables with units or categories, and I chose survey, observational study, or experiment and said why.
☐
Assignment: if my aim is cause, I described random assignment, a comparison group, blinding (or why not), replication, and blocks if needed. If I did not assign anything, I said why not.
☐
Risks: I named at least two risks (bias, confounding, nonresponse, measurement error) and what my design does about each.
☐
Limits: my last paragraph says who the claim covers, whether it supports cause, and one thing the study leaves open. It does not claim more than the design earned.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Part A: auto-graded
3 pts		 1 pt per item. Answer key: (1) c; (2) b; (3) d. Not applicable: each item is right or wrong. Not applicable. 3 pts
Part B: population and sampling plan
1 pt		 Names the population exactly and gives a specific, workable plan for choosing subjects (for example a stratified random sample with the allocation shown and adding to n, or all available subjects with an honest note that they are not a random sample). The plan fits the prompt. (0.5 pt) Population or plan is vague (“ask some students”), or arithmetic is missing or does not add up. No population named, or a plan with no way of choosing subjects. 1 pt
Part B: variables and design type with justification
2 pts		 Names the explanatory and response variables with units or categories, and chooses survey, observational study, or experiment with a reason tied to the aim (describe, link, or cause) and, where relevant, to ethics or practicality. Variables are named but lack units, or the design is correct but the reason is thin (“because it is an experiment”), or one variable is mislabeled. Design does not match the aim (for example a survey for a cause question) or no variables are identified. 2 pts
Part B: assignment plan, or the reason it is observational
1 pt		 For a cause question: random assignment with the procedure (for example RAND and sort), a comparison group, and at least two of blinding, replication, and blocks. For a survey or observational design: a clear statement that nothing is assigned and why, plus what is measured instead (other factors). (0.5 pt) Says “randomly assign” with no procedure or no comparison group, or says nothing is assigned without saying why. No assignment plan and no reason. 1 pt
Part B: bias, confounding, and how it is addressed
1 pt		 Names at least two relevant risks (bias, confounding, nonresponse, measurement error, or reverse direction) and, for each, says specifically what the design does about it. (0.5 pt) Names one risk with a fix, or names two or more risks without saying what the design does. No risks named, or the only fix is “use a bigger sample.” 1 pt
Part B: honest limits statement
2 pts		 Says who the claim covers, whether the design supports cause or only a link, and at least one thing the study leaves open. The strength of the claim matches the design (for example, no cause claim from an observational design; no generalizing beyond the subjects if they were not randomly chosen). Mostly honest but overreaches in one place (for example generalizes to everyone from volunteers), or is correct but omits what is left open. Claims cause from an observational design, claims the result applies to everyone from a non-random group, or gives no limits. 2 pts
Total (3 + 1 + 2 + 1 + 1 + 2): 10 pts
▶  Teacher exemplar: model response for Prompt A
Model response for Prompt A (a strong 7-point design).
1. Question and aim. Does adding compost to the soil make bean plants grow taller in 6 weeks? Aim: cause.
2. Population and sampling. Bean plants of this variety grown in the Cedar Lane greenhouse. I will use all 36 available seedlings, which are the same variety and about the same size. They are not a random sample of all bean plants, so I will limit my claim.
3. Variables and design. Explanatory: soil type (compost added or not). Response: plant height at 6 weeks, in centimeters, measured from the soil to the tip of the tallest leaf. Other variables: light, water, pot size, seedling size. I will run a randomized experiment, because I want to know about cause and I can assign soil to pots with no harm to anyone.
4. Assignment. Block by shelf, because the bright and shaded shelves get different light. On each shelf I number the 18 pots 1 to 18, put =RAND() beside each, freeze the numbers, and sort. The first 9 pots on each shelf get compost soil and the other 9 get the usual soil, giving 18 pots per treatment (replication). The usual-soil pots are the comparison group: same seeds, same pots, same water, same schedule. A classmate who measures heights sees only pot codes, so the measurement is blind.
5. Risks. Light differences could be confounded with compost, so blocks give each shelf 9 and 9. Hidden differences between seedlings are spread across groups by random assignment. A measurer who hopes for tall compost plants could measure generously, so the measurer is blind. A seedling that dies is recorded and reported, not quietly dropped.
6. Conclusion. If the compost pots end up taller by more than random assignment alone would likely produce, I can conclude that compost caused extra growth for these bean plants, in this greenhouse, over six weeks. I cannot say it works for other plants, outdoors, or for a longer time, because the 36 seedlings were not a random sample, and 36 is a small study.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 32.3 — Design a Study
Enter the three multiple-choice letters for Part A, and type your one-page design for Part B in the text box. Start with the prompt letter you chose. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company
PROBABILITY & STATISTICS HONORS
Quarter / Module
Q4 · Module 11
Sampling & Study Design
Type
VR Module Lab
Optima · Week 32 · the module's capstone in headset
Time in headset
25–35 minutes
One session, one submission
Points
Rubric-scored
15 pts
Module 11 · VR Lab
The Sampling Orchard
VR Lab · 15 pts · rubric-graded
🥼 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
This module's virtue is responsibility: whoever picks a sample owns what it says about the whole. Today you walk an orchard. In the Location, one hundred made-up apple trees stand in ten rows of ten, and each tree carries a sign with the number of apples on it. The orchard's true average number of apples per tree is sealed on a whiteboard, and you will not open it until you have made three estimates. You pick ten trees by convenience (the ten nearest the gate), ten by a systematic plan (every tenth tree from a random start), and ten by simple random sampling (random tags from a card). You record the three estimates on a Whiteboard IFX method-comparison board, open the seal, and compute each estimate's error. You finish with a short spatial recording that names which method came closest in your run, says why one run proves little, and states one limit. The orchard, the trees, and every apple count are constructed (made up). They are not a real farm.
📋 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset with Optima installed (desktop Optima works if a headset is unavailable, but walking the rows and seeing how the orchard changes from the gate to the far end is the heart of this lab).
▶
Your Week 30, 31, and 32 notes (notebook page): population versus sample, parameter versus statistic, the seven sampling methods and which are random, bias versus sampling variation, and why random selection protects against a lopsided sample. Review them before you put the headset on; re-reading inside a headset is hard.
▶
To do at your desk before the session: the orchard has N = 100 trees and you will pick n = 10. For a systematic sample, the step between picks is k = N ÷ n = 100 ÷ 10 = 10. Write the error formula you will use all session: error = estimate − true value (positive means too high, negative means too low). Check that you can compute the mean of ten whole numbers on your calculator without a mistake.
▶
A calculator or the Desmos scientific calculator, and about 35 uninterrupted minutes.
🚀 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (preferred) or desktop Optima
Session type: Persistent Session (your work saves between visits)
Session ID: [SESSION ID — teacher enters before publishing]
Location: [LOCATION NAME — an open, flat-floored Location with room for an 18 m by 18 m orchard and a gate area; teacher enters before publishing]
On arrival: Find the Whiteboard IFX at the orchard gate labeled “The Sampling Orchard — start here.” Beyond the gate, one hundred trees stand in 10 rows of 10. Row 1 is the row right inside the gate, and Row 10 is the far end. Every tree has a sign showing its tree number (T1 to T100, counted left to right along each row, starting with Row 1) and the number of apples on it. Near the gate wait the Draw Cards (cards A to H, each with a random start and ten random tags), a Whiteboard IFX labeled “Method-Comparison Board” for your numbers, and a sealed whiteboard labeled “Orchard truth — open after step 4.” Do not open it early: the whole lab depends on you not knowing the true average until your three estimates are written down.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Pick up your Draw Card and harvest by convenience. Your teacher assigns you a card letter on the Canvas page for this assignment (if none is assigned, pick any one and write its letter on your submission). Then do the easy thing: stand at the gate and take the ten trees nearest the gate, which is all of Row 1 (T1 to T10). Read the apples off each sign, write the ten counts on the Method-Comparison Board, and compute the sample mean. Call this your convenience estimate.
2
Harvest systematically. Your Draw Card gives a random start from 1 to 10. Take that tree, and then every 10th tree after it (start, start + 10, start + 20, and so on up to the 90s and 100), ten trees in all. Write the tree numbers and counts on the board and compute the mean. Then stop and look at where you walked: which column of the orchard did all ten of your trees land in? Say aloud why. (Each row is 10 trees wide and your step was 10, so every pick fell in the same position in its row.) Write one sentence on the board: what could go wrong with this plan if something about the orchard changes from column to column, such as a ditch or a shady edge?
3
Harvest by simple random sampling. Your Draw Card also lists ten random tags, drawn in advance from the numbers 1 to 100 with no repeats. Walk to each of those ten trees (they will be scattered across the orchard), read the signs, and write the counts on the board. Compute the mean. Notice that your ten trees are not all in one row and not all in one column.
4
Fill the Method-Comparison Board. The board has three rows, one per method, with columns method / trees picked / sample mean / error. Fill in the first three columns for convenience, systematic, and simple random. Leave the error column blank for now. Before you open the seal, write one sentence predicting which of your three estimates will be closest to the truth, and why.
5
Open the seal and compute the errors. Open the sealed whiteboard. It posts the orchard's true mean number of apples per tree (the parameter) and the reference numbers listed there. For each of your three methods compute error = estimate − true, to one decimal, and write it in the error column with its sign. Circle the method with the smallest error, ignoring sign, in your run.
6
Read the pooled results. The sealed whiteboard also posts what happens beyond your one run: the mean you get from convenience with the ten nearest trees and with the thirty nearest (Rows 1 to 3); the systematic mean for each of the ten possible starts; and how far the means of many simple random samples of ten typically scatter around the truth. Write three short statements on the board: (a) why the convenience error is the same for every student (the same ten trees every time) and which direction it points; (b) whether taking 30 trees by convenience fixed it, and why or why not; (c) how your systematic start compares with the other nine starts, and why a random start still helps even though one start sits in one column.
7
Capture the board. Stand where one snapshot catches the Method-Comparison Board with all three rows (trees, means, and errors) readable, and the orchard behind it. Take it and check it before moving on; every number must be readable. If not, retake it from closer.
8
Narrate. Stand where the orchard is in view and start a spatial recording. Speak for 60 to 90 seconds, in your own words, covering all three: (a) which method had the smallest error in your run, with your three errors as evidence; (b) why one run proves little: for example, a random method can still land on a lucky or unlucky set of trees, so one close estimate does not prove a method is good, while a method with a built-in tilt, such as convenience here, is off in the same direction every time; and (c) one limit, such as that ten random trees can still miss, that this orchard has only 100 trees and one made-up pattern, or that sampling variation means a different random draw gives a different answer. Use your own numbers. Do not read your sticky notes aloud; look at the orchard and tell what you see. Stop the recording. Then leave the Draw Cards, tree signs, and the sealed board as you found them, so the next student finds the orchard as it was built.
💬 OPTIONAL TWIST
If you have time, take a second simple random sample: pick ten new tags with a calculator or spreadsheet (no repeats), harvest those ten trees, and compute the mean and its error. Is it close to your first random mean? Say in one sentence what that tells you about sampling variation. Not required, and not graded unless it is in your recording.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Canvas Assignment Name: VR Lab — The Sampling Orchard
Upload two things: (1) your snapshot from step 7 (image file) showing the Method-Comparison Board with all three methods, trees picked, sample means, and errors; and (2) your spatial recording from step 8 (60–90 seconds of narration), shared as a link or file exactly as your teacher shows on the Canvas page for this assignment.
Below them, in the text entry box, write one line giving your numbers: your card letter and random start; your three sample means; the true mean you read from the sealed board; your three errors; and the column your systematic trees landed in. Then add one sentence: which method had the smallest error in your run, and why that does not settle which method is best.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment. · Estimated time: 25–35 minutes in headset.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
CriteriaFull creditPartial creditMinimal creditPts
Accuracy of the estimates and errors
5 pts		 All three sample means match the key for the student's card (convenience 59.90 for everyone; systematic and simple random per the card, within 0.1); the true mean (41.40) is recorded; each error is estimate minus true with the correct sign, to one decimal; and the column of the systematic trees is named correctly. One part wrong while the rest is correct: for example, one mean miscomputed, errors computed as true minus estimate (every sign flips), or the wrong column named. Several parts wrong or missing: most means or errors incorrect, no true mean, or no errors recorded. 5 pts
Evidence of using all three methods correctly
5 pts		 The snapshot shows the Method-Comparison Board with three rows (convenience, systematic, simple random), the correct trees picked for each (Row 1; start, start + 10, and so on; the card's ten tags), the sample means, and the errors; the board text shows the column sentence and the pooled-results statements about convenience and about the n = 30 sample. Most of the work is visible but one element is missing: one method's trees not listed or listed wrongly, the error column blank, or the pooled statements absent or without a reason. Little visible evidence that all three methods were used, or a snapshot that cannot be read. 5 pts
Quality of the narration, including the limit
5 pts		 The narration is in the student's own words and uses their own numbers: it names the method with the smallest error in their run and gives the three errors as evidence, explains why one run proves little (random draws vary; a lucky or unlucky draw is possible; convenience is off in the same direction every time), and names a specific, true limit. A correct narration that is generic or read from notes, misses one of the three parts, or gives a vague limit (“it might be wrong”). Narration missing most parts, much under about 45 seconds, or no evident engagement with the orchard. 5 pts
Total: 15 pts
👋 FACILITATOR NOTE
Stage the Location before publishing. Orchard: one hundred tree IFX in 10 rows of 10 on a flat floor, 2 m apart in both directions, so the orchard is 18 m by 18 m between outer trees. Use x = 2 × (column − 1) m across and z = 2 × (row − 1) m away from the gate, so Row 1 is at z = 0 and Row 10 is at z = 18 m; tree number T = 10 × (row − 1) + column. Gate: a gate or arch IFX at about x = 9 m, z = −3 m, with a low fence line along z = −1.5 m; the start whiteboard stands beside it, labeled “The Sampling Orchard — start here,” with the legend (“100 made-up trees; 10 rows of 10; Row 1 is nearest the gate; tree number = 10 × (row − 1) + column; made-up data”). Signs: every tree has a locked sign or text IFX reading its tree number and its apple count, as in the table below (for example, “T1: 60 apples”); if you want fruit to see, add a small apple-cluster IFX scaled by count, but the sign is what students record. Draw Cards: eight locked sticky notes or small boards, A to H, each showing one line of the card table below (the same for every student, so give each student a different letter in Canvas; eight letters cover eight students, and with a larger class reuse letters and say so). Method-Comparison Board: a Whiteboard IFX near the gate pre-drawn with three rows (Convenience, Systematic, Simple random) and four columns (method / trees picked / sample mean / error). Sealed truth board: a second Whiteboard IFX with a cover sticky note “Orchard truth — open after step 4” (the honor system is enough); post on it: true mean 41.40 apples per tree; convenience, n = 10 (Row 1), mean 59.90; convenience, n = 30 (Rows 1 to 3), mean 55.67; the ten systematic means by start (table below); and the spread of simple random sample means (SD about 3.8 apples over 1,000 draws of ten trees, middle range about 33.9 to 48.9). Confirm the IFX names and sizes, how to put text on a sign IFX, how to cover a whiteboard, and where to start and stop a spatial recording against the current IFX library and ENGAGE app before publishing; we have not verified these in ENGAGE. The data are constructed (made up): a 100-tree orchard with a gradient (trees near the gate carry more apples), a mild column pattern (the first and last columns carry a little less than the middle), and a few apples of random scatter, generated once and fixed. But any one start is one column, and the columns differ (the first and last columns are lower because of the made-up pattern). Spread of the ten start means: SD 2.35, range 36.50 to 44.70 (best start 4, error −0.3; worst start 10, error −4.9). Over 1,000 simple random samples of ten trees (fixed seed, drawn without replacement), the sample means average 41.55 (true 41.40), with SD 3.77 (check: the orchard's SD of 12.26 gives 3.70 after the finite-population correction) and range 27.80 to 51.80; about 95% of the draws fall within two such SDs of the truth. So a simple random draw is centered on the truth but can miss by several apples; the eight cards' simple random means range from 39.30 to 44.40. What to expect in the narration. Which method wins in a student’s run depends on their card; accept any method named if it matches their own errors. Do not accept “random is always closest” or “convenience is closest because it is easiest.” Accept limits such as: ten random trees can still miss; N = 100 is small and the orchard is one made-up pattern; the answer would change with another random draw (sampling variation); one student’s run cannot show a method is best. Common sticking points: computing true minus estimate (every sign flips); calling Row 1 a random sample because it “looks mixed”; saying the systematic sample “is biased” because it sits in one column (a random start makes it unbiased over starts, even though each start is one column); and treating the n = 30 convenience sample as an improvement because it is bigger. What to demo: reading a tree sign, writing on a Whiteboard IFX, lifting a sticky note, and starting and stopping a spatial recording. If a student finishes early, ask what would change if the trees were numbered down columns instead of across rows (then k = 10 would pick one row, the row means range from 22.10 to 59.90, and a systematic sample could miss by far more).

Lesson
Lesson 33.1
Paired Lesson
Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem
Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 33.1
Assignment 33.1 — Sampling Distributions and the CLT
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Telling the three piles apart, computing a standard error, and finding the chance that a sample mean or proportion lands in a range
Seven auto-graded items · one short written item
Covers: parent, sample, and sampling distributions; what the Central Limit Theorem does and does not say; standard error for a mean; how sample size changes the standard error; probabilities for a sample mean and a sample proportion with NORM.DIST.
Lesson focus: Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (7 pts, auto-graded): five multiple-choice questions and two numeric answers. Part B (3 pts, teacher-scored): one short written response. All scenarios are constructed (made up). Items 6 and 7 are best done in Excel with NORM.DIST, as in the lesson; a calculator with a normal table also works. You do not need to upload a workbook.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
If one sample gives one number, how do we know how far a number like it could have strayed?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
Describe the pile. A made-up town has 40,000 adult commute times, and their histogram is strongly skewed to the right. A planner draws many random samples of 50 commuters and records the mean of each sample. Which description fits the histogram of those sample means?
(a) Strongly skewed to the right, just like the individual commute times
(b) Approximately bell-shaped, centered near the population mean, and narrower than the histogram of individual commute times
(c) Uniform, with every mean about equally likely
(d) Bell-shaped, but wider than the histogram of individual commute times
2
Name the distribution. Which one is the sampling distribution of the sample mean?
(a) The histogram of the 50 values in one random sample
(b) The histogram of every individual value in the population
(c) The distribution of the sample mean across many random samples of the same size from the same population
(d) The single mean computed from one sample
3
Standard error. A made-up population has a standard deviation of σ = 12. Random samples of n = 36 are drawn and the mean of each is recorded. What is the standard error of the sample mean?
(a) 2
(b) 6
(c) 12
(d) 0.33
4
What the CLT says. A classmate says, “I took one sample of 200 very lopsided waiting times, so by the Central Limit Theorem the histogram of my 200 waiting times will be bell-shaped.” What is wrong with this?
(a) Nothing; 200 is larger than 30, so the data become normal
(b) The Central Limit Theorem only applies to proportions, not to waiting times
(c) A sample of 200 is too small for the theorem to apply to anything
(d) The theorem is about the distribution of sample means over many samples, not about the data in one sample; her 200 waiting times will still look lopsided
5
Sample size. With random samples of size 25 from a made-up population, the standard error of the sample mean is 4. About what sample size would cut the standard error to 2?
(a) 50
(b) 100
(c) 200
(d) 625
6
Compute a probability for a sample mean. The heights of a made-up bean plant variety are bell-shaped with mean μ = 30 cm and standard deviation σ = 6 cm. A random sample of n = 36 plants is measured. What is the probability that the sample mean is greater than 31.5 cm? Find the standard error first (it is used in place of σ), then use =1-NORM.DIST(31.5,30,SE,TRUE) in Excel with your standard error in place of SE. Give your answer as a percent to one decimal place; enter a number from 0 to 100 (no % sign).
7
Compute a probability for a sample proportion. In a made-up town, 40% of households compost (p = 0.40). A random sample of n = 200 households is chosen. First check that np and n(1 − p) are both at least 10. Then find the probability that the sample proportion who compost is greater than 0.45. In Excel, use the standard error √(p(1 − p) ÷ n) as the third item of NORM.DIST. Give your answer as a percent to one decimal place; enter a number from 0 to 100 (no % sign).
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (3 PTS)
8
Application: the garden club. A made-up community garden club wants to estimate the average height of the bean plants in the town’s gardens. The heights are bell-shaped with mean μ = 30 cm and standard deviation σ = 6 cm. Member A will measure random samples of 9 plants. Member B will measure random samples of 36 plants.

In three to five sentences, write: (a) the standard error of the sample mean for each member, with the formula you used; (b) which member’s sample mean is more likely to land within 2 cm of 30 cm, and why; and (c) one sentence explaining, for a younger student, the difference between the histogram of the heights in one sample and the sampling distribution of the sample mean.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I asked, for each question, which pile of numbers it is about: the individuals, one sample, or the sample means.
☐
My answers to items 6 and 7 used the standard error, not the standard deviation of individuals, and I checked the condition for the proportion.
☐
My written answer shows the formula and the two standard errors, not only the final choice of member.
☐
My explanation in (c) says that the sampling distribution is made of sample means, not of the plants themselves.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Part A: auto-graded
7 pts		 1 pt per item. Answer key: (1) b; (2) c; (3) a; (4) d; (5) b; (6) 6.7; (7) 7.4. Items 6 and 7 are numeric percents. Item 6: SE = 6 ÷ √36 = 1, z = 1.5, probability 0.0668 (accept 6.6 to 6.8). Item 7: np = 80, n(1 − p) = 120, SE = √(0.24 ÷ 200) = 0.0346, z = 1.44, probability 0.0745 (accept 7.3 to 7.5). Not applicable: each item is right or wrong. Not applicable. 7 pts
Part B: standard errors
1 pt		 Gives SE = 6 ÷ √9 = 2 cm for Member A and SE = 6 ÷ √36 = 1 cm for Member B, with the formula σ ÷ √n shown or named. Gets one standard error right, or gives both values with no formula, or uses σ = 6 for both. Gives no standard errors, or divides by n instead of √n for both. 1 pt
Part B: which member is likelier to land within 2 cm
1 pt		 Chooses Member B (n = 36) and gives a reason tied to the smaller standard error (1 cm versus 2 cm: the sample means of B are less spread out around 30). A student who adds the numbers, about 68% for A and about 95% for B (within 1 and within 2 standard errors; exact values 68.3% and 95.4%), earns full credit, but numbers are not required. Chooses B with no reason, or with a reason that is only “bigger samples are better.” Chooses A, or gives no choice. 1 pt
Part B: one sample versus the sampling distribution
1 pt		 Says in one clear sentence that a histogram of one sample shows the heights of that sample’s plants (individuals), while the sampling distribution is the pile of sample means from many samples, and is narrower and more bell-shaped. Describes only one of the two piles, or says “the sampling distribution is bigger / more accurate” without saying what it is made of. Treats them as the same thing, or says the data themselves become normal. 1 pt
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 33.1 — Sampling Distributions and the CLT
Enter the five multiple-choice letters and the two numeric answers for Part A, and type your Part B response in the text box. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Margin of Error: How Far Can a Poll Miss?
Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 33.2
Assignment 33.2 — Read the Poll, Plan the Poll
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Computing a margin of error, planning how many people to ask, and reading a poll without overclaiming
Eight auto-graded items · one Excel formula answer · one short AI-check item
Covers: the safe rule 1 ÷ √n; the formula 1.96 × √(p(1 − p) ÷ n); four times the sample, half the margin; sample size for a target margin; clear lead versus too close to call; what the margin does not cover; the meaning of “plus or minus.”
Lesson focus: Margin of Error: How Far Can a Poll Miss?
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (8 pts, auto-graded): seven multiple-choice questions and one numeric answer. Part B (2 pts, quick teacher check): one typed Excel formula and one short AI-check response. All polls, percents, and candidates are constructed (made up). A calculator or Excel is fine for the arithmetic; use the safe rule 100 ÷ √n points unless an item says to use the formula. You do not need to upload a workbook.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
How far can a fair poll miss by chance, how many people does it take to shrink that, and what can a margin of error never fix?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
Safe rule. A made-up poll surveys 625 randomly chosen residents. Using the safe rule 100 ÷ √n, what is the margin of error?
(a) 25 points
(b) 6.25 points
(c) 4 points
(d) 1.6 points
2
Four times the people. A made-up poll of 400 people has a margin of error of about 5 points. The pollster wants the margin to be about 2.5 points. About how many people should be surveyed?
(a) 800
(b) 1,600
(c) 2,000
(d) 3,200
3
The formula. A made-up poll of n = 900 finds that 30% (p = 0.30) favor a plan. Use the formula 1.96 × √(p(1 − p) ÷ n). What is the margin of error?
(a) About 1.5 points
(b) About 3.3 points
(c) About 6.0 points
(d) About 3.0 points
4
Is the lead real? A made-up poll of 1,000 people finds Candidate Lee at 52% and Candidate Park at 48%. Use the safe rule and the “lead versus twice the margin” rule of thumb. Which statement is best?
(a) The race is too close to call: the 4-point lead is smaller than about twice the margin of error (about 6.3 points)
(b) Lee is clearly ahead, because 52 is more than 48
(c) Park is clearly ahead, because the margin of error is subtracted from Lee
(d) Lee is clearly ahead, because the margin of error (about 3.2 points) is smaller than the 4-point lead
5
Is the lead real? A made-up poll of 400 people finds Candidate Lee at 57% and Candidate Park at 43%. Using the safe rule and the same rule of thumb, which statement is best?
(a) The race is too close to call, because the margin of error is 5 points
(b) A poll can never show a clear lead
(c) Lee has a clear lead: the 14-point gap is larger than about twice the margin (10 points)
(d) Lee’s lead cannot be trusted, because a poll of 400 people is always too small
6
What the margin does not cover. A made-up radio station invites listeners to phone in. Of 2,500 callers, 64% support a new stadium. The station reports “plus or minus 2 points.” Which is the best reading?
(a) The city’s support is certainly between 62% and 66%
(b) The margin of error should be larger, because callers are a small share of the city
(c) With 2,500 callers the poll must be accurate, because large samples are never biased
(d) The “2 points” describes only chance variation among callers; because callers chose themselves, the poll could be badly biased, and the margin of error cannot repair that
7
Reading “plus or minus.” A made-up poll reports 46% support with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 points. Which statement best describes what the margin of error means?
(a) There is a 4% chance that the 46% figure is wrong
(b) If many polls were taken the same way, about 95 of every 100 would land within 4 points of the true percent
(c) The true percent is certainly between 42% and 50%
(d) Four percent of the people refused to answer
8
Plan the sample. A made-up city office wants a margin of error of no more than 4.5 percentage points. Use n = (100 ÷ m)² with m = 4.5, and round up to a whole person. How many people should it survey? Enter a whole number.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (1 PT EACH)
9
Excel formula. In a worksheet, a poll’s sample proportion (as a decimal) is in cell B2 and the sample size is in cell C2. Type the exact Excel formula that gives the formula margin of error, 1.96 × √(p(1 − p) ÷ n), as a proportion. (Typed as you would type it in a cell, beginning with =.)
10
Check an AI. A made-up AI tool was asked about a poll of 400 randomly chosen people. It replied: “The margin of error is 5%, which means there is a 5% chance the poll result is wrong. Because 400 is a large sample, the poll cannot be biased.” In two or three sentences, say what the AI got right, and correct what it got wrong. Use the ideas about 95 of 100 polls and what the margin does not cover.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I used the safe rule 100 ÷ √n and the formula for the right items, and checked each answer for size.
☐
I remembered that four times the people gives half the margin, and that sample sizes are rounded up.
☐
For the lead items I compared the gap with about twice the margin, and called a small gap too close to call.
☐
My answers to items 6, 7, and 10 say that the margin covers chance variation only, not bias or bad wording.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Part A: auto-graded
8 pts		 1 pt per item. Answer key: (1) c; (2) b; (3) d; (4) a; (5) c; (6) d; (7) b; (8) 494. Item 8 is numeric (100 ÷ 4.5 = 22.22…; squared is 493.8…; rounded up is 494). Accept 494 only; 493 or 493.8 is not credited because the sample size must be rounded up to a whole person. Not applicable: each item is right or wrong. Not applicable. 8 pts
Part B: Excel formula (item 9)
1 pt		 Types =1.96*SQRT(B2*(1-B2)/C2). Accept equivalent forms, such as 1.96*SQRT(B2*(1-B2)/C2) with absolute references, =1.96*(B2*(1-B2)/C2)^0.5, or 1.96 written as NORM.S.INV(0.975). Right idea with a small slip: omits the leading equals sign, or leaves out the 1.96, or writes SQRT(B2*(1-B2))/C2 (square root applied to the wrong part). Uses 1/SQRT(C2) only (the safe rule), or multiplies p by n, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Part B: AI check (item 10)
1 pt		 Gets both parts right. Credits the AI for the number: about 5 percentage points (1 ÷ √400 = 0.05). Corrects at least two errors: (a) the margin is a distance, not a 5% chance of being wrong; it means about 95 of 100 such polls land within 5 points, so about 5 in 100 miss by more by chance alone; (b) a large sample does not prevent bias, and the margin of error covers only chance variation (not bias, nonresponse, or wording). Corrects only one of the two errors (for example, explains the 95-in-100 meaning but says nothing about bias, or the reverse), or corrects both but gives no credit for the correct 5-point figure. Agrees with the AI, or says only that 400 is “too small” or that the AI is “confusing.” 1 pt
Total: 10 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

Answer items 1 to 8 in Canvas (seven multiple-choice letters and one whole number), then type your Excel formula for item 9 and your short response for item 10 in the text boxes. You do not need to upload a workbook.

4
Intervals: link to the polls. Each poll gets a block of three rows (Poll 1 in rows 2 to 4, Poll 2 in rows 5 to 7, Poll 3 in rows 8 to 10, Poll 4 in rows 11 to 13). In the first row of a block, type three formulas that point at that poll’s row on the Polls sheet. For Poll 1, in A2 type =Polls!A2, in B2 type =Polls!D2, and in C2 type =Polls!E2. In the next two rows of the block, link to the cell above: in A3 type =A2, in B3 type =B2, and in C3 type =C2; then select A3:C3 and drag the fill handle down one row. 6

A made-up random sample of 49 sunflower seedlings has a mean height of 29.6 cm, and the population standard deviation is known (made up) to be 6 cm. In A1 type Sample size n and in B1 type 49; in A2 Sample mean and B2 29.6; in A3 Known sigma and B3 6; in A4 Standard error and B4 =B3/SQRT(B1). In A6 to F6 type Level, z*, Margin, Lower, Upper, Width. In A7 to A9 type 0.9, 0.95, 0.99. In row 7 type: B7 =NORM.S.INV((1+A7)/2), C7 =B7*$B$4, D7 =$B$2-C7, E7 =$B$2+C7, F7 =E7-D7. Select B7:F7 and fill down to row 9.
7
Notes sheet. Add a sheet named Notes. In A1 type your name. Then write short answers in your own words (to keep a long sentence readable, click the cell and choose Home > Wrap Text). A3: Using your Intervals sheet, which poll has the narrowest 95% interval and which has the widest? Explain the pattern using the sample sizes (one or two sentences). A4: Poll 4’s 95% interval contains 0.50. In two sentences, say what you can and cannot conclude about whether the town is split exactly 50/50. A5: A classmate says, “Poll 2’s 95% interval means there is a 95% probability that the true share is inside it.” Correct this statement in two sentences, using the idea of the method.
8
Part B — numeric answers (type into the Canvas text box). Label each answer. B1: the lower and upper endpoints of the Poll 2 95% interval, each to 3 decimals. B2: the poll with the widest 95% margin of error and that margin to 4 decimals. B3: the 95% interval for the mean from your Mean sheet, endpoints to 2 decimals. B4: the z* for the 99% level to 3 decimals. B5 (Desmos check): in Desmos Scientific, find Poll 1’s standard error by arithmetic: type 0.44 × 0.56 ÷ 300, then use the square-root button on the result. Report it to 4 decimals and say whether it matches your Polls sheet.

Part C — applied report (type into the Canvas text box). The made-up Hollow Creek town board will vote on a park bond and has asked you for a short written summary of Poll 2. In four to six sentences, write it for the board members, who are not statisticians. Include: (a) the poll result and your 95% interval in plain words; (b) what “95% confident” means (about the method, not a probability for this one interval); (c) what the interval does not cover (one thing from this module such as bias, nonresponse, or wording); and (d) one honest sentence about whether 50% is a plausible value for the park bond’s support.

☐

☐

Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company
PROBABILITY & STATISTICS HONORS
Quarter / Module

Type
VR Solo Activity

Module 12 · VR Solo Activity
The Interval Walk
VR Activity · 5 pts · completion
🥼 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
A poll that reports a number without a margin is only half a report. Lessons 33.2 and 33.3 showed you that a confidence interval has a width, and that the width shrinks as the sample grows, but only like a square root: four times the people for half the width. Today you stop reading that on a page and walk it. A town council in Cedar Landing (a made-up town) is deciding how big a poll to pay for on a made-up question. On the floor of the Location you will find three lanes, one for a poll of 25 people, one for 100 and one for 400. Each lane is marked with the 95% confidence interval that poll would give. You will pace each interval, feel how long it is, and then spend the council’s money: plant a flag at the sample size you would pay for to hit the council’s precision target, and say why. Service here means using what you know to help people decide well with limited money, so you will weigh cost against precision honestly. Every town, number and price in this activity is made up for the exercise; nothing in it comes from a real poll.
📋 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset with Optima installed (desktop Optima works if a headset is unavailable, but walking along each interval and standing at its ends is the point of the activity).
▶
Your Lesson 33.2 and 33.3 notes (notebook page): the margin of error, how it changes with sample size, and what “95% confident” means. Review them before you put the headset on; re-reading inside a headset is hard.
▶
A pencil and notebook beside you for after the session. You will not need a calculator inside the headset: every number you need is posted on a sign.
▶
About 25 uninterrupted minutes.
🚀 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (preferred) or desktop Optima
Session type: Persistent Session (your work saves between visits)
Session ID: [SESSION ID — teacher enters before publishing]
Location: [LOCATION NAME — an open, flat-floored Location with a clear strip of floor at least 5.5 m long and 4 m wide for three marked lanes, plus a Price Board and a Reading Board; teacher enters before publishing]
On arrival: Find the Whiteboard IFX near the spawn point labeled “The Interval Walk — start here.” Ahead of you, three lanes run side by side across the floor, labeled n = 25, n = 100 and n = 400. Each lane has a left post and a right post marking the two ends of its interval, a center post at 50%, and a flag post beside it. To one side stand the Price Board and the Reading Board.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Read the briefing. At the starting whiteboard, read the made-up scenario: Cedar Landing has asked residents one made-up yes-or-no question, and each poll in the three lanes found 50% yes. Each lane shows the 95% confidence interval for that sample size. Read the council’s target (a margin of about plus or minus 5 points, no wider), and read the Price Board: each person polled costs $4, and the council has $2,000.
2
Stand at the center post of the n = 25 lane and read the signs. The left and right posts show the two ends of the interval in percent. The signs also say how the floor is scaled: 0.1 meter for every 1 percentage point. Before you move, guess: is this interval longer or shorter than the lane beside it, and by how much?
3
Pace the interval. Walk from the left post to the right post of the n = 25 lane, counting your steps. Notice where your feet end up compared with the center post. Then walk back and stand at the center post.
4
Pace the other two lanes. Repeat for n = 100 and then n = 400. The sample is four times as large each time. Before the second and third walk, say aloud how long you expect the new interval to be compared with the one you just paced. Then check. You should feel the pattern: four times the people, half the walk.
5
Choose your sample size. Go to the Price Board and read the cost of each of the three polls. Decide which lane the council should pay for to meet its target of about plus or minus 5 points without wasting money. Walk to that lane’s flag post and plant your flag: attach a sticky note to the flag post that reads n = ___ — cost $___ — margin about ___ points.
6
Justify it in one sentence. On the same sticky note (or a second one on the same post), write one sentence on cost against precision. Say what you gave up by not choosing the lane just below yours, and what you would pay for the lane above. Mention the square-root pattern in your own words.
7
Answer at the Reading Board. Create one more sticky note and place it on the Reading Board under the heading “What does 95% confident mean?” Write, in your own words, the correct reading of “I am 95% confident” for one of these intervals. Do not copy a sentence from your notes.
8
Capture the walk. Stand behind the three center posts so a single snapshot catches all three lanes with their interval posts, your flag and its sticky note. Take it and check it; every sticky note must be readable. If anything is too small to read, retake it from closer, or take a second snapshot of the Reading Board.
9
Leave the floor as you found it. Do not move, turn or resize any post, lane marking or board, and do not remove anyone else’s notes or flag. Keep your notes on your own flag post and your own spot on the Reading Board.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Canvas Assignment Name: VR Activity — The Interval Walk
Upload your snapshot (an image file) from step 8, showing the three lanes with their interval posts, your flag and its sticky note, and your 95% sticky note, all readable. You may upload a second snapshot if the Reading Board does not fit in the first.
Below it, in the text entry box, write 2–3 sentences: (1) the sample size you chose, what it would cost, and the margin it gives; and (2) how the interval changed as the sample grew from 25 to 100 to 400, and what that means for the price of getting twice as precise.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment. · Estimated time: 20–30 minutes in headset.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA (COMPLETION)
☐
The snapshot shows all three lanes (n = 25, 100 and 400) with your flag planted at one of them and your sticky note readable.
☐
Your flag note gives the sample size, its cost, and its margin, and one sentence weighing cost against precision.
☐
Your Reading Board sticky note states in your own words what “95% confident” means.
☐
The text entry names your choice and its cost, and says how the interval changed as the sample grew.
☐
You left the floor as you found it (nothing moved, nobody else’s notes or flag removed).
👋 FACILITATOR NOTE
Stage the Location before publishing. Layout: a clear strip of floor with three parallel lanes, each 5.0 m long (the strip covers 25% to 75% on a scale of 0.1 m per percentage point) and 1.0 m apart, with at least 1.5 m clear around the strip so the student can walk end to end. Each lane carries three tall, thin posts (a left post, a center post at 50% and a right post), with a large percent label (digits at least 0.08 m) on each post, and a flag post beside the lane where the student attaches a sticky note. Between the end posts, mark the interval on the floor as a colored strip (a flat bar or a line of floor markers), so the three different lengths are obvious. Use one color for all three; label each lane “n = 25,” “n = 100,” “n = 400.” Put a sign at the strip: “CONSTRUCTED (made up) for this activity. Not real data.” Lock posts, lane markings and boards so students cannot move or resize them. Spacing: the three lanes must fit in one snapshot taken from behind the center posts; if not, change the number of snapshots in the submission text and success criteria together.
Scenario (all made up). Cedar Landing (made up) is a town of 12,000 adults. The council wants to ask one yes-or-no question (made up: “Should the town keep its shared-bike program?”) and must choose how many residents to poll. In each lane the poll result is 50% yes (the scenario fixes the result so the intervals differ only by sample size; 50% also gives the widest interval at each n). Each interval is 50% plus or minus 1.96 × √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ n) × 100 points. Target: a margin of about plus or minus 5 points. Price: $4 per person polled. Budget: $2,000. Post this text on the starting Whiteboard IFX and the prices on the Price Board.

Which n meets the target: n = 400, the only one of the three with a margin (4.9 points) at or under 5. It costs $1,600, inside the $2,000 budget. n = 100 costs $400 but gives plus or minus 9.8, about twice the target, so it misses; n = 25 costs $100 and gives plus or minus 19.6. A student who notes that a sample of 385 would just reach 5.0 points (n = (1.96 × 0.5 ÷ 0.05)² = 384.16, rounded up to 385) shows understanding, but only three lanes exist on the floor, so accept 400 as the answer. Width ratios: full widths are 39.2, 19.6 and 9.8 points, so each step up in sample size (four times as many people) halves the width; from 25 to 400 the width falls by a factor of 4 while the sample grows 16 times. Walk lengths are 3.92 m, 1.96 m and 0.98 m. Cost ratios: $100, $400, $1,600; each halving of the width costs four times as much. A student who asks what it would take to halve 4.9 again should say n = 1,600, margin about 2.45, cost $6,400, which is over the $2,000 budget. Accept any choice justified by the numbers on the board; award full credit if the justification compares cost with precision. If a student chooses n = 100 on cost grounds, the note should say it misses the target.
Correct reading of 95% confident (Reading Board). Accept any wording that says: if the whole polling method were repeated many times with fresh random samples, about 95 out of 100 of the intervals built this way would capture the true percent; the 95% describes the method, not the chance that this one interval holds the truth. Reject: “there is a 95% chance the true value is in this interval,” “95% of residents are in this interval,” and “95% of the sample answers fall in this interval.” Count a note that is correct but clumsy as correct.
Expected common errors: reading the lane length as the margin rather than the full width (the walk is twice the margin); expecting the n = 400 walk to be a quarter as long as n = 100 (it is half); choosing n = 400 “because bigger is better” with no cost reasoning; choosing the cheapest lane without noticing it misses the target; forgetting that the intervals assume a random sample, so no sample size repairs a biased method (Module 11). Common sticking points: not knowing where to attach the flag note, taking a snapshot too far away to read, and moving a post while attaching a note. What to demo: creating a sticky note and attaching it to a post, writing on a Whiteboard IFX, and taking and reviewing a snapshot. If a student finishes early, ask them what the council would pay to get to plus or minus 2.5 points.
Items to confirm in the IFX library and in ENGAGE before publishing (none of this has been tested in ENGAGE): how to build the three floor strips and the posts at the exact lengths above (floor markers, thin boxes or lines); whether the walked distance can be checked in the headset or only paced by feel (the page says to count steps); whether a “flag post” is a separate object or just a post that takes a sticky note; how a sticky note attaches to a post and whether students can create and attach notes in their own Session; whether a persistent Session keeps each student’s notes (if not, use a fresh Session per student and say so in the Session ID line); how to lock posts, markings and boards; whether one snapshot catches all three lanes legibly at your spacing; and whether 20–30 minutes holds. The page asks for one snapshot; adjust if your Location needs a different plan.

Spreadsheet lab · graded on a correct, consistent workbook and careful reasoning
Covers: group summaries with AVERAGE, STDEV.S, and COUNT; the difference of two means (B minus A); the standard error of a difference; an approximate 95% range for the true difference; a cross-check with the resampling interactive; reading a range next to zero; and what comparing two existing groups can and cannot show.
Lesson focus: Comparing Two Populations from Two Random Samples
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
This is the week’s Excel lab. You will upload one workbook with three sheets (Backpacks, Steps, Notes). 4
Cross-check with resampling (optional but recommended). Open the Two-Sample Comparison interactive from the lesson, choose Paste my own data, paste the two columns into Group A values and Group B values, press Use my data, and on the Two random samples tab press Resample 1000 a few times. The plausible range from the interactive should be close to your Excel range (it will move a little each run). If it is far off, recheck your formulas.
5
Notes sheet. Add a sheet named Notes. In A1 type your name. Then write short answers in your own words (to keep a long sentence readable, click the cell and choose Home > Wrap Text). A3: Look at the Backpacks range. Does it contain 0? In two sentences, say what you can conclude about the two grades’ backpack weights and what you cannot conclude about why they differ. A4: Look at the Steps range. Does it contain 0? In two sentences, say what that does and does not tell you about the two offices. A5: A classmate writes, “The Backpacks range runs from about 2 to 4 pounds, so there is a 95% chance the true difference is in it, and being in grade 11 makes backpacks heavier.” Find the two problems and rewrite the sentence correctly.
6
Part B — numeric answers (type into the Canvas text box). Label each answer. B1: the observed difference (B minus A) for the Backpacks data, to 2 decimals. B2: the standard error of that difference, to 3 decimals. B3: the lower and upper ends of the Backpacks approximate 95% range, each to 2 decimals. B4: the lower and upper ends of the Steps approximate 95% range, each to 2 decimals. B5 (Desmos check): in Desmos Scientific, find the Backpacks standard error from the rounded group SDs (1.083 and 1.108, both with n = 10) by arithmetic: type 1.083 × 1.083 ÷ 10 + 1.108 × 1.108 ÷ 10, then use the square-root button on the result. Report it to 3 decimals and say whether it matches your Excel value.
7
Part C — applied report (type into the Canvas text box). The made-up school principal is deciding whether the upper grades need bigger lockers and has asked you for a short written summary of the Backpacks result. In four to six sentences, write it for someone who is not a statistician. Include: (a) the two sample averages and the plausible range for the true difference, in plain words; (b) why it is fair to talk about all students in the two grades (what must be true about the samples); (c) one thing the range does not tell the principal (for example, why the weights differ, or whether the difference is important for lockers); and (d) one honest sentence about how confident you are in the size of the gap.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The workbook has Backpacks, Steps, and Notes sheets. Each data sheet uses formulas (not typed numbers) for n, mean, SD, the difference (B minus A), the standard error, the two range ends, and the width.
☐
The values match the answer ranges, and the ranges are built as difference ± 1.96 × standard error.
☐
Part B numbers match the workbook and include the Desmos check of the Backpacks standard error.
☐
My Notes and Part C say what a plausible range for a difference means, treat 0 correctly (neither “proved” nor “accepted”), do not claim a cause from two existing groups, and name at least one thing the range does not cover.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
CriteriaFull creditPartial creditMinimal creditPts
Workbook & numeric answers
6 pts		Structure: both data sheets use formulas for the counts, means, SDs, difference (B minus A), standard error, both range ends, and width, with the correct ranges and a consistent layout. Values: the difference, standard error, and range for each data set match the teacher key (the data are fixed, so values should match within rounding). Part B: B1 to B5 match the workbook, and B5 reports the Desmos check. (Grade against the teacher key below.)One sheet or block missing, a few values wrong because of a slip (for example, a wrong range such as A2:A11 on the Steps sheet, the standard error without the square root, endpoints reversed, A and B swapped so the sign flips), or one or two Part B numbers wrong or missing the Desmos check.Two or more parts missing, results typed in as numbers with no formulas, or numbers that do not come from the student’s own workbook.6 pts
Reasoning & report
4 pts		1 pt each for Notes A3, A4, A5 and Part C, each fully correct (see the teacher key for the expected content). Each correct response reads the range as plausible values for the true difference between populations, treats 0 with care, avoids causal claims from existing groups, and avoids saying “95% chance this interval holds the truth.”Each item is partly right: correct reading of the range but a causal word slips in; says 0 is “plausible” but also “proved”; names the idea but also says “95% chance this interval holds the truth.”No reasoning, a claim that being in a grade or office causes the difference, or a claim that the range contains 95% of individual values.4 pts
Total (6 + 4): 10 pts
▶  Teacher key: expected values, formulas, and model answers
Backpacks sheet (Excel will show more decimals; accept ±0.01 on the difference and range ends and ±0.002 on the standard error): n = 10 and 10; means 10.340 and 13.430; SDs 1.083 and 1.108; difference (B minus A) = 3.090; SE = √(1.083² ÷ 10 + 1.108² ÷ 10) = 0.490; range = 3.090 ± 1.96 × 0.490 = 2.130 to 4.050; width 1.921. Resampling in the interactive gives a similar range, about 2.2 to 4.0.

Steps sheet: n = 12 and 12; means 7.150 and 7.450; SDs 1.045 and 1.087; difference (B minus A) = 0.300; SE = 0.435; range = 0.300 ± 1.96 × 0.435 = -0.553 to 1.153; width 1.706. The interactive gives a similar range, about −0.5 to 1.1.

Part B expected: B1 3.09; B2 0.490; B3 2.13 to 4.05; B4 -0.55 to 1.15; B5 0.490 (matches Excel to within rounding).

Formulas to expect (each data sheet): E2 =COUNT(A2:A11), F2 =COUNT(B2:B11), E3 =AVERAGE(A2:A11), F3 =AVERAGE(B2:B11), E4 =STDEV.S(A2:A11), F4 =STDEV.S(B2:B11), E6 =F3-E3, E7 =SQRT(E4^2/E2+F4^2/F2), E8 =E6-1.96*E7, E9 =E6+1.96*E7, E10 =E9-E8 (ranges are rows 2 to 11 on Backpacks and rows 2 to 13 on Steps). Accept an equivalent correct formula.

Notes A3. The Backpacks range (about 2.13 to 4.05) does not contain 0, so a real difference between the two grades’ mean backpack weights is plausible: eleventh graders plausibly carry about 2 to 4 pounds more on average. Because both samples are random, the claim is about all students in the two grades. It does not say why (more books, different class schedules, bigger bodies); comparing two existing groups does not show cause. A4. The Steps range (about −0.55 to 1.15) contains 0, so the data are consistent with no difference between the offices (and with a modest difference either way); it does not show the offices are the same, and it does not show Office B walks more. A larger sample would narrow the range. A5. Problem 1: the 95% belongs to the method, not to a probability about this one range (about 95 of 100 ranges built this way would capture the true difference). Problem 2: grade level is an existing group, so the difference does not show that being in grade 11 causes heavier backpacks. Example: “In random samples, eleventh graders’ backpacks averaged about 3.1 lb heavier, and a plausible range for the true difference is about 2.1 to 4.1 lb; this describes the two grades but does not show why they differ.” Part C must include: the two sample means (10.34 lb and 13.43 lb) and the plausible range (about 2.1 to 4.1 lb heavier for grade 11); that random samples let the claim extend to the two grades; one limit (does not explain why; does not say whether 3 lb matters for lockers; bias would not be repaired); and an honest statement about the size of the gap (for example, plausibly anywhere from about 2 to 4 lb with a best guess near 3 lb).

Optima Academy Online
An Education Experience Company

Quarter / Module

Inference & Statistical Reasoning
Lesson
Lesson 34.2
Paired Lesson
Comparing Two Treatments in a Randomized Experiment
Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 34.2
Assignment 34.2 — Beat Chance, or Not?
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Reading shuffle results from a randomized experiment, and writing an honest conclusion
Eight auto-graded items · one Excel formula answer · one short applied conclusion
Covers: what random assignment allows; what one shuffle of the group labels does; the share of shuffles at least as big as the observed gap, in either direction; the 5-in-100 rule of thumb; the same gap with different spread; what an unremarkable result does not show; the limits of a cause claim.
Lesson focus: Comparing Two Treatments in a Randomized Experiment
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (8 pts, auto-graded): seven multiple-choice questions and one numeric answer. Part B (2 pts, quick teacher check): one typed Excel formula and one short written conclusion. All experiments, groups, and numbers are constructed (made up). A calculator or Excel is fine for the arithmetic. In every item, “at least as big” means as big as the observed gap or bigger, in either direction, and the rule of thumb is: unusual if chance alone makes a gap that big in fewer than about 5 of every 100 shuffles. You do not need to upload a workbook.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
When groups are formed by chance, how do you decide whether a gap is more than luck, and what may you honestly say afterward?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
Why random assignment. A made-up researcher randomly assigns 60 volunteers to one of two exercise programs. Which statement best explains why random assignment lets a gap that chance alone would rarely produce be credited to the program?
(a) It guarantees the two groups are exactly equal before the programs begin
(b) It tends to spread other differences between people evenly across the two groups, so those differences are unlikely to explain a large gap
(c) It makes the results apply to every person in the city
(d) It makes each person’s measurement more precise
2
What a shuffle does. In a shuffle test for a randomized experiment, what does one shuffle do?
(a) Draws brand-new subjects from the population and repeats the experiment with the treatment
(b) Removes the highest outcome from each group and recomputes the gap
(c) Pools all the outcomes, deals them back at random into groups of the original sizes as if the treatment made no difference, and records the gap
(d) Repeats the original experiment on the same subjects with the groups swapped
3
Reading a share. A made-up experiment randomly assigned runners to two warm-up routines. The observed gap in mean sprint time was 0.30 seconds. In 2,000 shuffles of the group labels, 46 gave a gap at least as big as 0.30 in either direction. Which statement is correct?
(a) The share is 0.46, so the gap is not unusual
(b) The share is 0.023, so the gap is not unusual, because 0.023 is less than 1
(c) The share is 0.977, so the gap is unusual
(d) The share is 0.023, so the gap is unusual: chance alone makes a gap this big in fewer than 5 of every 100 shuffles
4
A large share. In another made-up randomized experiment, 540 of 1,000 shuffles gave a gap at least as big as the observed gap in either direction. Which statement is best?
(a) The share is 0.54, so chance alone makes a gap this big more often than not. This experiment does not show a difference beyond chance, and it does not show that the treatment has no effect
(b) The share is 0.54, so the treatment has no effect
(c) The share is 0.54, so there is a 54% chance that the treatment works
(d) The share is 0.46, so the treatment works for 46% of people
5
Same gap, different spread. Two made-up experiments each randomly assigned 16 people to two groups of 8. In both, group B’s mean was exactly 6 points higher than group A’s. In Experiment 1 the scores within each group are tightly packed (standard deviation about 1.3). In Experiment 2 they are widely scattered (standard deviation about 12). Which statement is best?
(a) The two gaps are equally convincing, because both are 6 points
(b) Experiment 2 is more convincing, because more scatter leaves more room for a real difference
(c) Experiment 1 is more convincing: shuffling the labels would rarely recreate a 6-point gap among such tightly packed scores
(d) Neither can be judged, because the two experiments have the same number of people
6
What you may conclude. A made-up researcher recruits 60 volunteers from one school and randomly assigns 30 to a new tutoring method and 30 to the usual method. The tutoring group scores higher by a gap that chance alone would rarely produce. Which conclusion is best supported?
(a) The tutoring caused the higher scores among these volunteers; saying it works for all students would need more evidence, such as a random sample of students
(b) The tutoring will raise scores for every student in the state
(c) The tutoring and the scores are related, but a cause cannot be claimed for these volunteers even though assignment was random
(d) The result means nothing, because the volunteers were not a random sample
7
No random assignment. At a made-up school, students chose whether to attend a weekend workshop. The attenders scored 8 points higher on average, and shuffling the group labels produced a gap that big in only about 1 of 1,000 shuffles. Which statement is best?
(a) The workshop caused the higher scores, because the share is so small
(b) The workshop did not matter, because students chose it
(c) The share is meaningless, because 0.001 is too small to be real
(d) Chance alone is an unlikely explanation for the gap, but because students chose whether to attend, other differences (such as motivation) may explain it, so the shuffle cannot show that the workshop caused it
8
Compute the share. A made-up experiment ran 4,000 shuffles of the group labels, and 120 gave a gap at least as big as the observed gap in either direction. What is the share of shuffles that were at least as big? Enter it as a decimal.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (1 PT EACH)
9
Excel formula. In a worksheet, the observed gap (a positive number) is in cell D2, and 100 shuffled gaps are in cells F2:F101. Type the exact Excel formula that counts how many of the shuffled gaps are at least as big as the observed gap in either direction. (Type it as you would type it in a cell, beginning with =.)
10
Write the conclusion. A made-up researcher recruited 24 volunteer students at one school and randomly assigned 12 to study vocabulary with flashcards (group A) and 12 with practice quizzes (group B). On a 20-point vocabulary test, the group means were 14.2 (A) and 16.1 (B), so the observed gap, B minus A, was +1.9 points. In 2,000 shuffles of the group labels, 62 gave a gap at least as big as 1.9 in either direction. In three or four sentences, (1) give the share and say whether the gap is unusual by the 5-in-100 rule, (2) say what the random assignment lets you conclude, and (3) say one thing you may not conclude from this experiment.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I found each share as a count divided by the number of shuffles, and counted both directions.
☐
I compared each gap with the spread of the data, not just the size of the gap.
☐
My answers to items 4, 6, 7, and 10 do not say “no effect” from a large share, and do not claim more than the design allows.
☐
My conclusion in item 10 separates what chance can explain, what random assignment supports, and what remains unknown.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Part A: auto-graded
8 pts		 1 pt per item, scored automatically in Canvas. Item 8 is numeric and needs the share as a decimal. Not applicable: each item is right or wrong. Not applicable. 8 pts
Part B: Excel formula (item 9)
1 pt		 Types a complete formula, beginning with =, that adds a count of shuffled gaps at or above the observed gap and a count of shuffled gaps at or below its negative, using the cell references given. Right idea with one small slip: leaves off the equals sign, counts only one direction, or has a small reference or punctuation error. Counts all the shuffled gaps, divides when no division is asked for, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Part B: written conclusion (item 10)
1 pt		 Covers all three parts in three or four sentences: gives the share and the verdict, says what random assignment supports about cause, and names a correct limit on what may not be concluded. Covers two of the three parts correctly, or covers all three but one statement is wrong or overclaims. Covers only one part, says the treatment “proves” or “has no effect,” or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Total: 10 pts
▶  Teacher key: answers and grading notes (not shown to students)
Part A answer key: (1) b; (2) c; (3) d; (4) a; (5) c; (6) a; (7) d; (8) 0.03. Item 3: 46 ÷ 2000 = 0.023, under 0.05, so unusual. Item 4: 540 ÷ 1000 = 0.54; distractor (b) is the “no effect” error, (c) misreads the share as the probability that the treatment works. Item 5 (computed by script from every possible split of 16 scores into 8 and 8): tightly packed scores give 2 of 12,870 splits at least as extreme (about 0.0002); widely scattered scores give 4,608 of 12,870 (about 0.36). Item 7: random sampling is not the issue here; the missing random assignment is. Item 8: 120 ÷ 4000 = 0.03; accept 0.03 only (3 or 3% is not the decimal asked for; if the Canvas numeric field allows, also accept 0.030).

Item 9 key: =COUNTIF(F2:F101,">="&D2)+COUNTIF(F2:F101,"<="&-D2). Accept equivalent forms, such as =COUNTIF(F2:F101,">="&ABS(D2))+COUNTIF(F2:F101,"<="&-ABS(D2)), =COUNTIF(F2:F101,">="&$D$2)+COUNTIF(F2:F101,"<="&-$D$2), or a SUMPRODUCT that counts ABS(F2:F101)>=D2. Partial: one direction only, or missing the leading =. Minimal: COUNT(F2:F101), or no formula.

Item 10 key (computed: 62 ÷ 2000 = 0.031): Full credit mentions (1) the share 0.031, about 3 in 100, below the 5-in-100 rule, so the gap is unusual (chance alone rarely makes a gap this big); (2) because students were randomly assigned, the practice quizzes likely caused the higher scores among these 24 students (not “proves”); (3) any one correct limit: the 24 volunteers are not a random sample, so the result may not apply to all students; one test and one school; the share does not say how large or important the 1.9-point gap is; or the result does not prove the method works for everyone. Do not give full credit for “the quizzes work for all students” or “there is a 3% chance the quizzes do not work.”
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 34.2 — Beat Chance, or Not?
Answer items 1 to 8 in Canvas (seven multiple-choice letters and one decimal), then type your Excel formula for item 9 and your short conclusion for item 10 in the text boxes. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.
