Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 34.3
Assignment 34.3 — Boring Worlds and Honest Reports
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Reading simulated p-values, applying a rule fixed in advance, and reporting a result honestly
Seven auto-graded items · one short written item with three parts
Covers: the empirical p-value as a share of simulated boring worlds; what a p-value means and does not mean; the 5% convention; the effect of sample size at the same percent; statistically significant versus practically important; false alarms from many tests; counting extreme shuffled differences in Excel.
Lesson focus: Is the Difference Real? Significance by Simulation
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (7 pts, auto-graded): five multiple-choice questions and two numeric answers, one point each. Part B (3 pts, teacher check): one written item with three parts, one point each. All coins, studies, and clubs are constructed (made up). A calculator or Excel is fine for the arithmetic. You do not need to upload a workbook.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
When a result looks surprising, how do we find out how surprising it really is, and how do we describe it without claiming more than we know?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
Count to a p-value. A made-up student simulated 2,000 boring worlds. In 130 of them the result was at least as extreme as the observed result, in either direction. What is the empirical p-value? Enter it as a decimal.
2
What the p-value says. A made-up randomized study reports a p-value of 0.04 for a new reading program. Which statement is the most accurate?
(a) There is a 4% chance that the reading program does nothing
(b) If the program did nothing, chance alone would produce a gap this big or bigger about 4 times in 100
(c) There is a 96% chance that the program works
(d) The program raises scores by 4%
3
An ordinary result. A made-up coin lands heads 55 times in 100 flips. Simulating many fair-coin worlds of 100 flips, about 37% of them have 55 or more heads or 45 or fewer. Which statement is best?
(a) The coin is proved fair
(b) The coin is proved unfair
(c) A result like this is ordinary for a fair coin, so it gives no good reason to doubt the coin
(d) The p-value of 0.37 means there is a 37% chance the coin is fair
4
More flips, same percent. Two made-up coins both land heads 60% of the time in the flips tested. Coin X was flipped 100 times (60 heads); coin Y was flipped 1,000 times (600 heads). Compared with a fair coin, which statement is best?
(a) The two results are equally convincing, because both are 60%
(b) Coin X’s result is more convincing, because 100 is a nicer number
(c) Coin Y’s result is far more convincing: with more flips, a fair coin rarely strays 10 points from 50%, so the p-value is much smaller
(d) Neither result can be judged without knowing the weight of the coin
5
Significant is not the same as important. A made-up online game company randomly assigns 50,000 players to each of two menu designs. Design B players spend 0.3 minutes more per session, on a base of about 40 minutes, and the shuffle share (p-value) is below 0.001. Which statement is best?
(a) The gap is statistically significant, but a 0.3-minute difference may be too small to matter in practice
(b) The gap is large, because the p-value is so small
(c) The gap is not statistically significant, because it is small
(d) The company must adopt design B, because the p-value proves it is better
6
Many tests. A made-up club runs 20 independent comparisons, and in every one of them the boring world is true (no real effect). Each comparison uses the 5% rule. What is the chance that at least one comparison looks statistically significant by luck alone? Use 1 − 0.9520. Enter a decimal rounded to two places.
7
Excel counting. In a worksheet, cells A1:A1000 hold 1,000 shuffled differences, and cell D1 holds a positive observed difference. Which formula gives the share of shuffled differences at least as big as the observed one in either direction?
(a) =COUNTIF(A1:A1000,">="&D1)/1000
(b) =(COUNTIF(A1:A1000,">="&D1)+COUNTIF(A1:A1000,"<="&-D1))/1000
(c) =AVERAGE(A1:A1000)/D1
(d) =COUNTIF(A1:A1000,D1)/1000
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (3 PTS)
8
Report it honestly. A made-up school club ran 20 different comparisons of two randomly assigned groups. One of them, a comparison of two study playlists, gave a shuffle share (p-value) of 0.03. The club wants to announce, “Playlist B works! There is a 97% chance it works.” and say nothing about the other 19 comparisons. Answer in your own words, in a few sentences each:
(a) What does a p-value of 0.03 actually mean? Use the idea of a boring world in your answer. (1 pt)
(b) Why is “97% chance it works” a misreading? (1 pt)
(c) Using the number 20, explain why reporting only this one comparison is misleading, and say what the club should report to serve the people who will read it honestly. (1 pt)
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I found each empirical p-value by dividing a count of extreme worlds by the number of worlds, and I checked that my answer is a decimal between 0 and 1.
☐
I read every p-value as a statement about how often chance alone would do this in the boring world, not as the probability that a claim is true or false.
☐
I remembered that more data makes the same percent more convincing, and that a significant result can still be too small to matter.
☐
My written answer uses the idea of a boring world, corrects the misreading, and mentions the number of comparisons.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Part A: auto-graded
7 pts		 1 pt per item (items 1 to 7). Five multiple-choice items, one numeric empirical p-value, and one numeric probability. Not applicable: each item is right or wrong. Not applicable. 7 pts
Part B (a): meaning of p = 0.03
1 pt		 Says that if nothing were going on (the boring world), results at least this extreme would occur about 3 times in 100. States the “3 in 100” idea but leaves out the boring world, or the reverse. Describes the p-value as the chance the claim is true or false, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Part B (b): the misreading
1 pt		 Explains that the p-value is computed assuming the boring world, so it is not the probability that the playlist works (and so 97% is not justified). Says the 97% claim is wrong but gives no reason. Accepts the 97% claim, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Part B (c): many tests, honest report
1 pt		 Uses the number 20 (about 1 false alarm expected, or about a 64% chance of at least one by luck) to explain the selection problem, and says the club should report all 20 comparisons, including the non-significant ones. Gives only one of the two: the selection problem or what to report. Says only that the club should “be honest” with no reasoning, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Total (7 + 3): 10 pts
▶  Teacher key (not for students)
Part A. (1) 0.065 (130 ÷ 2000 = 0.065; accept 0.065 only, or 6.5% if the platform allows). (2) b. (3) c (the other choices claim proof or misread the p-value). (4) c (exact two-sided p-values: 0.057 at 60 of 100, about 0.0000000003 at 600 of 1,000). (5) a. (6) 0.64 (1 − 0.9520 = 1 − 0.3585 = 0.6415; accept 0.64 or 0.642). (7) b (it counts both tails; choice a counts only one tail).

Part B, model answer. (a) If the playlists made no difference (the boring world, where the group labels are arbitrary), shuffling the labels would produce a gap at least as big as the one seen in about 3 of every 100 shuffles. (b) The p-value is computed assuming nothing is going on, so it cannot also be the probability that something is going on. It is not “a 97% chance it works.” (c) With 20 comparisons and a 5% rule, about 1 false alarm is expected even if no playlist does anything, and the chance of at least one is about 1 − 0.9520 = 0.64. Showing only the one that looked good hides how many tries it took. The club should report all 20 comparisons, say how many were run, include the non-significant ones, and describe the 0.03 result as one of many tests (a result worth testing again with new data), not as a proven discovery. Part B scoring is by the rubric above: 1 point per part.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 34.3 — Boring Worlds and Honest Reports
Answer items 1 to 7 in Canvas (five multiple-choice letters and two numbers), then type your written response for item 8 in the text box. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Computing false-alarm rates and power from a decision rule, using the language of a decision, and telling the two schools apart
Seven auto-graded items · one short written item with three parts
Covers: the Type I rate of a two-tail coin rule; power against a particular true value; Type I versus Type II errors; what raises power; “reject” versus “fail to reject”; what a frequentist test and a Bayesian analysis each answer; the BINOM.DIST pattern in Excel.
Lesson focus: The Logic of Hypothesis Testing: Two Schools Revisited
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (7 pts, auto-graded): two numeric answers and five multiple-choice questions, one point each. Part B (3 pts, teacher check): one written item with three parts, one point each. All coins, spinners, councils, and studies are constructed (made up). Excel (the BINOM.DIST pattern from the lesson) or a calculator is fine for the arithmetic. You do not need to upload a workbook.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
If you must decide before seeing the data, how do you measure the two ways your rule can go wrong, and what can your verdict honestly say?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
Type I rate of a rule. A made-up game flips a coin 50 times and rejects “the coin is fair” if it shows 33 or more heads, or 17 or fewer. What is the chance this rule rejects when the coin really is fair (the Type I rate)? Enter a decimal rounded to three places.
2
Power against a particular coin. A made-up referee flips a coin 100 times and rejects “the coin is fair” if it shows 62 or more heads, or 38 or fewer. If the coin really lands heads 70% of the time, what is the chance the rule rejects (the power)? Enter a decimal rounded to three places.
3
Which error? A made-up council flips its coin 100 times and will replace it only if it sees 61 or more heads or 39 or fewer. The coin is truly biased (it lands heads 60% of the time), but in the council’s 100 flips it shows 57 heads, and the council keeps the coin. Which statement is correct?
(a) The council made a Type I error: a false alarm
(b) The council made a correct decision, because 57 is close to 50
(c) The council made a Type II error: a miss
(d) The council made no error, because the rule was followed
4
Raising power. For the council’s 100-flip rule in item 3, which change would raise the chance of catching a coin that lands heads 60% of the time, while keeping the false-alarm rate about the same?
(a) Flip fewer times and use a rule of the same shape
(b) Flip many more times (for example 400) and use a rule built to keep the false-alarm rate near the same level
(c) Decide on the rule after seeing the flips
(d) Tighten the rule to 64 or more heads or 36 or fewer
5
The language of a decision. A made-up study of a tutoring method reports a p-value of 0.11, and the 5% level was fixed before the data were collected. Which statement is best?
(a) The null hypothesis is accepted, so the tutoring has no effect
(b) There is an 11% chance that the null hypothesis is true
(c) The study proves that the tutoring does not work
(d) We fail to reject the null hypothesis: the data are not strong evidence against it, but a real effect could still be there
6
Two schools. A made-up randomized study reports a p-value of 0.03. Which statement correctly separates what a frequentist test offers from what a Bayesian analysis offers?
(a) The test says that if nothing were going on, results this extreme would occur about 3 times in 100; a probability that nothing is going on would also need a prior
(b) The test says there is a 3% chance that nothing is going on, and a Bayesian analysis says the same thing
(c) A Bayesian analysis ignores the data and uses only the prior
(d) The two schools always give the same number, so it does not matter which is used
7
Excel pattern. The rule in item 2 rejects at 62 or more heads or 38 or fewer in 100 flips. Which formula gives the Type I rate of this rule (the chance of rejecting when the coin is fair)?
(a) =1-BINOM.DIST(62,100,0.5,TRUE)+BINOM.DIST(38,100,0.5,TRUE)
(b) =1-BINOM.DIST(61,100,0.5,TRUE)
(c) =1-BINOM.DIST(61,100,0.5,TRUE)+BINOM.DIST(38,100,0.5,TRUE)
(d) =BINOM.DIST(61,100,0.5,TRUE)-BINOM.DIST(38,100,0.5,TRUE)
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (3 PTS)
8
Report it honestly. A made-up club claims its spinner lands on red half the time. A skeptic plans 40 spins and writes this rule before spinning: reject the claim if the spinner shows 27 or more reds, or 13 or fewer. (For a spinner that really is fair, this rule falsely rejects about 3.85 times in 100.) The skeptic spins and gets 25 reds. Answer in your own words, in a few sentences each:
(a) Write the null hypothesis and the alternative hypothesis in words, and explain why the rule has to be written before the spinning. (1 pt)
(b) Describe a Type I error and a Type II error in this scenario. Say which one is the false alarm, and what its long-run rate is when the spinner really is fair. (1 pt)
(c) State the decision for 25 reds in the correct language, and explain why it would be wrong to conclude that the spinner is fair. (1 pt)
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I computed each rejection chance by adding the two tails of the rule, using the true heads chance (0.5 for a false-alarm rate) in the formula.
☐
I kept Type I (rejecting a true null) and Type II (missing a false null) straight, and I remembered that power is one minus the Type II rate.
☐
I wrote every verdict as “reject” or “fail to reject,” and I did not read a p-value as the probability that a hypothesis is true.
☐
My written answer states both hypotheses, explains the rule-first habit, and refuses to say the spinner is proved fair.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Part A: auto-graded
7 pts		 1 pt per item (items 1 to 7). Two numeric items and five multiple-choice items. Not applicable: each item is right or wrong. Not applicable. 7 pts
Part B (a): hypotheses and the rule-first habit
1 pt		 States a null (the spinner lands on red half the time) and an alternative (it does not), and explains that the rule is fixed before the data so the data cannot choose the rule or the false-alarm rate. States both hypotheses but gives no reason for writing the rule first, or the reverse. Hypotheses missing or confused, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Part B (b): the two errors
1 pt		 Describes a Type I error as rejecting a fair spinner and a Type II error as failing to reject a spinner that is not fair; names Type I as the false alarm; gives its rate for a fair spinner as about 0.04 (4 in 100). Describes the two errors correctly but leaves out the rate, or swaps the two names. Gives only a vague description, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Part B (c): the decision and its limits
1 pt		 States “fail to reject” for 25 reds, and explains that this does not show the spinner is fair (small sample, modest bias can be missed, weak evidence is not no effect). States fail to reject but gives no explanation of why it does not prove the spinner is fair, or the reverse. Says the spinner is fair or proved fair, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Total (7 + 3): 10 pts
▶  Teacher key (not for students)
Part A. (1) 0.033 (exact 0.0328: P(33 or more in 50 at 0.5) = 0.0164, doubled by symmetry; accept 0.032 to 0.034). (2) 0.966 (exact 0.9660; accept 0.965 to 0.967). (3) c (the null is false but the rule failed to reject: a miss). (4) b (more flips gives more power; option d lowers both the false-alarm rate and the power). (5) d. (6) a. (7) c (62 or more is 1 minus the chance of 61 or fewer; option a is off by one; option b counts one tail only; option d is the chance of the middle).

Part B, model answer. (a) Null: the spinner lands on red half the time (the boring world). Alternative: it does not land on red half the time. The rule is written first so the data cannot choose the rule: if the skeptic picked the cutoffs after seeing 25 reds, any result could be made to look significant or not, and the stated false-alarm rate would mean nothing. (b) A Type I error is rejecting the claim when the spinner really is fair (a false alarm). A Type II error is failing to reject when the spinner really is not fair (a miss). For a fair spinner, the long-run Type I rate of this rule is about 0.0385, roughly 4 times in 100. (c) 25 reds is not 27 or more and not 13 or fewer, so the decision is to fail to reject the claim that the spinner is fair. It would be wrong to say the spinner is fair or the claim is proved: 40 spins is a small sample, and a spinner that is biased by a modest amount would often slip past this rule (for a spinner that lands on red 70% of the time, the rule rejects only about 70% of the time). Failing to reject means the evidence was not strong enough, not that nothing is going on. Part B scoring is by the rubric above: 1 point per part.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 35.1 — Rules, Errors, and Power
Answer items 1 to 7 in Canvas (two numbers and five multiple-choice letters), then type your written response for item 8 in the text box. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Evaluating Data-Based Reports in the Wild
Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Lesson 35.2
Assignment 35.2 — Spot the Flaw: Reading Reports Fairly
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Spotting flaws in data-based reports, matching claims to what a study design allows, and recomputing a report’s own numbers
Seven auto-graded items · one short written critique with three parts
Covers: the six-question reader’s checklist; naming flaws (voluntary response, causal verbs from observational data, truncated axes, many tests, and more); which verb a study design allows; recomputing a margin of error, an interval, and a percent change; statistically significant versus big enough to matter; writing a fair critique.
Lesson focus: Evaluating Data-Based Reports in the Wild
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (7 pts, auto-graded): two matching items, two multiple-choice items, and three numeric answers. Each item is worth one point. Part B (3 pts, teacher check): one written critique with three parts, one point each. Every article, study, company, and number is constructed (made up). A calculator or Excel is fine for the arithmetic. You do not need to upload a workbook.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
When a report quotes a study, how do we find out what the evidence really supports, and say so fairly?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
Name the flaw. Match each excerpt from a made-up report to the flaw that best describes it. Flaws: A voluntary response; B a causal claim from observational data; C a truncated axis; D reporting only one of many tests; E extrapolation beyond the data; F a tiny effect called significant.
(1) “The bars start at 95%, so the bar for 97% is drawn twice as tall as the bar for 96%.”
(2) “Listeners were invited to call a hotline to vote on the new bridge toll.”
(3) “The team measured 40 outcomes; the report highlights the one with p = 0.03.”
(4) “Teens who sleep with a fan on have higher grades, so a bedroom fan raises grades.”
Enter the four letters in order for excerpts 1 to 4, for example B A E F.
2
Which checklist question? The six questions are 1 who and how many; 2 how was it measured; 3 what kind of study and which verbs; 4 is the display honest; 5 uncertainty and size; 6 who benefits or what is missing. Match each made-up excerpt to the question that catches the problem.
(1) “The study was paid for by the company that sells the product; the report mentions this in its last line.”
(2) “The poll reports 52% in favor, with no sample size and no margin of error.”
(3) “Only the 1,000 customers who left reviews were counted.”
(4) “Students were asked to recall how many hours they slept last week.”
Enter the four question numbers in order for excerpts 1 to 4, for example 3 1 2 5.
3
Which verb is allowed? In a made-up study, 500 adults were randomly chosen from a city and asked about their own coffee habits and stress. Those who drink more coffee reported lower stress. Which statement is best supported?
(a) Coffee lowers stress in adults
(b) Stress makes people drink less coffee
(c) Coffee drinking is associated with lower reported stress among adults in this sample, but the study cannot show that coffee is the reason
(d) The study proves that coffee protects adults from stress
4
Recompute a margin. A made-up report says only, “a survey of 625 students found 61% favor the new schedule.” Using the safe rule 1 ÷ √n, what is the margin of error in percentage points? Enter a number.
5
Recompute an interval. A made-up random sample of 1,600 residents finds 52% in favor of a plan (p-hat = 0.52). Using p-hat ± 1.96 × √(p-hat(1 − p-hat) ÷ n), find the low end of the 95% interval as a decimal rounded to three places.
6
Check the headline. A made-up headline says a walking program “cuts sick days in half.” The report’s own numbers are 3.1 sick days per year for program households and 4.0 for the others. By what percent are the program households’ sick days lower than the others’? Enter a number rounded to one decimal place (for example 12.5).
7
Significant is not the same as important. In a made-up study, 40,000 students were randomly assigned to a tutoring program or to no program. The program raised average scores by 0.2 points on a 100-point test, with a p-value below 0.001. Which critique is strongest?
(a) The result is not statistically significant, because the gap is so small
(b) The gap is statistically significant, but 0.2 points may be too small to matter; the report should state the size of the gain and ask whether it is worth the cost
(c) Because the p-value is so small, the program has a large effect
(d) The p-value shows a 99.9% chance that the program works
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (3 PTS)
8
Critique the report. Read this made-up report.
Made up. The Cedar Falls Dispatch, Cedar Falls, the Cedar Falls Learning Center, and every person and number are invented.
Chess Makes Kids Smarter, Study Finds. CEDAR FALLS. Students who play chess score higher in math, according to a study by Dr. Rafael Ortiz of the Cedar Falls Learning Center. A flyer invited students to volunteer; 90 chess club members and 90 non-members signed up. The members averaged 88 on a math test, against 84 for the non-members, a difference called “statistically significant” (p = 0.02). “Chess makes kids smarter, and every school should require it,” Ortiz said. The Learning Center sells chess lessons.
Answer in your own words, in a few sentences each:
(a) Name two flaws. For each, give the number of the checklist question that catches it and say in one sentence why it is a problem. (1 pt)
(b) Write one sentence saying what the evidence in this report does support. (1 pt)
(c) Describe a study design or extra evidence that could settle whether chess raises math scores, and say what the report should state about it (for example, sample sizes or the size of the gap). (1 pt)
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I used the six questions to look for what is missing, not only for what is wrong, and I matched each flaw to the question that catches it.
☐
I checked each verb against the study design: random sample, observational, or experiment.
☐
I recomputed numbers from the report itself, and I kept “statistically significant” separate from “big enough to matter.”
☐
My written critique names specific flaws, says what the evidence does support, and describes evidence that would settle the question, without sneering at anyone.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Full credit Partial credit Minimal credit Pts
Part A: auto-graded
7 pts		 1 pt per item (items 1 to 7). Two matching items (all four letters or numbers correct), two multiple-choice items, and three numeric answers. Not applicable: each item is right or wrong. Not applicable. 7 pts
Part B (a): two flaws
1 pt		 Names two real flaws in the report, gives the correct checklist question number for each, and explains in a sentence why each is a problem. Names two flaws but gives the wrong question numbers or no reasons, or names one flaw well. Lists vague complaints (“it is biased”) with no specific flaw, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Part B (b): what the evidence supports
1 pt		 Writes a sentence limited to the volunteers in the study (members who volunteered scored about 4 points higher on average) and does not say chess is the reason. Writes a sentence that is mostly fair but slips in a causal word or applies the result to all students. Restates the headline claim, says the study is useless, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Part B (c): evidence that would settle it
1 pt		 Describes random assignment to chess lessons or not (or a comparable design) and says what should be reported (the number of students in each group, the size of the gap, an interval). Gives only a design or only what to report, or suggests a bigger volunteer sample. Says “do more research” with no specifics, or leaves it blank. 1 pt
Total (7 + 3): 10 pts
▶  Teacher key (not for students)
Part A. (1) C A D B (truncated axis; voluntary response; many tests, one reported; causal claim from observational data; E and F are distractors). (2) 6 5 1 2 (funder is who benefits; no n or margin is uncertainty and size; only reviewers is who and how many; recalled hours is how it was measured). (3) c (random sample of adults but no assignment, so “associated with” is the allowed verb; a and d are causal; b reverses the cause without evidence). (4) 4 (1 ÷ √625 = 1 ÷ 25 = 0.04, or 4 points; accept 4 or 4.0). (5) 0.496 (margin = 1.96 × √(0.52 × 0.48 ÷ 1600) = 0.0245; interval 0.4955 to 0.5445; accept 0.495 or 0.496). (6) 22.5 ((4.0 − 3.1) ÷ 4.0 = 0.225; accept 22.5 or 22.5%; the headline’s “in half” would be 50%). (7) b (significant but tiny; c and d misread the p-value; a says not significant when it is).

Part B, model answer. (a) Voluntary response (Question 1): students volunteered after seeing a flyer, so the members and non-members who signed up are self-selected and may differ in motivation or interest; nothing can be said about students in general. Causal verb from observational data (Question 3): “makes kids smarter” is not allowed because students chose chess; students who already like math and school may be the ones who join. Other acceptable flaws: who benefits (Question 6), since the Center sells chess lessons and the point is mentioned last; no margin of error, interval, or size beyond a 4-point gap (Question 5); “every school should require it” goes beyond a volunteer sample. (b) Example: “Among the 180 students who volunteered, the chess club members averaged about 4 points higher on a math test than the non-members, and the study cannot say whether chess is the reason.” (c) Example: randomly assign a group of willing students to chess lessons or to no lessons, measure math scores from school records for everyone, and report how many students were in each group, the size of the gap with an interval, and who paid for the study. Random assignment is what would allow a cause claim for those students. Part B scoring is by the rubric above: 1 point per part.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 35.2 — Spot the Flaw: Reading Reports Fairly
Answer items 1 to 7 in Canvas (two matching items with four answers each, two multiple-choice letters, and three numbers), then type your written response for item 8 in the text box. You do not need to upload a workbook.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Assignment 35.3 — The Capstone Critique
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
Recomputing a report’s numbers, then writing a fair seven-part critique and comparing it with an AI
Three auto-graded warm-ups · one written critique · one AI-comparison reflection
Covers: the seven-part critique template (data and displays; summaries; models and fit; relationships and causation; sampling and design; inference; verdict), recomputing a difference and a percent change, matching a study design to the verb it allows, writing fairly (steelman first), and documenting disagreements with an AI.
Lesson focus: Capstone: The Complete Statistical Critique
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Part A (3 pts, auto-graded): two numeric answers and one multiple-choice item, one point each. Part B (7 pts, teacher scored with a rubric): a written seven-part critique (6 pts) and a short AI-comparison reflection (1 pt). The report, school, researchers and every number are constructed (made up). A calculator or Excel is fine for the arithmetic. You do not upload a workbook.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
How much of a report’s claim can its evidence carry, and how can you say so fairly?
📰 THE REPORT TO CRITIQUE (ITEMS 1 TO 5 USE THIS REPORT)
Read the made-up report, then use the data and the summary under it. The data are each homeroom’s average tardies per week over the four weeks, rounded to a whole number (made up).
📰 MADE-UP REPORT · The Harbor Hill Gazette (a made-up newspaper about a made-up school)
QUIET START CUTS TARDIES BY 20%, SCHOOL STUDY SHOWS
Harbor Hill Middle School tested “Quiet Start,” a five-minute silent-reading routine at the beginning of homeroom, researchers Marisol Quade and Tobias Wren said. (The school, the researchers and every quotation here are made up.) The researchers flipped a coin for each of the school’s 14 homerooms: 7 were assigned to Quiet Start and 7 kept the usual routine. After four weeks, the average number of tardies per week was 8 in Quiet Start homerooms and 10 in the others, “a 20% drop,” the report says.
“Chance alone would rarely produce a gap this large: p = 0.037,” Quade said. The researchers’ bar chart, which shows one bar for each group, has a vertical axis that starts at 7 tardies. “If every school in the state adopted Quiet Start, we would expect about two fewer tardies per homeroom each week, and a better school year for everyone,” Wren said.
A note at the end of the report says the team also tracked four other measures (absences, nurse visits, discipline referrals, and homework completion) that “showed no clear pattern and are not reported here.” The study was run at one school.
The data (made up):
Homeroom1234567
Usual routine10129101298
Quiet Start81078896
The summary (made up, computed from the data above):
Groupn (homerooms)Mean tardies per weekSD
Usual routine710.01.53
Quiet Start78.01.29
One more fact (made up): if the 14 homeroom values are shuffled between the two groups in every possible way (3,432 ways to pick which 7 homerooms form one group), 126 of the 3,432 splits give a gap in group means of at least 2 tardies per week in either direction. 126 ÷ 3,432 is about 0.037, the report’s p-value.
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART A (1 PT EACH)
1
Recompute the gap. Using the data table, find the mean tardies per week for each group and subtract: Quiet Start mean minus Usual routine mean. Enter the number (it may be negative).
2
Recompute the percent. The report says Quiet Start produced “a 20% drop.” Using the two means, find the drop as a percent of the Usual routine mean. Enter a whole number (without the percent sign).
3
Which verb is allowed? Which statement about the study design is correct?
(a) An observational study, so the report may say only that Quiet Start homerooms were associated with fewer tardies
(b) A randomized experiment on homerooms, so a gap larger than chance could produce may be attributed to Quiet Start in these 14 homerooms
(c) A sample survey, so the result describes every middle school
(d) A randomized experiment, so it proves Quiet Start works in every school
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS · PART B (7 PTS)
4
Write the critique (6 pts). In your own words, write a short critique of the report using the seven parts of the template, with a label for each: 1 Data and displays; 2 Summaries; 3 Models and fit; 4 Relationships and causation; 5 Sampling and design; 6 Inference; 7 Verdict. Write a few sentences for each part (you may combine parts 2 and 3). If a part has nothing to critique, say so in one sentence. Follow the fairness rules from the lesson: begin by stating the strongest honest version of the report’s claim, say what the evidence does support, name each limit, and finish with what additional evidence would settle the question. Use at least two numbers you recomputed yourself (for example, from the data table or the summary). Do not sneer at the researchers.
5
Compare with an AI (1 pt). Only after you have finished item 4, ask an AI tool to critique the same report. In a short list, (a) say that you wrote your critique first, (b) list every disagreement between your critique and the AI’s (a point only you made, a point only it made, or a point you both made with different conclusions), and (c) for each disagreement, say who was right and give the evidence (a number you recomputed, a line in the report, or a rule from the course). If the AI and you agree on everything, say what you checked to make sure it was not simply repeating you.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
I recomputed the numbers I used, and I can show where each one came from.
☐
My critique has a label for each of the seven parts, begins with a fair statement of the claim, and says what the evidence does support.
☐
I named the study design and the verb it allows, and I separated random assignment from random sampling.
☐
I said what would settle the question, ranked my points, and avoided sneering.
☐
I wrote my critique before I asked the AI, and I listed every disagreement with the evidence for who was right.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
CriteriaFull creditPartial creditMinimal creditPts
Part A: auto-graded

3 pts		1 pt per item (items 1 to 3): two numeric answers and one multiple-choice item.Not applicable: each item is right or wrong.Not applicable.3 pts
Data and displays
1 pt		Checks the chart against the honesty checklist (the axis that starts at 7, not 0) and says how it exaggerates the gap, or checks the display honestly.Notices the axis problem but does not say how it affects the reader, or the reverse.Does not address the display, or only says the chart is “misleading” with no reason.1 pt
Summaries and models
1 pt		Uses the summaries correctly (means 8 and 10, a gap of 2, a 20% drop, small n = 7 per group, SDs near 1.5), notes that nothing odd stands out, and states at least one number recomputed from the data.Uses the numbers but does not comment on spread or sample size, or the reverse.Repeats the headline without checking any number, or leaves it blank.1 pt
Relationships and causation
1 pt		Names the study as a randomized experiment, says that random assignment allows a causal statement about these 14 homerooms (beyond chance), and does not wrongly call it “only correlation.”Names the design but gives the wrong verb, or gives the verb without the design.Says “correlation is not causation” with no reference to random assignment, or leaves it blank.1 pt
Sampling and design
1 pt		Says the study covers one school and 14 homerooms (n = 7 per group), that randomization is not random sampling, and that the statewide claim is not supported.Gives only one of these limits.Says “the sample is too small” with no further reasoning, or leaves it blank.1 pt
Inference
1 pt		Reads p = 0.037 correctly (chance alone would give a gap this big about 4 times in 100 if the routine did nothing), comments on the size or uncertainty (a rough range of about −3.5 to −0.5 tardies per week, or the small gap of 2), and notes that five measures were tracked but only one reported (about a 23% chance that at least one of five empty tests looks significant).Does two of the three: the p-value reading, the size or interval, the many-tests point.Calls 0.037 “a 3.7% chance the routine does nothing,” or leaves it blank.1 pt
Verdict and fairness
1 pt		Begins with a fair statement of the claim, says what is supported and what is not, says what would settle it (for example, repeating the experiment in several schools and reporting all five measures), and has no sneering.Has a verdict but lacks either the fair opening or the settling evidence.Only says the study is “good” or “bad,” or leaves it blank.1 pt
AI comparison
1 pt		States that the critique was written first, lists every disagreement, and decides who was right on each with evidence.Lists disagreements but gives no evidence, or misses some obvious ones.Pastes the AI’s answer with no comparison, or leaves it blank.1 pt
Total (3 + 7):10 pts
▶  Teacher key (not for students)
Part A. (1) −2 (Quiet Start mean 56 ÷ 7 = 8.0; Usual mean 70 ÷ 7 = 10.0; 8 − 10 = −2; accept −2 or −2.0). (2) 20 (2 ÷ 10 = 0.20; accept 20 or 20%). (3) b (a is wrong because the homerooms were randomly assigned; c is wrong because it is not a survey and covers one school; d is wrong because “proves” and “every school” go beyond the evidence).

Part B, model critique (a student answer need not match; check it against the rubric). Opening, fair claim. The strongest honest claim is that, in these 14 homerooms over four weeks, homerooms randomly given Quiet Start had about 2 fewer tardies per week than homerooms that kept the usual routine, and that is more than a chance-only split would usually produce. 1 Data and displays. The bar chart’s axis starts at 7. The Quiet Start bar is 8 − 7 = 1 unit tall and the usual bar is 10 − 7 = 3 units tall, so the usual bar looks 3 times as tall, while the real ratio is 10 ÷ 8 = 1.25. This exaggerates the gap. 2 and 3 Summaries and models. The means are 8.0 and 10.0, so the gap is 2 tardies per week, a 20% drop, which checks out. The SDs (1.29 and 1.53) are small and nothing looks like an outlier. With only 7 homerooms per group, the numbers are fragile, but nothing needs a model here. 4 Relationships and causation. This is a randomized experiment (a coin flip assigned each homeroom), so random assignment makes the groups comparable on average, and a gap beyond chance can be attributed to Quiet Start in these homerooms. Dismissing it with “correlation is not causation” would be wrong. 5 Sampling and design. One school and 14 homerooms; the homerooms were not randomly sampled from schools in the state, so the statewide claim (“every school in the state”) goes beyond the evidence (extrapolation to a population the study did not sample). Random assignment is not random sampling. Everyone knew which homerooms had the new routine, which may matter if tardies are recorded by hand. 6 Inference. The p-value of about 0.037 means: if Quiet Start did nothing, shuffling the homerooms would give a gap at least this big, either direction, in about 4 splits in 100 (126 of 3,432). It is not “a 3.7% chance Quiet Start does nothing.” The size is small: SE = √(1.53² ÷ 7 + 1.29² ÷ 7) = 0.756, so a rough 95% range for the gap is −2 ± 1.96 × 0.756, about −3.5 to −0.5 tardies per week, which is wide compared with the gap. The report tracked 5 measures and reported only the one that worked. If all 5 had no real effect, the chance that at least one looks significant by luck is 1 − 0.955 = 0.226, about 23%, so a lone p of 0.037 among 5 tries is weaker evidence than it looks. 7 Verdict. Supported: in these homerooms, Quiet Start probably reduced tardies by something between about half a tardy and three and a half per week. Not supported: the exact 20%, a statewide rollout, or a “better school year for everyone.” To settle it: repeat the experiment in several schools with random assignment, pre-register the one main outcome (tardies) in advance, and report all five measures, including the ones that did not move.

Item 5 model. (a) “I wrote my critique before asking the AI.” (b) Disagreements might include: the AI said “correlation is not causation” but the study is randomized (the student was right, the evidence is the coin-flip assignment); the AI missed the five-measures point and the student caught it (evidence: the last paragraph of the report and 1 − 0.955 = 0.226); the AI called p = 0.037 “a 3.7% chance of no effect” (the AI was wrong; a p-value assumes the boring world). (c) Each disagreement is settled with a number or a line in the report. Credit the documentation, not whether the AI agreed. Part B is scored by the rubric above: 6 points for the critique rows and 1 point for the AI comparison.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Assignment 35.3 — The Capstone Critique
Answer items 1 to 3 in Canvas (two numbers and one letter), then type your written responses for items 4 and 5 in the text boxes. You do not need to upload a workbook. Write your critique before you ask an AI.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment.

Type
VR Module Lab
Optima · Week 35 · the module's capstone in headset

25–35 minutes
One session, one submission
Points
Rubric-scored
15 pts
Module 12 · VR Lab
The Gallery of Samples
VR Lab · 15 pts · rubric-graded
🥼 WHAT YOU'RE DOING
This module's virtue is service: statistics is a way of serving others with honest numbers, and honest numbers come with an honest account of how sure we are. Today you build a gallery and test a promise. In the Location, forty made-up bean-plant studies hang as placards, each posting the mean height of a made-up sample of 25 plants. You place the forty placards into a wall histogram, then hang a confidence-interval hoop (a bar exactly as wide as a 95% interval) on ten chosen placards. A sealed cover hides the made-up population's true mean height. You open it, check which hoops caught the truth, and count how many of all forty would have. You finish with a short spatial recording about the shape and spread of your gallery, what “95%” really promises, and one limit of the whole method. The plants, the studies, and every number are constructed (made up). They are not real measurements.
📋 WHAT YOU'LL NEED
▶
Your VR headset with Optima installed (desktop Optima works if a headset is unavailable, but standing in front of a wall of forty samples and sliding hoops along the axis is the heart of this lab).
▶
Your notes from Lessons 33.1 and 33.3 (the sampling distribution of a sample mean, its center and its spread; the interval formula and what a confidence level means) and from Lesson 35.3 (how to critique a statistical claim and name its limits). Review them before you put the headset on; re-reading inside a headset is hard.
▶
To do at your desk before the session: the made-up population of bean-plant heights has a known standard deviation σ = 6 cm, and every sample has n = 25 plants. Compute the standard error σ ÷ √n, then the 95% margin 1.960 × σ ÷ √n, then the full hoop width 2 × margin, to two decimals. Write all three on paper. Check that you can compute a mean and a standard deviation of a list of numbers with your calculator or a spreadsheet.
▶
A calculator or the Desmos scientific calculator, and about 35 uninterrupted minutes.
🚀 HOW TO JOIN
Device: VR headset (preferred) or desktop Optima
Session type: Persistent Session (your work saves between visits)
Session ID: [SESSION ID — teacher enters before publishing]
Location: [LOCATION NAME — an open, flat-floored Location with a clear wall about 8 m wide and room to step back 6 m; teacher enters before publishing]
On arrival: Find the Whiteboard IFX labeled “The Gallery of Samples — start here.” It tells you the made-up setup: bean-plant heights in a made-up population with a known standard deviation of 6 cm, and forty studies of 25 plants each. Along the wall is the Gallery Wall: a number-line axis from 29.0 to 35.0 cm with twelve bins, each 0.5 cm wide, and a mark every 0.5 cm. In front of it, on the Placard Table, lie forty placards labeled P01 to P40, each posting one sample mean. Ten hoops hang on a rail beside the wall, each labeled with one placard (P02, P05, P08, P13, P17, P20, P23, P29, P31, P40). One Sample Card shows the 25 individual heights behind placard P01. Near the wall is a Whiteboard IFX called “Gallery Board” for your numbers, and a sealed cover labeled “Population truth — open after step 5.” Do not open it early: the whole lab depends on you committing your hoops before you know where the truth is.
📝 WHAT TO DO, IN ORDER
1
Read the setup and study the Sample Card. Read the start board. Then look at the Sample Card: the 25 individual plant heights behind placard P01. Write on the Gallery Board the smallest and largest height on the card, and the card's mean (it should match the P01 placard). This is what individual plants look like. You will compare it with the gallery in a moment.
2
Build the wall histogram. Pick up the forty placards one at a time and set each into the bin on the Gallery Wall that holds its value (a bin includes its left edge and not its right: a placard reading 30.0 goes in the 30.0 to 30.5 bin). Stack them in the bin, one on top of another. When all forty are placed, write the count in every bin on the Gallery Board and check that the counts add to 40.
3
Describe the gallery. Step back and look at the wall. On the Gallery Board write three short things: where the gallery is centered, its shape (symmetric, skewed, bell-like?), and its spread (the smallest and largest placard). Then write one sentence comparing the gallery's spread with the spread of the individual plants on the Sample Card. Which is tighter, and by roughly how many times?
4
Hang the ten hoops. Each hoop is a bar exactly as wide as the 95% interval you computed at your desk, scaled to the axis. For each of the ten labeled hoops, find that placard's value, slide the hoop so its center sits exactly under the value on the axis, and write the hoop's two endpoints (value − margin and value + margin, to two decimals) on the Gallery Board. Do all ten before you move on.
5
Predict, then open the cover. First write one line on a sticky note: how many of your ten hoops do you expect to catch the true mean, and how many of all forty, and why, using what a 95% interval is built to do. Then lift the sealed cover. It posts the made-up population's true mean height (the parameter) and shows it as a vertical line across the axis.
6
Check each hoop. For each of your ten hoops, decide whether the line passes through the bar. Place a sticky note on each hoop: C if it captured the truth, M if it missed. Write the number captured out of ten on the Gallery Board.
7
Count all forty. The cover also posts a capture window: the range of placard values whose hoop would catch the truth. Use it to decide, for each of the forty placards, whether its hoop would have captured (a placard whose value is in the window would; one outside would not). Placards in the bins at the window edges need a careful look, one by one, by value and not by bin. Write the number out of forty on the Gallery Board, and its percent. Do not round it to 95%: write what you actually count. This is one simulated run of the method.
8
Read the spreads. The cover also posts the standard deviation of the individual plants on your Sample Card and the standard deviation of the forty placard values. Write both on the Gallery Board. Compare the gallery's spread with σ ÷ √n from your desk work, and say in one line whether they agree.
9
Capture the gallery. Stand where one snapshot catches the whole Gallery Wall: the histogram, the ten hoops with their C and M marks, and the Gallery Board with your counts. Take it and check it; the bin counts and capture marks must be readable. If not, retake it from closer.
10
Narrate. Stand where the wall is in view and start a spatial recording. Speak for 60 to 90 seconds, in your own words, covering all three: (a) the shape and spread of the gallery compared with individual plants, using your numbers; (b) what “95% confident” does and does not mean, using your own hoop count as an example; and (c) one limit of this model, such as what it assumes or what it cannot fix. Do not read your sticky notes aloud; look at the wall and tell what you see. Stop the recording. Then leave the placards, hoops, and sealed cover as you found them (return the placards to the table and the hoops to the rail), so the next student finds the gallery as it was built.
💬 OPTIONAL TWIST
If you have time, imagine each sample used n = 100 plants instead of 25. Before using the formula, write on a sticky note how the hoop width and the spread of the gallery would change, then check your claim with the formula. Not required, and not graded unless it is in your recording.
📤 WHAT TO SUBMIT
Canvas Assignment Name: VR Lab — The Gallery of Samples
Upload two things: (1) your snapshot from step 9 (image file) showing the wall histogram, the ten hoops with their C and M marks, and the Gallery Board with your counts; and (2) your spatial recording from step 10 (60–90 seconds of narration), shared as a link or file exactly as your teacher shows on the Canvas page for this assignment.
Below them, in the text entry box, write one line giving your numbers: your hoop width (to two decimals); your count in each bin; the number of your ten hoops that captured; the number of all forty that would capture, with its percent; and the standard deviation of the forty placards. Then add one sentence: why your capture count does not have to be exactly 95%.
Due: See the due date on this Canvas assignment. · Estimated time: 25–35 minutes in headset.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
CriteriaFull creditPartial creditMinimal creditPts
Gallery accuracy
5 pts		 All forty placards sit in the correct bins and the bin counts on the Gallery Board match the key and add to 40; the Sample Card's smallest, largest, and mean are recorded; and the description names the center (near the true mean), a roughly symmetric, bell-like shape, and a spread much tighter than the individual plants. One part wrong while the rest is correct: for example, one or two placards in a neighboring bin, a bin count that does not match the wall, or a description that gets the center and shape right but leaves out the spread comparison. Several parts wrong or missing: many placards misplaced, counts that do not add to 40, or no description of the gallery. 5 pts
Hoops and capture check
5 pts		 All ten hoops are centered on their placards (within about 0.1 cm) with endpoints correct to two decimals (margin 2.35); every C and M mark is correct against the truth line; the count out of ten and the count out of forty (37) are correct; and the student reports the count actually found rather than forcing 95%. Most hoops and marks are correct but one element is off: one hoop off-center, one wrong mark, a margin or width computed incorrectly, or a count out of forty off by one or two. Little visible evidence that the hoops were hung and checked, several wrong marks, or no count out of forty. 5 pts
Narration, including the limit
5 pts		 The narration is in the student's own words and uses their own numbers: it compares the gallery's spread with the individual spread (about σ ÷ √n versus σ), says that 95% describes the method's long-run capture rate and not the chance that this one hoop holds the truth, and names a specific, true limit. A correct narration that is generic or read from notes, misses one of the three parts, or gives a vague limit (“it might be wrong”). Narration missing most parts, much under about 45 seconds, or no evident engagement with the wall. 5 pts
Total: 15 pts
👋 FACILITATOR NOTE
Stage the Location before publishing. The data are constructed (made up): a population of bean-plant heights with true mean 32.0 cm and standard deviation 6.0 cm (both fixed and made up), and forty samples of n = 25 generated once by a seeded script (seed 1202, normal draws, each height rounded to 0.1 cm; each placard is the mean of its 25 rounded heights, rounded to 0.1 cm). There are no real plants or studies behind them. Gallery Wall: a number-line axis on a wall from 29.0 to 35.0 cm at 1 m per cm (6 m wide), tick marks every 0.5 cm, twelve bin slots 0.5 m wide, each outlined with stack guides every 0.25 m up to about 2.5 m (the tallest bin holds 8 placards). Bins include their left edge. Placards: forty small locked sign or text IFX labeled P01 to P40, each reading its value, for example “P01: mean 32.6 cm (n = 25)”, set loose on a Placard Table so students can carry them. Hoops: ten bar or ring IFX, each 4.70 m wide (2 × 1.960 × 6 ÷ √25 = 2 × 2.35 cm, at 1 m per cm), labeled P02, P05, P08, P13, P17, P20, P23, P29, P31, P40, hung on a rail beside the wall; the student slides each so its center sits under the placard's value. Accept a hoop centered within about 0.1 m. Sample Card: a locked Whiteboard IFX reading the 25 heights behind P01 (listed below). Gallery Board: an open Whiteboard IFX for student numbers. Sealed cover: a cover panel or sticky note “Population truth — open after step 5” (the honor system is enough) over a locked Whiteboard IFX posting: true mean 32.0 cm; a vertical line IFX across the axis at 32.0; the capture window 29.65 to 34.35 cm (a hoop captures the truth exactly when its placard value lies in this window); the SD of the 25 heights on the Sample Card (5.98); and the SD of the forty placard values (1.18). Confirm the IFX names and sizes, how to put text on a placard IFX, how to cover a whiteboard, whether objects stack or snap into bins, and where to start and stop a spatial recording against the current IFX library and ENGAGE app before publishing; we have not verified these in ENGAGE. Answer key. Of the ten hoops, 7 capture and 3 miss (the misses are P02, P20, P40). Of all forty, 37 of 40 capture (92.5%); the 3 misses are P02 (34.4), P20 (29.5), P40 (34.4). This is one simulated run, not a result to force toward 95%: the method promises about 95% in the long run, and a run of forty can land at 36, 37, 38, 39, or 40. Accept the student's counts if they equal this key. P02 and P40 (34.4) sit just above the window top 34.35 and P20 (29.5) just below the window bottom 29.65, and each is in an edge bin with placards that do capture, so a student who judges by bin instead of by value can flip them. What to expect in the narration. (a) The gallery is centered near the true mean, roughly bell-shaped, and much tighter than individual plants: its SD is about 1.18 (theory 1.20) against about 5.98 (σ = 6) for single plants, a factor of about 5 = √25. (b) The correct reading of 95%: the method captures the true mean about 95% of the time over many samples; it is not a 95% chance that a particular hoop, once drawn and compared, holds the truth (each one either does or does not); and it does not say 95% of the plants lie inside the hoop. Reject “95% of the data is in the hoop” and “there is a 95% chance the true mean is in this hoop.” Accept the student's own count (7 of 10, 37 of 40) used as an example. (c) Accept any specific, true limit: the hoop assumes a random sample and does nothing to fix a biased one; it assumes σ is known (in practice it is estimated); with a small n the normal model for the sample mean needs care when the data are skewed; this population and this run are made up, and forty samples is only one run; and the 3 misses are the method working as designed, not an error. Do not accept “it might be wrong” with nothing more. Common sticking points: centering the hoop on the truth instead of on the placard (the hoop moves with the data, the truth stays still); using the margin as the full width; judging a placard at the window edge by its bin; reading 95% as the probability for one hoop; and forcing the count to 95% because “it should be 95%.” What to demo: carrying a placard and setting it into a bin, sliding a bar along an axis, lifting a cover, placing a sticky note, and starting and stopping a spatial recording. If a student finishes early, ask what would change if every sample came from a convenience sample that over-represents tall plants (every hoop would shift the same way, the capture rate would fall well below 95%, and the hoop would give no warning).

Optima Academy Online

PROBABILITY & STATISTICS HONORS
Quarter / Module
Q4 · Semester 2 Finals
Finals Week
Lesson
Review Lesson
Paired Lesson
From One Sample to a Population, Carefully
Complete the lesson before starting
Points
Assignment
10 pts
Semester 2 Review
Review Activity — The Whole Course, Once Through
Assignment · 10 pts
📖 CONTENT FOCUS
One problem from every room of the semester — and one flawed analysis to catch
Mixed-practice set · graded on complete, honest work
Covers: data displays; five-number summaries, outliers, and choosing a center; the normal model; regression and residuals; two-way tables; sampling methods and bias; study design; sample means and the Central Limit Theorem; margin of error and confidence intervals; shuffle tests and Type I error; diagnosing a flawed statistical report.
Lesson focus: From One Sample to a Population, Carefully
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Ten items, one from each room of the semester, in the mixed order a final exam would deal them. Work every item in your notebook with the work visible: the model named, the z-scores and standard errors written out, the intervals built term by term, and the Desmos entry or Excel formula reported where you used one. (Excel work here is written as the formula you would type; you do not upload a workbook.) This is a practice set — it is scored on completeness and visible reasoning, not on perfection — but treat it as a dress rehearsal: no notes open, Desmos and Excel only, and check your answers against the lessons afterward. Every dataset, name, and scenario in this activity is made up for practice. Each item stands alone; you may work them in any order.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Can you recognize which room of the course a problem lives in — when nobody tells you — and say only what the evidence supports?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS — WORK ALL TEN ITEMS, WORK VISIBLE
1
The normal model. Apple sacks packed at a made-up orchard, “Hollowell Orchard,” have weights that are well described by a normal model with mean \(\mu = 450\) g and SD \(\sigma = 20\) g. (a) Find the z-score of a 485 g sack and the percent of sacks heavier than 485 g. (b) Find the percent of sacks between 430 g and 470 g, and say which rule of thumb it matches. (c) The orchard labels the heaviest 10% of sacks “Extra Large.” Find the cutoff weight. Show the z-score arithmetic, the picture (a sketched bell with the area shaded), and your tool entry: Desmos (485-450)/20 for z; Excel =1-NORM.DIST(485,450,20,TRUE), =NORM.DIST(470,450,20,TRUE)-NORM.DIST(430,450,20,TRUE), and =NORM.INV(0.90,450,20). Round areas to three decimals and the cutoff to one decimal.
2
Two-way table. A made-up survey of 240 students at “Cedar Ridge High” asked two yes/no questions: do you play an instrument, and are you on a sports team? You are told only this: 240 students answered; 90 play an instrument; 114 are on a team; 54 do both. (a) Rebuild the full two-way table, all four cells and all totals. (b) Find \(P(\text{team} \mid \text{instrument})\) and \(P(\text{instrument} \mid \text{team})\) as fractions of counts and as decimals, and say in one sentence why these two numbers are not the same. (c) Compare the team rate among instrument players with the team rate among students who do not play, and say what that comparison does and does not show about cause.
3
Reading and choosing displays. A made-up survey of 40 workers in the fictional town of “Marlowe Falls” recorded two variables: how each worker travels to work (car, bus, bike, walk) and the minutes of the trip. The trip times are summarized below. (a) Classify each variable as categorical or numerical. (b) Name the best display for each variable and give one reason; say why a histogram would be the wrong choice for the travel method. (c) Use the table to find how many workers travel under 30 minutes, name the interval that contains the median (show how you found it), and describe the shape of the distribution.
Trip time (minutes)Workers
0 to under 104
10 to under 2012
20 to under 3011
30 to under 407
40 to under 504
50 to under 602
4
Margin of error and sample size. A made-up random poll by the fictional “Larch County Survey Desk” asks \(n = 625\) registered voters whether they favor a new bridge; \(y = 350\) say yes. (a) Find \(\hat{p}\), the standard error, the margin of error, and the 95% interval, using \(\hat{p} \pm 1.96\sqrt{\hat{p}(1-\hat{p})/n}\); Desmos sqrt(0.56*0.44/625), then 1.96*0.0199. Round to four decimals. (b) Does the interval contain 0.50? Say what that tells you and what it does not. (c) Give the correct one-sentence reading of “95% confident,” and name one source of error the margin of error does not cover. (d) A later poll wants a margin of error of at most 0.03 with no information about \(p\) beforehand. Use \(n = \left(\frac{1.96}{0.03}\right)^2(0.5)(0.5)\) and report the smallest whole sample size that works; Desmos (1.96/0.03)^2*0.5*0.5. Excel for the interval endpoints (proportion in B1, n in B2): =B1-1.96*SQRT(B1*(1-B1)/B2) and =B1+1.96*SQRT(B1*(1-B1)/B2).
5
Five numbers, fences, and the right center. Daily visitor counts at a made-up library branch, “Maple Hollow,” for 12 days: 21, 24, 18, 27, 22, 25, 19, 23, 26, 20, 22, 71. Use the by-hand convention: order the data, take the median, then find Q1 and Q3 as the medians of the lower and upper halves (with 12 values, each half has 6). (a) Write the five-number summary and the IQR. (b) Compute the outlier fences \(Q1 - 1.5 \times IQR\) and \(Q3 + 1.5 \times IQR\) and name any outlier. (c) Compute the mean and the median. Which better describes a typical day, and why? (d) Recompute the mean without the outlier and say what the change shows. Excel check: =MEDIAN(A1:A12) and =QUARTILE.INC(A1:A12,1). The spreadsheet's quartile rule may differ slightly from the by-hand rule; report your by-hand values and, if the two differ, say so.
6
Sampling and study design. (a) The fictional town of “Larkspur Hollow” wants opinions on a new park. Three plans are proposed. Plan 1: post a survey link on the town website and use everyone who answers. Plan 2: interview people who walk past the farmers market on one Saturday morning. Plan 3: number the 2,400 households on the town's utility list from 1 to 2,400 and pick 150 using =RANDBETWEEN(1,2400) (redrawing any repeat). Name the sampling method in each plan, name the likely bias in Plans 1 and 2, and say which plan you would use and why. (b) Under Plan 3, what is the probability that any one household is chosen? Write it as a fraction and a decimal. (c) Classify each of these made-up studies as a survey, an observational study, or an experiment, and for each say whether the words “is associated with” or “causes” are permitted. Study X: the fictional “Quill Valley Clinic” mails a sleep-and-mood questionnaire to 300 randomly chosen patients. Study Y: a researcher compares the grades of students who happen to eat breakfast with those who do not, using school records. Study Z: 60 volunteers are assigned by coin flip to either a 10-minute walk or 10 minutes of sitting after lunch, and afternoon alertness is scored for everyone.
7
Regression in context. A made-up school study of 30 students (weekly study time from 2 to 10 hours) gives the fitted line \(\hat{y} = 52 + 3.5x\), where \(x\) is hours studied per week and \(\hat{y}\) is the predicted quiz score out of 100. (a) Interpret the slope and the intercept in context, and say whether the intercept is trustworthy here. (b) Predict the score for a student who studies 6 hours. (c) Predict the score for a student who studies 20 hours and explain why that prediction should be flagged. (d) A student who studies 8 hours scores 76. Find the residual (observed minus predicted), state its sign, and say what the sign means. Desmos: 52+3.5*6; Excel for real data: =SLOPE(y_range,x_range) and =INTERCEPT(y_range,x_range).
8
Shuffle test and Type I error. At the fictional “Brightwater Academy,” 16 students were randomly split into two groups of 8. Group A studied with self-quizzing; Group B reread their notes. Quiz scores (out of 20) were A: 14, 16, 15, 18, 17, 13, 16, 15 and B: 12, 14, 13, 15, 11, 14, 12, 13. (a) Find each group's mean and the observed difference (A minus B). (b) A class shuffled all 16 scores at random into two groups of 8, 2,000 times, and recorded the difference in means each time. The difference was at least as large as the observed one in 17 of the 2,000 shuffles. Estimate the p-value, and say in plain words what one shuffle represents and what the p-value measures. (c) At the 5% level, what is the decision? (d) Say what a Type I error would mean in this experiment, and why the 5% level means such an error will happen about 5% of the time when nothing is going on. (e) A friend says “the p-value is the probability that self-quizzing does nothing.” Explain what is wrong with that sentence.
9
A sample mean and the Central Limit Theorem. Waiting times at a made-up urgent-care clinic, “Pinegate Clinic,” are right-skewed with population mean \(\mu = 18\) minutes and SD \(\sigma = 9\) minutes. A random sample of \(n = 49\) patients is taken. (a) Find the standard error of the sample mean. (b) Find the probability that the sample mean exceeds 20 minutes: write the z-score on the sample-mean scale, then the area to the right. (c) If the sample size were quadrupled to 196, what would happen to the standard error, and why? (d) Explain why the normal model may be used for the sample mean in part (b) even though individual waiting times are skewed — and why you could not use the same normal model to find the chance that one patient waits more than 20 minutes. Desmos: 9/sqrt(49), (20-18)/(9/sqrt(49)); Excel: =1-NORM.DIST(20,18,9/SQRT(49),TRUE). Round areas to three decimals.
10
Diagnose the flawed analysis. Read this short report. It is made up: the town, the newspaper, and every number are invented for practice.
DUNHALLOW (made up) — The Fenwick Bugle (made up) reports: (A) The Fenwick Bugle posted a link to its website, and 412 readers chose to click it and answer; 84% said they back the new riverfront arcade, so the Bugle declares that “84% of Dunhallow supports the arcade.” (B) In a look at school records, students who visit the arcade have higher grades, so “the arcade raises grades.” (C) A bar chart of the school budget “shows spending skyrocketing”: its vertical axis starts at $4.90 million instead of zero, so a rise from $4.92 million to $5.00 million makes one bar tower over the other. (D) The arcade's brain-training game produced a “highly significant” improvement of 0.2 points on a 100-point test; the sample size is not given. (E) Town population has grown by about 300 people a year since 2015, so the Bugle predicts exactly 40,000 residents in the year 2090.
Each of the five passages (A) through (E) contains one planted flaw. For each, write: (1) the flaw, named precisely; (2) which idea from this semester it breaks (name the module’s topic: displays, descriptive statistics, the normal model, regression and association, sampling and study design, or inference); and (3) how to fix the claim so that it says only what the evidence supports. One to three sentences per passage is enough; the diagnosis is the deliverable.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA

▶  Teacher answer key (all data made up; not for students)
1. Normal model (made up). z = (485 − 450)/20 = 1.75. P(X > 485) = 1 − 0.9599 = 0.040 (accept 0.040 to 0.041; about 4.0%). (b) z = −1 and +1; area 0.683 (accept 0.682 to 0.683); matches the 68% part of the empirical rule. (c) top 10% means area 0.90 below; 475.6 g (accept 475.5 to 475.7; z ≈ 1.282, 450 + 1.282(20)).
2. Two-way table. Instrument and team 54; instrument, no team 36; no instrument, team 60; no instrument, no team 90. Row totals 90 and 150; column totals 114 and 126; grand total 240. (b) P(team | instrument) = 54/90 = 0.600 (3/5); P(instrument | team) = 54/114 = 0.474 (9/19, accept 0.474 or 0.473 to 0.474). They differ because they condition on different groups (different denominators, 90 versus 114). (c) Team rate among non-players = 60/150 = 0.40 versus 0.60 among players (overall 0.475): the two traits are associated in these 240 students; observational survey data, so no cause is shown (a lurking variable such as time, interest or school involvement could drive both).
3. Displays. Travel method: categorical. Trip time: numerical (continuous). Best displays: bar chart (or circle graph) for travel method; histogram (or box plot) for trip time. A histogram is wrong for travel method because its categories have no numerical order or scale and the bars would imply one. (c) Under 30 minutes: 4 + 12 + 11 = 27. n = 40, so the median is the mean of the 20th and 21st values; cumulative counts are 4, 16, 27, 34, 38, 40, so both fall in 20 to under 30. Shape: skewed right (a long tail toward longer trips; the tallest bar is 10 to under 20).
4. Margin of error. p-hat = 350/625 = 0.56; SE = √(0.56 × 0.44/625) = 0.0199; margin = 1.96 × 0.0199 = 0.0389 (accept 0.0389 to 0.0390); interval (0.521, 0.599) (accept 0.521 to 0.599). (b) 0.50 is not inside, so 50% is not a plausible value for the population proportion at this confidence level, but this says nothing about bias or about the exact size of support. (c) 95% describes the method: about 95% of intervals built this way from repeated random polls would capture the true proportion; it is not a 95% probability that this one interval does, and not that 95% of voters are in it. Not covered: bad wording, nonresponse, an incomplete voter list. (d) n = 1067.11, so 1068 (always round up; accept 1,068). Using p-hat = 0.56 instead would give 1051.7, so 1052; accept this only if the student explains the planning value was chosen from the earlier poll.
5. Five numbers. Ordered: 18, 19, 20, 21, 22, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 71. Min 18; Q1 = (20 + 21)/2 = 20.5; median = (22 + 23)/2 = 22.5; Q3 = (25 + 26)/2 = 25.5; max 71. IQR = 5.0. Fences: 20.5 − 7.5 = 13.0 and 25.5 + 7.5 = 33.0; 71 is the only outlier (above 33). Mean = 318/12 = 26.5; median = 22.5. The median is the better typical day because the outlier pulls the mean above 10 of the 12 days. Without 71: mean = 247/11 = 22.45 (accept 22.45 to 22.46); a single value moved the mean by about 4.0, while the median moves only to 22. Excel's QUARTILE.INC gives Q1 = 20.75 and Q3 = 25.25; small differences from the by-hand rule are expected and fine if noted; the outlier conclusion is unchanged either way.
6. Sampling and design. (a) Plan 1: voluntary response (self-selected); bias: only motivated people answer, and people without the website are excluded. Plan 2: convenience sample; bias: one place and time, so people who shop at the market (and are free Saturday morning) are overrepresented. Plan 3: simple random sample from the utility list (best choice; the list is not the whole town, so a small coverage gap remains: households without utility accounts). (b) 150/2400 = 1/16 = 0.0625. (c) Study X: survey; association words only (and it describes the surveyed group; a random sample lets it speak about the patient population). Study Y: observational study; “is associated with” only, since breakfast eaters may differ in many other ways. Study Z: experiment (random assignment by coin flip, with a control group); “causes” is permitted, but because the 60 were volunteers the result applies only to people like them; no blinding is possible for walking versus sitting, which is worth one sentence.
7. Regression. (a) Slope: each additional hour studied per week goes with a predicted 3.5-point increase in quiz score. Intercept: predicted score of 52 for 0 hours; 0 hours is outside the observed 2 to 10 hours, so it is a starting value of the line, not a trustworthy prediction. (b) 52 + 3.5(6) = 73. (c) 52 + 3.5(20) = 122, above the 100-point maximum; 20 hours is far outside 2 to 10: extrapolation. (d) predicted at 8 hours = 80; residual = 76 − 80 = -4; negative: the student scored 4 points below what the line predicts for that study time.
8. Shuffle test. (a) Mean A = 124/8 = 15.5; mean B = 104/8 = 13.0; difference = 2.5. (b) p ≈ 17/2,000 = 0.0085 (this exact simulation count was produced by a seeded run; the exact p-value from all 12,870 equally likely splits is 0.0041 (53/12,870); accept 0.0085, or any value from 0.004 to 0.013 if the student reports the count given as a fraction; this is a one-sided count of shuffles at least as large as the observed difference). One shuffle = one world in which the study method has no effect, the 16 scores are just reassigned to groups by chance. The p-value is the fraction of such worlds that produce a difference at least as large as the one observed. (c) p is below 0.05: reject the idea that chance alone explains it; the result is statistically significant at 5%. (d) Type I error: concluding self-quizzing helps when in fact it makes no difference; when nothing is going on, 5% of the shuffled worlds still land beyond the cutoff by luck. (e) The p-value assumes “nothing is going on” and asks how surprising the data are; it is not the probability that the assumption is true.
9. Sample mean. (a) SE = 9/√49 = 9/7 = 1.2857 (accept 1.286). (b) z = (20 − 18)/1.2857 = 1.556 (accept 1.56); P(mean > 20) = 0.060 (accept 0.059 to 0.060; about 6%). (c) SE = 9/√196 = 9/14 = 0.6429 (accept 0.643): quadrupling n halves the SE, because SE has √n in the denominator. (d) By the Central Limit Theorem, means of samples of decent size (n = 49) are approximately normal whatever the population's shape; a single waiting time is not an average, so the skewed shape still governs it and the normal model would misstate the chance.
10. Diagnose. One point of credit per item is earned by naming each flaw, its module idea, and a workable fix; accept equivalent wording. The five planted flaws:
  • (A) Voluntary-response sample (self-selected, from one website) treated as all residents; no margin of error either. Module idea: sampling and study design (and inference). Fix: Say “of the 412 readers who chose to respond”; to speak for the town, use a random sample and report a margin of error.
  • (B) Causal verb (“raises”) from observational data; confounding (students who visit arcades may differ in other ways). Module idea: regression and association (correlation is not causation) and study design. Fix: “Students who visit the arcade tend to have higher grades,” or run a randomized experiment.
  • (C) Truncated vertical axis (starts at $4.90 million, not zero); the visual exaggerates a rise of about 1.6%. Module idea: data displays. Fix: Start the bars at zero, or state the real change: $4.92M to $5.00M is about 1.6%.
  • (D) “Significant” with a tiny effect (0.2 points of 100) and no sample size; statistical significance is not practical importance. Module idea: inference (significance) and descriptive statistics. Fix: Report the effect size and n and the p-value; call 0.2 points tiny; do not say “highly significant” as if it were large.
  • (E) Extrapolation (a linear trend carried 65 years beyond the data) stated as an exact prediction. Module idea: regression (extrapolation). Fix: Predict only inside or near the data range, use hedged language, and say growth may not stay linear.
Arithmetic behind the planted flaws: the budget rise is (5.00 − 4.92)/4.92 = 0.016, about 1.6%; a straight line through 300 people per year over 2015 to 2090 is 75 years, or about 22,500 added people.

quizzes.title: Module 7: Begin Here — Data and Data Displays
quizzes.description: Welcome to Semester 2. For a semester you studied chance: what could happen. Now you turn to what did happen. Statistics begins with data, and data begins to speak only when someone draws it. In the oldest case in this course, a London haberdasher named John Graunt read the weekly lists of burials in his city and saw patterns no one had drawn before him. Over the next three weeks you will learn to sort data, tally it, and draw it as bar charts, histograms, box plots, and scatter plots. You will also learn the harder lesson: the same numbers can be drawn to tell the truth or to mislead, and the difference is often a few quiet choices. Before you start, answer the few questions below. There are no wrong answers; your teacher reads these to meet you where you are.

questions.text: Here is the question this module keeps asking: When is a picture of data honest, and when does it lie? Write your first answer now, in 3–5 sentences. If you can, describe a graph you have seen (news, social media, a classroom) that you trusted or doubted, and why. You will meet this question again at the end of the module and compare.

By the end of Module 7 you will be able to: tell numerical from categorical data and one-variable from two-variable data; build and read frequency and relative frequency tables; draw and interpret bar charts, circle graphs, line plots, stem-and-leaf plots, histograms, box plots, and scatter plots; choose the display that fits a question and defend the choice; spot the common ways a graph misleads; and use a spreadsheet to build clear, honestly labeled charts. Have you read this list?

quizzes.description: You have finished the module that began with a haberdasher counting burials and ended with you building your own charts and telling the truth with them. You have drawn data seven ways, chosen among those ways on purpose, and learned five quiet tricks that make a graph lie. This module's virtue is Honesty. A graph can mislead without a single false number: a cut-off axis, an uneven scale, a hand-picked window of time. Name one place in this module where the honest choice was less impressive than the dishonest one (a bar chart whose differences looked small when drawn from zero, a histogram that hid its clumps, a trend that disappeared in the full range). Describe what the honest picture cost you, and what it protected.

quizzes.title: Module 8: Begin Here — Descriptive Statistics
quizzes.description: Last module you drew data. This module you measure it. A picture shows everything and a number shows one thing, and the art of descriptive statistics is choosing the few numbers that tell a reader the most without telling them anything false. Over three weeks you will find the center of a dataset two ways, measure its spread three ways, decide when a lone far-off value is a mistake and when it is the whole story, and compare one group with another. You will also meet a hard question you will keep asking all year: when a single number stands in for twenty values, what has been left out, and who is owed the truth about it? Before you start, answer the few questions below. There are no wrong answers; your teacher reads these to meet you where you are.

questions.text: Here is the question this module keeps asking: What does a fair summary of a dataset keep, and what does it hide? Write your first answer now, in 3–5 sentences. If you can, describe a time you saw a single number (an average, a typical value, a rating) that gave you the wrong idea. You will meet this question again at the end of the module and compare.

By the end of Module 8 you will be able to: find and explain the mean and the median and say when each fits; find percentiles, quartiles, and the five-number summary and draw a box plot; measure spread with the range, the interquartile range, and the standard deviation; use the 1.5 × IQR rule to flag possible outliers and decide what to do about them; describe a distribution's shape; compare two or more distributions with numbers and words; and use a spreadsheet to build a summary table and write an honest data story. Have you read this list?
