quizzes.title: Quiz 22.1 — Measures of Center: Mean and Median

questions.text: What is the mean of the data set 3, 5, 8, 12, 17?
What is the median of the data set 7, 2, 11, 4, 9, 15?
The data set 20, 22, 25, 26, 27 has mean 24 and median 25. If the largest value is changed from 27 to 270, which statement is true?

answers.text: the mean changes a great deal, but the median stays 25
the median changes a great deal, but the mean stays 24
both the mean and the median stay the same
both the mean and the median change by the same amount

questions.text: The prices of homes in a (made-up) town are strongly skewed to the right because a few mansions cost far more than the rest. Which statistic better describes a typical home price, and why?

answers.text: the mean, because it uses every value, so it is not affected by the mansions
the median, because it is resistant to a few extremely large values
the mean, because the mean is always larger than the median
the median, because it equals the total price divided by the number of homes

questions.text: Four friends have 2, 4, 9, and 13 dollars. They pool all their money and share it equally. How much does each friend get?

answers.text: 6.5 dollars
6 dollars
7 dollars
28 dollars

quizzes.title: Quiz 22.2 — Percentiles, Quartiles, and Box Plots

questions.text: Dana's score on a 50-point quiz is at the 80th percentile of her class. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: Dana answered 80 percent of the questions correctly.
About 80 percent of the students in her class scored the same as or lower than Dana.
About 80 percent of the students in her class scored higher than Dana.
Dana scored 40 points.

questions.text: The number of values is odd. Using the median-of-each-half method, with the median left out of both halves, what is Q3 for the ordered data 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 12, 15?
Find the five-number summary (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum) of the ordered data 4, 6, 7, 10, 12, 15, 19, 20 using the median-of-each-half method.

Two datasets of the same size have these five-number summaries (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum): Set A is 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and Set B is 10, 27, 30, 33, 50. Which statement do the box plots support?

answers.text: Set B has a larger median than Set A.
Set B has more values in its upper whisker than Set A.
The middle half of Set A is more spread out than the middle half of Set B.
Set A has a larger range than Set B.

questions.text: For the ordered data 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10, 13, 15, 16, 20, a student finds Q1 = 5 by the median-of-each-half method. A spreadsheet's QUARTILE.INC gives 5.5. What is the best explanation?

answers.text: The student made an arithmetic error, and the spreadsheet's answer is correct.
The two methods use different conventions for locating Q1, and neither answer is a mistake.
The spreadsheet is rounding up to the next half.
The data must be re-ordered before QUARTILE.INC can be used.

quizzes.title: Quiz 22.3 — Range, IQR, and Outliers

questions.text: What is the range of the data set 6, 9, 10, 12, 13, 40?
Which pair of statistics is resistant, meaning it changes very little when an extreme value is added to a data set?

answers.text: the median and the interquartile range (IQR)
the mean and the range
the mean and the IQR
the median and the range

questions.text: For the data set 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 40, use the median-of-each-half method for quartiles (Q1 = 5.5, Q3 = 11.5) and the 1.5 × IQR rule. In a box plot of these data, where does the upper whisker end?

answers.text: at 40
at 12

questions.text: A data set has Q1 = 24 and Q3 = 34. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which of the values 8, 12, 49, and 52 are flagged as outliers?

answers.text: 52 only
8 and 52
all four values

questions.text: A value in a data set of delivery times is flagged as an outlier by the 1.5 × IQR rule. Which is the best next step?

answers.text: delete it automatically, because outliers are always errors
keep it and say nothing, because the rule is only a guide
find out why it is so far from the others, correct or remove it only if it is an error or does not belong, and report the summary with and without it
replace it with the mean of the other values

quizzes.title: Quiz 23.1 — Standard Deviation

questions.text: The data set 3, 5, 7 has mean 5. What is its sample standard deviation (divide the sum of squared deviations by n − 1)?

answers.text: about 1.63
about 2.83

questions.text: When computing a standard deviation, why are the deviations from the mean squared before they are averaged?

answers.text: to make the answer a whole number
because the mean is the middle value of the ordered data
to remove outliers from the data
because the deviations from the mean always add to zero, so they would cancel without squaring

questions.text: A researcher measures the heights of 25 students chosen from a school of 900 students and wants to describe the spread of heights for the whole school. Which Excel function matches the standard deviation she should compute from her data?

answers.text: STDEV.S
STDEV.P
AVERAGE
MEDIAN

questions.text: Delivery Service X has delivery times (in minutes) 48, 49, 50, 51, 52, and Delivery Service Y has delivery times 30, 40, 50, 60, 70. Both have a mean of 50 minutes. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: the two services have equal standard deviations because their means are equal
Service X has the larger standard deviation because its values are closer together
Service Y has the larger standard deviation because its values are farther from the mean on average
the standard deviation of Service Y is 0 because its values increase by the same amount each time

questions.text: The data set 4, 5, 7, 8, 11, 13 has a sample standard deviation of about 3.46 and an IQR of 6 (using the median of each half to find Q1 and Q3). If the value 13 is changed to 40, which statement is true?

answers.text: the standard deviation and the IQR both stay the same
the IQR stays 6, but the standard deviation increases a great deal
the IQR increases a great deal, but the standard deviation stays about 3.46
both the IQR and the standard deviation decrease

quizzes.title: Quiz 23.2 — Shape: Symmetry, Skewness, and Clusters

questions.text: A histogram of made-up waiting times has its tallest bars on the left and a long, thin stretch of short bars trailing off to the right. How is this distribution described?

answers.text: symmetric
skewed left
skewed right
bimodal

questions.text: A made-up data set has a mean of 38 and a median of 31. Which shape is the most likely?

answers.text: skewed right
skewed left
symmetric
This combination of mean and median is impossible.

questions.text: Twelve made-up scores are 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 86, 87, 88, 88, 89, 90. Both the mean and the median equal 50. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: The scores are symmetric with one peak, so 50 is a typical score.
The score 50 is an outlier.
The scores are skewed right.
The scores form two clusters with a gap, so 50 describes no actual score.

questions.text: Which pair of summaries best describes a strongly right-skewed data set with a few very large values?

answers.text: the mean and the standard deviation
the median and the interquartile range (IQR)
the mean and the IQR
the median and the standard deviation

questions.text: A made-up histogram of 40 students' reading times is skewed right. The median is 22 minutes, the IQR is 9 minutes, and two students read for more than an hour. Which sentence is the most complete description?

answers.text: The mean is 22 minutes.
The reading times are skewed right.
Most students read about 22 minutes, give or take.
The reading times are skewed right with a median of 22 minutes; the middle half spans 9 minutes (IQR), and two students read for over an hour, far above the rest.

quizzes.title: Quiz 23.3 — Descriptive Statistics by Spreadsheet

questions.text: The values 1, 3, and 5 are a sample from a much larger group, and they are typed in cells A1:A3 of an Excel sheet. Which entry gives the sample standard deviation, and what does it return?

answers.text: =STDEV.P(A1:A3), which returns 1.63
=STDEV.S(A1:A3), which returns 1.63
=STDEV.S(A1:A3), which returns 2
=STDEV.P(A1:A3), which returns 2

questions.text: An Excel summary of the commute times, in minutes, of 30 riders (a sample) shows: mean 62.4, median 55, Q1 41, Q3 70. Which conclusion and choice of summary is best supported?

answers.text: The mean is above the median, so the data are skewed left; report the mean and standard deviation.
The mean is above the median, which suggests a right skew; the median and IQR are the safer summary of a typical rider.
The mean and median are far apart, so the data must contain an error and should be thrown out.
The mean is above the median, so the data are symmetric; either summary is equally good.

questions.text: In Excel, the values 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 14 are in cells A1:A7. What does the formula =QUARTILE.INC(A1:A7,3) return?
In Excel, cell C2 holds =IF(OR(B2<$F$9,B2>$F$10),"outlier","") and is copied down to C5. What formula appears in C5?

answers.text: =IF(OR(B5<$F$12,B5>$F$13),"outlier","")
=IF(OR(B5<$F$9,B5>$F$10),"outlier","")
=IF(OR(B2<$F$9,B2>$F$10),"outlier","")
=IF(OR(B5<F12,B5>F13),"outlier","")

130 only
12 only
neither value

quizzes.title: Quiz 24.1 — Comparing Two or More Distributions

questions.text: Group A has a median of 40 and an IQR of 10. Group B has a median of 52 and an IQR of 22. Which statement correctly compares the center and the spread?

answers.text: B's median is 12 higher than A's, and B's IQR is 12 narrower than A's
A's median is 12 higher than B's, and A's IQR is 12 wider than B's
B's median is 12 higher than A's, and B's IQR is 12 wider than A's
B's median is 12 higher than A's, and the two IQRs are about the same

questions.text: Group 1 has the values 4, 5, 5, 6, 7, 8, 40 and Group 2 has the values 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 8, 9. Which pair of summaries is the better choice for comparing the two groups fairly?

answers.text: median and IQR, because Group 1 has an extreme value (40) that would distort its mean and standard deviation
mean and standard deviation, because they use every value
mean and standard deviation, because both groups have 7 values
the minimum and maximum only, because the 40 is an error and should be ignored

questions.text: Five-number summaries (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum) are Group A: 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 and Group B: 35, 45, 55, 65, 75. The two box plots are drawn on one axis. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: the boxes overlap, so the two groups have about the same center
B's median is 10 higher than A's
A's IQR is 20 and B's IQR is 30
B's lower quartile (45) is above A's upper quartile (40), so the boxes do not overlap

questions.text: A student surveys 12 students from School X and 12 students from School Y. In these samples, the median time spent on homework is 15 minutes higher at School X. Which conclusion is best supported by these data alone?

answers.text: School X assigns more homework because its teachers are stricter
In these two samples the median is 15 minutes higher at School X, but this alone does not tell us whether the two whole schools differ
the difference proves that the median homework time is 15 minutes higher for all students at School X
the difference in the population must be zero because the samples are small

questions.text: Class P has 40 students and 12 of them scored above 90 on a test. Class Q has 25 students and 10 of them scored above 90. Which comparison is fair?

answers.text: Class P did better because 12 is greater than 10
Class Q did better because it has fewer students
Compare proportions: 30% of Class P and 40% of Class Q scored above 90, so a larger share of Class Q did
the classes cannot be compared because they have different sizes

quizzes.title: Quiz 24.2 — Outliers and Their Effects on Center and Spread

questions.text: A made-up list of five values is 3, 5, 6, 8, 9. The largest value is changed from 9 to 90 and no other value changes. Which of these summaries does NOT change?

answers.text: the mean
the range
the median
the sample standard deviation

questions.text: In a made-up group of 20 values, one value is increased by 60 and no other value changes. By how much does the mean increase?

Every value in a data set is multiplied by 3 and then 5 is added to every value. The original mean is 10 and the original sample standard deviation is 4. What are the new mean and sample standard deviation?

answers.text: mean 35, standard deviation 12
mean 35, standard deviation 17
mean 35, standard deviation 4

questions.text: In a made-up list of 11 commute times in minutes, ten values lie between 12 and 35 and one value is 450. The 1.5 × IQR rule flags the 450, and the original record sheet is available. What is the best next step?

answers.text: Delete the 450, because the rule flagged it.
Check the record sheet to find out why the value is 450, then correct it, set it aside with a stated reason, or keep it, and report what was done.
Replace the 450 with the mean of the other ten values.

questions.text: Twelve made-up values are 20, 22, 23, 25, 26, 28, 29, 31, 33, 35, 36, 40. The largest value, 40, is changed to 60. Using the median-of-each-half method for quartiles, which statement is correct?

answers.text: The range and the IQR both stay the same.

The range increases by 20 and the IQR stays the same.
The median increases by 20 and the IQR stays the same.

quizzes.title: Quiz 24.3 — Telling a Dataset's Story Honestly

questions.text: The summary table for the minutes people waited in two shops (30 days each, a sample of days) reads: Shop A: mean 8.0, median 8, SD 1.5; Shop B: mean 8.0, median 5, SD 9.0, with three days flagged as unusually long. Which statement is the most honest report?

answers.text: The two shops have the same average wait, 8 minutes, so they are equally good.
Shop B is better because its median wait is lower, so the SD does not matter.
Shop B's typical wait is 3 minutes shorter (median 5 versus 8), but its waits vary far more (SD 9.0 versus 1.5) and include some very long days.
Shop A is better because its SD is smaller, so its mean must be smaller.

questions.text: A survey of 40 students (constructed) found that those who reported more sleep had higher test scores. Which sentence breaks the rules of an honest data story?

answers.text: Among these 40 students, more sleep went along with higher scores.
These data cannot tell us whether sleep affects scores or something else explains both.
The survey included 40 students, so the results describe only that group unless the students were chosen to represent a larger one.
More sleep raises test scores, as the survey proves.

questions.text: A summary table says: Q1 = 10, median = 14, Q3 = 18 (minutes), by the median-of-each-half method. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which of these values is flagged as an outlier?
A bar chart shows two group means, 52 and 55, with the vertical axis starting at 50. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: The bars are drawn to scale, so the 55 bar is about 6 percent taller than the 52 bar.
The 55 bar looks 2.5 times as tall as the 52 bar, but 55 is only about 6 percent more than 52; starting the axis at 0 would be fair.
The axis starts at 50, so the chart shows that the second group's mean is 2.5 times the first group's mean.
Cutting the axis changes the data, so the means are no longer 52 and 55.

questions.text: Ten constructed values are 18, 19, 20, 20, 21, 21, 22, 22, 23, and 44. The mean of all ten is 23.0 and the median is 21. Without the 44, the mean of the other nine is 20.67 and the median is still 21. Which report best follows the rules for outliers?

answers.text: Delete the 44 and report only the mean of 20.67, since it is the more typical number.
Report only the mean of 23.0, since it uses every value.
Report that the 44 is flagged by the 1.5 × IQR rule, give the mean with and without it (23.0 and 20.67) and the median (21), and say what is known about why the 44 occurred.
Report only the median, 21, and say nothing about the 44.

This module's virtue is Courtesy. A summary is a courtesy to a reader who cannot look at every value, and it becomes a discourtesy when it hides what the reader needed to see. quizzes.title: Module 9: Begin Here — The Normal Distribution
quizzes.description: Last module you summarized data with a center and a spread. This module you meet the shape that makes those two numbers do extraordinary work. Over two weeks you will learn to say exactly where a value stands in a group using a z-score, estimate what share of a population lies below, above, or between values, check a normal model against real-looking data, and watch a board of falling balls build the bell curve one bounce at a time. You will also keep asking a harder question: a normal curve can be a wonderful model, but when does it stop telling the truth? Before you start, answer the few questions below. There are no wrong answers; your teacher reads these to meet you where you are.

questions.text: Here is the question this module keeps asking: How can many small random events pile up into something orderly, and when does that order mislead us? Write your first answer now, in 3–5 sentences. If you can, describe something you have seen pile up into a pattern (heights, test scores, coin flips, anything) or a time a "typical" pattern did not fit. You will meet this question again at the end of the module and compare.

By the end of Module 9 you will be able to: describe the normal model and its two numbers; compute and interpret a z-score and compare values from different groups; use the Empirical Rule (68–95–99.7) to estimate shares of a population; estimate percents below, above, and between values and find cutoffs with a spreadsheet; judge whether a normal model fits a dataset; and explain how the binomial distribution turns into a bell. Have you read this list?

questions.text: On a test, the scores have a mean of 76 and a standard deviation of 6. What is the z-score of a student who scored 88?

questions.text: Test A has a mean of 70 and a standard deviation of 8. Test B has a mean of 80 and a standard deviation of 10. Jo scores 82 on Test A and Kim scores 90 on Test B. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: the heights of a large group of adults of the same age and sex, shown as a symmetric, single-humped histogram
the lengths of repeated measurements of one object with a careful instrument, shown as a symmetric, single-humped histogram
the waiting times at a service counter, shown as a histogram with most values short and a long tail to the right
the fill weights of boxes from a machine, shown as a symmetric, single-humped histogram

quizzes.title: Quiz 25.3 — Estimating Percentages with a Normal Model

questions.text: A machine fills jars so that the fill volumes are approximately normally distributed with mean 250 mL and standard deviation 3 mL. Using this model, about what percent of jars hold less than 247 mL?
A test is taken by 1200 students. Scores are approximately normally distributed with mean 70 and standard deviation 12. About how many students are expected to score above 88?

answers.text: about 80
about 1120
about 160
about 18

questions.text: The lengths of a batch of bolts are approximately normally distributed with mean 40 mm and standard deviation 0.5 mm. Using this model, about what percent of bolts are between 39.5 mm and 41 mm long?
Scaled exam scores are approximately normally distributed with mean 500 and standard deviation 100. Which score is closest to the cutoff for the lowest 25% of scores?
A normal model with mean 170 cm and standard deviation 8 cm says that about 78.9% of the students in a school are between 160 cm and 180 cm tall. Which statement is best?

answers.text: The percent is exact, because the area under a normal curve is computed exactly.
The percent holds for any population with that mean and standard deviation.
The percent is an estimate that is only as reliable as the fit of the normal model to the students' actual heights.
The percent is guaranteed, because the mean and standard deviation came from measured data.

quizzes.title: Quiz 26.1 — When the Normal Model Does Not Fit

questions.text: A set of 100 delivery times has a mean of 52 minutes and a median of 31 minutes. Which explanation of the gap between the mean and the median is most likely?

answers.text: The distribution is symmetric, so a normal model fits well
The distribution has two separate clusters of equal size
A few very long delivery times pull the mean above the median (right skew)
A few very short delivery times pull the mean above the median

questions.text: A large dataset (1,000 values) has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10. The percents of values within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean are 66%, 95%, and 99.6%. How do these compare with what a normal model predicts, and what do they suggest?

answers.text: They are close to 68%, 95%, and 99.7%, so this check gives no evidence against a normal model
They are far below 68%, 95%, and 99.7%, so the data are clearly not normal
They are far above 68%, 95%, and 99.7%, so the data are clearly not normal
They prove the data are exactly normal

questions.text: A normal model with a mean of 43 and a standard deviation of 28 is proposed for a quantity that can never be negative, such as the amount of money in a wallet. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: The model is fine, because the mean is positive
The model is fine, because the standard deviation is smaller than twice the mean
The model is fine, because normal curves never go below zero
The model is a poor fit, because mean − 2 × SD = 43 − 56 = −13, so it predicts values that are impossible

questions.text: A histogram of 200 values shows two separate humps, one near 30 and one near 70, with very few values near 50. The mean is 50 and the median is 50. Which description is best?

answers.text: A normal model with mean 50 fits well, because the mean and median are equal
A single normal model does not fit; the data look like two clusters, and one mean and SD would hide that
The data are right-skewed, so the median should be used
The data are normal, and the two humps are outliers

questions.text: Two datasets have the same mean and the same standard deviation. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: They must have the same shape, because the mean and standard deviation determine the shape
If one is normal, the other must be normal
They can have very different shapes, so matching the mean and SD does not show that a normal model fits
They must have the same median

quizzes.title: Quiz 26.2 — The Binomial and the Normal

questions.text: A count X follows a binomial distribution with n = 80 trials and a success probability of p = 0.25. What are its mean and standard deviation?

answers.text: mean 20, standard deviation 15
mean 60, standard deviation 3.87
mean 20, standard deviation about 3.87
mean 20, standard deviation about 4.47

questions.text: A common rule of thumb says a normal curve can reasonably approximate a binomial distribution when both np and n(1 − p) are at least 10. Which binomial setting meets this rule of thumb?
X is a binomial count, and a normal curve with the same mean and standard deviation is used to estimate P(X ≤ 30). With the continuity correction, the normal area is found below which value?
Balls fall through rows of pegs on a Galton board, bouncing left or right with equal chance at each peg, and land in slots at the bottom. What does the pile of many balls demonstrate?

answers.text: The balls prefer the middle slots because the board steers them there
Many small independent left-or-right chances add up to a bell-shaped pile, even though no single ball's slot can be predicted
Once the first ball lands, every later ball will land in the same slot
Dropping more balls makes the pile wider, because there are more balls to spread out

questions.text: Which statement about using a normal curve to approximate a binomial distribution is true?

answers.text: It gives the exact binomial probability whenever n is at least 10
It works just as well for n = 50 and p = 0.01 as for n = 50 and p = 0.5
For a fixed p, it generally improves as n increases, and it is poorer when p is close to 0 or 1 unless n is large
It can be used only if the continuity correction is left out

quizzes.title: Quiz 26.3 — Normal-Model Applications

questions.text: The battery lifetimes of a made-up device are approximately normally distributed with mean 400 hours and standard deviation 25 hours. Using this model, about what percent of batteries last between 390 hours and 440 hours?
Scores on a placement test are approximately normally distributed with mean 60 and standard deviation 8. Which score is closest to the cutoff for the top 5% of scores?

A fair coin is flipped 100 times. Let X be the number of heads. The conditions for the normal approximation hold (np = 50 and n(1 − p) = 50, with SD = 5). Using the normal approximation with the continuity correction, about what is the probability of getting at least 55 heads?

A made-up process makes a defective item with probability 0.04, independently each time. In a random sample of 50 items, a student wants the probability of at most 1 defective item. Which statement is best?

answers.text: Use the normal approximation with the continuity correction, because 50 is a large sample.
Use the normal approximation without the continuity correction, because the count is small.
Use the normal approximation, because n(1 − p) = 48 is greater than 10.
Do not use the normal approximation, because np = 2 is less than 10; use the exact binomial probability instead.

questions.text: For a binomial count with n = 100 and p = 0.4, the exact probability of at most 35 successes is 0.1795, and the normal approximation with the continuity correction gives 0.1792. Which statement is best?

answers.text: The two values differ, so the normal approximation must be wrong.
The approximation is a close estimate of the exact value because the conditions hold, but it is still an estimate, not the exact probability.
The normal approximation is exact whenever np is at least 10.
The exact value is an estimate and the normal value is the true probability.

quizzes.title: Module 9: Look Back — The Normal Distribution
quizzes.description: You have finished the module on the most famous shape in statistics. You placed values with z-scores, read the Empirical Rule, estimated shares of a population with a spreadsheet, tested whether a bell fits, and stood inside a bell the size of a room. Next module you will move from one variable to two: how two measurements travel together, and how to say honestly how well one predicts the other. Before you go on, look back honestly. Your teacher reads every one of these, and the confidence rating and "still unclear" answers directly shape what gets reviewed.

questions.text: At the start of this module you answered: How can many small random events pile up into something orderly, and when does that order mislead us? Answer it again now, and say specifically what changed in your answer. Use one of the module's own cases as your example (the Galton board filling as balls fall, the thousand plants in Inside the Bell, a dataset that matched a normal curve's mean and SD but not its shape).

How confident do you feel about this module's core skills (z-scores, the Empirical Rule, estimating areas and cutoffs with a spreadsheet, checking whether a normal model fits, the binomial-normal connection)?

answers.text: Very confident — I could teach it
Confident — I'd get most problems right
Shaky — I can follow along but couldn't do it alone yet
Lost — I need help before we build on this

answers.text: Computing and interpreting a z-score
Comparing values from different distributions
The Empirical Rule (68–95–99.7)
Estimating percents below, above, and between with a spreadsheet
Finding a cutoff from a percent
Deciding when a normal model does not fit
How the binomial turns into a bell, and the continuity correction
Using the normal model in applications (and stating what could make an estimate wrong)
None — I'm solid across the module

questions.text: What remains unclear? Name the specific moment a lesson lost you (a step in a worked example, a quiz question, an Excel formula that did not work, a widget result you could not explain). "Nothing" is an acceptable answer only if Q2 was one of the top two choices.

This module's virtue is Wonder. Wonder is not only delight; it is paying attention to what is actually there. Name one moment in this module when something made you stop and look (the bell appearing out of falling balls, two very different measurements landing on the same z-ruler, a bell that was close but not the same as the rule), and then say what it made you want to check. What did you do about it, or what would you do now?

quizzes.title: Module 10: Begin Here — Bivariate Data & Regression
quizzes.description: Until now you have studied one variable at a time. This module you study two together: how hours of practice relate to scores, how temperature relates to sales, how one category relates to another. Over three weeks you will describe a scatter plot, fit a line and use it to predict, measure the misses with residuals, put a number on strength with the correlation coefficient, fit a curve that grows by a steady percent, and organize two categories in a two-way table. You will also keep asking the careful question: when two things move together, what do we really know? Before you start, answer the few questions below. There are no wrong answers; your teacher reads these to meet you where you are.

questions.text: Here is the question this module keeps asking: When two things move together, what do we really know, and what are we only tempted to believe? Write your first answer now, in 3–5 sentences. If you can, describe two things you have noticed rising or falling together (in school, sports, weather, social media, anything) and say what you think is going on. You will meet this question again at the end of the module and compare.

By the end of Module 10 you will be able to: describe and make scatter plots; fit a line and interpret its slope and intercept in context; predict, and say when a prediction goes too far; read residuals to judge a fit; use and interpret the correlation coefficient; explain why correlation does not show causation; fit an exponential model with a log transform; and summarize two categorical variables with two-way tables. Have you read this list?

answers.text: I have read the module objectives and know where we're headed.

questions.text: Some later activities offer an optional collaborative path (shared persistent VR Sessions, discussion pairings). Would you like to be considered for group collaboration where it's offered?

answers.text: Yes — include me in group options
No — I prefer to work independently this module
Not sure yet — ask me again mid-module

questions.text: A news headline says: "Students who eat breakfast score higher on tests, so breakfast improves test scores." How do you respond?

answers.text: Agree: the data show breakfast causes higher scores
Agree, if the group of students studied was large
Disagree: the data show the two go together, but something else could explain it, and I'd want to know how the data were collected
I'm not sure what a good response would be

questions.text: A line fitted to data about 10 to 50 cups of hot chocolate sold at temperatures from 20°F to 60°F is used to predict sales at 110°F. What would you say?

answers.text: The line is a good guide anywhere, since it fits the data well
It is probably fine, since the line keeps going in the same direction

questions.text: Anything your teacher should know as you start this module? (Schedule constraints, how Module 9 and its Excel work went for you, how you learn best — anything.)

quizzes.title: Quiz 27.1 — Scatter Plots and Association

questions.text: Eight constructed pairs (x, y) are: (1, 9), (2, 8), (3, 8), (4, 6), (5, 5), (6, 5), (7, 3), (8, 2). Which description of the scatter plot is best?

answers.text: Positive association, roughly linear, strong
Negative association, roughly linear, strong
Negative association, roughly linear, weak
No association, no clear pattern

questions.text: In a scatter plot, the points rise from left to right and cluster fairly closely around an upward-sloping straight line, but with noticeable scatter on both sides of it (not all on the line). Which value is the best estimate of the correlation coefficient r?

For nine measurements, x runs from 1 to 9 and y rises from 4 up to 18 and then falls back to 4, so the points trace a smooth arch (a curve). The correlation coefficient is r = 0.00. Which conclusion is best?

answers.text: There is no straight-line trend, but there is a clear curved relationship between x and y
x and y are completely unrelated
The points must lie exactly on a horizontal line
The relationship is strong and linear

questions.text: Nine points lie close to a rising straight line, and for those nine points alone r is about +0.99. A tenth point is then added far below the line at the right-hand end of the plot. Which effect on r is most likely?

answers.text: r stays about +0.99, because one point is a small share of the data
r becomes about −0.99, because the new point is low
r drops noticeably, because one far-off point can pull r away from +0.99
r becomes exactly 0

questions.text: In a made-up sample of 20 students, hours of sleep and quiz score have a correlation of r = +0.6. Which statement is the most careful way to report this?

answers.text: Getting more sleep causes higher quiz scores
In this sample, students who slept more tended to have higher scores; this does not show that sleep caused the difference
Sixty percent of the students raised their scores by sleeping more
Because the data are only a sample, the association is not real

quizzes.title: Quiz 27.2 — Fitting a Line and Reading Slope and Intercept

questions.text: A constructed model predicts a quiz score in points from the number of hours studied: ŷ = 50 + 6.5x, where x is hours studied. Which statement about the slope is best?

answers.text: Each additional hour of studying causes a student's score to rise by 6.5 points.
For each additional hour studied, the model predicts a quiz score about 6.5 points higher.
A student who studies 6.5 hours is predicted to score 50 points.
For each additional hour studied, the model predicts the score to rise by 6.5 percent.

questions.text: A constructed model predicts weight in kilograms from height in centimeters for adults whose heights in the data range from 150 cm to 190 cm: ŷ = −80 + 0.85x. What is the best statement about the intercept, −80?

answers.text: An adult who is 0 cm tall is predicted to weigh −80 kg, so the model is correct only for very short people.
Each additional centimeter of height lowers the predicted weight by 80 kg.
The average weight of the adults in the data is −80 kg.
It is the predicted value at a height of 0 cm, which lies far outside the data, so it has no sensible meaning here and only positions the line.

questions.text: A straight line passes through the points (2, 24) and (10, 8). Which equation describes it?
For a scatter plot of data, what does the least-squares line minimize?

answers.text: The number of points that lie off the line
The difference between the number of points above the line and the number below it
The sum of the squared vertical distances from the points to the line
The distance between the first point and the last point

questions.text: In a constructed set of 40 parent and child heights, each measured in standard deviations from the average, the least-squares line is approximately ŷ = 0.5x, where x is the parent's height and ŷ is the predicted child's height. Which statement about a parent who is 2 standard deviations above average is best?

answers.text: The child will be exactly 1 standard deviation above average.
The model predicts a child about 1 standard deviation above average, which is closer to the average than the parent; this is a statistical pattern in the data, not a force pulling families back.
The child of a tall parent will be shorter than the child of an average parent.
Each generation must be 0.5 times as tall as the one before it.

quizzes.title: Quiz 27.3 — Prediction: Interpolation and Extrapolation

questions.text: A line is fitted to data in which the values of x (hours of practice) range from 2 to 9. Which prediction is an extrapolation?

answers.text: A prediction at x = 2
A prediction at x = 5.5
A prediction at x = 9.5
A prediction at x = 8

questions.text: A fitted line is ŷ = 12.5 + 3.2x, based on data with x from 1 to 10. What does the line predict at x = 7, and is the prediction an interpolation?

answers.text: 34.9, and yes, it is an interpolation
22.4, and yes, it is an interpolation
34.9, and no, it is an extrapolation
87.5, and yes, it is an interpolation

questions.text: A fitted line for daily sales is ŷ = 95 − 4.5x, where x is the price in dollars and the data use prices from 2 to 12. Daily sales cannot be negative. Which prediction is both an extrapolation and an impossible value?

answers.text: x = 3, which predicts 81.5 sales
x = 8, which predicts 59 sales
x = 15, which predicts 27.5 sales
x = 25, which predicts −17.5 sales

questions.text: Which statement about extrapolation is correct?

answers.text: It is always accurate when the correlation is high
It can be unreliable, because the pattern in the data may not continue outside the range of the data
It is safer than interpolation, because it uses more of the line
It cannot be done with a fitted line

questions.text: A fitted line predicts a test score from the hours of sleep reported by a group of students, and the points follow the line closely. Which statement is correct about using the line to predict?

answers.text: The close fit shows that more sleep causes higher scores
A prediction from the line is a guaranteed result for any student
The prediction is an estimate based on a pattern in the data; it does not show that changing the hours of sleep would cause the score to change
Predictions are only allowed when the cause is known

quizzes.title: Quiz 28.1 — Residuals: Assessing a Linear Fit

questions.text: A constructed model predicts a value from x: ŷ = 12 + 3x. An observation has x = 5 and y = 31. What is the residual (observed minus predicted), and what does it mean?

answers.text: +4; the observed value is above the line, so the model underpredicted
−4; the observed value is below the line, so the model overpredicted
+4; the observed value is below the line, so the model overpredicted
27; it is the value the model predicted

questions.text: A least-squares line is fitted to 8 constructed points. In order of x from smallest to largest, the residuals are positive for the first two points, negative for the next four points, and positive for the last two points. What is the best conclusion?

answers.text: The residuals show random scatter, so the straight line is adequate.
The residuals form a curved pattern, so a straight line is not an adequate model for these data.
The residuals fan out, so the line is accurate only for small x.
The line must have been computed incorrectly, because residuals cannot change sign.

questions.text: Which statement is true of the residuals of a least-squares line (one with an intercept) fitted to any small data set, apart from rounding?

answers.text: They add to zero, because the points above the line and the points below it balance out.
They add to the number of data points.
They are all positive if the correlation is positive.
They add to zero only when the line is a perfect fit.

questions.text: Six constructed points, (1, 3), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 7), (5, 6), (6, 8), have a least-squares slope of about +0.89. A seventh point at (14, 3), far to the right of the others and well below their trend, is added, and the slope of the least-squares line becomes about −0.06. Which description of the new point is best?

answers.text: It is an influential point: it is far from the others in the x direction and pulls the line toward itself.
It is not influential, because its own residual is small.
It is an outlier only in the middle of the x values, so it cannot change the slope.
It cannot affect the line, because the least-squares line always passes through the mean of the original six points.

questions.text: Two lines are fitted to the same five constructed points. Line A leaves residuals +1, −2, +2, −1, 0. Line B leaves residuals +2, −1, +1, −2, +2. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: Line A fits better by the least-squares rule: its sum of squared residuals is 10, and Line B’s is 14.
Line B fits better, because its residuals are larger.
Both lines fit equally well, because each has residuals of both signs.
Line B fits better, because its residuals add to a smaller number than Line A’s do.

quizzes.title: Quiz 28.2 — Correlation: Strength, Direction, and r

questions.text: For a made-up sample of used cars, the correlation between age in years and asking price is r = −0.92. Which description is best?

answers.text: A weak positive straight-line association
A strong negative straight-line association: older cars tend to have lower asking prices
A strong positive straight-line association
A weak negative straight-line association, because −0.92 is less than +0.5

questions.text: In a made-up data set, the correlation between two variables is r = 0.80. What is the best interpretation of r-squared = 0.64?

answers.text: 64% of the points lie exactly on the line
About 64% of the variation in y is accounted for by the straight-line relationship with x
Changes in x cause 64% of the changes in y
The relationship is 80% reliable and 64% of the time it is correct

questions.text: For a data set, r = 0.8, the standard deviation of x is sx = 5, and the standard deviation of y is sy = 10. What is the slope b of the least-squares line for predicting y from x?
A spreadsheet has the x values in cells A2:A11 and the y values in cells B2:B11. Which formula gives the slope of the least-squares line for predicting y from x?

answers.text: =SLOPE(A2:A11,B2:B11)
=SLOPE(B2:B11,A2:A11)
=CORREL(B2:B11,A2:A11)

questions.text: For a made-up data set with variables P and Q, the correlation is r = +0.70 when P is used as x and Q as y. The roles are now swapped, so that Q is x and P is y. Which statement is true?

answers.text: r is still +0.70, but the slope of the least-squares line is generally different
r becomes −0.70, and the slope is the same
r becomes 1 / 0.70, about 1.43
Both r and the slope are exactly the same as before

quizzes.title: Quiz 28.3 — Correlation Is Not Causation

questions.text: In made-up fire records, fires that had more fire trucks sent to them had more damage (a strong positive association). Which is the most plausible explanation?

answers.text: Sending more trucks causes more damage
Fire size is a third variable: bigger fires get more trucks and also cause more damage
Damage causes fire trucks to be built
The pattern must be a coincidence

questions.text: In made-up clinic records, patients who take more pain medicine report more pain. Which explanation involves reverse direction?

answers.text: Pain medicine causes pain
A third variable, such as temperature, drives both
People in more pain tend to take more pain medicine
The association is entirely due to chance

questions.text: In a made-up set of ten towns, the correlation between ice cream sales and pool incidents is about +0.88 overall. answers.text: Ice cream sales cause pool incidents, but only in warm weather
Most of the overall association comes from the difference between the two weather groups, which is consistent with weather driving both variables
There is no relationship between ice cream sales and pool incidents of any kind

questions.text: Which study design can best support the claim that a new teaching method causes higher test scores?

answers.text: A survey asking students which method they like and what their scores are
Students choose their own method, and their scores are then compared
Students are randomly assigned to the new method or the usual method, and their scores are then compared

questions.text: A made-up observational study of 90 adults found that those who owned more houseplants reported better moods. Which headline is the most careful?

answers.text: Houseplants Boost Your Mood
Want to Feel Better? Buy a Plant
In One Study of 90 Adults, Those With More Houseplants Reported Better Moods; the Study Cannot Say Why
Proof: Happy People Buy More Plants

quizzes.title: Quiz 29.1 — Exponential Fits and the Log Transform

questions.text: A constructed (simulated) quantity is measured at steps x = 0, 1, 2, 3 and has the values 50, 60, 72, 86.4. Which description is best?

answers.text: A straight-line pattern: it adds the same amount, 10, each step
Exponential growth: each value is about 1.2 times the one before, an increase of about 20% per step
Exponential decay: each value is 20% smaller than the one before
Exponential growth with b = 0.2, because the increase is 20%

questions.text: A straight line fitted to (x, ln y) for a constructed data set gives ln ŷ = 3 + 0.2x. Converting back to the model ŷ = a·bx, which statement is correct?

answers.text: a = 3 and b = 0.2, so the model is ŷ = 3·0.2x
a = 3 and b = e0.2, so the model is ŷ = 3·1.2214x
a = e3 ≈ 20.09 and b = e0.2 ≈ 1.2214, an increase of about 22% per step
a = e3 ≈ 20.09 and b = 0.2, a decrease of about 80% per step

questions.text: A student fits a straight line to a constructed data set and the residual plot shows a clear smile (residuals positive, then negative, then positive). She then takes ln of y, fits a straight line to (x, ln y), and finds that the new residuals look like random scatter with no pattern. What is the best conclusion?

questions.text: A model ŷ = 112.8·1.95x was fitted to simulated bacteria counts at hours x = 0 to 6, and the fit looks excellent on the log scale. Someone uses it to predict the count at hour 30. What is the best response?

questions.text: A student wants to fit y = a·bx by taking ln of y, but one of the constructed y values is 0. What is the problem, and what is the honest response?

ln(0) does not exist, so that point cannot be transformed; the student should report the problem and say how it was handled rather than silently delete it

quizzes.title: Quiz 29.3 — Conditional Relative Frequencies, Segmented Bars, and Association

answers.text: About 43%
About 4%

questions.text: A made-up town has 600 residents. A tree diagram has first branches "Junior" with 0.30 and "Not junior" with 0.70. From "Junior" the second branches are "attends" with 0.50 and "does not attend" with 0.50. How many residents are in the cell "Junior and attends" of the matching two-way table?

A made-up observational survey of 200 teens found that 80% of the teens who use a study app passed their last math test, compared with 60% of the teens who do not use the app. Teens chose for themselves whether to use the app. Which conclusion is the most careful?

answers.text: The app raises pass rates by 20 percentage points.
In this survey, teens who used the app passed at a higher rate than teens who did not; the survey cannot show whether the app is the reason.
Because the rates differ, teens who do not use the app are less capable.
Using the app and passing are independent.

quizzes.title: Module 10: Look Back — Bivariate Data & Regression
quizzes.description: You have finished the module on how two variables travel together. You described scatter plots, fitted lines and predicted with them, read residuals, measured strength with r, fitted a curve that grows by a steady percent, and organized two categories in tables and segmented bars. In the VR lab you walked a cloud of points and saw how one far-out point can drag a line. Next module you will ask where data come from in the first place: how a sample is chosen, how a study is designed, and what kind of study can honestly support a claim about cause. Before you go on, look back honestly. Your teacher reads every one of these, and the confidence rating and "still unclear" answers directly shape what gets reviewed.

questions.text: At the start of this module you answered: When two things move together, what do we really know, and what are we only tempted to believe? Answer it again now, and say specifically what changed in your answer. Use one of the module's own cases as your example (a residual plot that curved, a strong r that fooled you in the correlation game, the far-out point in The Scatter Field, a two-way table where the bars differed, the cones-and-pool-incidents example).

How confident do you feel about this module's core skills (reading scatter plots, fitting and interpreting a line, residuals, the correlation coefficient, correlation versus causation, the log transform for exponential data, two-way tables and conditional relative frequencies)?

answers.text: Very confident — I could teach it
Confident — I'd get most problems right
Shaky — I can follow along but couldn't do it alone yet
Lost — I need help before we build on this

questions.text: Which topic most deserves another pass?

answers.text: Describing a scatter plot (direction, form, strength, unusual points)
Interpreting slope and intercept in context
Interpolation versus extrapolation
Residuals and residual plots
The correlation coefficient and r-squared
Correlation is not causation, and confounding variables
The log transform and exponential fits
Two-way tables: joint and marginal frequencies
Conditional relative frequencies, segmented bars, and association
None — I'm solid across the module

questions.text: What remains unclear? Name the specific moment a lesson lost you (a step in a worked example, a quiz question, an Excel formula that did not work, a widget result you could not explain). "Nothing" is an acceptable answer only if Q2 was one of the top two choices.

This module's virtue is Responsibility. Responsibility here means claiming only what the evidence supports. Name one moment in this module when you caught yourself, or a number, claiming too much (a headline that overreached, a prediction far outside the data, a high r that proved less than it seemed). What would the careful version of that claim say? And where might you be tempted to overclaim in your own life?

quizzes.title: Module 11: Begin Here — Sampling & Study Design
quizzes.description: Every statistic you have met so far started somewhere: someone decided who to ask, what to ask, and what to measure. This module is about those decisions. Over three weeks you will tell a parameter from a statistic, draw samples by seven different methods and see which ones can be trusted, watch how much random samples vary from one to the next, learn how samples and questions go wrong, see why randomly assigning treatments is what lets an experiment speak about cause, and design a study of your own. Before you start, answer the few questions below. There are no wrong answers; your teacher reads these to meet you where you are.

questions.text: Here is the question this module keeps asking: How can a small piece of the world tell us the truth about the whole, and how do we know when it is lying to us? Write your first answer now, in 3–5 sentences. If you can, describe a poll, a survey, or a "studies show" claim you have seen and say whether you trusted it and why. You will meet this question again at the end of the module and compare.

By the end of Module 11 you will be able to: tell a parameter from a statistic; describe and carry out simple random, stratified, cluster, systematic, and other sampling methods; explain sampling variation and why bias is different; spot biased samples and biased questions; tell a survey, an observational study, and an experiment apart; explain why random assignment supports causal claims; and design a sound study. Have you read this list?

answers.text: I have read the module objectives and know where we're headed.

questions.text: Some later activities offer an optional collaborative path (shared persistent VR Sessions, discussion pairings). Would you like to be considered for group collaboration where it's offered?

answers.text: Yes — include me in group options
No — I prefer to work independently this module
Not sure yet — ask me again mid-module

questions.text: A local news site asks readers to vote online on whether the town should build a new stadium. 4,000 people vote, and 78% say yes. How should you read that result?

answers.text: It is reliable, since 4,000 is a big sample
It is reliable, as long as no one voted twice
It tells us how the people who chose to vote feel, but not necessarily how the whole town feels
I'm not sure how to judge that

questions.text: A study finds that students who join a chess club get better math grades. A reporter writes, "Chess club improves math grades." What would you want to know before agreeing?

answers.text: Nothing more: the data show chess club works
How many students were in the study
Whether students were randomly assigned to the club, or chose it themselves
I'm not sure what a good response would be

questions.text: Anything your teacher should know as you start this module? (Schedule constraints, how Module 10 and its Excel work went for you, how you learn best — anything.)

quizzes.title: Quiz 30.1 — Parameter or Statistic? Why We Sample

questions.text: A made-up school has 900 students. A survey asks 60 of them how many hours they sleep, and the mean of the 60 answers is 7.4 hours. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: 7.4 is a parameter, because it is a mean
7.4 is the population mean μ, because the sample was part of the school
7.4 is a parameter, because the 60 students were all asked the same question
7.4 is a statistic, because it describes a sample of 60 students

questions.text: A made-up company tests how long its batteries last by running each tested battery until it is completely drained. Why does the company test a sample of batteries instead of every battery it makes?

answers.text: A census is never allowed in statistics
Testing a battery until it is drained uses it up, so testing every battery would leave none to sell
A sample is always more accurate than a census
Batteries are numerical, and numerical variables cannot be tested all at once

questions.text: A made-up survey asks each of 40 sampled students whether they walk to school (yes or no). Which statistic summarizes the answers, and what symbol is used?

answers.text: A sample mean, written x̄
A population proportion, written p
A sample proportion, written p̂
A population mean, written μ

questions.text: Two different samples of 30 students are taken from the same made-up school. The first has a mean of 6.8 hours of sleep and the second has a mean of 7.3 hours. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: One of the two samples must have been done wrongly
The population mean μ changed between the two samples
The sample means differ because a statistic changes from sample to sample, while the population mean μ is one fixed value
The average of the whole population is 6.8, because that sample was taken first

questions.text: A club president asks the five friends sitting nearest her whether they will attend a dance. Four say yes, and she announces, "80% of the school will attend." Which response is the most careful?

answers.text: Four of the five friends asked said yes; that is a statistic from a small, convenient sample, and it gives little reason to trust it as the share for the whole school
She is right, because 4 divided by 5 is 0.80
80% is the parameter, because every one of the five friends answered
The statement would be correct if she rounded 80% to 100%

quizzes.title: Quiz 30.2 — Random Sampling and Representativeness

questions.text: A constructed (made-up) club has 40 members. Which method produces a simple random sample of 5 members?

answers.text: Ask the first 5 members who arrive at the meeting
Flip a coin: heads, take members 1 to 5; tails, take members 36 to 40
Let the president choose 5 members who seem typical
Number the members 1 to 40 and use random numbers to choose 5 different members, so that every group of 5 is equally likely

questions.text: A constructed club of 60 has exactly 30 members who own a library card, so the true share is 50%. A simple random sample of 8 members is drawn. The chance that the sample share is exactly 50% (4 of 8) is about 0.29. What does this show?

answers.text: The method must be biased, since most samples do not give exactly 50%
A random sample of 8 will often be near 50% but usually is not exactly 50%, so a fair method does not guarantee that one sample mirrors the population
A random sample is representative on average, so each sample will look just like the population
Only samples that give exactly 50% count as random

questions.text: A researcher surveys the first 200 people who walk into a made-up shop and gets a mean of 40 minutes spent shopping, while the true mean for all customers is 55 minutes. She then surveys the first 2,000 people through the door and gets a mean of 41 minutes. What is the best conclusion?

answers.text: The larger sample removed most of the bias, so 41 is close enough to 55
The larger sample is now representative because it is ten times as big
The method leans the same way regardless of size, so a bigger sample from the same convenient group does not fix the bias; choosing people by a random method would
The first sample was wrong and the second sample was right

questions.text: A student draws 8 IDs from 1 to 60 using =RANDBETWEEN(1,60) in eight cells and sees that the ID 23 appears twice. What should the student do?

answers.text: Keep both, since a member can be counted twice
Redraw until no ID repeats (or use =RAND with a sort so repeats cannot happen), because a simple random sample needs 8 different members
Delete one 23 and leave only 7 members
Replace the second 23 with the next ID, 24

questions.text: A student uses =RANDBETWEEN to pick her sample and computes a sample mean. After she types a note in another cell, her sample mean changes. What should she have done after the draw?

answers.text: Nothing, since RANDBETWEEN values stay fixed once they are drawn
Press F9 until the mean looks close to the true value
Copy the picks and use Paste Special > Values to freeze them before computing anything from them
Switch to =RAND, which does not recalculate

quizzes.title: Quiz 30.3 — Sampling Methods

questions.text: A made-up factory has an assembly line with numbered units. An inspector picks a random number from 1 to 25, tests that unit, and then tests every 25th unit after it. Which sampling method is this?

answers.text: Simple random sampling
Stratified sampling
Cluster sampling
Systematic sampling

questions.text: A made-up town has four neighborhoods, each with a complete list of residents. A survey team draws 10 residents at random from each neighborhood's list. Which description is best?

answers.text: Stratified sampling: the sample is drawn from every group
Cluster sampling: every neighborhood is included
Quota sampling: the same number is taken from each group
Convenience sampling: the lists make it easy

questions.text: Which of the following is a non-probability sampling method?

answers.text: Drawing 50 names at random from a complete list
Taking a random sample from each grade level, in proportion to the grade's size
Choosing 5 classrooms at random and surveying every student in them
Telling an interviewer to collect 40 responses from men and 40 from women, from whoever agrees to stop

questions.text: A made-up bakery keeps a daily sales log listing every day in order. An analyst takes every 7th day's record, starting from a random day. The bakery always sells far more on Saturdays than on other days. What is the main danger with this plan?

answers.text: Because the start was random, the plan has no danger
Every 7th day falls on the same weekday, so the sample could be all Saturdays or contain no Saturdays, and the average would be biased
Systematic sampling always includes too many Saturdays
The sample size is too large for a bakery

questions.text: A made-up club has 900 members, of whom 360 are beginners. A stratified sample of 50 members is drawn in proportion to group size. How many beginners should be in the sample?

quizzes.title: Quiz 31.1 — Sampling Variation: Many Samples, Many Estimates

questions.text: A made-up school has exactly 40% of its students walking to school. Two classmates each take their own simple random sample of 25 students and find 36% and 52% who walk. Which statement is the best explanation of the difference?

answers.text: One of the two classmates must have used a biased method
The true percentage of walkers changed between the two samples
The two sample proportions differ because of sampling variation, which is expected even when both samples are random and unbiased
The larger sample proportion is always the one closer to the truth

questions.text: A made-up population has a true proportion of 0.40. Simple random samples of size n = 25 give sample proportions with a typical swing (standard deviation) of about 0.098. If the sample size is increased to n = 100, four times as large, about what typical swing should be expected?

answers.text: About 0.196, because a larger sample is more variable
About 0.049, because four times the sample size cuts the typical swing to about half
About 0.098, because the typical swing depends only on the population
About 0.025, because the typical swing falls to one quarter

questions.text: The owner of a made-up website invites visitors to vote on whether a new rule is fair. A total of 10,000 visitors respond, and the owner says, "With this many responses, the result must be accurate." Which statement is best?

answers.text: Yes, because 10,000 is larger than any sample a researcher would need
Yes, because a large sample removes every kind of error
No, because a sample larger than 1,000 is always biased
No, because a large sample shrinks sampling variation but does not remove bias from self-selected responses

questions.text: A population has a true proportion of 0.50. Using the formula √(p(1 − p) ÷ n), what is the typical swing of the sample proportion for simple random samples of size n = 400?

Suppose 1,000 simple random samples, each of size n = 100, are drawn from a population whose true proportion is 0.40, and the 1,000 sample proportions are plotted in a dot plot. Which description is most accurate?

answers.text: Centered near 0.40 but skewed far to the right
Centered near 0.50, because 0.50 is the middle of the possible values
Centered near 0.40, roughly bell-shaped, with most of the sample proportions within about 0.10 of 0.40
Every sample proportion is exactly 0.40

quizzes.title: Quiz 31.2 — Bias: How Samples and Questions Go Wrong

questions.text: Two honest methods are used many times on the same made-up town. Method X gives estimates that scatter above and below the true value, and the average of its estimates is very close to the truth. Method Y gives estimates that are tightly bunched but all about 8 points above the truth. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: Method X is biased and Method Y is not, because X scatters more
Method Y is biased, because it tends to miss the truth in the same direction every time
Both are unbiased, because both give estimates that are close to each other
Neither is biased, because bias only exists when every estimate is wrong by the same amount in both directions

questions.text: A made-up web page asks visitors, "Should the town add a skate park?" Anyone may click once or many times, and 600 votes are recorded. Which statement is the most careful?

answers.text: The result estimates the town's opinion well, because 600 is a large number of votes
The result is a voluntary-response poll: people chose themselves, so it describes only those who voted and is not a reliable estimate for the whole town
The result is a simple random sample, because the vote was open to everyone
The result is unbiased because the page did not choose who answered

questions.text: A made-up call-in poll of a town reports 70% in favor of a proposal, while the true share in the town is 55%. The station repeats the same call-in method and collects 10 times as many calls. What is the best prediction?

answers.text: The new result will be close to 55%, because more calls reduce bias
The new result will still tend to lean above 55%, because more replies from the same self-selecting group do not remove the lean
The new result will lean below 55%, because the bias reverses with more calls
The new result will be exactly 55%

questions.text: Which rewrite of the question "Don't you agree that our overcrowded, noisy cafeteria is a disgrace?" is the most neutral?

answers.text: "Do you agree that the cafeteria is overcrowded and noisy, or do you disagree?"
"How would you describe the cafeteria at lunch: very comfortable, comfortable, uncomfortable, or very uncomfortable?"
"How satisfied are you with the cafeteria at lunch? (Very satisfied, Satisfied, Neither satisfied nor dissatisfied, Dissatisfied, Very dissatisfied)"
"Is the cafeteria a disgrace, or is it merely overcrowded and noisy?"

questions.text: A made-up school draws 100 student names at random from its complete roster and mails each a survey about school lunches. Only 30 students return it. Which statement about this survey is correct?

answers.text: Random selection guarantees the 30 replies are representative of all 100
Random selection removes nonresponse bias, since the names were chosen by chance
Nonresponse can still bias the result, because the 30 who replied may differ from the 70 who did not, and a random draw does not prevent that
The survey is biased because the sample was chosen at random

quizzes.title: Quiz 31.3 — Is the Model Consistent with the Data?

questions.text: A made-up game company claims that its spinner has 4 equal sections and lands on section A with chance 25% on every spin. Which statement best describes this claim as a model (a data-generating process)?

answers.text: A rule for how the data could have been produced: each spin lands on A with chance 25%, independent of the other spins
A prediction that section A will come up exactly once in every four spins
A record of the spins that have already happened
A proof that the spinner is fair

questions.text: A made-up game claims its coin is fair. The coin is flipped 50 times and lands heads 28 times (3 above the expected 25). The exact chance of a result at least this far from 25, on either side, is 0.480. Which conclusion is the most careful?

answers.text: The result proves the coin is fair
The result is not unusual under the claimed model, so it is consistent with a fair coin, though it does not prove the coin is fair
The result is unusual under the claimed model, so the coin is biased
The result proves the coin favors heads, because 28 is more than 25

questions.text: A made-up game claims its coin is fair. It is flipped 50 times and lands heads 36 times. The exact chance of a result at least this far from 25 on either side (36 or more, or 14 or fewer) is 0.002602, about 1 in 384. Which statement is the most careful?

answers.text: The result is not unusual, because 36 heads can happen with a fair coin
The result proves the coin is rigged, because 0.002602 is less than 0.05
The result is unusual under the claimed model, which is a strong reason to doubt the coin is fair, but it does not prove the coin is rigged
The result proves that the next 50 flips will also give about 36 heads

questions.text: Two made-up checks use the rule of thumb "unusual if a result at least this far from expected happens in fewer than 5 in 100 runs." A fair-coin claim checked against 60 heads in 100 flips has an exact chance of 0.0569. A 25% spinner claim checked against 19 landings on section A in 50 spins has an exact chance of 0.0481. Which statement is the most sensible?

answers.text: The first result is clearly not unusual and the second is clearly unusual, because they fall on opposite sides of 0.05
Both results are unusual, because both chances are close to 0.05
Both results are borderline: they sit very near the 5-in-100 line, and the line is a rule of thumb rather than a law
Neither result can be judged, because a simulation never gives the same count twice

questions.text: A made-up lab checks 20 different models that are all true, each against its own independent result. For each check, the chance that a true model lands in the unusual zone (the 5-in-100 tail) is 0.05. What is the chance that at least one of the 20 checks lands in its unusual zone?

answers.text: 0.05, the same as for a single check
About 0.36, because 0.95<sup>20</sup> ≈ 0.358
About 0.64, because 1 − 0.95<sup>20</sup> ≈ 0.642

quizzes.title: Quiz 32.1 — Surveys, Experiments, and Observational Studies

questions.text: A made-up orchard owner numbers her 24 trees, draws 12 numbers from a hat, and puts Fertilizer X on those 12 trees and Fertilizer Y on the other 12. At harvest she compares the weight of apples from each tree. What kind of study is this?

answers.text: A sample survey
A randomized experiment
An observational study
A census

questions.text: A made-up researcher selects 300 students at random from a school of 1,500 and records each student's weekly screen time and hours of sleep. No one is asked to change any habit. Which conclusion is best supported?

answers.text: Less screen time causes more sleep for students at this school
The result cannot be generalized because the students were not assigned to groups
Because the sample is random, the study shows that screen time causes lost sleep
Screen time and sleep may be associated among the school's students, but the study cannot show that one causes the other

questions.text: In a made-up study, 12 runners are assigned to Shoe A or Shoe B by a draw from a hat. Each runs 5 km, and the researchers compare the times. Which choice correctly names the explanatory variable and the response variable?

answers.text: Explanatory: the shoe type; response: the 5 km time
Explanatory: the 5 km time; response: the shoe type
Explanatory: the number of runners; response: the shoe type
Explanatory: the draw from the hat; response: the number of runners

questions.text: A made-up school finds that students who chose optional tutoring have higher test scores than students who did not. Why can the school NOT conclude that tutoring caused the higher scores?

answers.text: The sample must have been too small
Observational studies are always biased in the same direction
Students who chose tutoring may differ in other ways, such as motivation, that also affect scores, so the effect of tutoring is confounded
Test scores cannot be compared between two groups

questions.text: In a made-up study, 40 volunteers from one running club are assigned to Shoe A or Shoe B by random draw, and the Shoe A group runs faster on average. Which conclusion is best supported?

answers.text: Shoe A makes all runners faster
Nothing can be concluded about the shoes because the runners were volunteers
Shoe A and speed are associated, but the study cannot suggest a cause
Shoe A likely caused the faster times among these volunteers, but the result could not be generalized to all runners without a random sample of them

quizzes.title: Quiz 32.2 — Randomized Assignment: The Key to Causal Claims

questions.text: In a made-up experiment, 40 volunteers are assigned to a new study app or to their usual method by a random number generator. Which statement best explains why this assignment lets a difference in test scores support a causal claim about the app?

answers.text: Random assignment guarantees that the two groups are exactly equal on every characteristic
Chance, not anyone's choice, decides the groups, so on average characteristics (measured or not) that could affect scores are balanced between them
Random assignment makes the sample representative of all students in the country
Random assignment proves that any difference in scores was caused by the app

questions.text: A researcher testing a new warm-up gives it to the first 10 volunteers who sign up and uses the last 10 volunteers as the comparison group. The first volunteers turn out to be keener and to perform better even without a warm-up. What is the main problem with this design?

answers.text: The groups are too small to compute a mean
A placebo was not used, so the volunteers could tell which group they were in
The experiment is not double-blind, which alone makes causal claims impossible
Eagerness is confounded with the warm-up, so the difference in results cannot be credited to the warm-up alone

questions.text: In a made-up medical study, patients receive either a new pill or an identical-looking pill with no active ingredient. Neither the patients nor the staff who record each patient's symptoms know who received which pill. Which description is correct?

answers.text: The inactive pill is a placebo, and the study is double-blind
The inactive pill is the treatment, and the study is single-blind
The inactive pill is a placebo, and the study is single-blind
There is no control group because every patient received a pill

questions.text: A researcher must split 20 subjects into two groups and decides to flip a fair coin for each subject, with heads meaning Treatment. The number of ways to choose which 10 of the 20 flips are heads is 184,756, and there are 220 = 1,048,576 equally likely sequences of 20 flips. About how likely is it that this method produces two groups of exactly 10?

answers.text: About 0.50
About 0.05
About 0.18
About 0.82

questions.text: In a made-up experiment, 60 subjects are randomly assigned to a new exercise plan or to no plan. Many subjects who find the plan unpleasant quit during the study and their final results are never recorded, while few subjects in the comparison group quit. Which statement is best?

answers.text: Random assignment guarantees that dropout cannot affect the comparison
Dropout is harmless as long as the group sizes at the start were equal
Uneven dropout can leave the remaining groups unlike each other, so random assignment alone does not fully protect the comparison
The study can no longer be called an experiment because some subjects quit

quizzes.title: Quiz 32.3 — Designing a Study

questions.text: A made-up researcher wants to know whether a new study routine causes higher quiz scores. She uses a random number generator to assign each of 60 volunteers to the new routine or the usual routine. What is the main purpose of the random assignment?

answers.text: To make the sample of volunteers representative of all students
To make the two groups alike, on average, in both measured and unmeasured ways, so that a difference in scores is less likely to come from some other factor
To guarantee that the new routine will produce higher scores
To make the volunteers unaware of which routine they are using

questions.text: In a made-up observational study of a randomly chosen sample of teens, those who slept fewer hours per school night tended to have lower grade point averages. Which conclusion is best supported?

answers.text: Sleeping fewer hours causes lower grades
Lower grades cause teens to sleep fewer hours
Shorter sleep is associated with lower grades in this group, but the study alone cannot show that one causes the other
There is no relationship between sleep and grades, because the study was not an experiment

questions.text: A made-up school has 800 students: 320 in Group X, 280 in Group Y, and 200 in Group Z. A stratified random sample of 40 students is to be taken, with the number from each group proportional to the size of the group. How many students should be chosen from Group Y?

A greenhouse has a sunny bench and a shady bench, and the light is expected to affect plant growth. A researcher randomly assigns half of the plants on each bench to a new fertilizer and the other half to the usual fertilizer. What is the design called, and why was it used?

answers.text: A completely randomized design, because plants were assigned by chance
An observational study, because the benches already existed
A matched survey, because every bench was asked the same question
A block design, because the benches are blocks, and randomizing within each bench keeps the difference in light from favoring one fertilizer

questions.text: A made-up school draws a simple random sample of 200 students for a survey, but only 80 return the survey. The principal says, "The sample was random, so the results represent all students." Which response is best?

answers.text: Correct, because a random sample always represents the population
Not necessarily, because only 40% responded, and the students who answered may differ from those who did not (nonresponse bias)
Correct, because 80 is a large enough sample for any survey
Not necessarily, because a random sample is never a good way to choose students

quizzes.title: Module 11: Look Back — Sampling & Study Design

questions.text: At the start of this module you answered: How can a small piece of the world tell us the truth about the whole, and how do we know when it is lying to us? Answer it again now, and say specifically what changed in your answer. This module's virtue is Responsibility. Responsibility here means that whoever picks the sample, writes the question, or assigns the treatment is answerable for what the result can honestly say. Name one decision in this module (a way of sampling, a wording, an assignment) that could have tilted a result, and say how a responsible researcher would make it differently.
