quizzes.title: Module 12: Begin Here — Inference & Statistical Reasoning
quizzes.description: Every module so far has led here. You can describe data, model it, and judge where it came from. Now the question is how far a number from a sample can be trusted. Over three weeks you will watch sample results pile up into a predictable shape, turn that shape into a margin of error and a confidence interval, compare two groups by resampling and by shuffling, ask whether a difference is real or just chance, and finish by writing a full critique of a data-based report. Before you start, answer the few questions below. There are no wrong answers; your teacher reads these to meet you where you are.

questions.text: Here is the question this module keeps asking: How far can we trust a number that comes from a sample, and what do we owe the people who will rely on it? Write your first answer now, in 3–5 sentences. If you can, describe a poll, a "studies show" headline, or a "statistically significant" claim you have seen and say how much you trusted it. You will meet this question again at the end of the module and compare.

By the end of Module 12 you will be able to: explain how sample results vary and why larger samples vary less; compute and read a margin of error; build and correctly interpret a confidence interval; compare two groups by resampling and by shuffling; explain what a p-value does and does not say; tell a significant result from an important one; and write a fair, complete critique of a data-based report. Have you read this list?

answers.text: I have read the module objectives and know where we're headed.

questions.text: Some later activities offer an optional collaborative path (shared persistent VR Sessions, discussion pairings). Would you like to be considered for group collaboration where it's offered?

answers.text: Yes — include me in group options
No — I prefer to work independently this module
Not sure yet — ask me again mid-module

questions.text: A poll of 800 randomly chosen voters reports Candidate Rivera at 52% and Candidate Okafor at 48%, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.5 points. How should you read that result?

answers.text: Rivera is clearly ahead, since 52 is bigger than 48
The race is too close to call: the lead is within what random sampling alone could produce
There is a 3.5% chance the poll is wrong
I'm not sure how to judge that

questions.text: A report says, "We are 95% confident that between 40% and 50% of students walk to school." What does the 95% describe?

answers.text: The chance that the true percent is in that range, now that the range is written down
How often intervals built this way, from fresh random samples, would capture the true percent
The percent of students who walk
I'm not sure what it means

questions.text: Anything your teacher should know as you start this module? (Schedule constraints, how Module 11 and its Excel work went for you, how you learn best — anything.)

quizzes.title: Quiz 33.1 — Sampling Distributions and the Central Limit Theorem

questions.text: A made-up bakery weighs every loaf it bakes, and the weights are slightly skewed to the right. A statistician draws 500 random samples of 40 loaves each and records the mean weight of each sample. The histogram of these 500 sample means is best described as:

answers.text: The distribution of the population of loaf weights
The distribution of the weights in one sample of 40 loaves
A census of all the loaves the bakery has ever made
An approximation to the sampling distribution of the sample mean

questions.text: A made-up population has a standard deviation of 20. Random samples of size 64 are drawn, and the mean of each sample is recorded. What is the standard deviation of these sample means (the standard error)?

The scores on a made-up test have mean 100 and standard deviation 15. A random sample of 25 test takers is chosen. Assume the sample mean is approximately normal. What is the probability that the sample mean is greater than 103?

The values in a made-up population are strongly skewed to the right, with mean μ and standard deviation σ. Many random samples of size 100 are drawn, and the mean of each sample is recorded. Which statement is best supported by the Central Limit Theorem?

answers.text: The 100 values in each sample will form a bell-shaped histogram
The sample means will be skewed to the right, just like the population
The sample means will be approximately normal, centered at μ, with standard deviation σ ÷ √100
The sample means will be approximately normal, centered at μ, with standard deviation σ

questions.text: In a made-up town, 30% of residents own a bicycle. For random samples of 100 residents, what is the standard error of the sample proportion?

quizzes.title: Quiz 33.2 — Margin of Error: How Far Can a Poll Miss?

questions.text: A made-up poll of n = 400 randomly chosen residents finds that 20% (p = 0.20) favor a plan. Using the formula 1.96 × √(p(1 − p) ÷ n), what is the margin of error?

answers.text: About 2.0 points
About 5.0 points
About 3.9 points
About 7.8 points

questions.text: A made-up poll of 250 randomly chosen people has a margin of error of about 6.3 points (by the rule 100 ÷ √n). A second poll of the same kind surveys 1,000 people. About what is the second poll's margin of error?

answers.text: About 3.2 points, half as large, because the sample is four times as big
About 1.6 points, one quarter as large, because the sample is four times as big
About 5.0 points, because adding people only helps a little
About 6.3 points, because the margin of error does not depend on the sample size

questions.text: A made-up city office wants a poll with a margin of error of no more than 6 percentage points. Using n = (100 ÷ m)² with m in points, and rounding up to a whole person, about how many people must it survey?

A made-up poll of 800 randomly chosen voters finds Candidate Vega at 49% and Candidate Hale at 45%, with the rest undecided. Use the safe rule 100 ÷ √n for the margin of error and the rule of thumb that a lead smaller than about twice the margin is too close to call. Which statement is best?

answers.text: Vega is clearly ahead, because 49 is larger than 45
The race is too close to call: the 4-point lead is smaller than about twice the margin of error (about 3.5 points, so about 7.1)
Hale is clearly ahead, because the margin of error is subtracted from Vega's 49
Vega is clearly ahead, because the margin of error (about 3.5 points) is smaller than the 4-point lead

questions.text: A made-up poll reports that 55% of residents favor a ballot measure, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 points. Which statement is the most accurate reading?

answers.text: The poll has a 3% chance of being wrong
If many polls were taken the same way, about 95 of every 100 would land within 3 points of the true percent; the margin does not account for bias, nonresponse, or poor question wording
The true percent of residents who favor the measure is certainly between 52% and 58%
Because the margin of error is small, the poll cannot be biased

quizzes.title: Quiz 33.3 — Confidence Intervals and Confidence Levels

questions.text: A made-up polling team builds a 95% confidence interval for the proportion of voters in a town who favor a plan, using a random sample. Which statement gives the correct meaning of the 95% confidence level?

answers.text: There is a 95% probability that the true proportion lies inside this particular interval
If the team repeated the whole process many times with fresh random samples, about 95% of the intervals built this way would capture the true proportion
95% of all voters in the town have values inside the interval
The next random sample's estimate will land inside this interval 95% of the time

questions.text: In a made-up random poll, 156 of 300 students say they would join a new club. Both counts (yes and no) are at least 10. Which is the 95% confidence interval for the proportion of all students who would join (use z* = 1.960)?

A made-up 95% confidence interval for a proportion, from a random sample of 250 people, has a width of about 0.12. A second random sample of 1,000 people gives the same sample proportion. About how wide is its 95% confidence interval?

answers.text: About 0.24
About 0.12
About 0.06
About 0.03

questions.text: A made-up random sample of 64 plants has a mean height of 72 cm, and the population standard deviation is known to be 10 cm. Which is the 90% confidence interval for the population mean height (use z* = 1.645)?
A made-up claim says that exactly half of the residents of a town support a plan. A 95% confidence interval from a random sample of residents is 0.47 to 0.59. Which statement is the most careful?

answers.text: The interval contains 0.50, so the data prove that exactly half of the residents support the plan
The interval contains 0.50, so the claim is rejected
There is a 95% probability that exactly 0.50 of the residents support the plan
The interval contains 0.50, so 50% is a plausible value that the data cannot rule out, but the data do not show that the true proportion is exactly 50%

quizzes.title: Quiz 34.1 — Comparing Two Populations from Two Random Samples

questions.text: A researcher takes a random sample from each of two large populations and wants a plausible range for the true difference between the two population means. To build that range by the bootstrap, which procedure is correct?

answers.text: Draw a new Group A and a new Group B by sampling with replacement from the values in each original sample (keeping each group's size), record the difference in means, repeat many times, and take the middle 95% of the differences
Pool all the values, shuffle which values belong to Group A and Group B, and record the difference in means each time
Draw new groups by sampling without replacement, using every value in each original sample exactly once, and record the difference in means each time
Compute the difference in means once and repeat the same calculation many times

questions.text: Random samples from two made-up populations give these summaries. Group A: n = 36, mean 50, standard deviation 6. Group B: n = 49, mean 60, standard deviation 14. What is the standard error of the difference in sample means (B minus A), √(s_A²/nA + s_B²/nB)?

In a made-up study, a random sample of 100 people from Town A and a random sample of 100 people from Town B were asked whether they favor a plan. In Town A, 40 favored it; in Town B, 55 favored it. Using difference ± 1.96 × SE, what is an approximate 95% range for the true difference in proportions (Town B minus Town A)?
A plausible range (middle 95% of bootstrap differences) for the true difference in means, B minus A, is −1.5 to 6.1. Which statement is best supported?

answers.text: Group B's population mean is 6.1 higher than Group A's
The data are consistent with no difference, and also with Group B being somewhat higher (or slightly lower) than Group A
There is a 95% probability that the true difference is exactly 2.3
The data prove that the two populations have the same mean

questions.text: A researcher takes a random sample of 50 students who walk to school and a random sample of 60 students who ride the bus in a made-up district. The walkers' mean sleep time is higher, and a 95% range for the difference in means does not contain 0. Which conclusion is best supported?

answers.text: Walking to school causes students to sleep more
Students who ride the bus should be told to walk so that they sleep more
A real difference in mean sleep between all walkers and all bus riders in the district is plausible, but the study does not show that walking is the cause
The difference applies only to the 110 students in the samples and says nothing about the district

quizzes.title: Quiz 34.2 — Comparing Two Treatments in a Randomized Experiment

questions.text: In a made-up randomized experiment, 40 seeds were assigned to each of two soil mixes. In mix A, 18 of the 40 seeds sprouted. In mix B, 27 of the 40 seeds sprouted. What is the observed difference in sprout proportions, B minus A?

In a made-up randomized experiment, subjects were randomly assigned to two treatments and an outcome was measured for each. A researcher wants to see how large a gap between the two group means chance alone would produce if the two treatments had exactly the same effect. Which procedure does this?

answers.text: Draw many new random samples from the population and compute each sample mean
Pool all the measured outcomes, deal them at random into two groups of the original sizes, record the gap between the group means, and repeat many times
Remove the largest outcome from each group and recompute the gap
Repeat the experiment many times, giving the same treatments to the same subjects

questions.text: A made-up experiment randomly assigned subjects to two diets. The researcher shuffled the group labels 5,000 times, and 215 of the shuffles gave a gap at least as big as the observed gap, in either direction. What is the share of shuffles that were at least as big?
In a made-up randomized experiment, 3,000 shuffles of the group labels were run, and 18 of them gave a gap at least as big as the observed gap in either direction. Which statement is best supported?

answers.text: Chance alone rarely makes a gap this big (about 6 in 1,000 shuffles), so, because subjects were randomly assigned, there is evidence the treatment made a difference among these subjects
There is a 0.6% chance that the treatment does nothing
The treatment raises the outcome by 0.6 units
The gap is not unusual, because 18 is a small number

questions.text: A made-up randomized experiment assigned 5 subjects to each of two treatments. After 1,000 shuffles of the group labels, 350 gave a gap at least as big as the observed gap in either direction. Which statement is best?

answers.text: The treatment has no effect
There is a 35% chance that the treatment works
Chance alone often makes a gap this big, so the experiment did not find a difference beyond chance; with so few subjects it could miss a real effect, so it does not show the treatment has no effect
The gap is unusual, because 350 is a large count

quizzes.title: Quiz 34.3 — Is the Difference Real? Significance by Simulation

questions.text: A made-up student simulates 2,000 "boring worlds" in which nothing interesting is going on. In 90 of them, the result is at least as extreme as the one actually observed, in either direction. Using the 5% convention, which statement is best?

answers.text: The empirical p-value is 0.045, which is below 0.05, so the result is called statistically significant
The empirical p-value is 0.955, so the result is statistically significant
The empirical p-value is 0.045, which means there is a 4.5% chance the boring world is true
The empirical p-value is 90, so the result is statistically significant

questions.text: A made-up randomized study reports a p-value of 0.03 for a new tutoring method. Which statement is the most accurate reading?

answers.text: There is a 3% chance that the tutoring method does nothing
There is a 97% chance that the tutoring method works
If the method did nothing, random assignment alone would produce a gap at least this large in about 3 of every 100 repetitions
The tutoring method raises scores by 3%

questions.text: A made-up coin lands heads 60 times in 100 flips. Simulations of many fair-coin worlds of 100 flips show that about 5.7% of them have 60 or more heads or 40 or fewer. Using a 5% rule chosen in advance, which statement is best?

answers.text: The result is not statistically significant, but it is near the edge, so more flips would be a sensible next step
The coin is proved fair
The result is statistically significant, because 5.7% is close to 5%
The result is statistically significant, because 60 is more than 50

questions.text: Two made-up coins each land heads 60% of the time in the flips tested. Coin X was flipped 100 times (60 heads) and coin Y was flipped 1,000 times (600 heads). Compared with a fair coin, which statement is best?

answers.text: Both results are equally convincing, because the percents are equal
Coin Y's result is far more convincing, because with more flips a fair coin rarely strays 10 points from 50%
Coin X's result is more convincing, because it needed fewer flips
Neither result is convincing, because 60% is not far from 50%

questions.text: A made-up club runs 20 independent comparisons in which no real effect exists. Each comparison uses the 5% rule. Which is closest to the chance that at least one comparison looks statistically significant by luck alone?

quizzes.title: Quiz 35.1 — The Logic of Hypothesis Testing: Two Schools Revisited

questions.text: A made-up referee flips a coin 100 times and will reject "the coin is fair" if it shows 61 or more heads, or 39 or fewer. Using exact binomial probabilities, which value is closest to the chance that this rule rejects when the coin really is fair (the Type I error rate)?

A made-up clinic tests whether a new reminder text changes how many patients keep their appointments. The reminder truly does help, but the clinic's test fails to reject the null hypothesis of no effect. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: The clinic made a Type I error: a false alarm
The clinic made no error, because the test followed its rule
The clinic made a Type II error: a miss
The clinic has shown that the reminder has no effect

questions.text: A made-up decision rule for 100 flips of a coin rejects "the coin is fair" at 61 or more heads or 39 or fewer. If the coin truly lands heads 70% of the time, the rule rejects with probability 0.979. What is the probability of a Type II error for this coin?

A test of a fair-coin claim uses a rule built to keep the false-alarm rate near 4%. Which change would most increase the chance of detecting a coin that really lands heads 60% of the time, while keeping the false-alarm rate near 4%?

answers.text: Flip the coin 25 times instead of 100, with a rule of the same kind
Use the same rule, but decide the cutoffs after seeing the data
Tighten the rule so that it rejects only at far more extreme counts
Flip the coin 400 times instead of 100, with a rule of the same kind

questions.text: A made-up randomized study of a study technique reports a p-value of 0.11. The 5% significance level was fixed before the data were collected. Which statement is best?

answers.text: We fail to reject the null hypothesis: the data are not strong evidence against it, but a real effect could still exist
We accept the null hypothesis, so the technique has no effect
There is an 11% chance that the null hypothesis is true
The study proves that the technique does not work

quizzes.title: Quiz 35.2 — Evaluating Data-Based Reports in the Wild

questions.text: A made-up town website invites visitors to click a link and rate a new park. Of the 2,000 people who clicked and rated it, 85% gave it five stars. What is the biggest reason this 85% should not be treated as the opinion of all town residents?

answers.text: 2,000 people is always too few to describe a town
Only people who chose to respond are counted, so the group is self-selected and may differ from residents in general
A percentage cannot describe a rating
Five-star ratings cannot be averaged or compared

questions.text: In a made-up experiment, 80 student volunteers were randomly assigned to one of two study lessons. After the lesson, the group with the new lesson scored higher, and a shuffle test showed that chance alone would produce a gap this large in only about 1 of every 100 shuffles. Which statement is best supported?

answers.text: The new lesson raises scores for all students in the country
The study proves that the new lesson is better than every other lesson
In these volunteers, the new lesson caused the higher scores; because the volunteers were not a random sample, the study does not show the same effect for all students
The scores are associated with the lesson, but random assignment cannot support any statement about cause

questions.text: A made-up headline says, "Program doubles reading time." The report's own numbers show that average daily reading rose from 20 minutes to 22 minutes. By what percent did the average reading time rise?

A made-up bar chart has a vertical axis that starts at 50 instead of 0. One bar represents the value 52 and the other represents 54. About how many times as tall does the taller bar look compared with the shorter bar?

answers.text: 1.04 times
1.5 times
4 times
2 times

questions.text: A made-up club runs 10 independent comparisons. In every one of them, nothing real is going on, and each comparison uses the 5% rule for statistical significance. What is the chance that at least one comparison looks statistically significant by luck alone?

quizzes.title: Quiz 35.3 — Capstone: The Complete Statistical Critique

questions.text: A made-up newsroom posts a link in a neighborhood chat group asking, "Do you support the new bike lane?" In one weekend, 412 people click the link and answer; 78% say yes. The story's headline reads "Residents back the bike lane" and says the margin of error is plus or minus 5 points. Which is the strongest critique of the report?

answers.text: A sample of 412 is too small to estimate a percent
A percent as high as 78% is too large to be real
The respondents chose themselves from one group, so the poll may not represent residents, and a margin of error covers only sampling variation, not this bias
The report should have given the median instead of a percent

questions.text: In a made-up study, researchers recorded the nightly sleep and the unit-test scores of 200 students who were not asked to change anything. Students who slept more tended to score higher. Which statement does the study design justify?

answers.text: Sleeping more causes higher test scores
Students who slept more tended to score higher, but this design cannot show that sleep is the cause
Sleep has no effect on test scores
Making students sleep an extra hour will raise their scores

questions.text: A made-up random survey of 400 students finds that 45% ride the bus. The report gives a 95% interval of 40% to 50%. Which statement is the best reading of the interval?

answers.text: 95% of the 400 students ride the bus between 40% and 50% of days
There is a 95% chance that the true percent is between 40% and 50% for this one interval, and the sample percent will be between those values 95% of the time
The true percent of all students who ride the bus is exactly 45%
If surveys like this were repeated many times, about 95 in 100 of the intervals built this way would capture the true percent, and values from about 40% to 50% are plausible for it

questions.text: A made-up report measures 40 children aged 6 to 12 and fits the line height = 80 + 6.2 × age (height in centimeters, age in years). Using the line, the report predicts that a 30-year-old will be 266 cm tall. What is the best critique?

answers.text: The prediction is an extrapolation far beyond the ages studied (6 to 12), and the impossible 266 cm shows the line does not hold there
The line should have been fitted to a larger number of adults before it can be used at all
The line must be wrong for children, because the slope is positive
The prediction is acceptable, because the line fits the children well

questions.text: A made-up company reports that students who chose to use its flashcard app scored 9 points higher on unit tests than students who did not. Which additional evidence would best settle whether the app raises scores?

answers.text: A survey of more app users about whether they like the app
A larger group of app users, all of whom chose the app
An experiment that randomly assigns students to use the app or not, then compares scores in the two groups
A test of whether the 9-point gap is statistically significant in the same data

quizzes.title: Module 12: Look Back — Inference & Statistical Reasoning
quizzes.description: You have finished the last module of the course. You watched sample means form a bell, turned that bell into margins of error and confidence intervals, compared groups by resampling and by shuffling labels, met p-values and the two kinds of error, learned to judge a data-based report, and wrote a full critique. In the VR lab you built a gallery of samples and hung interval hoops to see which ones caught the truth. Next comes the finals week review, which pulls the whole semester together. Before you go on, look back honestly. Your teacher reads every one of these, and the confidence rating and "still unclear" answers directly shape what gets reviewed.

questions.text: At the start of this module you answered: How far can we trust a number that comes from a sample, and what do we owe the people who will rely on it? Answer it again now, and say specifically what changed in your answer. Use one of the module's own cases as your example (the poll where a lead sat inside the margin, the gallery where some hoops missed the truth, the experiment where chance could easily make the gap, the report you critiqued).

How confident do you feel about this module's core skills (sampling distributions, margin of error, confidence intervals, comparing two groups, p-values and the logic of testing, evaluating reports, writing a critique)?

answers.text: Very confident — I could teach it
Confident — I'd get most problems right
Shaky — I can follow along but couldn't do it alone yet
Lost — I need help before we build on this

questions.text: Which topic most deserves another pass?

answers.text: Sampling distributions and the Central Limit Theorem
Margin of error and choosing a sample size
Confidence intervals and confidence levels
Comparing two populations from two random samples
Comparing two treatments in a randomized experiment
Is the difference real? Significance by simulation
The logic of hypothesis testing (null and alternative, Type I and Type II errors)
Evaluating data-based reports
Writing the complete statistical critique
None — I'm solid across the module

questions.text: What remains unclear? Name the specific moment a lesson lost you (a step in a worked example, a quiz question, an Excel formula that did not work, a widget result you could not explain). "Nothing" is an acceptable answer only if Q2 was one of the top two choices.

This module's virtue is Service. Service here means that people will act on the numbers you report, so you owe them honesty about uncertainty and about what the evidence can and cannot show. Name one place in this module where reporting a number carelessly (leaving out a margin of error, writing "proves," calling a result significant without its size) could mislead someone who trusts it, and say how you would report it instead. Who, in your own life, relies on numbers you might pass along?

quizzes.title: Semester 2 Final Exam
quizzes.description: Fifty questions, fifty points, one attempt, 90 minutes. Every question on this exam is drawn from the lesson quizzes you have already taken this semester — nothing here is new. Questions come from every module, in proportion to its size. Have your Desmos Scientific Calculator (desmos.com/scientific) and Excel open in other tabs, and pencil and paper at hand for summaries, tables, and interval work. Answer choices are shuffled; read each choice fully. When you finish, you are done with Probability and Statistics — well earned.

questions.text: Which of these variables is categorical, even though its values are written as numbers?

answers.text: a student's height in centimeters
a student's locker number
the number of siblings a student has
the minutes a student spent on homework

questions.text: A frequency table has categories with frequencies 12, 9, 6, and 3. What is the percent for the category with frequency 9?
You want to compare the number of students in each of 12 school clubs. Which display is the better choice?

answers.text: a circle graph with 12 slices
a bar chart
a single number
a circle graph, because it shows percents

questions.text: Which dataset is best displayed with a line plot?

answers.text: the exact weights in grams of 400 apples
the favorite colors of 30 students
a student's height measured every month for five years
the number of books read last month by each of 15 students

questions.text: A histogram uses bins in which each bin includes its left endpoint but not its right endpoint. A value of exactly 30 belongs in which bin?

answers.text: neither bin

questions.text: Which statement describes a weakness of a box plot?

answers.text: it cannot show the median
it can only be used for categorical data
it can hide clusters or gaps inside the box
it requires every individual value to be written on the graph

questions.text: In a (made-up) town, monthly ice-cream sales and monthly swimming-pool visits are strongly associated. Which conclusion is justified by this data alone?

answers.text: ice-cream sales cause people to swim
swimming causes people to buy ice cream
the two variables are associated, but the data alone do not show that one causes the other
the variables are unrelated

questions.text: A bar chart shows two bars, 52 and 55, on a vertical axis that starts at 50. How does this affect a reader's impression?

answers.text: it makes the difference between the bars look much larger than it is
it makes the difference look smaller than it is
it has no effect on the impression
it makes the values larger

questions.text: After inserting a column chart in Excel, which setting should you check to keep the chart honest?

answers.text: that the vertical axis minimum is 0
that the bars are different colors
that the chart has a legend
that the chart is as wide as the page

questions.text: The data set 20, 22, 25, 26, 27 has mean 24 and median 25. If the largest value is changed from 27 to 270, which statement is true?

answers.text: the mean changes a great deal, but the median stays 25
the median changes a great deal, but the mean stays 24
both the mean and the median stay the same
both the mean and the median change by the same amount

questions.text: Dana's score on a 50-point quiz is at the 80th percentile of her class. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: Dana answered 80 percent of the questions correctly.
About 80 percent of the students in her class scored the same as or lower than Dana.
About 80 percent of the students in her class scored higher than Dana.
Dana scored 40 points.

questions.text: For the data set 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 40, use the median-of-each-half method for quartiles (Q1 = 5.5, Q3 = 11.5) and the 1.5 × IQR rule. In a box plot of these data, where does the upper whisker end?

answers.text: at 40
at 12

questions.text: When computing a standard deviation, why are the deviations from the mean squared before they are averaged?

answers.text: to make the answer a whole number
because the mean is the middle value of the ordered data
to remove outliers from the data
because the deviations from the mean always add to zero, so they would cancel without squaring

questions.text: Twelve made-up scores are 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 14, 86, 87, 88, 88, 89, 90. Both the mean and the median equal 50. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: The scores are symmetric with one peak, so 50 is a typical score.
The score 50 is an outlier.
The scores are skewed right.
The scores form two clusters with a gap, so 50 describes no actual score.

questions.text: An Excel summary of the commute times, in minutes, of 30 riders (a sample) shows: mean 62.4, median 55, Q1 41, Q3 70. Which conclusion and choice of summary is best supported?

answers.text: The mean is above the median, so the data are skewed left; report the mean and standard deviation.
The mean is above the median, which suggests a right skew; the median and IQR are the safer summary of a typical rider.
The mean and median are far apart, so the data must contain an error and should be thrown out.
The mean is above the median, so the data are symmetric; either summary is equally good.

questions.text: A student surveys 12 students from School X and 12 students from School Y. In these samples, the median time spent on homework is 15 minutes higher at School X. Which conclusion is best supported by these data alone?

answers.text: School X assigns more homework because its teachers are stricter
In these two samples the median is 15 minutes higher at School X, but this alone does not tell us whether the two whole schools differ
the difference proves that the median homework time is 15 minutes higher for all students at School X
the difference in the population must be zero because the samples are small

questions.text: In a made-up list of 11 commute times in minutes, ten values lie between 12 and 35 and one value is 450. The 1.5 × IQR rule flags the 450, and the original record sheet is available. What is the best next step?

answers.text: Delete the 450, because the rule flagged it.
Check the record sheet to find out why the value is 450, then correct it, set it aside with a stated reason, or keep it, and report what was done.
Replace the 450 with the mean of the other ten values.
Keep it and report only the mean, since the mean uses every value.

questions.text: A bar chart shows two group means, 52 and 55, with the vertical axis starting at 50. Which statement is correct?

answers.text: The bars are drawn to scale, so the 55 bar is about 6 percent taller than the 52 bar.
The 55 bar looks 2.5 times as tall as the 52 bar, but 55 is only about 6 percent more than 52; starting the axis at 0 would be fair.
The axis starts at 50, so the chart shows that the second group's mean is 2.5 times the first group's mean.
Cutting the axis changes the data, so the means are no longer 52 and 55.

questions.text: A machine fills boxes so that the weights are approximately normal with a mean of 50 ounces and a standard deviation of 8 ounces. A box has a z-score of -1.5. What is its weight?

answers.text: 62 ounces
41.5 ounces
38 ounces
48.5 ounces

questions.text: Which of the following data sets is the poorest candidate for using the Empirical Rule (68–95–99.7)?

answers.text: the heights of a large group of adults of the same age and sex, shown as a symmetric, single-humped histogram
the lengths of repeated measurements of one object with a careful instrument, shown as a symmetric, single-humped histogram
the waiting times at a service counter, shown as a histogram with most values short and a long tail to the right
the fill weights of boxes from a machine, shown as a symmetric, single-humped histogram

questions.text: A machine fills jars so that the fill volumes are approximately normally distributed with mean 250 mL and standard deviation 3 mL. Using this model, about what percent of jars hold less than 247 mL?

A large dataset (1,000 values) has a mean of 50 and a standard deviation of 10. The percents of values within 1, 2, and 3 standard deviations of the mean are 66%, 95%, and 99.6%. How do these compare with what a normal model predicts, and what do they suggest?

answers.text: They are close to 68%, 95%, and 99.7%, so this check gives no evidence against a normal model
They are far below 68%, 95%, and 99.7%, so the data are clearly not normal
They are far above 68%, 95%, and 99.7%, so the data are clearly not normal
They prove the data are exactly normal

questions.text: A common rule of thumb says a normal curve can reasonably approximate a binomial distribution when both np and n(1 − p) are at least 10. Which binomial setting meets this rule of thumb?

The battery lifetimes of a made-up device are approximately normally distributed with mean 400 hours and standard deviation 25 hours. Using this model, about what percent of batteries last between 390 hours and 440 hours?

Nine points lie close to a rising straight line, and for those nine points alone r is about +0.99. A tenth point is then added far below the line at the right-hand end of the plot. Which effect on r is most likely?

answers.text: r stays about +0.99, because one point is a small share of the data
r becomes about −0.99, because the new point is low
r drops noticeably, because one far-off point can pull r away from +0.99
r becomes exactly 0

questions.text: A straight line passes through the points (2, 24) and (10, 8). Which equation describes it?
A fitted line is ŷ = 12.5 + 3.2x, based on data with x from 1 to 10. What does the line predict at x = 7, and is the prediction an interpolation?

answers.text: 34.9, and yes, it is an interpolation
22.4, and yes, it is an interpolation
34.9, and no, it is an extrapolation
87.5, and yes, it is an interpolation

questions.text: A least-squares line is fitted to 8 constructed points. In order of x from smallest to largest, the residuals are positive for the first two points, negative for the next four points, and positive for the last two points. What is the best conclusion?

answers.text: The residuals show random scatter, so the straight line is adequate.
The residuals form a curved pattern, so a straight line is not an adequate model for these data.
The residuals fan out, so the line is accurate only for small x.
The line must have been computed incorrectly, because residuals cannot change sign.

questions.text: A spreadsheet has the x values in cells A2:A11 and the y values in cells B2:B11. Which formula gives the slope of the least-squares line for predicting y from x?

answers.text: =SLOPE(A2:A11,B2:B11)
=SLOPE(B2:B11,A2:A11)
=CORREL(B2:B11,A2:A11)

questions.text: In a made-up set of ten towns, the correlation between ice cream sales and pool incidents is about +0.88 overall. After splitting the towns into a warm-week group and a hot-week group, the correlation is about +0.19 within the warm group and about −0.08 within the hot group. Which conclusion is best supported?

answers.text: Ice cream sales cause pool incidents, but only in warm weather
Most of the overall association comes from the difference between the two weather groups, which is consistent with weather driving both variables
There is no relationship between ice cream sales and pool incidents of any kind
The within-group correlations prove that ice cream sales have exactly zero effect on pool incidents

questions.text: A student wants to fit y = a·bx by taking ln of y, but one of the constructed y values is 0. What is the problem, and what is the honest response?

answers.text: There is no problem, because ln(0) = 0
ln(0) does not exist, so that point cannot be transformed; the student should report the problem and say how it was handled rather than silently delete it
ln(0) is a very large positive number, so the point will pull the line up and should be kept
The problem is that the natural log can only be used on x values, never on y

questions.text: Which situation is best summarized with a two-way frequency table rather than a scatter plot?

answers.text: The height (in inches) and arm span (in inches) of 30 students
The hours of sleep and the quiz score of 25 students
The age (in years) and the price (in dollars) of 40 used cars
The grade level (9, 10, 11, or 12) and the lunch choice (cafeteria, packed, or off-campus) of 24 students

questions.text: A made-up survey of 400 club members asked two questions. Of the 150 members who bike to work, 60 also own a car. Of the 250 members who do not bike to work, 150 own a car. Of the members who own a car, what percent bike to work?

answers.text: About 28.6%

questions.text: A club president asks the five friends sitting nearest her whether they will attend a dance. Four say yes, and she announces, "80% of the school will attend." Which response is the most careful?

answers.text: Four of the five friends asked said yes; that is a statistic from a small, convenient sample, and it gives little reason to trust it as the share for the whole school
She is right, because 4 divided by 5 is 0.80
80% is the parameter, because every one of the five friends answered
The statement would be correct if she rounded 80% to 100%

questions.text: A student uses =RANDBETWEEN to pick her sample and computes a sample mean. After she types a note in another cell, her sample mean changes. What should she have done after the draw?

answers.text: Nothing, since RANDBETWEEN values stay fixed once they are drawn
Press F9 until the mean looks close to the true value
Copy the picks and use Paste Special > Values to freeze them before computing anything from them
Switch to =RAND, which does not recalculate

questions.text: Which of the following is a non-probability sampling method?

answers.text: Drawing 50 names at random from a complete list
Taking a random sample from each grade level, in proportion to the grade's size
Choosing 5 classrooms at random and surveying every student in them
Telling an interviewer to collect 40 responses from men and 40 from women, from whoever agrees to stop

questions.text: The owner of a made-up website invites visitors to vote on whether a new rule is fair. A total of 10,000 visitors respond, and the owner says, "With this many responses, the result must be accurate." Which statement is best?

answers.text: Yes, because 10,000 is larger than any sample a researcher would need
Yes, because a large sample removes every kind of error
No, because a sample larger than 1,000 is always biased
No, because a large sample shrinks sampling variation but does not remove bias from self-selected responses

questions.text: A made-up call-in poll of a town reports 70% in favor of a proposal, while the true share in the town is 55%. The station repeats the same call-in method and collects 10 times as many calls. What is the best prediction?

answers.text: The new result will be close to 55%, because more calls reduce bias
The new result will still tend to lean above 55%, because more replies from the same self-selecting group do not remove the lean
The new result will lean below 55%, because the bias reverses with more calls
The new result will be exactly 55%

questions.text: A made-up game claims its coin is fair. It is flipped 50 times and lands heads 36 times. The exact chance of a result at least this far from 25 on either side (36 or more, or 14 or fewer) is 0.002602, about 1 in 384. Which statement is the most careful?

answers.text: The result is not unusual, because 36 heads can happen with a fair coin
The result proves the coin is rigged, because 0.002602 is less than 0.05
The result is unusual under the claimed model, which is a strong reason to doubt the coin is fair, but it does not prove the coin is rigged
The result proves that the next 50 flips will also give about 36 heads

questions.text: A made-up researcher selects 300 students at random from a school of 1,500 and records each student's weekly screen time and hours of sleep. No one is asked to change any habit. Which conclusion is best supported?

answers.text: Less screen time causes more sleep for students at this school
The result cannot be generalized because the students were not assigned to groups
Because the sample is random, the study shows that screen time causes lost sleep
Screen time and sleep may be associated among the school's students, but the study cannot show that one causes the other

questions.text: In a made-up experiment, 60 subjects are randomly assigned to a new exercise plan or to no plan. Many subjects who find the plan unpleasant quit during the study and their final results are never recorded, while few subjects in the comparison group quit. Which statement is best?

answers.text: Random assignment guarantees that dropout cannot affect the comparison
Dropout is harmless as long as the group sizes at the start were equal
Uneven dropout can leave the remaining groups unlike each other, so random assignment alone does not fully protect the comparison
The study can no longer be called an experiment because some subjects quit

questions.text: A made-up researcher wants to know whether a new study routine causes higher quiz scores. She uses a random number generator to assign each of 60 volunteers to the new routine or the usual routine. What is the main purpose of the random assignment?

answers.text: To make the sample of volunteers representative of all students
To make the two groups alike, on average, in both measured and unmeasured ways, so that a difference in scores is less likely to come from some other factor
To guarantee that the new routine will produce higher scores
To make the volunteers unaware of which routine they are using

questions.text: In a made-up town, 30% of residents own a bicycle. For random samples of 100 residents, what is the standard error of the sample proportion?

A made-up poll of 250 randomly chosen people has a margin of error of about 6.3 points (by the rule 100 ÷ √n). A second poll of the same kind surveys 1,000 people. About what is the second poll's margin of error?

answers.text: About 3.2 points, half as large, because the sample is four times as big
About 1.6 points, one quarter as large, because the sample is four times as big
About 5.0 points, because adding people only helps a little
About 6.3 points, because the margin of error does not depend on the sample size

questions.text: A made-up random sample of 64 plants has a mean height of 72 cm, and the population standard deviation is known to be 10 cm. Which is the 90% confidence interval for the population mean height (use z* = 1.645)?

A researcher takes a random sample of 50 students who walk to school and a random sample of 60 students who ride the bus in a made-up district. The walkers' mean sleep time is higher, and a 95% range for the difference in means does not contain 0. Which conclusion is best supported?

answers.text: Walking to school causes students to sleep more
Students who ride the bus should be told to walk so that they sleep more
A real difference in mean sleep between all walkers and all bus riders in the district is plausible, but the study does not show that walking is the cause
The difference applies only to the 110 students in the samples and says nothing about the district

questions.text: In a made-up randomized experiment, 40 seeds were assigned to each of two soil mixes. In mix A, 18 of the 40 seeds sprouted. In mix B, 27 of the 40 seeds sprouted. What is the observed difference in sprout proportions, B minus A?

A test of a fair-coin claim uses a rule built to keep the false-alarm rate near 4%. Which change would most increase the chance of detecting a coin that really lands heads 60% of the time, while keeping the false-alarm rate near 4%?

answers.text: Flip the coin 25 times instead of 100, with a rule of the same kind
Use the same rule, but decide the cutoffs after seeing the data
Tighten the rule so that it rejects only at far more extreme counts
Flip the coin 400 times instead of 100, with a rule of the same kind

questions.text: A made-up headline says, "Program doubles reading time." The report's own numbers show that average daily reading rose from 20 minutes to 22 minutes. By what percent did the average reading time rise?

A made-up report measures 40 children aged 6 to 12 and fits the line height = 80 + 6.2 × age (height in centimeters, age in years). Using the line, the report predicts that a 30-year-old will be 266 cm tall. What is the best critique?

answers.text: The prediction is an extrapolation far beyond the ages studied (6 to 12), and the impossible 266 cm shows the line does not hold there
The line should have been fitted to a larger number of adults before it can be used at all
The line must be wrong for children, because the slope is positive
The prediction is acceptable, because the line fits the children well
